questions.explanation: Oranges are counted in whole numbers; you cannot have a fraction of an orange, so the data is discrete.

questions.stem: Explain why the mass of a bag of rice is continuous data.

criteria.description: States that mass is measured, not counted
Explains that mass can take any value within a range

hints: Can rice have a mass of 5.25 kg?
questions.explanation: Mass is measured and can take any value, so it is continuous.
questions.misconception: Thinking mass is discrete because we round it.

questions.stem: Explain why the number of matchsticks in a pattern is discrete data.

criteria.description: States that matchsticks are counted in whole numbers
Explains that you cannot have part of a matchstick

questions.explanation: Matchsticks are counted in whole numbers, so the data is discrete.
questions.misconception: Thinking the pattern makes it continuous.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'The temperature at 2.5 minutes is 35°C.' Explain why this is possible on a line graph.

criteria.description: States that temperature and time are continuous
Explains that intermediate values can be estimated from the line

hints: Can temperature be between two readings?
questions.explanation: Both time and temperature are continuous, so the line between plotted points represents intermediate values.
questions.misconception: Thinking the line only connects whole-number points.

questions.stem: Why is a line graph suitable for showing temperature over time but not for showing the number of pupils in different classes?

criteria.description: Number of pupils in different classes is discrete/categorical

questions.explanation: Temperature over time is continuous, so a line graph is appropriate. Class sizes are discrete categories, so a bar chart is better.
questions.misconception: Thinking any data can use a line graph.

questions.stem: A table shows water temperature recorded every 2 minutes. Can a line graph be used? Explain.

criteria.description: Explains that a line graph can show the trend and estimate between readings

hints: Temperature can be measured between the 2-minute intervals.
questions.explanation: Yes, because temperature is continuous, a line graph can show the trend and allow estimation between readings.
questions.misconception: Thinking recording at intervals makes it discrete.

questions.stem: Which graph is best for showing how temperature changes over 10 minutes?
hints: We want to show change over time.
A line graph connects points to show a trend.
questions.explanation: A line graph is best for showing change over time.
questions.misconception: Choosing a bar chart, which is better for comparing categories.

questions.stem: Which graph is best for showing the number of pupils who like different fruits?
questions.explanation: A bar chart is best for comparing categories.
questions.misconception: Choosing a line graph, which implies continuity.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to show the number of matchsticks used for patterns 1 to 5. Should they use a line graph or a scatter of points?
hints: Matchsticks are counted in whole numbers.
questions.explanation: Since matchsticks are discrete, a series of points is more appropriate than a continuous line.
questions.misconception: Joining the points with a line as if the data were continuous.

questions.stem: A pupil records the mass of a baby every month for a year. Which representation is best?
hints: We want to show growth over time.
questions.explanation: A line graph is best because mass is continuous and we want to show growth over time.
questions.misconception: Using a pie chart for continuous data.

questions.stem: A table shows the number of goals scored in 5 matches. A pupil draws a line graph joining the points. What is wrong?
options: Goals are discrete, so points should not be joined
The line graph is always correct
The graph needs a pie chart
hints: Goals are counted in whole numbers.
There is no meaning to 2.5 goals between matches.
questions.explanation: Goals are discrete; joining the points implies continuous data, which is misleading.
questions.misconception: Thinking a line always makes the graph better.

indicator.subject: Mathematics
indicator.sub_strand: Data Collection, Organization, Presentation, Interpretation and Analysis
indicator.content_standard: Select, justify, and use appropriate methods of collecting data, including questionnaires, interview, observation, experiments, databases, electronic media, etc.
indicator.objective: Select a method for collecting data to answer a given question and justify the choice

skills.description: Pick questionnaire, interview, observation, experiment, database, or electronic media.
Give a reason for the choice of method.
State one weakness of a chosen method.

misconceptions: Choosing a method that cannot answer the question
Confusing observation with interview
Ignoring sample size

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know the favourite drink of pupils in Basic 6. Which method is best?
hints: You need to ask many pupils their preference.
questions.explanation: A questionnaire is best for collecting preferences from many pupils.
questions.misconception: Choosing observation, which cannot reveal preferences.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know how many cars pass the school gate in one hour. Which method is best?
hints: The pupil needs to watch and count.
No one needs to be asked.
questions.explanation: Observation is best for counting passing cars.
questions.misconception: Choosing a questionnaire, which cannot count cars.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know the most common shoe size in the class. Which method is best?
hints: Pupils need to report their shoe sizes.
questions.explanation: A questionnaire is best for collecting shoe sizes.
questions.misconception: Choosing observation, which cannot determine shoe size.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to find out which of two fertilizers makes plants grow taller. Which method is best?
hints: The pupil needs to test both fertilizers.
questions.explanation: An experiment is best to compare the effects of two fertilizers.
questions.misconception: Choosing observation only, which does not test a hypothesis.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know the population of Ghana. Which method is best?
hints: Look in official records or online.
questions.explanation: A database or electronic media is best for existing population data.
questions.misconception: Choosing a questionnaire, which would take too long.

questions.stem: A pupil wants detailed reasons why some pupils are absent from school. Which method is best?
questions.explanation: An interview is best for detailed reasons and follow-up questions.
questions.misconception: Choosing a questionnaire, which may not capture detailed reasons.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to compare the rainfall in two towns over six months. Which method is best?
hints: Rainfall data is recorded by weather stations.
questions.explanation: A database is best for comparing recorded rainfall data.
questions.misconception: Choosing a questionnaire, which cannot measure rainfall.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know the average number of hours pupils in the school spend on homework each week. Which method is best?
hints: Pupils need to report their homework hours.
Many pupils can answer a questionnaire.
questions.explanation: A questionnaire is best for collecting homework hours from many pupils.
questions.misconception: Choosing observation, which cannot see homework done at home.

questions.stem: Why is a questionnaire a good method for finding out the favourite subject of pupils in a class?

criteria.description: States that a questionnaire can collect answers from many pupils quickly

hints: Think about how many pupils need to answer.
Questionnaires are fast to give out and collect.
questions.explanation: A questionnaire can reach many pupils quickly and collect their opinions.

questions.stem: Why is an experiment better than a questionnaire for testing which soap cleans better?

criteria.description: States that an experiment allows controlled testing and observation of results
Explains that opinions cannot determine cleaning power

hints: Cleaning power is tested, not asked.
questions.explanation: An experiment tests the soaps under controlled conditions and measures results, while a questionnaire only collects opinions.
questions.misconception: Thinking soap cleaning power can be decided by asking people.

questions.stem: Why is observation better than a questionnaire for counting the number of pupils who use the library at break time?

criteria.description: States that observation directly counts the pupils
Explains that a questionnaire would not give accurate counts

hints: Asking pupils later may give wrong counts.
questions.explanation: Observation directly counts pupils as they enter, giving accurate data that a questionnaire could not guarantee.
questions.misconception: Thinking pupils can accurately recall how many times they visited the library.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know the average daily temperature in Accra for a year. Why is a database better than a questionnaire?

criteria.description: States that official temperature records already exist
Explains that a questionnaire cannot measure temperature accurately

hints: Records are kept by weather stations.
questions.explanation: Official temperature records already exist in databases and are more accurate than asking people.
questions.misconception: Thinking people can accurately report daily temperatures from memory.

questions.stem: Why is an interview better than a questionnaire when finding out why a pupil walks to school instead of taking a trotro?

criteria.description: States that an interview allows detailed answers and follow-up questions

hints: Interviews allow the interviewer to ask 'why' again.
questions.explanation: An interview allows the interviewer to probe deeper and get detailed reasons, which a questionnaire may not capture.
questions.misconception: Thinking a questionnaire gives more detail than an interview.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'I will use a questionnaire to measure how much water each pupil drinks in a day.' Is this a good choice? Explain.

criteria.description: States that a questionnaire is not reliable for measuring amounts

hints: People may not remember exact amounts.
Measuring cups would give better data.
questions.explanation: A questionnaire relies on memory and may be inaccurate. Measurement with a cup would give better data.
questions.misconception: Thinking people can accurately estimate their water intake.

questions.stem: What is one weakness of a questionnaire?
options: Some pupils may not return it or may answer carelessly
hints: Think about what can go wrong when people fill in forms.
questions.explanation: A weakness of questionnaires is that respondents may return incomplete or careless answers.

questions.stem: What is one weakness of observation as a data-collection method?
options: It may be time-consuming and the observer may miss events
It always gives too much data
hints: One person cannot watch everything at once.
questions.explanation: Observation can be time-consuming and events may be missed.
questions.misconception: Thinking observation is always quick and easy.

questions.stem: What is one weakness of an interview?
options: It takes a long time and may only cover a few people
hints: They take more time than questionnaires.
questions.explanation: Interviews are time-consuming and often cover only a small sample.
questions.misconception: Thinking interviews are fast for large groups.

questions.stem: What is one weakness of using a database from the internet?
options: The data may be outdated or from an unreliable source
It cannot be accessed by teachers
It always takes too long to find
hints: Not everything online is correct or current.
questions.explanation: Online databases may contain outdated or unreliable information.
questions.misconception: Thinking all online data is accurate.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to find the average height of pupils in the class using a questionnaire. What is the main weakness?
options: Pupils may not know their exact height
hints: A tape measure gives better data.
questions.explanation: Pupils may not know their exact height, so measuring is more accurate.
questions.misconception: Thinking pupils always know their exact height.

indicator.subject: Mathematics
indicator.sub_strand: Data Collection, Organization, Presentation, Interpretation and Analysis
indicator.content_standard: Select, justify, and use appropriate methods of collecting data, including questionnaires, interview, observation, experiments, databases, electronic media, etc.
indicator.objective: Design and administer a questionnaire for collecting data to answer given question(s), record the data, analyse and graph the results to solve problems

skills.description: Write a clear survey question.
Organise tallies into a frequency table.
Draw a bar or line graph from frequency data.

misconceptions: Asking leading or double-barrelled questions
Miscounting tallies
Choosing the wrong graph type

questions.stem: Which is the best survey question to find the favourite drink of pupils in a class?
options: Do you drink Fanta or Coke?
hints: A good question is open and clear.
It should not suggest an answer.
questions.explanation: 'What is your favourite drink?' is clear and does not lead the respondent.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'Do you like Fanta?', which is a yes/no question that favours one drink.

questions.stem: Which is the best survey question to find out how pupils travel to school?
options: How do you travel to school?
Why do you take a trotro?
Do you walk or take a trotro?
hints: A good question allows many possible answers.
It should not limit choices to two.
questions.explanation: 'How do you travel to school?' allows all forms of transport to be reported.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'Do you walk or take a trotro?', which ignores other transport.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know the favourite subject of each classmate. Which question is best?
options: Do you like Maths or English?
Why is Maths your favourite subject?
hints: A good question is open to all subjects.
It should not assume a subject.
questions.explanation: 'What is your favourite subject?' is clear and open.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'Why is Maths your favourite subject?', which assumes Maths is the favourite.

questions.stem: What is wrong with the survey question: 'Do you agree that Fanta is the best drink?'
options: It leads the respondent to agree
questions.explanation: The question is leading because it suggests Fanta is the best.
questions.misconception: Thinking the question is fine because it mentions a popular drink.

questions.stem: A pupil asks: 'Do you walk or take a trotro to school?' What is the problem with this question?
options: It is double-barrelled and leaves out other options
It is not a survey question
hints: Some pupils may cycle or be driven.
The question limits answers to two options.
questions.explanation: The question only allows two answers and ignores other ways of travelling.
questions.misconception: Thinking two options are always enough.

questions.stem: A pupil asks: 'How many minutes do you spend on homework and what is your favourite subject?' What is wrong?
options: It is double-barrelled (asks two questions in one)
hints: Count how many things are being asked.
A respondent can only answer one part.
questions.explanation: The question asks two different things, making it double-barrelled.

questions.stem: Write one clear survey question to find out how many hours per week pupils spend reading at home.

criteria.description: The question is clear and not leading
The question asks about hours per week and reading at home

hints: Include 'hours per week' and 'reading at home'.
questions.explanation: Example: 'How many hours per week do you spend reading at home?'
questions.misconception: Writing 'Do you read a lot at home?', which is vague.

questions.stem: A tally chart shows: Fanta |||| (5), Coke ||| (3), Sprite || (2). How many pupils chose Fanta?
hints: Count the tally marks for Fanta.
questions.explanation: Fanta has 5 tallies, so 5 pupils chose it.

questions.stem: Tallies: Maths |||| (5), English ||| (3), Science || (2). What is the total number of pupils surveyed?
questions.explanation: 5 + 3 + 2 = 10 pupils.

questions.stem: A frequency table shows: Walk 8, Trotro 12, Car 4. How many pupils travel by trotro?
questions.explanation: 12 pupils travel by trotro.

questions.stem: Tally chart: Red |||| || (7), Blue |||| (5), Green ||| (3). Which colour has the highest frequency?
questions.explanation: Red has the highest frequency (7).
questions.misconception: Choosing Blue because it is a common colour.

questions.stem: A frequency table shows: Football 15, Athletics 10, Basketball 5. What fraction of pupils chose Football?
questions.misconception: Using only the other categories to find the denominator.

questions.stem: A frequency table shows: Boys 18, Girls 12. What is the ratio of boys to girls in simplest form?
A tally chart shows: Fanta |||| (5), Coke ||| (3), Sprite || (2). Complete a frequency table and explain how you would use it to draw a bar graph.

criteria.description: Explains that the x-axis shows drinks and the y-axis shows frequency

hints: List each drink and its count.
The bar height equals the frequency.
questions.explanation: Frequency table: Fanta 5, Coke 3, Sprite 2. Draw bars of heights 5, 3, 2 above each drink.

questions.stem: A frequency table shows: Maths 6, English 4, Science 5. Which type of graph is best to display this data?
questions.explanation: A bar graph is best for comparing categories.
questions.misconception: Choosing a line graph, which suggests continuity.

questions.stem: A bar graph shows Fanta 5, Coke 3, Sprite 2. Which drink has the lowest bar?
questions.explanation: Sprite has the lowest frequency (2).
questions.misconception: Choosing Coke because it is a well-known brand.

questions.stem: A pupil draws a bar graph of favourite subjects with bars Maths 6, English 4, Science 5. What should the y-axis be labelled?
questions.explanation: The y-axis should show 'Number of pupils'.
questions.misconception: Labelling the y-axis with subject names.

questions.stem: A bar graph shows 8 pupils walk, 12 take a trotro, 4 come by car. How many pupils were surveyed in total?
A bar graph shows: Football 15, Athletics 10, Basketball 5. What conclusion can you draw?
options: Football is the most popular sport
hints: The tallest bar shows the most popular.
questions.explanation: Football has the highest bar, so it is the most popular.
questions.misconception: Choosing Basketball because it is well-known.

questions.stem: A pupil draws a bar graph with unequal gaps between bars and no title. What two improvements should be made?
options: Equal gaps between bars and add a title
Add more bars and a key
Change colours and add a title
Use a line graph and add a title
questions.explanation: Use equal gaps between bars and add a clear title.
questions.misconception: Thinking colours matter more than equal spacing.

indicator.subject: Mathematics
indicator.content_standard: Demonstrate an understanding of probability by identifying all possible outcomes of a probability experiment, determining the theoretical and experimental probability of outcomes in a probability experiment
indicator.objective: List the possible outcomes of a probability experiment, such as tossing a coin, rolling a die with a given number of sides, spinning a spinner with a given number of sectors and determine the theoretical probability of an outcome occurring for a given probability experiment

skills.description: List all outcomes for a coin, die, or spinner.
Find P(event) as a fraction.
Count favourable outcomes.

misconceptions: Thinking a coin always alternates
Confusing favourable with total outcomes
Writing probability as a ratio of sides

questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed once. What are all the possible outcomes?
hints: The sides are called head and tail.
questions.explanation: The possible outcomes are Head and Tail.
questions.misconception: Thinking there are more than two outcomes.

questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. How many possible outcomes are there?
hints: A die has faces numbered 1 to 6.
questions.explanation: There are 6 possible outcomes: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
questions.misconception: Thinking there are 12 outcomes because of edges.

questions.stem: A spinner has 4 equal sectors numbered 1, 2, 3, 4. What are the possible outcomes when it is spun once?
hints: List the numbers on the sectors.
questions.explanation: The possible outcomes are 1, 2, 3, 4.

questions.stem: A bag contains 3 red balls and 2 blue balls. One ball is picked at random. What are the possible outcomes in terms of colour?
hints: The balls are of two colours.
questions.explanation: The possible outcomes are Red and Blue.
questions.misconception: Thinking only one colour can be picked.

questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed twice. What are all the possible outcomes?
hints: First toss can be H or T.
Second toss can be H or T.
questions.explanation: The possible outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT.
questions.misconception: Listing only the first toss outcomes.

questions.stem: A spinner has 5 equal sectors numbered 1 to 5. What is the probability of landing on an even number?
hints: Even numbers on the spinner: 2 and 4.
There are 2 favourable outcomes out of 5.
questions.explanation: P(even) = 2/5.

questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 4?
hints: Two favourable outcomes out of six.

questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed once. What is the probability of getting a Head?
hints: One favourable outcome (Head) out of two.
questions.explanation: P(Head) = 1/2.
questions.misconception: Thinking probability can be greater than 1.

questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability of rolling a 3?
A spinner has 4 equal sectors labelled A, B, C, D. What is the probability of landing on B?
questions.misconception: Writing 2/4 because B is a consonant.

questions.stem: A bag has 5 red balls and 3 blue balls. What is the probability of picking a blue ball?
questions.explanation: P(blue) = 3/8.
questions.misconception: Using only the number of blue balls over red balls.

questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability of rolling an even number?
hints: Three favourable outcomes out of six.

questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed twice. What is the probability of getting two Heads?
hints: Possible outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT.
questions.misconception: Thinking 1/2 because two heads are possible.

questions.stem: A spinner has 8 equal sectors numbered 1 to 8. What is the probability of landing on a number less than 3?
hints: Two favourable outcomes out of eight.

questions.stem: A bag has 4 green, 6 yellow, and 2 red balls. What is the probability of picking a red ball?
questions.misconception: Using only the other colours in the denominator.

questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability of rolling a number that is not 6?
A fair coin is tossed. How many outcomes give a Head?
questions.explanation: There is 1 favourable outcome (Head).

questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled. How many outcomes give a number greater than 4?
questions.explanation: There are 2 favourable outcomes: 5 and 6.

questions.stem: A bag has 3 red, 2 blue, and 5 yellow balls. How many outcomes give a blue or red ball?
questions.explanation: 3 + 2 = 5 favourable outcomes.
questions.misconception: Counting only blue (2) or only red (3).

questions.stem: A spinner has 10 equal sectors numbered 1 to 10. How many outcomes give a multiple of 3?
questions.explanation: There are 3 favourable outcomes: 3, 6, 9.

indicator.subject: Mathematics
indicator.content_standard: Demonstrate an understanding of probability by identifying all possible outcomes of a probability experiment, determining the theoretical and experimental probability of outcomes in a probability experiment
indicator.objective: Predict the probability of a given outcome occurring for a given probability experiment by using theoretical probability

skills.description: Predict the likely result of an experiment using theoretical probability.
Compare theoretical and experimental probability.
Predict from a spinner with unequal sectors.

misconceptions: Expecting exact results from few trials
Ignoring unequal sector sizes
Confusing 'likely' with 'certain'

questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed 100 times. About how many times would you expect to get a Head?
questions.misconception: Thinking it must be exactly 50 every time.

questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled 60 times. About how many times would you expect to roll a 3?
A spinner has 4 equal sectors: Red, Blue, Green, Yellow. If spun 40 times, about how many times would you expect Red?
A fair coin is tossed 20 times. About how many Tails would you expect?
questions.misconception: Thinking it must be more than 10.

questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled 30 times. About how many times would you expect an even number?
A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls. If a ball is picked 50 times with replacement, about how many red balls would you expect?
questions.misconception: Using only the number of red balls (4).

questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled 120 times. About how many times would you expect a number greater than 4?
A fair coin is tossed 200 times. About how many times would you expect to get a Head?
questions.misconception: Thinking it must be exactly 100 every time.

questions.stem: A coin is tossed 10 times and 7 Heads are recorded. What is the experimental probability of Head?
hints: Experimental probability = number of Heads / total tosses.
questions.explanation: Experimental P(Head) = 7/10.

questions.stem: A fair coin has theoretical probability of Head = 1/2. In 20 tosses, 8 Heads are recorded. How does the experimental probability compare with the theoretical?
questions.explanation: 2/5 < 1/2, so experimental is lower.
questions.misconception: Thinking any result close to half is equal.

questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled 60 times. The number 6 appears 12 times. What is the experimental probability of rolling a 6?
A fair coin is tossed 100 times. Theoretical P(Head) = 1/2. If 45 Heads are recorded, what is the experimental probability and how does it compare?
questions.explanation: 0.45 < 0.5, so slightly lower.
questions.misconception: Thinking 45/100 is equal to 1/2 because 45 is close to 50.

questions.stem: A spinner with 4 equal sectors is spun 80 times. The theoretical probability of Red is 1/4. If Red appears 30 times, what is the experimental probability?
A fair die is rolled 600 times. Theoretical P(6) = 1/6. If 80 sixes are recorded, what is the experimental probability and how does it compare?
A spinner has 5 equal sectors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Which outcome is most likely?
hints: The sectors are equal in size.
questions.explanation: All outcomes have the same probability (1/5).
questions.misconception: Thinking larger numbers are more likely.

questions.stem: A spinner has 3 sectors: Red (half the spinner), Blue (quarter), Green (quarter). Which colour is most likely?
hints: Probability is proportional to sector size.
questions.explanation: Red has the largest sector, so it is most likely.
questions.misconception: Thinking all colours are equally likely.

questions.stem: A spinner has 8 equal sectors: 5 are Red and 3 are Blue. What is the probability of landing on Red?
questions.misconception: Using the number of blue sectors.

questions.stem: A spinner has sectors: Red (1/2), Blue (1/4), Green (1/4). If spun 80 times, about how many times would you expect Blue?
A spinner has 10 equal sectors: 6 are Red and 4 are Blue. If spun 50 times, about how many times would you expect Blue?
questions.misconception: Using the number of red sectors (6/10) to predict blue.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.1.1.1: Show understanding of the physical features and life processes of living things and use this understanding to classify them
indicator.objective: Observe and describe different kinds of things in the environment.

skills.description: Observe and name things found in the immediate environment
Describe observable features of a named thing
Group observed things by simple observable criteria

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Only animals are living things; plants are not living.
Anything that moves is living.
Things in the environment are only what we can see inside the classroom.
Confusing 'describe' with 'name'.

questions.stem: What is the name of the thing in the sky that gives us light during the day?
hints: It is very bright and yellow.
questions.explanation: The sun is the bright object in the sky during the day. It gives us light and warmth.
questions.misconception: Some pupils think the moon gives light during the day, but the moon is mainly seen at night.

questions.stem: Which of these things can you find in a classroom?
hints: Think about what you sit at in school.
questions.explanation: A desk is a piece of furniture found in a classroom. Cars, rivers, and goats are found outside.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name things from home or outside instead of focusing on the classroom.

questions.stem: Name one thing you can see in your school compound.
hints: It can be a plant or an object.
questions.explanation: There are many things in the school compound, such as trees, grass, stones, or the school building.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name things inside the classroom instead of the compound.

questions.stem: Which is a thing you see in a market?
hints: Think about where people buy food.
It is a red food item.
questions.explanation: Tomatoes are sold in markets. Blackboards are for schools, and beds are for homes.
questions.misconception: Pupils might choose blackboard because it is a familiar object, but it is not found in a market.

questions.stem: Which of these is found in the sky at night?
hints: Think about when it is dark.
It is round and shines at night.
questions.explanation: The moon is seen in the sky at night. The sun is seen during the day.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose the sun, forgetting that the sun is for the day.

questions.stem: A stone is usually...
hints: It is not soft like a pillow.
questions.explanation: A stone is hard. It does not bend or flow like water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the hardness of a stone with other properties.

questions.stem: How would you describe the colour of a typical leaf?
hints: It is the colour of grass.
questions.explanation: Most healthy leaves are green.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all leaves are the same colour as flowers.

questions.stem: Adwoa sees a mango. How can she describe its shape?
hints: Think about the shape of a ball.
It is not flat like paper.
questions.explanation: A mango is round in shape.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse shape with other features like size or colour.

questions.stem: Describe one thing about a goat.
hints: Think about what a goat looks like.
Does it have horns or wings?
questions.explanation: A goat has four legs, horns, and eats grass. These are observable features.
questions.misconception: Pupils may describe what a goat does instead of what it looks like.

questions.stem: Look at a pencil and a piece of paper. Describe how they are different in colour and how they feel.

criteria.description: States a correct colour difference (e.g., pencil is yellow/wood, paper is white)
States a correct difference in how they feel (e.g., pencil is hard, paper is soft/smooth)

hints: Touch them gently. Which is harder?
questions.explanation: This requires observation and description of two features.

questions.stem: We can put things into groups. Which group does a chair belong to?
hints: Think about what you sit on.
It is not something you eat.
questions.explanation: A chair is furniture. It is used for sitting.
questions.misconception: Pupils may group items by where they are found instead of what they are.

questions.stem: Kwame has a cup, a plate, and a spoon. What group can they all belong to?
hints: Think about what you do with them.
They are used in the kitchen.
questions.explanation: A cup, plate, and spoon are all used when eating or drinking.
questions.misconception: Pupils may group them by material or colour instead of their use.

questions.stem: Sort these into two groups: dog, cat, stone, chair.
answer: living: dog cat, non-living: stone chair
animals: dog cat, objects: stone chair
hints: Which ones can move and grow?
questions.explanation: Dogs and cats are living things (animals). Stones and chairs are non-living things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may struggle to find the common criteria for grouping.

questions.stem: Where would you find fish?
questions.explanation: Fish live in water. They need water to breathe and swim.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fish can live anywhere like land animals.

questions.stem: Which of these words describes a balloon?
hints: Think about the shape of a ball.
questions.explanation: A blown-up balloon is round. It is not square or flat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think of a deflated balloon which is flat.

questions.stem: Ama found an object. It is round, small, and used to buy things. What is it?
questions.explanation: A coin is round, small, and used as money to buy things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose another round object like a stone, ignoring the clue about buying things.

questions.stem: Why do we put a dog and a cat in the same group?
hints: They both have fur and breathe.
questions.explanation: A dog and a cat are both animals. They share features like moving, breathing, and eating.
questions.misconception: Pupils may group them by size or colour instead of fundamental characteristics.

questions.stem: Draw a tree and a stone. Write one word to describe the tree and one word to describe the stone.

criteria.description: Uses a correct describing word for the tree (e.g., tall, green)
Uses a correct describing word for the stone (e.g., hard, grey)

hints: What does a tree look like?
questions.explanation: This tests observation, drawing, and description.

questions.stem: Tell me three things you can see outside the window right now.

criteria.description: Names a second correct object outside
Names a third correct object outside

hints: Name what you see on the ground or in the sky.
questions.explanation: This tests real-time observation skills.

questions.stem: Which of these does NOT belong with the others?
hints: Think about what you can eat.
One of these is not a fruit.
questions.explanation: Mango, orange, and banana are fruits. A stone is not a fruit.
questions.misconception: Pupils may sort by colour instead of category.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.1.1.2: Understand the differences between living things, non-living things, and things which have never been alive
indicator.objective: Know the basic needs of living things (food, water and air)

skills.description: Identify food, water and air as basic needs
Give examples of living things and say what they need
Explain simply why living things need food, water and air

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Only people need food, water and air.
Shelter and toys are basic needs.
Plants get all their food from the soil only.
Air is not needed because we cannot see it.

questions.stem: What do all living things need to stay alive?
questions.explanation: Food is a basic need for all living things. Toys, cars, and shoes are not needed for survival.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose toys because they like them, but toys are not a basic need.

questions.stem: Which of these is a basic need of a plant?
questions.explanation: Plants need water to grow. They do not need meat, books, or milk.
questions.misconception: Pupils might choose meat because animals eat meat.

questions.stem: To stay alive, people need to breathe...
hints: You do this all the time without thinking.
questions.explanation: People need air to breathe. We cannot see air, but we need it to live.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose water because they know it is a basic need, but the question asks what we breathe.

questions.stem: Which of these living things needs food?
questions.explanation: A dog is a living thing and needs food to survive. Stones, cups, and chairs are non-living.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think non-living things like cars need food because they need fuel.

questions.stem: Why do we drink water?
hints: You feel thirsty when you need it.
questions.explanation: We drink water because it is a basic need that keeps us alive and healthy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think we only drink water for fun or because we are thirsty, missing the survival aspect.

questions.stem: A potted plant is not watered for many days. What is it missing?
hints: What do you give a plant to help it grow?
questions.explanation: The plant is missing water. Without water, plants will wilt and die.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants only need soil and forget that they need water.

questions.stem: Which of these living things needs water to survive?
questions.explanation: A fish lives in water and needs water to survive. Stones, pencils, and books are non-living.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all animals only need food and forget about water.

questions.stem: Why do we need air?
hints: You do this with your nose and mouth.
questions.explanation: We need air to breathe. Breathing keeps us alive.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the need for air with the need for food or water.

questions.stem: Name two things a baby needs to stay alive.
questions.explanation: A baby needs food (milk), water, and air to stay alive and grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may list toys or clothes instead of basic needs.

questions.stem: Give one example of a living thing and say what it eats.
questions.explanation: A goat is a living thing that eats grass.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name a non-living thing like a car.

questions.stem: Kofi has a plant, a dog, and a fish. What do all three need?
questions.explanation: Plants, dogs, and fish are all living things, so they all need water. Meat, bones, and grass are specific to certain animals.
questions.misconception: Pupils may focus on the dog or fish and choose meat or bones.

questions.stem: Ama has a cat, a bird, and a fish. Which one needs air but does NOT live on land?
questions.explanation: A fish lives in water but still needs air (from the water) to breathe. It does not live on land.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fish do not need air because they live in water.

questions.stem: Explain why a person cannot live without water.

criteria.description: States that we need water to drink
States that water keeps us alive or healthy

hints: Think about what happens when you are very thirsty.
questions.explanation: This tests the understanding of water as a basic need.

questions.stem: What happens to a plant if it does not get air?
hints: Without it, living things cannot survive.
questions.explanation: Plants need air to survive. Without air, a plant will die.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants do not need air because they are not animals.

questions.stem: Which of these things needs food?
hints: It cries when it is hungry.
questions.explanation: A baby is a living thing and needs food to grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think objects that 'use up' things (like a car using fuel) need food.

questions.stem: A farmer gives his goats food, water, and a place to sleep. But the goats are still dying. What basic need is missing?
questions.explanation: All living things need air. If the goats are in a place without fresh air, they will die.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think shelter or water is missing because those are visible, but air is invisible yet essential.

questions.stem: Why is food important for living things?
options: It gives them energy to grow and work
hints: What happens when you don't eat?
questions.explanation: Food gives living things the energy they need to grow, move, and stay healthy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think food is just for satisfying hunger without understanding its role in energy.

questions.stem: Draw a living thing and write two things it needs to survive.

criteria.description: Writes one correct need (e.g., food, water, air)

hints: Draw a plant or an animal.
What does it need to live?
questions.explanation: This tests drawing and recall of basic needs.

questions.stem: Tell me three things that all living things need to survive.
questions.explanation: This tests verbal recall of the three basic needs.

questions.stem: A fish is taken out of water and placed on a table. What will happen to the fish and why?
options: It will die because it cannot breathe
It will turn into a stone
questions.explanation: A fish needs water to breathe. On a table, it cannot get the water it needs and will die.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a fish can breathe air on land like humans.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.1.1.2: Understand the differences between living things, non-living things, and things which have never been alive
indicator.objective: Describe the differences between living and non-living things

skills.description: State simple differences between living and non-living things
Decide whether a given thing is living or non-living and give a simple reason
Choose the best reason for grouping a thing as living or non-living

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Non-living things are the same as dead things.
A car moves, so it is living.
A tree does not move from place to place, so it is non-living.
If something does not eat, it is not living.

questions.stem: Living things grow. Which of these grows?
questions.explanation: A tree is a living thing and it grows. Stones, cars, and cups do not grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a car grows because it gets bigger when more people enter.

questions.stem: Is a dog living or non-living?
questions.explanation: A dog is a living thing. It eats, grows, breathes, and reproduces.
questions.misconception: Pupils may hesitate if they think of a toy dog.

questions.stem: Why is a stone non-living?
hints: Think about how a stone changes over time.
questions.explanation: A stone is non-living because it does not grow, eat, or breathe.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stones move when they roll, so movement equals life.

questions.stem: Which of these is something living things do that non-living things do not?
questions.explanation: Living things reproduce (make babies or new plants). Non-living things cannot do this.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose 'move' because they have seen cars move.

questions.stem: Which of these is non-living?
hints: Which one does not eat or grow?
questions.explanation: A chair is a non-living thing. It does not grow, eat, or breathe.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wooden things are living because they come from trees.

questions.stem: How do living things differ from non-living things in terms of eating?
options: Non-living things eat food, living things do not
Living things eat food, non-living things do not
hints: Do you eat? Does a stone eat?
Living things need food for energy.
questions.explanation: Living things eat food to get energy. Non-living things do not eat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cars 'eat' fuel so they are living.

questions.stem: A car moves. Why is a car not a living thing?
options: It does not grow or make babies
hints: Can a car grow? Can it have baby cars?
questions.explanation: A car is non-living because it cannot grow, eat, breathe, or reproduce, even though it can move.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think movement is the only sign of life.

questions.stem: Kwame has a mango tree, a stone, and a bird. Which group does the mango tree belong to?
questions.explanation: A mango tree is a living thing because it grows, needs water, and makes seeds.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants are non-living because they do not move.

questions.stem: Name one thing that living things can do, but a stone cannot do.
hints: Think about how you change as you get older.
questions.explanation: Living things can grow, eat, and breathe. A stone cannot do any of these.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say 'move' but stones can roll if pushed.

questions.stem: Why do we call a plant a living thing?
hints: What does it need to survive?
questions.explanation: A plant is a living thing because it grows, needs water and air, and reproduces.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants are non-living because they do not move around.

questions.stem: Look at these things: fish, stone, tree, book. Which pair are both living?
hints: A fish swims and a tree grows.
questions.explanation: A fish and a tree are both living things. A stone and a book are non-living.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a book is living because it is made of paper from a tree.

questions.stem: A dead branch is on the ground. Which statement is true?
options: It is non-living because it never lived
It does not grow because it is dead
It is a living thing because it is wood
It will grow into a new tree
hints: Is it still part of a living tree?
questions.explanation: A dead branch was once part of a living tree, but now it is dead and will not grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils often confuse 'dead' with 'non-living' or think wood is always living.

questions.stem: Ama says 'My cup is a living thing because it can hold water.' Is she right? Explain why.

criteria.description: Explains that the cup does not grow, eat, or breathe

questions.explanation: A cup is non-living because it cannot grow, eat, breathe, or reproduce.

questions.stem: Put these into two groups: goat, stone, cup, tree.
answer: living: goat tree, non-living: stone cup
living: goat, tree; non-living: stone, cup
questions.explanation: A goat and a tree are living things. A stone and a cup are non-living things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may struggle to group a plant with an animal as 'living'.

questions.stem: Which of these shows that a living thing is different from a non-living thing?
options: A baby grows into a child
hints: Think about how people change over time.
questions.explanation: A baby growing into a child shows growth, which is a characteristic of living things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may pick 'breaking' as a change, but breaking is not growth.

questions.stem: Why is a moving car NOT considered a living thing?
options: It cannot make its own food or reproduce
hints: Can a car have baby cars?
Living things eat and make babies.
questions.explanation: A car cannot eat, grow, or reproduce, so it is non-living even though it moves.
questions.misconception: Pupils may focus on what makes the car move rather than the characteristics of life.

questions.stem: A boy sees a tall object in the garden. It has green leaves and brown stems. Is it living or non-living?
hints: Leaves and stems are parts of a plant.
questions.explanation: The object is a plant (living thing) because it has leaves and stems.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it is non-living if it does not move.

questions.stem: Write two ways a goat is different from a stone.

criteria.description: States one correct difference (e.g., goat grows, stone does not)
States a second correct difference (e.g., goat eats, stone does not)

hints: What does a goat do that a stone cannot do?
questions.explanation: This tests comparison of living and non-living things.

questions.stem: Tell me why a stone is not a living thing.
questions.explanation: A stone is non-living because it does not grow, eat, or breathe.

questions.stem: Which of these is a thing that has NEVER been alive?
hints: A table was once a tree.
A leaf was once on a plant.
questions.explanation: A stone has never been alive. Wood, leaves, and fish were once alive.
questions.misconception: Pupils often confuse non-living things that come from living things (like wood) with things that have never been alive.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.1.2.1: Recognise materials as important resources for providing human needs
indicator.objective: Identify and name a variety of everyday materials in their immediate environment

skills.description: Name everyday materials commonly found in the home, school and community
Identify/recognise a named material from a picture or simple description
Say where a given material is commonly found in the immediate environment
Link a simple everyday material to one common use

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Metal and plastic are the same thing.
Glass is the same as plastic because both are shiny.
Soil and stone are not materials.
Cloth is only for clothes.
Confusing the name of an object with the name of the material.

questions.stem: Which of these is a material?
hints: A material is used to make things.
questions.explanation: Wood is a material used to make tables, chairs, and doors.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name objects or living things instead of materials.

questions.stem: A bottle of water is usually made from which material?
hints: It is light and can be squeezed.
Water bottles are made from this.
questions.explanation: Plastic is a common material used to make water bottles.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse plastic with glass.

questions.stem: Name one material you can find in your classroom.
questions.explanation: There are many materials in the classroom, such as wood for desks and glass for windows.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name objects like a desk instead of the material.

questions.stem: Which of these is a piece of cloth?
hints: What do you wear to school?
questions.explanation: A school uniform is made of cloth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse objects made of cloth with other objects.

questions.stem: Which material is hard and used to make nails?
questions.explanation: Metal is a hard material used to make nails.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any hard material is metal.

questions.stem: Where do we usually get wood from?
questions.explanation: Wood comes from trees.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wood is dug from the ground.

questions.stem: What is plastic commonly used for?
hints: You can put water in it.
questions.explanation: Plastic is used to make buckets, cups, and many other things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse what a material is with what you do with it.

questions.stem: Which of these is a glass object?
questions.explanation: A windowpane is made of glass.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse transparent plastic with glass.

questions.stem: Where is soil usually found?
hints: It is the dirt on the ground.
questions.explanation: Soil is found on the ground.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think soil is only in farms.

questions.stem: What is cloth used for?
questions.explanation: Cloth is used to make clothes, bags, and curtains.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cloth is only for clothes.

questions.stem: What material is a stone usually made of?
hints: You find it on the ground.
questions.explanation: A stone is a hard material found naturally.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stones are made by people.

questions.stem: Look at a ruler. What material is it made of?
questions.explanation: Rulers can be made of plastic, wood, or metal.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all rulers are plastic.

questions.stem: Why is glass used for windows?
questions.explanation: Glass is used for windows because it is transparent and lets light into a room.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think glass is used because it is pretty.

questions.stem: Why is metal used to make cooking pots?
options: It is hard and can withstand heat
hints: You put pots on a fire.
questions.explanation: Metal is hard and can handle high heat, making it good for cooking pots.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any material can be put on fire.

questions.stem: Kofi has a chair, a bucket, and a shirt. What materials are they made from?
questions.explanation: A chair is often wood, a bucket is plastic, and a shirt is cloth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may mix up the materials for each object.

questions.stem: Name one material found in your kitchen and say what it is used for.

criteria.description: Names a correct material (e.g., metal, plastic, glass)
States a correct use for it

questions.explanation: This tests identifying materials and linking them to uses.

questions.stem: Yaw needs to carry water. Which material is best for making a bucket?
questions.explanation: Plastic is strong and waterproof, making it best for a water bucket. Glass breaks, paper tears, and cloth leaks.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose glass because it holds water, but it breaks easily.

questions.stem: Go outside and collect three different materials (e.g., a leaf, a stone, a piece of plastic). Show them to your teacher and name them.

criteria.description: Collects three items from the environment
Correctly names the material of each item

questions.explanation: This tests real-world observation and naming of materials.

questions.stem: Which statement about materials is TRUE?
options: Materials can only be found in shops
Different materials have different properties and uses
Materials are only made by humans
questions.explanation: Materials have different properties (hard, soft, transparent) which makes them useful for different things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all materials can be used for the same purposes.

questions.stem: Why would you NOT use paper to make a cup for drinking water?

criteria.description: States that paper gets wet and tears
States that water will leak out

hints: What happens to paper when it touches water?
questions.explanation: Paper is not waterproof; it gets soft and tears when it gets wet, so water would leak out.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.1.2.2: Know that substances can exist in different physical state (Solid, Liquid, Gas). Many substances can be changed from one state to another by heating or cooling
indicator.objective: Identify and classify materials as solid, liquid or gas

skills.description: Identify whether a named material is a solid, liquid or gas
Sort a small set of materials into solid, liquid and gas groups
Give an example of a solid, a liquid and a gas
Give a simple reason why a material belongs to a given state

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Air is nothing, so it is not a gas.
Sand is a liquid because it pours.
All liquids are water.
Steam is not a gas because we can see it.
A solid cannot change shape at all.

questions.stem: Which of these is a solid?
hints: You can hold it in your hand.
questions.explanation: A stone is a solid. It has a fixed shape.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any object is a solid, including liquids in a cup.

questions.stem: Which of these is a liquid?
questions.explanation: Water is a liquid. It flows and takes the shape of its container.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water is the only liquid.

questions.stem: What state of matter is the air we breathe?
questions.explanation: Air is a gas. It fills the space around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air is nothing, not a gas.

questions.stem: Which of these is a gas?
questions.explanation: Steam is a gas. It is water in its gaseous state.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think steam is liquid water.

questions.stem: Why is a table called a solid?
hints: Can you change its shape easily?
questions.explanation: A table is a solid because it has a fixed shape and does not flow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think solids must be heavy.

questions.stem: Which group has only liquids?
questions.explanation: Water, milk, and juice are all liquids.
questions.misconception: Pupils may include stones in the liquids group if they think of pouring them.

questions.stem: Is a balloon filled with air a solid, liquid, or gas?
questions.explanation: The air inside the balloon is a gas.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the balloon itself is the gas because it is round.

questions.stem: Why is water called a liquid?
options: It takes the shape of its container
hints: Does it take the shape of the cup?
questions.explanation: Water is a liquid because it flows and takes the shape of whatever container it is in.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water is liquid because it is wet, not because of its shape.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a solid?
questions.explanation: Milk is a liquid. You can pour it. The others are solids.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think anything white is a solid (like chalk).

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a solid?
questions.explanation: Wood is a solid. It has a fixed shape.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think only hard things are solids.

questions.stem: What state of matter is ice?
questions.explanation: Ice is a solid. It is frozen water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think ice is a liquid because it melts.

questions.stem: Give one example of a gas.
hints: What comes from a boiling pot?
questions.explanation: Air, steam, and smoke are examples of gases.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think gas is only petrol.

questions.stem: Ama has three items: a piece of chalk, a glass of water, and a balloon full of air. What are their states?
questions.explanation: Chalk is a solid, water is a liquid, and air is a gas.
questions.misconception: Pupils may get confused by the balloon, thinking the balloon is the gas.

questions.stem: Why does a gas not have a fixed shape?
options: It fills any container it is in
hints: Think about the air in a tyre.
questions.explanation: A gas spreads out to fill any container it is put into, so it does not have a fixed shape.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think gas has no shape because they cannot see it.

questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE?
options: Liquids take the shape of their container
Solids do not take up space
hints: Think about water in a cup.
questions.explanation: Liquids take the shape of their container. Solids keep their shape, and gases fill their container.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think liquids keep their shape like solids.

questions.stem: Kwesi blows into a balloon. What state of matter fills the balloon?
hints: What comes out of his mouth?
questions.explanation: The air Kwesi blows into the balloon is a gas.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the balloon is filled with liquid because it can burst.

questions.stem: Why is a stone a solid?
questions.explanation: A stone is a solid because it has a fixed shape and does not flow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stones are solids because they are heavy.

questions.stem: Explain why a liquid is different from a solid.

criteria.description: States that liquids take the shape of their container (while solids keep their shape)

hints: What happens when you pour water?
questions.explanation: Liquids flow and take the shape of their container, while solids keep their own shape.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT true about gases?
options: They fill the space they are in
They can be compressed into a smaller space
hints: Think about the air in a tyre.
questions.explanation: Gases do not have a fixed shape; they spread out to fill their container.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think gases have a shape because they are inside objects.

questions.stem: Look around your classroom. Write down one solid and one liquid you can see.

criteria.description: Names a correct solid from the classroom
Names a correct liquid from the classroom (e.g., water in a bottle)

questions.explanation: Desks are solids, and water in a bottle is a liquid.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.1.2.3: Understand mixtures, the types, their formation, uses and ways of separating them into their components
indicator.objective: Demonstrate understanding that a mixture is two or more objects or materials put together

skills.description: State in simple words that a mixture is two or more things put together
Identify whether a given example is a mixture or a single material
Give an example of a mixture from everyday life
Recognise that when two materials are mixed, no new material is formed

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: When you mix two things, they always make a new thing.
A mixture is only when you mix the same kind of thing.
Sugar and water is not a mixture because the sugar disappears.
Any two objects placed together are a mixture.

questions.stem: What is a mixture?
options: Two or more things put together
hints: Think about mixing gari and sugar.
questions.explanation: A mixture is formed when two or more materials are put together.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a mixture is only when things dissolve.

questions.stem: Which of these is a mixture?
hints: Which one has two things combined?
You can mix them in a bowl.
questions.explanation: Gari and sand is a mixture of two materials.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any two things placed next to each other are mixed.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a mixture?
options: A cup of tea with sugar
hints: Think about what is in the cup.
questions.explanation: A cup of tea with sugar is a mixture of tea and sugar.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water is a mixture because it is liquid.

questions.stem: When you mix two materials together, you get a...
hints: What is the word for things put together?
questions.explanation: A mixture is formed when two or more materials are combined.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think mixing creates a brand new element.

questions.stem: Is a bowl of plain rice a mixture?
options: Yes, because it has many grains
No, it is a single material
questions.explanation: A bowl of plain rice is just one material (rice). It is not a mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think many grains of the same thing make a mixture.

questions.stem: Which of these is a mixture?
hints: Which one has two different things?
questions.explanation: Milo and milk powder mixed together is a mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any powder is a mixture.

questions.stem: Kofi puts stones and sand in a bucket. Is this a mixture?
options: Yes, because there are two materials
No, because they are both hard
No, because they are from the ground
hints: How many different things are in the bucket?
questions.explanation: Stones and sand is a mixture of two different materials.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think things must dissolve to be a mixture.

questions.stem: When you mix sugar and water, do you make a new material?
options: No, the sugar and water are still there
hints: The sugar is still there, just dissolved.
questions.explanation: Mixing sugar and water forms a mixture, but no new material is made. The sugar and water are still there.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sugar disappears completely and a new liquid is formed.

questions.stem: Give an example of a mixture you can make in the kitchen.
hints: What do you put in tea?
questions.explanation: Mixing milo and milk, or sugar and water, creates a mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name a single food item like 'rice'.

questions.stem: What is formed when you put two or more things together?
questions.explanation: A mixture is formed when two or more things are put together.
questions.misconception: Pupils may answer with a specific object name instead of the concept.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a mixture?
options: A bowl of gari and beans
A cup of tea with milk
A mix of sand and stones
hints: Which one is only one thing?
Is there anything else in the water?
questions.explanation: A glass of pure water is a single material. The others are mixtures of different materials.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think liquids are always mixtures.

questions.stem: Ama mixes sand and iron filings. What is true about the mixture?
options: The sand and iron are still separate materials
hints: Can you still see the sand?
Can you still see the iron?
questions.explanation: In a mixture, the original materials are still there. No new material is formed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think mixing always creates a completely new substance.

questions.stem: Which of these is a mixture of a solid and a liquid?
hints: One is solid, one is liquid.
questions.explanation: Sand (solid) and water (liquid) form a mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify the states of matter in a mixture.

questions.stem: You mix gari and sugar. Explain why no new material is formed.

criteria.description: States that the gari and sugar are still there
States that it is only a combination, not a new substance

hints: Can you still taste the gari?
Can you still taste the sugar?
questions.explanation: The gari and sugar are just mixed together. They keep their own properties, so no new material is formed.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes a mixture?
options: Two or more materials combined without forming a new material
hints: Are the original materials still there?
questions.explanation: A mixture is formed when two or more materials are combined, and the original materials keep their own properties.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a mixture is always a new substance.

questions.stem: Kwame mixes oil and water in a bottle. What type of mixture is this?
questions.explanation: Oil and water are both liquids, so it is a liquid-liquid mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think oil is a solid because it is thick.

questions.stem: Write down two different mixtures you can find in your home.

criteria.description: Gives one correct example of a mixture
Gives a second correct example of a mixture

hints: Is there a mix of things?
questions.explanation: Examples include tea with sugar, gari and beans, or sand and stones.

questions.stem: A student claims: 'When I mix sand and water, the sand turns into water.' Why is this FALSE?
options: Because sand is a solid and cannot turn into water
Because the sand is still in the water, just settled at the bottom
Because sand is not a material
hints: What happens if you leave the mixture to stand?
questions.explanation: The sand does not turn into water. It is a mixture, and the sand sinks to the bottom. Both materials are still there.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think that because the sand is covered by water, it has changed into a new material.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a mixture?
options: A bucket of sand and stones
A cup of tea with sugar
A bowl of gari and milk
hints: Which one is only one material?
questions.explanation: A bar of pure gold is a single material, not a mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all solid objects are mixtures.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: BI.2.1.1: Recognize that some events in our environment occur recurrently
indicator.objective: Explain that some natural phenomena, such as day and night, occur repeatedly

skills.description: Recognise that day and night come one after the other, again and again
Give examples of things seen in the day and things seen at night
Put simple day/night events in the correct order

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Day and night happen only once.
The sun goes away completely at night.
The moon only appears on some nights.

questions.stem: What do we see in the sky during the day?
questions.explanation: The sun is seen in the sky during the day.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon is only seen at night, but it is sometimes visible in the day too; however, the sun is the main object seen in the day.

questions.stem: What do we usually see in the sky at night?
hints: It is round and gives light at night.
questions.explanation: The moon and stars are usually seen at night.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon is always full and bright every night.

questions.stem: After night, what comes next?
hints: When you wake up, it is bright.
questions.explanation: Day comes after night. This happens over and over again.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think night lasts forever.

questions.stem: Which of these activities is done during the day?
hints: What do you do in the morning?
questions.explanation: Going to school is an activity done during the day.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sleeping is only done at night.

questions.stem: Does day and night happen once or many times?
questions.explanation: Day and night happen repeatedly, over and over again.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think day and night happen only once.

questions.stem: When it is dark outside and you can see the moon, it is...
hints: What time do people usually sleep?
questions.explanation: When it is dark and the moon is out, it is night.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse evening with night.

questions.stem: Which of these comes first in a day?
questions.explanation: Morning comes first in a day.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think afternoon comes before morning.

questions.stem: What comes after evening?
questions.explanation: Night comes after evening.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think morning comes right after evening.

questions.stem: Kofi woke up and saw the sun shining. What time of day is it?
questions.explanation: When the sun is shining, it is day.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse morning with night if they wake up early.

questions.stem: Ama sees stars in the sky. What time is it?
hints: Stars are seen when it is dark.
questions.explanation: Stars are seen at night.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stars are seen in the day.

questions.stem: What happens every morning?
questions.explanation: The sun comes out every morning.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon comes out in the morning.

questions.stem: Write the word that comes after morning.
hints: The sun is high in the sky.
questions.explanation: Afternoon comes after morning.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think night comes immediately after morning.

questions.stem: Why do we say day and night occur repeatedly?
options: Because they happen over and over again
Because they happen once a year
questions.explanation: Day and night occur repeatedly, meaning they happen over and over again in a cycle.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'repeatedly' means only twice.

questions.stem: Which of these is the correct order of a full day?
hints: Start with when you wake up.
questions.explanation: The correct order is morning, afternoon, evening, then night.
questions.misconception: Pupils may mix up the order of the day.

questions.stem: If it is night now, what will come next?
hints: What happens when you wake up?
questions.explanation: After night comes day (or morning).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it stays night forever.

questions.stem: Draw a picture of something you see in the day and something you see at night.

criteria.description: Draws a correct day object (e.g., sun)
Draws a correct night object (e.g., moon, stars)

hints: What is in the sky in the day?
What is in the sky at night?
questions.explanation: This tests the understanding of day and night objects.

questions.stem: Ama says 'Day and night happen only once.' Why is she wrong?
hints: Does it happen today? Did it happen yesterday?
questions.explanation: Day and night happen every day. They are repeated over and over.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand the concept of recurrence.

questions.stem: If it is afternoon now, which of these will happen next?
hints: The sun starts to go down.
questions.explanation: Afternoon is followed by evening.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think morning comes after afternoon.

questions.stem: Tell me what happens to the sun and the moon over a whole day.

criteria.description: States the sun comes out in the day
States the moon comes out at night

hints: When do you see the sun?
When do you see the moon?
questions.explanation: The sun is out during the day, and the moon is seen at night.

questions.stem: Which of these happens in a repeating cycle?
questions.explanation: Day and night occur in a repeating cycle.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all daily activities are natural cycles.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: BI.2.1.2: Recognize the relationship between the Earth and the Sun
indicator.objective: Know that the sun is the main source of light to the Earth

skills.description: Identify the sun as the main source of light to the Earth
Name other sources of light
Explain simply why light from the sun is important

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: The moon makes its own light like the sun.
A torch is the main source of light.
We do not need the sun because we have electric lights.
The sun is only for heat, not light.

questions.stem: What is the main source of light to the Earth?
hints: It is in the sky during the day.
questions.explanation: The sun is the main source of light to the Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon is the main source of light.

questions.stem: Which of these is a source of light at home?
hints: It gives light when you switch it on.
questions.explanation: An electric bulb is a source of light.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all objects give light.

questions.stem: What do we use to see in the dark when there is no electricity?
hints: It gives a beam of light.
questions.explanation: A torch is a source of light used in the dark.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they can see in the dark without a light source.

questions.stem: Why do we need light from the sun?
hints: When it is dark, can you see well?
questions.explanation: We need light to see things around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think light is only for keeping warm.

questions.stem: Is the sun a source of light?
questions.explanation: Yes, the sun is a natural source of light.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sun is only for heat.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a source of light?
hints: Does the moon make its own light?
It reflects light from the sun.
questions.explanation: The moon does not make its own light. It reflects light from the sun.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think the moon makes its own light.

questions.stem: During the day, what gives us the most light?
hints: You see it in the sky.
questions.explanation: The sun gives us the most light during the day.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stars give us light in the day.

questions.stem: Which of these is a natural source of light?
hints: It is not made by people.
questions.explanation: The sun is a natural source of light. Torches, candles, and bulbs are artificial (made by people).
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse natural and artificial light sources.

questions.stem: Why is the sun important for plants?
hints: Plants need light to make food.
questions.explanation: Plants need sunlight to grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants only need water and soil.

questions.stem: Ama lights a candle in a dark room. What is the candle doing?
questions.explanation: A candle gives light when it is lit.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the candle only gives heat.

questions.stem: What is the main source of light for the Earth?
hints: It comes out in the day.
questions.explanation: The sun is the main source of light for the Earth.

questions.stem: Name one source of light you use at night.
hints: What helps you see in the dark?
questions.explanation: A torch, candle, or electric bulb can be used at night.
questions.misconception: Pupils may answer with the sun.

questions.stem: Kwame says 'The moon is the main source of light.' Why is he wrong?
options: Because the moon is not bright
Because the sun is the main source
Because the moon is far away
Because the moon only comes out at night
hints: Which one comes out in the day?
questions.explanation: The sun is the main source of light. The moon reflects light from the sun.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon is the main source because they see it at night.

questions.stem: What would happen if the sun stopped giving light?
hints: Think about what happens at night.
Without the sun, it would be like that all the time.
questions.explanation: If the sun stopped giving light, the Earth would be dark.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think electric lights could replace the sun for everything.

questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE about light sources?
options: The sun is the only light source
The moon makes its own light
The sun is a natural light source and a torch is artificial
hints: Think about the difference between the sun and a bulb.
Is the sun made by people?
questions.explanation: The sun is natural, while a torch is artificial (made by people).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all light sources are natural.

questions.stem: Write one reason why we need the sun's light.

criteria.description: States that the sun helps us see
States that the sun helps plants grow

hints: What does light help us do?
questions.explanation: The sun helps us see and helps plants grow.

questions.stem: Why is the sun called the main source of light?
options: Because it gives the most light to the Earth
Because it is in the sky
hints: Is there another light source as bright as the sun?
It lights up the whole Earth.
questions.explanation: The sun gives the most light to the Earth, making it the main source.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand the concept of 'main' source.

questions.stem: Ama is in a dark room. She needs light. Which of these will work best?
hints: Which one gives its own light?
questions.explanation: A torch is a source of light and will work best in a dark room.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a mirror gives light, but it only reflects it.

questions.stem: Write the name of the main source of light for the Earth and one other source of light.

criteria.description: Names the sun as the main source
Names another correct source (e.g., torch, candle, bulb)

hints: What is in the sky in the day?
What do you use in the dark?
questions.explanation: The sun is the main source, and a torch is another source.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: BI.2.1.3: Show understanding of the roles of condensation, evaporation, transpiration and precipitation in the hydrological cycle
indicator.objective: Observe the disappearance of mist and pools of water after rains

skills.description: Observe and describe what happens to mist or a pool of water after rain
Say where the water goes
Predict what will happen to water left in the sun or shade

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: The water just vanishes into nothing.
Mist is smoke.
Water only disappears when it is hot.
