Puddles go into the ground only and never into the air.

questions.stem: After it rains, puddles of water form on the ground. Later, what happens to the puddles?
questions.explanation: Puddles disappear after some time because the water dries up.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the water stays forever.

questions.stem: What is mist?
options: Small drops of water in the air
hints: It looks like a cloud near the ground.
questions.explanation: Mist is made of tiny drops of water in the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think mist is smoke.

questions.stem: When a puddle of water dries up, where does the water go?
options: Into the sky as a cloud
Both into the ground and into the air
hints: Some goes up into the air.
questions.explanation: Puddle water can soak into the ground or evaporate into the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the water just vanishes.

questions.stem: What happens to wet clothes when you hang them in the sun?
questions.explanation: Wet clothes dry in the sun because the water evaporates (goes into the air).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think clothes only dry when it is windy.

questions.stem: If you leave a cup of water in the sun for a long time, what will happen?
options: The water will turn into juice
hints: The water goes into the air.
questions.explanation: The water will decrease because it evaporates into the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the water level stays the same.

questions.stem: Kofi sees mist early in the morning. A few hours later, the mist is gone. What happened to the mist?
questions.explanation: The mist disappeared into the air (it evaporated).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the mist turned into something else.

questions.stem: Where does water from a drying puddle go?
hints: It goes into the air or ground.
questions.explanation: The water goes into the air (evaporation) or into the ground.

questions.stem: Why do puddles dry up faster on a sunny day than on a cloudy day?
options: Because the sun helps the water evaporate faster
Because it rains on sunny days
Because the wind blows the puddles away
questions.explanation: The sun provides heat, which helps water evaporate faster.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sun directly 'drinks' the water.

questions.stem: What is the process called when water turns into gas and goes into the air?
hints: It happens when puddles dry up.
questions.explanation: Evaporation is when water turns into gas and goes into the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse evaporation with boiling.

questions.stem: If you put two identical puddles of water, one in the sun and one in the shade, which will dry up first?
options: Both will dry at the same time
questions.explanation: The puddle in the sun will dry up first because the heat from the sun helps water evaporate faster.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think shade helps water dry.

questions.stem: What happens to wet clothes when you hang them outside on a sunny day?
hints: The water goes into the air.
questions.explanation: Wet clothes dry when hung in the sun because the water evaporates.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the clothes stay wet until it rains.

questions.stem: Ama leaves a glass of water outside for two days. The water level goes down. Why?
options: The water evaporated into the air
The water turned into a solid
questions.explanation: The water evaporated into the air because of the heat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the glass absorbed the water.

questions.stem: You see a puddle of water on the ground in the morning. What do you predict it will look like in the afternoon? Explain why.

criteria.description: States the puddle will be smaller or gone
Explains that the water evaporates into the air

questions.explanation: The puddle will get smaller or disappear because the sun helps the water evaporate.

questions.stem: Put a little water on two plates. Put one plate in the sun and one in the shade. Check them after an hour. Tell your teacher what you observed.

criteria.description: Observes and states that the plate in the sun dried faster
States that the heat from the sun helps water disappear

hints: Does heat make water dry faster?
questions.explanation: The plate in the sun will dry faster because heat from the sun helps the water evaporate.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a way water disappears from the ground?
hints: Think about what actually happens to puddles.
questions.explanation: Water does not turn into stone. It evaporates or soaks into the ground.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand the limits of transformation.

questions.stem: What causes mist to disappear after the sun comes out?
options: The mist is blown away by the wind
The tiny water drops in the mist evaporate into the air
The mist falls to the ground as rain
hints: The tiny water drops dry up.
questions.explanation: The tiny water drops in the mist evaporate into the air when the sun heats them.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the mist is always blown away by the wind.

questions.stem: Why is it easier to dry clothes on a windy, sunny day than on a still, cloudy day?
options: The wind blows the water away
The wind and sun help the water evaporate faster
The sun makes the clothes heavier
The wind makes the clothes dry faster
questions.explanation: Both wind and sun help water evaporate faster, so clothes dry more quickly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the wind physically 'blows' the water off, which is partly true but evaporation is the main process.

questions.stem: A student puts a small puddle of water in the freezer. What will happen to the water?
hints: Water freezes when it gets cold.
questions.explanation: The water will freeze and turn into ice because the freezer is very cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water always evaporates regardless of temperature.

questions.stem: Write two places where puddle water goes when it dries up.

criteria.description: States it goes into the air (evaporates)
States it goes into the ground

questions.explanation: The water goes into the air (evaporation) and into the ground.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.2.1.4: Recognize water and air as important natural resources
indicator.objective: Identify sources and uses of water in the home and at school

skills.description: Name sources of water at home, school and community
Name uses of water
Match a use to the correct setting or to a source

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Water only comes from taps.
Rain is not a source of water.
We only use water for drinking.
The sea is good for drinking water.

questions.stem: Where do we usually get water in our homes?
hints: It is in the kitchen or bathroom.
questions.explanation: We usually get water from a tap in our homes.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water only comes from rivers.

questions.stem: What do we use water for?
hints: You need it to stay alive.
questions.explanation: We use water for drinking.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water is only for washing.

questions.stem: Which of these is a source of water?
hints: It is a body of water.
questions.explanation: A river is a source of water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water only comes from taps.

questions.stem: What do we use to wash our hands?
questions.explanation: We use water and soap to wash our hands.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any liquid can be used for washing.

questions.stem: Where do we get rain from?
questions.explanation: Rain falls from clouds in the sky.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think rain comes from the ground.

questions.stem: Ama wants to cook rice. What does she need?
hints: You boil the rice in it.
questions.explanation: Ama needs water to cook rice.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cooking only needs fire.

questions.stem: Which of these is a source of water in a village?
questions.explanation: A borehole is a source of water in a village.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think boreholes are only in cities.

questions.stem: Where is water used for watering plants?
questions.explanation: Water is used for watering plants in the school garden.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water is only for drinking.

questions.stem: Why do we use water in the school toilet?
hints: It helps keep the toilet clean.
questions.explanation: Water is used to flush the toilet.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think toilets use sand.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a source of water?
hints: Which one does not hold or give water?
questions.explanation: A stone is not a source of water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stones hold water because they are found in water.

questions.stem: Write one way you use water at school.
hints: What do you do after using the toilet?
What do you do before eating?
questions.explanation: There are many ways to use water at school, such as washing hands or flushing the toilet.
questions.misconception: Pupils may only think of drinking.

questions.stem: Name one source of water in your community.
questions.explanation: A tap, river, well, borehole, or rain are all sources of water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water only comes from shops.

questions.stem: Kofi has a bucket. He wants to get water from the ground. Which source should he go to?
hints: It is dug in the ground.
questions.explanation: A well is a source of water dug in the ground.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know what a well is.

questions.stem: Why is water important for our health?
options: It keeps us hydrated and clean
hints: What happens if you don't drink water?
What do you use to wash?
questions.explanation: Water keeps us hydrated and helps us stay clean, which is important for health.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water is only for fun.

questions.stem: Which of these sources of water is safe to drink without treating it?
options: Rain that has just fallen on the ground
hints: Which one is cleaned by the government?
questions.explanation: Tap water is treated and usually safe to drink. River and stream water may contain dirt and germs.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all natural water is safe to drink.

questions.stem: Write two uses of water at home.

criteria.description: Names one correct use (e.g., drinking, cooking)

hints: What do you do when you are thirsty?
What do you do before cooking?
questions.explanation: We use water for drinking and cooking.

questions.stem: Why would a farmer need water on a farm?
questions.explanation: A farmer needs water to water the crops so they can grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think farms only need rain.

questions.stem: Which of these is a natural source of water?
hints: It is not made by people.
questions.explanation: Rain is a natural source of water. Taps and bottled water are man-made.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all water sources are man-made.

questions.stem: Tell me one way you use water at home and one way you use it at school.
hints: What do you do in the bathroom?
What do you do in the school toilet?
questions.explanation: Water is used for many things at home and school, like drinking, cooking, washing, and flushing.

questions.stem: Write the name of one source of water you can find in your community and one use of water.

criteria.description: Names a correct source (e.g., river, tap)
Names a correct use (e.g., drinking, washing)

hints: What do you use it for?
questions.explanation: A river is a source, and drinking is a use.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.2.1.4: Recognize water and air as important natural resources
indicator.objective: Demonstrate the existence of air in the environment

skills.description: Recognise simple evidence that air exists
Name uses of air
Know that air is all around us, even though we cannot see it

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Air is nothing because we cannot see it.
Air only exists outside.
A balloon is empty when deflated.
Wind is not air; it is a separate thing.

questions.stem: Can we see air?
hints: You breathe it but cannot see it.
questions.explanation: We cannot see air, but it is all around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air is visible.

questions.stem: What do we use air for?
hints: You do it all the time.
You need it to stay alive.
questions.explanation: We use air to breathe.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think we only need air for blowing balloons.

questions.stem: How do you know air is in a balloon?
options: The balloon is big and hard
hints: What happens when you blow into a balloon?
questions.explanation: When a balloon is blown up, air fills it and makes it big and hard.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a balloon is empty when it is blown up.

questions.stem: Is there air in the classroom?
options: Only if the window is open
Only if the fan is on
questions.explanation: Yes, there is air in the classroom. Air is all around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air only comes from outside.

questions.stem: What do you need air for when you are playing?
hints: You get tired and breathe faster.
questions.explanation: You need air to breathe, especially when playing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they only need air when they are resting.

questions.stem: When you wave a piece of paper in front of your face, what do you feel?
questions.explanation: Waving paper moves the air around, and you can feel it on your face.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand that moving air creates a breeze.

questions.stem: What do we use to blow up a balloon?
questions.explanation: We use air from our lungs to blow up a balloon.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think you use water to blow up a balloon.

questions.stem: Is there air outside your house?
questions.explanation: Yes, there is air everywhere outside.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air is only inside.

questions.stem: Ama switches on a fan. What does the fan do?
questions.explanation: The fan makes air move, which creates a breeze.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the fan creates new air.

questions.stem: Which of these uses air?
hints: It goes up in the sky.
questions.explanation: Flying a kite uses air (wind) to lift the kite.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not see the connection between kites and air.

questions.stem: What do you fill a balloon with to make it big?
questions.explanation: You fill a balloon with air to make it big.

questions.stem: Is air everywhere around us?
hints: Can you breathe anywhere in the room?
questions.explanation: Yes, air is everywhere around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air is only in some places.

questions.stem: How can you show that air is inside a deflated balloon?
options: Squeeze the balloon and feel the air come out
questions.explanation: Squeezing a deflated balloon can push the air out, showing that air is inside.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a deflated balloon has no air inside.

questions.stem: Why do we need air to breathe?
hints: What happens if you hold your breath?
questions.explanation: We need air to stay alive. Without air, we cannot breathe.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think we only need air for play.

questions.stem: Describe one way you can show that air exists.

criteria.description: Describes a valid activity (e.g., waving a paper, blowing a balloon, feeling the wind)
States what is observed (e.g., paper moves, balloon gets big)

hints: What happens when you wave a paper?
What happens when you blow up a balloon?
questions.explanation: Waving paper moves the air, and you can feel it. This shows that air exists.

questions.stem: What happens to a paper fan when you move it back and forth?
questions.explanation: Moving a paper fan pushes the air, creating a breeze.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the fan creates air.

questions.stem: Why can we not see air?
questions.explanation: Air is transparent and colourless, so we cannot see it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air is invisible because it doesn't exist.

questions.stem: Ama says 'A balloon that is not blown up has no air in it.' Why is she wrong?
options: Because the balloon is still there
Because the balloon is actually full of air even when not blown up
Because the balloon is made of air
hints: Is there space inside the balloon?
Does the balloon look completely flat?
questions.explanation: Even a balloon that is not blown up has some air inside it. Air is all around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a deflated balloon is completely empty.

questions.stem: Demonstrate to your teacher one way to show that air exists (e.g., blowing a balloon, waving a paper, or using a fan).

criteria.description: Explains what they observed to show air is present

hints: What can you do with a balloon?
questions.explanation: This tests the practical demonstration of air's existence.

questions.stem: Write two ways we use air in our daily lives.

criteria.description: Names one use (e.g., breathing, blowing balloons, flying kites)

hints: What do you do to stay alive?
What do you blow into a balloon?
questions.explanation: We use air for breathing, flying kites, and blowing up balloons.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.2.2.1: Demonstrate understanding of the life cycle of plants
indicator.objective: Examine the structure of plants

skills.description: Name the main external parts of a plant
Identify plant parts from a picture, drawing, or real plant
State simply what each part does
Draw and label a simple plant showing at least three parts

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Plants only have leaves and stems; roots are not part of the plant.
Flowers are only for decoration; they have no job.
The stem is just a stick; it does not carry water.
Confusing 'root' with 'stem' when looking at a plant pulled from the soil.

questions.stem: Which part of a plant is usually found under the ground?
hints: It holds the plant in the soil.
You cannot see it when the plant is growing.
questions.explanation: The roots are the part of the plant that grows under the ground.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the stem goes all the way underground.

questions.stem: Which part of a plant is usually green and flat?
questions.explanation: Leaves are usually green and flat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse leaves with the stem.

questions.stem: What do we call the colourful part of a plant?
hints: It can be red, yellow, or pink.
questions.explanation: The flower is the colourful part of the plant.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the flower is only for looking at.

questions.stem: Look at a plant. Which part holds the leaves up to the sun?
hints: It connects the roots to the leaves.
questions.explanation: The stem holds the plant up, including the leaves.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the roots hold the leaves up.

questions.stem: Which part of the plant takes in water from the soil?
questions.explanation: The roots take in water from the soil.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the stem takes in water directly from the soil.

questions.stem: Kofi pulls a small plant from the ground. He sees a part with tiny hairs on it that was in the soil. What part is this?
questions.explanation: The part with tiny hairs that was in the soil is the root.
questions.misconception: Pupils may call it a stem because it looks like a thin stick.

questions.stem: Why do plants have leaves?
questions.explanation: Leaves help the plant make food using sunlight.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think leaves are only for decoration.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a main part of a plant?
questions.explanation: A stone is not a part of a plant. Roots, stems, and leaves are plant parts.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stones are part of the plant because they are in the soil.

questions.stem: Ama sees a plant with roots, a stem, and green leaves. She does not see any flowers. Is this a plant?
options: No, it is not a plant
Yes, but it is missing a flower
hints: Does it have roots and leaves?
Can a plant live without flowers?
questions.explanation: Yes, it is still a plant. Some plants do not have flowers, or they have not grown flowers yet.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all plants must have flowers to be a plant.

questions.stem: What job does the stem do for the plant?
options: It takes in water from the soil
It carries water to the leaves
hints: It connects the roots and the leaves.
questions.explanation: The stem carries water from the roots to the leaves.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the stem only holds the plant up and does nothing else.

questions.stem: Name two parts of a plant.
hints: What is under the ground? What is green?
questions.explanation: Two parts of a plant are roots and leaves (or stem and flower).
questions.misconception: Pupils may name non-plant parts like soil.

questions.stem: What part of the plant is found under the soil?
hints: You cannot see it above the ground.
questions.explanation: The roots are found under the soil.
questions.misconception: Pupils may answer 'stem' because stems can be near the ground.

questions.stem: If you remove the roots of a plant, what will happen to the plant?
options: It will not get water and may die
It will turn into a flower
hints: Where does the plant get water?
questions.explanation: Roots take in water. Without roots, the plant cannot get water and may die.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think roots are not important.

questions.stem: Kwame is drawing a plant. He draws a line going straight up from the ground. He adds leaves to the sides. What is the line he drew?
questions.explanation: The line going straight up is the stem.
questions.misconception: Pupils may call the stem a root.

questions.stem: Why does a plant need flowers?
hints: What do we plant to grow new plants?
questions.explanation: Flowers help the plant make seeds so new plants can grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think flowers are just for beauty.

questions.stem: Adwoa has a leaf and a flower. How are they different?
options: The leaf is usually green, the flower is colourful
The leaf is usually colourful, the flower is green
The leaf is under the ground
The flower is under the ground
questions.explanation: Leaves are usually green, while flowers can be many colours like red, yellow, or pink.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not have observed flowers closely.

questions.stem: Draw a plant showing the roots, stem, and one leaf. Label the three parts.
hints: Start with the root at the bottom.
Add the stem and a leaf.
questions.explanation: This tests observation and drawing of plant parts.

questions.stem: Explain why a plant is called a living thing because of its parts.

criteria.description: Mentions that it has parts that help it grow or make food
Mentions that it takes in water or air

hints: What does the plant do with its leaves?
questions.explanation: A plant is a living thing because its parts help it grow, take in water (roots), and make food (leaves).

questions.stem: Draw a flower and label it.
questions.explanation: This tests identification and drawing of the flower.

questions.stem: A plant has roots, a stem, and leaves. It does NOT have flowers. What can we say about this plant?
options: It is a plant that may not grow flowers
hints: Are roots and leaves enough to make it a plant?
Do all plants have visible flowers all the time?
questions.explanation: Not all plants have visible flowers. As long as it has roots, a stem, and leaves, it is a plant.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all plants must have flowers.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.2.2.1: Demonstrate understanding of the life cycle of plants
indicator.objective: Observe different kinds of seeds

skills.description: Name common seeds found in the environment
Describe simple differences between seeds
Match a seed to the fruit or plant it comes from
Draw and label one or two seeds observed

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: All seeds look the same.
A seed is the same as a fruit.
Only big seeds can grow into plants.
Confusing 'seed' with 'nut' or 'stone' in everyday language.

questions.stem: Which of these is a seed?
hints: You plant it to grow a new plant.
It can be cooked and eaten.
questions.explanation: A bean is a seed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any small object is a seed.

questions.stem: Where do we find the seed of an orange?
questions.explanation: The seed of an orange is found inside the fruit.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think seeds grow outside the fruit.

questions.stem: Which of these seeds is eaten as a snack in Ghana?
questions.explanation: Groundnut is a seed that is commonly eaten as a snack.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know that groundnuts are seeds.

questions.stem: Which seed comes from a maize plant?
questions.explanation: The corn seed (maize) grows on a cob.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse corn with other yellow foods.

questions.stem: Are all seeds the same size?
options: Only the ones in the ground
hints: Compare a mango seed and a bean seed.
Some are big, some are small.
questions.explanation: No, seeds come in different sizes. A mango seed is big, and a bean seed is smaller.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all seeds look alike.

questions.stem: Which fruit has a large, hard seed in the middle?
hints: The seed is big and flat.
questions.explanation: The mango has a large, hard seed in the middle.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think bananas have large seeds.

questions.stem: How is a maize seed different from a bean seed?
options: The maize seed is yellow and the bean seed is red/brown
The maize seed is small and the bean seed is huge
hints: What colour is a typical bean?
questions.explanation: Maize seeds are usually yellow or white, while bean seeds are often red, brown, or black.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all seeds are brown.

questions.stem: Where do we find seeds?
options: Inside fruits and in the soil
questions.explanation: Seeds are found inside fruits and in the soil (after planting).
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize seeds come from fruits.

questions.stem: Ama has an orange seed and a groundnut. How are they different?
options: The orange seed is inside a fruit and the groundnut is a seed we eat
The groundnut is inside an orange
The orange seed is big and hard
hints: Where do you find each one?
Can you eat a groundnut directly?
questions.explanation: An orange seed is found inside the orange fruit, while a groundnut is a seed we can eat directly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand the difference between a seed inside a fruit and a seed we eat.

questions.stem: Name one seed you can find in your home.
questions.explanation: Seeds like beans, maize, and groundnuts are commonly found in homes.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name rice, but rice is also a seed; accept it.

questions.stem: What fruit does a pawpaw seed come from?
hints: It has many small black seeds.
questions.explanation: A pawpaw seed comes from a pawpaw fruit.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know what a pawpaw is.

questions.stem: Kwame has two seeds. Seed A is very small. Seed B is large and hard. Which could be a mango seed?
questions.explanation: Mango seeds are large and hard, so Seed B is likely the mango seed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think small seeds are the only ones that grow.

questions.stem: Why do some seeds have a hard outer cover?
questions.explanation: The hard outer cover protects the inside of the seed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the hard cover is just for decoration.

questions.stem: Which of these statements is TRUE?
options: Seeds can grow into new plants
Seeds do not need soil to grow
hints: What happens when you plant a seed?
questions.explanation: Seeds can grow into new plants when planted.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think seeds are just food and do not grow.

questions.stem: Draw a bean seed and a maize seed. Write 'bean' under the bean and 'maize' under the maize.
hints: Maize is like a small yellow tooth.
questions.explanation: This tests observation and drawing of two different seeds.

questions.stem: Name two seeds that you can eat and two seeds that you cannot eat.

criteria.description: Names one non-edible seed (e.g., mango seed, orange seed)

hints: Think about mango and orange seeds.
questions.explanation: Beans and groundnuts are edible. Mango and orange seeds are usually not eaten.

questions.stem: A farmer plants a maize seed. What will grow from it?
hints: The seed comes from the maize plant.
It grows into the same kind of plant.
questions.explanation: A maize seed grows into a maize plant.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a seed can grow into any plant.

questions.stem: Look at a mango seed and a bean seed. Write one way they are different.

criteria.description: States a valid difference (e.g., size, colour, hardness)

questions.explanation: A mango seed is larger and harder than a bean seed.

questions.stem: Draw a pawpaw seed and a groundnut. Colour them.

criteria.description: Draws a small black pawpaw seed

hints: Pawpaw seeds are small and black.
questions.explanation: This tests observation of seed colour and size.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.3.1.1: (Content standard garbled in source document)
indicator.objective: Identify the external human body parts by their appropriate names (e.g. eyes, ears, mouth, nose, legs, hands, shoulders, knees, fingers, toes and chest)

skills.description: Name external body parts correctly when shown or pointed to
Identify/point to a named body part on self or on a picture
Say where a body part is found
Draw and label at least three external body parts

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: The chest is the same as the stomach.
Fingers and toes are the same.
Shoulders are part of the arm only.
Confusing 'knee' and 'elbow'.

questions.stem: Which part of the body do we use to see?
questions.explanation: We use our eyes to see.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the eyes with other facial parts.

questions.stem: Which part of the body do we use to hear?
hints: It is on the side of your head.
questions.explanation: We use our ears to hear.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they hear with their eyes.

questions.stem: What is the name of the body part we use to walk?
questions.explanation: We use our legs to walk.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse legs with arms.

questions.stem: Point to the part of your body used for smelling. What is it called?
hints: It is in the middle of your face.
questions.explanation: The nose is used for smelling.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the mouth is for smelling.

questions.stem: Where are your fingers found?
hints: You use them to hold a pencil.
They are at the end of your arms.
questions.explanation: Fingers are found on the hand.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fingers are on the feet.

questions.stem: Which of these is a body part?
hints: Which one is part of you?
questions.explanation: The shoulder is a body part.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think external objects are body parts.

questions.stem: Kofi is touching the part of his body where his arm joins his neck. What part is he touching?
questions.explanation: Kofi is touching his shoulder.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the shoulder with the chest.

questions.stem: Where is your chest located?
options: At the back of your body
On the front of your body between your neck and stomach
hints: It is the front part of your upper body.
questions.explanation: The chest is on the front of the body between the neck and the stomach.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the chest is the same as the stomach.

questions.stem: Which part of the body is used to eat?
questions.explanation: We use the mouth to eat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the nose is used to eat because it is near the mouth.

questions.stem: What do we call the parts at the end of our arms?
questions.explanation: The parts at the end of our arms are the hands.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse hands with feet.

questions.stem: Where are your knees?
hints: You bend them when you walk.
They are in the middle of your legs.
questions.explanation: The knees are found on the legs.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse knees with elbows.

questions.stem: Name the body part you use to kick a ball.
hints: It is at the bottom of your body.
questions.explanation: We use our legs (and feet) to kick a ball.

questions.stem: Draw a human head. Label the eyes, nose, and mouth.
hints: Add the features you see on your own face.
questions.explanation: This tests drawing and identifying parts of the face.

questions.stem: Name three parts of the body that are on your face.
questions.explanation: The eyes, nose, mouth, and ears are found on the face.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name body parts not on the face, like knees.

questions.stem: Ama has a pain in the part of her body that connects her head to her shoulders. What part is this?
hints: It is between the head and shoulders.
questions.explanation: The neck connects the head to the shoulders.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the neck with the chest.

questions.stem: Which body parts work together when you clap your hands?
hints: They are at the end of your arms.
questions.explanation: You use your hands to clap.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think you clap with your legs.

questions.stem: Draw a hand and label the fingers.
hints: Draw an outline of your hand.
questions.explanation: This tests drawing and labeling the hand.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an external body part you can see on the outside?
hints: Can you see it from the outside?
questions.explanation: The heart is an internal organ. You cannot see it from the outside.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they can see their heart because they can feel it beating.

questions.stem: Write down three body parts you use when you wash your face.
hints: What do you use to scrub?
questions.explanation: You use your hands and fingers to wash your face, which includes your eyes and mouth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may list unrelated parts like knees.

questions.stem: Kwame is standing straight. Which body part is touching the ground?
questions.explanation: When standing, the feet touch the ground.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say knees, forgetting that feet are at the very bottom.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.3.2.1: Show understanding and appreciation of the interactions and interdependencies of organisms in an ecosystem
indicator.objective: Know the places where living things live (land, air, and water)

skills.description: Name the three main places where living things live
Match a living thing to its habitat
Give examples of living things found in each habitat
Give a simple reason why a living thing is found in a particular place

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: All animals live on land.
Birds live only in the air and never on land.
Fish can live on land if they are wet.
Plants are not living things, so they do not have a habitat.
Air is not a habitat because we cannot see it.

questions.stem: What are the three main places where living things live?
questions.explanation: Living things live on land, in the air, and in water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may list specific objects instead of the three main habitats.

questions.stem: Where does a fish live?
questions.explanation: A fish lives in water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fish live on land.

questions.stem: Where does a bird fly?
questions.explanation: Birds fly in the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think birds only live on land.

questions.stem: A goat lives on...
questions.explanation: A goat lives on land.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think goats live in the air.

questions.stem: Which of these living things lives in water?
questions.explanation: A fish lives in water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all animals live on land.

questions.stem: Match the animal to its home: A dog lives on...
questions.explanation: A dog lives on land.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think dogs can live in water.

questions.stem: Do plants grow on land or in the air?
questions.explanation: Plants can grow on land (in soil) or in water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all plants only grow on land.

questions.stem: Name one living thing that lives in the air.
questions.explanation: Birds and insects are living things that live in the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name things that cannot fly, like a dog.

questions.stem: Ama sees a fish, a bird, and a cow. Which one lives in water?
questions.explanation: The fish lives in water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think birds live in water because they drink it.

questions.stem: Is air a place where living things live?
options: Yes, birds and insects live in the air
Yes, only fish live in the air
questions.explanation: Yes, birds and insects are living things that live in the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air is not a habitat.

questions.stem: Which of these lives on land?
questions.explanation: A goat lives on land.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse land and water animals.

questions.stem: Where does a whale live?
hints: It is a very large animal in the sea.
questions.explanation: A whale lives in water (the sea or ocean).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think whales live on land because they breathe air.

questions.stem: Why does a fish live in water?
options: It needs water to swim and breathe
questions.explanation: A fish lives in water because it needs it to swim and breathe.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fish live in water just because they like it.

questions.stem: Why do birds fly in the air?
options: To move from place to place and find food
Because they are afraid of land
hints: Where do they find their food?
questions.explanation: Birds fly in the air to move around and find food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think birds only fly to hide.

questions.stem: Kwame says 'All living things live on land.' Is he correct?
options: No, some live in water and air
No, all living things live in water
questions.explanation: No, living things live on land, in water, and in the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think land is the only habitat.

questions.stem: A fish is taken out of water. Why will it die?
hints: Where does a fish get air?
It does not have lungs like us.
questions.explanation: A fish needs water to breathe. Out of water, it cannot breathe and will die.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fish can breathe air on land.

questions.stem: Name two living things that live on land.
hints: Think of animals you see on the ground.
Think of plants in the garden.
questions.explanation: Many living things live on land, such as goats, dogs, trees, and people.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name fish or birds.

questions.stem: Why can't a fish live on land?
options: It has no legs and needs water to breathe
It does not like the sun
questions.explanation: A fish cannot live on land because it has no legs to walk and needs water to breathe.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect the body parts of the fish to its habitat.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a place where living things live?
hints: Which one is dangerous and hot?
Can living things survive in it?
questions.explanation: Living things do not live in fire. They live on land, in water, and in the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fire is a habitat because it exists in the environment.

questions.stem: A bird has wings. How does this help it live in the air?
hints: How does a bird move in the air?
questions.explanation: Wings help a bird to fly, which allows it to live in the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wings are for swimming.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.4.1.1: Demonstrate understanding of the concept of energy, its various forms and sources and the ways in which it can be transformed and conserved
indicator.objective: Understand energy and give examples of its uses

skills.description: State in simple words that energy is what enables us to do work
Give examples of everyday activities that use energy
Name simple sources of energy for everyday activities
Explain simply what happens when there is no energy

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Energy is only electricity.
Only people need energy; animals and machines do not.
Food is not energy; it is just something we eat.
Energy is something you can always see.

questions.stem: What gives you the power to walk and run?
questions.explanation: Energy is what gives you the power to do things like walk and run.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think objects like chairs give them energy.

questions.stem: Which of these activities uses energy?
hints: You use your legs to push off the ground.
questions.explanation: Jumping uses energy because it requires your body to move and work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sitting quietly uses no energy at all.

questions.stem: Where do people get the energy to work and play?
questions.explanation: People get energy from the food they eat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they get energy from just resting.

questions.stem: What happens to a car when it runs out of fuel?
questions.explanation: A car stops moving when it runs out of fuel because it has no energy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a car can move without fuel.

questions.stem: Which of these uses energy from electricity?
questions.explanation: A fan uses electrical energy to spin and give breeze.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all objects use electricity.

questions.stem: Energy is best described as...
options: What enables us to do work
hints: Think about what you need to run.
questions.explanation: Energy is what enables us to do work, move, and play.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think energy is always visible.

questions.stem: What is the main source of energy for plants to make their food?
hints: It is in the sky during the day.
questions.explanation: The sun is the main source of energy for plants to make food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants only get energy from the soil.

questions.stem: Kofi is pushing a heavy box. What is he using?
hints: His body needs energy to push.
questions.explanation: Kofi is using energy to push the heavy box.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not associate physical work with energy.

questions.stem: Ama has not eaten all day. How will she feel?
hints: Without food, you have no energy.
questions.explanation: Ama will feel weak because she has no energy from food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think skipping meals makes you stronger.

questions.stem: Which of these activities does NOT need much energy?
questions.explanation: Sleeping in bed requires much less energy than running or playing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sleeping uses no energy at all, but the body still needs some.

questions.stem: Name one thing that gives you energy.
questions.explanation: Food is the main source of energy for people.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name things that do not provide energy, like a pencil.

questions.stem: What do we call the thing that helps us do work?
questions.explanation: Energy is what helps us do work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse energy with a physical object.

questions.stem: Why does a person need to eat food before playing football?
questions.explanation: Food provides the energy needed to run and play football.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think eating before playing makes you tired.

questions.stem: What happens to a torch when its battery runs out?
hints: The battery gives the torch energy.
questions.explanation: A torch stops giving light when its battery is dead because it has no energy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a torch can work without a battery.

questions.stem: Which of these is a source of energy for a moving car?
hints: The car goes to the petrol station.
questions.explanation: Petrol (fuel) is the source of energy for a car to move.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cars run on water.

questions.stem: Which of these shows the use of energy in the home?
options: A book lying on a table
hints: Energy is needed to change the food.
questions.explanation: Cooking food on a stove uses energy (heat energy).
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize cooking uses energy.

questions.stem: Explain what happens to a person who has not eaten for a long time.

criteria.description: States the person will feel weak or tired
Explains that the person has no energy from food

questions.explanation: A person who has not eaten for a long time will feel weak because they have no energy from food.

questions.stem: Why do we say energy is needed to do work?
options: Because energy gives us the strength to move and act
hints: Think about pushing a heavy object.
What gives you the power to push it?
questions.explanation: Energy gives us the strength and power to move and do work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think work requires no energy.

questions.stem: Tell me two activities you did today that used energy.
questions.explanation: Walking, playing, and writing are all activities that use energy.

questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE about energy?
options: Energy is only found in food
Energy can never be used up
Living things and machines need energy to work
questions.explanation: Both living things and machines need energy to work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think only humans use energy.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.4.1.2: Show understanding of the concept of heat energy in terms of its importance, effects, sources and transfer from one medium to another
indicator.objective: Explain the terms hot and cold

skills.description: Explain in simple words what 'hot' and 'cold' mean
Sort familiar items into hot and cold
Name simple sources of heat
Say what happens when something is heated or cooled

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Cold is a kind of energy that comes from ice.
If it is not on fire, it is cold.
Hot and cold are the same as hard and soft.
Objects become cold by gaining coldness, not by losing heat.

questions.stem: Which of these is usually hot?
hints: It is very dangerous to touch.
questions.explanation: Fire is very hot.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fire is cold.

questions.stem: Which of these is usually cold?
hints: It is kept in the fridge.
questions.explanation: Ice cream is cold because it is kept frozen.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all food is hot.

questions.stem: How does a hot cup of tea feel when you touch it?
questions.explanation: A hot cup of tea feels warm or hot to the touch.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse hot with just being wet.

questions.stem: When you touch a piece of ice, how does it feel?
hints: It makes your hand feel chilly.
questions.explanation: Ice feels cold to the touch.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think ice is hot because the sun melts it.

questions.stem: What is the main natural source of heat for the Earth?
hints: It gives us light during the day.
questions.explanation: The sun is the main natural source of heat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon gives heat.

questions.stem: Ama is sorting items. Which group is all cold?
hints: Which group has things from the fridge/freezer?
The other groups have fire or heat.
questions.explanation: Ice, cold water, and an ice block are all cold items.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water is always cold.

questions.stem: Which of these is a source of heat at home?
questions.explanation: A stove is a source of heat used for cooking.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think only the sun gives heat.

questions.stem: What happens to an ice block when you leave it in the sun?
questions.explanation: An ice block melts when left in the sun because the heat turns it into liquid water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think ice stays solid in the sun.

questions.stem: What happens to water when you put it in a fridge?
questions.explanation: Water becomes cold when placed in a fridge.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a fridge adds cold energy.

questions.stem: If something is NOT hot, we say it is...
hints: It is the opposite of hot.
questions.explanation: The opposite of hot is cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse temperature with texture (hard/soft).

questions.stem: Name one hot thing and one cold thing in your home.
answer: hot: fire/stove/iron, cold: ice/water in fridge
hints: What do you use to cook?
What do you use to cool a drink?
questions.explanation: A stove is hot, and ice is cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may list items that are room temperature.

questions.stem: Name one thing that gives us heat.
questions.explanation: The sun and fire are sources of heat.

questions.stem: Why do we put ice in a bottle of water on a hot day?
questions.explanation: We put ice in water to make it cold because ice is cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think ice adds flavor.

questions.stem: Kwame wants to make his water hot. Which of these can he use?
questions.explanation: An electric kettle is a source of heat used to boil water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a fan makes water hot.

questions.stem: What happens to a hot iron when you unplug it and leave it for a long time?
hints: It is no longer connected to electricity.
questions.explanation: The hot iron cools down when unplugged because it loses heat to the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the iron stays hot forever.

questions.stem: Explain how you can tell if something is hot or cold just by touching it.

criteria.description: States that hot things feel warm or burning
States that cold things feel chilly or cool

questions.explanation: We use our sense of touch to feel if something is hot (warm/burning) or cold (chilly/cool).

questions.stem: Which of these is true about a boiling pot of water and a piece of ice?
options: The water is hot and the ice is cold
The water is cold and the ice is hot
questions.explanation: Boiling water is hot, and ice is cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the two states.

questions.stem: Why does a metal spoon left in a hot cup of tea feel hot after some time?
options: The tea is hot and the heat moves to the spoon
The spoon makes its own heat
hints: The spoon is in the hot tea.
Heat moves from the tea to the spoon.
questions.explanation: The heat from the hot tea moves to the metal spoon, making the spoon feel hot.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the spoon generates heat.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a source of heat?
questions.explanation: A block of ice is not a source of heat; it is cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all solids give off heat.

questions.stem: Tell me one thing that is hot and one thing that is cold, and explain how you know.

criteria.description: Names a hot object and says it feels warm/burning
Names a cold object and says it feels chilly/cool

questions.explanation: This tests the understanding of hot and cold through touch.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.4.2.1: Demonstrate knowledge of generation of electricity, its transmission and transformation into other forms of energy
indicator.objective: Know the importance of electricity and identify common household appliances that require electricity to work

skills.description: Identify common household appliances that need electricity to work
Sort items into 'uses electricity' and 'does not use electricity'
Match an appliance to its use
Explain simply why electricity is important

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: All household items use electricity.
A torch uses electricity from a wall socket.
Electricity is only for lighting.
If an item has a wire, it must use electricity.

questions.stem: Which of these items uses electricity to work?
hints: It gives light when you switch it on.
questions.explanation: An electric bulb uses electricity to give light.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any item in the house uses electricity.

questions.stem: Which of these does NOT use electricity?
hints: Which one is from the ground?
It is hard and does not need power.
questions.explanation: A stone does not use electricity. It is a natural object.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all objects in the home use electricity.

questions.stem: What do we use an electric iron for?
hints: You use it on a table.
questions.explanation: An electric iron is used to iron clothes and remove creases.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the iron with a cooking pot.

questions.stem: Why is electricity important in our homes?
hints: Think about a fan or TV.
questions.explanation: Electricity is important because it makes appliances like fans, TVs, and fridges work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think electricity is only for light.

questions.stem: Which of these is a household appliance that uses electricity?
hints: It is found in the kitchen.
questions.explanation: A fridge is a household appliance that uses electricity to keep food cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think vehicles are household appliances.

questions.stem: Which of these uses electricity?
hints: It needs to be plugged in.
questions.explanation: A television uses electricity to show pictures and sound.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think things with screens don't need power.

questions.stem: Which of these does NOT use electricity?
hints: Which one is used for eating?
It does not have a plug.
questions.explanation: A spoon is a simple tool that does not use electricity.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all kitchen items use electricity.

questions.stem: What do we use a fan for?
questions.explanation: A fan uses electricity to spin and give breeze.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a fan produces cold water.

questions.stem: Why do we need electricity in the home?
hints: Think about how many things need a plug.
questions.explanation: We need electricity to power our appliances like lights, TVs, and fridges.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think electricity helps with manual tasks like sweeping.

questions.stem: Kwame wants to keep his food cold. What does he use?
questions.explanation: A fridge uses electricity to keep food cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a fan keeps food cold.

questions.stem: Which of these items uses electricity from a battery?
questions.explanation: A torch uses electricity from a battery to give light.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a torch plugs into a wall socket.

questions.stem: Which group has only items that use electricity?
hints: Look for the group where all items need power.
Which group has things that light up or spin?
questions.explanation: A fan, bulb, and TV all use electricity.
questions.misconception: Pupils may include non-electric items in the group.

questions.stem: Why does a television need electricity?
questions.explanation: A television needs electricity to show pictures and produce sound.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a TV works without power.

questions.stem: Ama plugs in her phone to charge. What is she using?
questions.explanation: Ama is using electricity from the socket to charge her phone.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think charging uses water.

questions.stem: What happens to a fan when there is no electricity?
questions.explanation: A fan stops working when there is no electricity because it has no power.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a fan can work without electricity.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an electrical appliance?
hints: It does not need a plug.
questions.explanation: A bicycle does not use electricity. It is powered by pedaling.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any machine is an electrical appliance.

questions.stem: Kofi says 'All things in the house use electricity.' Is he right?
options: No, only some things use it
questions.explanation: Kofi is not right. Only some things, like appliances, use electricity. Many things like chairs and cups do not.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all household items are electrical.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to touch a socket with wet hands?
options: Water can make electricity shock you
hints: Water and electricity do not mix well.
questions.explanation: Water can conduct electricity, so touching a socket with wet hands can cause a dangerous electric shock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water makes electricity safer.

questions.stem: Which of these appliances changes electricity into movement?
questions.explanation: A fan uses electricity to turn its blades, creating movement.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all appliances just produce heat or light.

questions.stem: If there were no electricity, which of these would still work?
hints: Which one is a simple tool?
You use it with your hands.
questions.explanation: A broom does not need electricity. It is a simple tool you use with your hands.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all household tasks require electricity.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.4.2.2: (Document prints '4.2.2' — missing 'B1.' prefix. Full code should be B1.4.2.2.)
indicator.objective: Know examples of common electronic devices and their uses

skills.description: Identify common electronic devices
State the use of a given electronic device
Match a device to its use or to a picture
Recognise simple differences between two electronic devices

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: All electronic devices do the same thing.
A torch is not electronic.
A wrist watch is not electronic.
A phone is only for calling.

questions.stem: Which of these is an electronic device?
hints: You use it to call people.
It has a screen and buttons.
questions.explanation: A mobile phone is an electronic device.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any object is an electronic device.

questions.stem: What do we use a camera for?
questions.explanation: A camera is used to take pictures.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the camera with a phone.

questions.stem: Which device do we use to call someone far away?
hints: You put it to your ear.
questions.explanation: We use a phone to call someone far away.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a torch is used for calling.

questions.stem: Which of these is a small electronic device you wear on your wrist?
questions.explanation: A wrist watch is an electronic device worn on the wrist to tell the time.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not consider a watch electronic.

questions.stem: Which of these devices gives light?
hints: You use it in the dark.
questions.explanation: A torch is an electronic device that gives light.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a radio gives light.

questions.stem: Match the device to its use: What is a torch used for?
questions.explanation: A torch is used to give light.
questions.misconception: Pupils may match the torch with calling.

questions.stem: Which device is used to take pictures?
questions.explanation: A camera is used to take pictures.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse a camera with a torch.

questions.stem: What is the main use of a radio?
options: To listen to news and music
questions.explanation: A radio is used to listen to news and music.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a radio is for watching videos.

questions.stem: Which of these is an electronic device?
questions.explanation: A wrist watch is an electronic device.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think natural or simple wooden objects are electronic.

questions.stem: How is a phone different from a camera?
options: A phone can call and take pictures, a camera only takes pictures
A camera can call and take pictures, a phone only takes pictures
hints: Can you make a call with a camera?
What can a phone do besides taking pictures?
questions.explanation: A phone can make calls and take pictures, while a camera is mainly for taking pictures.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a phone is only for calling.

questions.stem: Which device would you use to calculate numbers?
hints: It has numbers and a screen.
questions.explanation: A calculator is an electronic device used for calculating numbers.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a radio can calculate.

questions.stem: Match the device to its use: Which device is used for listening to music?
questions.explanation: A radio is used for listening to music and news.
questions.misconception: Pupils may match the camera with music.

questions.stem: Why is a mobile phone called an electronic device?
options: Because it uses electricity and chips to work
Because it is made of wood
hints: It has a screen and circuits inside.
questions.explanation: A mobile phone is an electronic device because it uses electricity and electronic components (chips) to work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think phones work by magic.

questions.stem: Ama wants to take a picture of her family. Which device should she use?
questions.explanation: Ama should use a camera to take a picture of her family.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a torch can take pictures.

questions.stem: Which of these devices can be used to call and send messages?
hints: It has a keypad or touchscreen.
questions.explanation: A mobile phone can be used to call and send messages.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize phones do more than just call.

questions.stem: Kwame says 'A torch is not an electronic device.' Is he right?
options: No, it has a bulb and uses electricity
Yes, it is only a light
No, it is a piece of wood
questions.explanation: Kwame is not right. A torch is an electronic device because it has a bulb and uses electricity from a battery.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think torches are too simple to be electronic.

questions.stem: Which device is used to watch cartoons?
hints: You sit in front of it.
questions.explanation: A television is used to watch cartoons and other programmes.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a camera is used to watch cartoons.

questions.stem: If you want to know the time, which device is best?
hints: You wear it on your arm.
questions.explanation: A wrist watch is the best device to tell the time.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the watch with a calculator.

questions.stem: Why is a camera different from a radio?
options: A camera takes pictures and a radio plays sound
A camera plays sound and a radio takes pictures
questions.explanation: A camera is for taking pictures, and a radio is for listening to sound (news/music).
questions.misconception: Pupils may mix up the functions.

questions.stem: Which of these is an electronic device that helps us see in the dark?
hints: It gives a beam of light.
You use it during a power outage.
questions.explanation: A torch is an electronic device that gives light to help us see in the dark.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a camera helps us see in the dark.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.4.3.1: Know that movement is caused by applied forces due to the release of stored energy
indicator.objective: Explain force as a pull or a push on an object

skills.description: Recognise pushing as a force that moves an object away from you
Recognise pulling as a force that moves an object towards you
Identify everyday activities that involve a push or a pull
Draw a picture showing a push or a pull in an everyday action

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: A push and a pull are the same thing.
Only pushing is a force; pulling is not.
You can only push or pull with your hands.
Kicking is not a push.
The wind does not push things.
Objects move on their own without any force.

questions.stem: When you push a door open, you are moving the door...
hints: You use your hands to move it forward.
You are not pulling it back.
questions.explanation: A push moves an object away from you.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think pushing moves an object towards them.

questions.stem: When you pull a rope towards you, you are...
hints: You are bringing it closer to you.
It is the opposite of pushing.
questions.explanation: Pulling moves an object towards you.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think bringing an object closer is pushing.

questions.stem: Which of these activities involves a pull?
options: Pulling a bucket from a well
questions.explanation: Pulling a bucket from a well involves a pull force.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think kicking is pulling.

questions.stem: Ama is pushing a wheelbarrow. Which direction is the force moving the wheelbarrow?
hints: She is not pulling it back.
questions.explanation: Ama is pushing the wheelbarrow forward, away from her.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the direction of a push.

questions.stem: Kwame is pulling a rope towards himself. What is he applying?
hints: He is not moving it away.
questions.explanation: Kwame is applying a pull force to bring the rope towards him.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse pulling with pushing.

questions.stem: Which of these is a push?
options: Opening a drawer by pulling the handle
hints: You move the ball away from you.
questions.explanation: Kicking a football is a push force because you move the ball away from you.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think kicking is a pull.

questions.stem: When you push a swing, you move it...
hints: You stand behind it and move it forward.
You are not pulling it back.
questions.explanation: Pushing a swing moves it away from you.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think pushing a swing moves it towards them.

questions.stem: Adwoa is pulling a suitcase behind her. Which way is the suitcase moving?
questions.explanation: Pulling a suitcase moves it towards her as she walks.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think pulling moves things away.

questions.stem: The wind blows and moves the leaves of a tree. Is this a push or a pull?
hints: The wind moves the leaves away.
The wind does not pull the leaves towards it.
questions.explanation: The wind pushes the leaves, moving them away.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wind only pulls things.

questions.stem: If you move a table away from you, are you pushing or pulling it?
hints: You are not bringing it towards you.
questions.explanation: Moving a table away from you is pushing.

questions.stem: If you bring a chair closer to you, are you pushing or pulling it?
hints: It is the opposite of pushing.
questions.explanation: Bringing a chair closer to you is pulling.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a pull?
options: A man pulling a donkey cart
hints: The man is behind the cart.
questions.explanation: A man pulling a donkey cart is an example of a pull force.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think throwing is a pull.

questions.stem: Kofi is trying to move a heavy box. He stands behind it and pushes. What happens to the box?
options: It stays in the same place
questions.explanation: When Kofi pushes the box from behind, it moves away from him.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think pushing pulls the box towards them.

questions.stem: Ama is pulling a bucket of water up from a well. She is applying a force...
options: That moves the bucket away from her
That moves the bucket towards her
That makes the bucket turn into a stone
hints: She is bringing the bucket up.
She wants the bucket to come to her.
questions.explanation: Pulling the bucket moves it towards Ama.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the direction of pull.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a push?
hints: Which action moves something towards you?
questions.explanation: Pulling a rope is a pull force, not a push.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all actions are pushes.

questions.stem: Why is a push considered a force?
options: Because it moves an object away from you
questions.explanation: A push is a force because it causes an object to move away from you.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a force is just the feeling of being tired.

questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE about a pull?
options: It moves an object away from you
It moves an object towards you
It has no effect on the object
questions.explanation: A pull moves an object towards you.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a pull pushes things away.

questions.stem: A boy is playing tug of war. He is pulling the rope towards his team. What force is he applying and in what direction is the rope moving?
options: A push, moving away from him
A pull, moving away from him
hints: He wants the rope to come to his side.
questions.explanation: He is applying a pull force, and the rope is moving towards him.
questions.misconception: Pupils may mix up the direction of the force.

questions.stem: Draw a picture of a person pushing a wheelbarrow. Show the direction the wheelbarrow is moving.

criteria.description: Draws a person behind a wheelbarrow
Shows the wheelbarrow moving away from the person

hints: Which way does the wheelbarrow move?
questions.explanation: This tests drawing a push force and its direction.

questions.stem: Draw a picture of a person pulling a bucket from a well.

criteria.description: Draws a person holding a rope and a bucket
Shows the bucket moving upwards towards the person

hints: Draw the rope going down to the bucket.
questions.explanation: This tests drawing a pull force and its direction.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.4.3.2: Recognise some simple machines used for making work easier, analyse their advantages and know their uses. E.g. levers, inclined planes and pulleys (Document prints '1.4.3.2.' — missing 'B')
indicator.objective: Understand what simple machines are and cite common examples

skills.description: Understand that simple machines are tools that help make work easier and faster
Identify common simple machines used in the home, school, or community
Match a simple machine to the task it makes easier
Describe simple safe practices when using a simple machine
Draw a simple machine and label it

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: A simple machine is a big engine or a car.
Scissors are just for cutting paper, not a machine.
All machines use electricity.
A broom is not a machine.
Machines work on their own without a person or force.

questions.stem: What is a simple machine?
options: A tool that makes work easier
questions.explanation: A simple machine is a tool that makes work easier and faster.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a machine must be big and use electricity.

questions.stem: Which of these is a simple machine?
questions.explanation: Scissors are a simple machine used for cutting.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think scissors are just a tool, not a machine.

questions.stem: What do we use a bottle opener for?
hints: It removes the cap from a bottle.
You use it in the kitchen.
questions.explanation: A bottle opener is a simple machine used to open bottles.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the opener with a spoon.

questions.stem: Why do we use simple machines?
options: To make work easier and faster
questions.explanation: We use simple machines to make work easier and faster.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think machines make work harder.

questions.stem: Which of these is a simple machine used for sweeping?
hints: You use it to clean the floor.
questions.explanation: A broom is a simple machine used for sweeping.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not think a broom is a machine.

questions.stem: Ama wants to cut a piece of paper. Which simple machine should she use?
questions.explanation: Scissors are used for cutting paper.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a hammer can cut paper.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a simple machine?
hints: Which one is a large vehicle?
questions.explanation: A car is a complex machine with an engine, not a simple machine.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all machines are simple machines.

questions.stem: Kwame wants to remove a nail from a piece of wood. Which simple machine should he use?
questions.explanation: A claw hammer is used to remove nails from wood.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose a tool that cannot grip the nail.

questions.stem: How does a wheelbarrow make work easier?
options: It helps carry heavy loads with less effort
hints: You put heavy things in it.
questions.explanation: A wheelbarrow makes work easier by helping you carry heavy loads with less effort.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a wheelbarrow is just for playing.

questions.stem: Which simple machine is used to cut cloth?
questions.explanation: Scissors are used for cutting cloth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a hammer is for cutting.

questions.stem: A farmer wants to pull water from a deep well. Which simple machine can help him?
hints: It has a wheel and a rope.
questions.explanation: A pulley is a simple machine that helps lift water from a well.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know what a pulley is.

questions.stem: What is a safe way to use scissors?
options: Point the blades at your friend
Use them carefully and do not run with them
questions.explanation: You should use scissors carefully and never run with them to avoid getting hurt.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize scissors are dangerous if misused.

questions.stem: Kofi is trying to open a bottle of soft drink but his hands are slippery. What should he use?
hints: It is specially made for this.
questions.explanation: A bottle opener is the correct simple machine for opening a bottle.
questions.misconception: Pupils may try to use improvised tools that are unsafe.

questions.stem: Which of these is a simple machine used for lifting water from a well?
hints: It uses a rope and a wheel.
questions.explanation: A pulley is used for lifting water from a well.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse a pulley with a wheelbarrow.

questions.stem: Why are simple machines important in our daily lives?
options: They help us do work faster and with less effort
They use a lot of electricity
questions.explanation: Simple machines are important because they help us do work faster and with less effort.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think machines are only for factories.

questions.stem: Ama wants to open a tin of tomatoes. Which simple machine should she use?
hints: It is designed to cut metal.
questions.explanation: A tin cutter is a simple machine used to open tins.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they can open a tin with a spoon.

questions.stem: Why should you not put your fingers near the blades of scissors?
options: They are sharp and can cut you
questions.explanation: You should keep your fingers away from the blades because they are sharp and can cut you.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not recognize the danger of sharp tools.

questions.stem: A student says 'A simple machine makes work easier.' What does this mean?
options: It helps you do a job with less effort
It does the job for you without you doing anything
It makes the job take more time
hints: Think about carrying a heavy load.
Does it help you or make it harder?
questions.explanation: A simple machine makes work easier by helping you do a job with less effort, though you still have to use some force.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a simple machine works completely on its own.

questions.stem: Draw a bottle opener and label it.
questions.explanation: This tests identifying and drawing a simple machine.

questions.stem: Draw a pair of scissors. Show what they are used for.

criteria.description: Draws a recognisable pair of scissors
Shows or indicates they are used for cutting (e.g., cutting paper)

hints: Draw the blades and the handles.
What do you cut with them?
questions.explanation: This tests identifying and drawing a simple machine and its use.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.5.1.1: Recognise the importance of personal hygiene
indicator.objective: Explain the need for bathing and know how it is done

skills.description: Explain why we bathe
Name items used for bathing
Describe the correct steps for bathing
Demonstrate bathing a doll correctly

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Bathing is just playing with water.
You only need to bathe when you are visibly dirty.
Using water alone is enough; soap is not needed.
You should share your sponge and towel with friends.

questions.stem: Why do we bathe?
hints: Think about what happens when you sweat.
questions.explanation: We bathe to remove dirt and sweat from our bodies.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think bathing is just for fun.

questions.stem: Which of these is used for bathing?
questions.explanation: Soap is used with water to clean the body.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any liquid is soap.

questions.stem: What do you use to dry your body after bathing?
hints: It is soft and absorbs water.
You hang it in the bathroom.
questions.explanation: A towel is used to dry the body after bathing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any cloth is a towel.

questions.stem: How often should you bathe?
questions.explanation: You should bathe every day to stay clean and healthy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think bathing once a week is enough.

questions.stem: What is the first step in bathing?
questions.explanation: The first step in bathing is to wet your body with water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think you apply soap to a dry body.

questions.stem: What happens if you do not bathe regularly?
options: You smell bad and can get sick
questions.explanation: If you do not bathe regularly, you will smell bad and germs can make you sick.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think skipping baths has no consequences.

questions.stem: Kofi is going to bathe. Which of these should he take with him?
questions.explanation: Kofi needs soap, a sponge, and a towel to bathe.

questions.stem: Why is it important to use soap when bathing?
options: Soap helps remove dirt and germs
hints: Water alone does not kill germs.
questions.explanation: Soap helps to remove dirt and germs from the skin.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water alone is enough.

questions.stem: After applying soap and scrubbing your body, what should you do next?
hints: You need to wash the soap off.
questions.explanation: After scrubbing with soap, you must rinse your body with clean water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may dry off without rinsing.

questions.stem: Which of these should you NOT share with a friend?
questions.explanation: You should not share your sponge because it can spread germs.
