questions.misconception: Pupils may share personal items without knowing the risks.

questions.stem: Ama played football and is sweating. What should she do?
hints: She needs to clean her body.
questions.explanation: Ama should bathe with soap and water to clean off the sweat and dirt.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sweating is fine without cleaning.

questions.stem: Name two items used for bathing.
questions.explanation: Soap, sponge, water, and towel are used for bathing.

questions.stem: Why should you bathe before going to school?
options: To look clean and stay healthy
hints: You don't want to smell bad.
questions.explanation: You should bathe before school to look clean and stay healthy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not see the link between hygiene and health.

questions.stem: What is the correct order for bathing?
options: Wet body, apply soap, scrub, rinse, dry
Dry body, apply soap, wet body, scrub
Apply soap, dry body, wet body, scrub
Scrub, wet body, dry body, apply soap
questions.explanation: The correct order is wet body, apply soap, scrub, rinse, and dry.
questions.misconception: Pupils may do steps out of order.

questions.stem: Which of these items is NOT used for bathing?
questions.explanation: A book is not used for bathing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any object in the bathroom is for bathing.

questions.stem: Kofi says 'I only bathe when I see dirt on my skin.' Why is this wrong?
options: Because dirt and germs can be on the skin without you seeing them
questions.explanation: You should bathe regularly because dirt and germs can be on your skin even if you cannot see them.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think visible dirt is the only reason to bathe.

questions.stem: Demonstrate to your teacher how to bathe a doll correctly.
hints: Don't forget to dry the doll.
questions.explanation: This tests the practical steps of bathing.

questions.stem: Draw some of the items you use for bathing.

criteria.description: Draws at least two correct items (e.g., soap, sponge, towel)

hints: What do you use in the bathroom?
questions.explanation: This tests identification of bathing items.

questions.stem: Write down two reasons why bathing is important.
hints: Think about how you feel after playing.
questions.explanation: Bathing removes dirt and prevents sickness.

questions.stem: Explain the steps you take to bathe.
hints: What do you do after scrubbing?
questions.explanation: The steps are wet, soap, scrub, rinse, and dry.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.5.1.1: Recognise the importance of personal hygiene
indicator.objective: Know the need for and how to clean the teeth

skills.description: Explain why we clean our teeth
Name items used to clean teeth
Describe the correct method for cleaning teeth
Demonstrate the correct method of brushing teeth

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Brushing hard is better than brushing gently.
You only need to brush in the morning.
Toothpaste alone is enough without a brush.
Sweet food cleans the teeth.

questions.stem: Why do we clean our teeth?
options: To keep them strong and white
questions.explanation: We clean our teeth to keep them strong and white.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think teeth cleaning is just for fun.

questions.stem: What do we use to brush our teeth?
hints: It is small enough for your mouth.
questions.explanation: A toothbrush is used to brush teeth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any brush can be used.

questions.stem: What do we put on the toothbrush to clean our teeth?
hints: It makes foam in your mouth.
questions.explanation: Toothpaste is used with a toothbrush to clean teeth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think soap is used on teeth.

questions.stem: How many times a day should you brush your teeth?
questions.explanation: You should brush your teeth at least twice a day.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think brushing once a week is enough.

questions.stem: Which direction should you move the toothbrush?
options: You don't need to move it
hints: Clean the top and bottom teeth.
questions.explanation: You should move the toothbrush in an upward and downward motion.
questions.misconception: Pupils may just scrub side to side.

questions.stem: What happens if you do not brush your teeth?
options: You can get cavities and bad breath
questions.explanation: If you do not brush your teeth, germs can cause cavities and bad breath.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize the consequences of poor oral hygiene.

questions.stem: Ama is going to brush her teeth. What does she need?
hints: She needs something to put on it.
questions.explanation: Ama needs a toothbrush and toothpaste to brush her teeth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may mix up items for different hygiene routines.

questions.stem: After brushing your teeth, what should you do?
hints: You need to spit out the foam.
questions.explanation: After brushing, you should rinse your mouth with water.

questions.stem: Which of these can be used to clean teeth if you don't have a toothbrush?
hints: It is a piece of wood.
People chew on it to clean.
questions.explanation: A chewing stick can be used to clean teeth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think only a plastic toothbrush works.

questions.stem: Why is brushing your teeth before bed important?
options: To remove food and germs from the day
To make your teeth fall out
questions.explanation: Brushing before bed removes food and germs, preventing them from staying on your teeth overnight.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think brushing in the morning is enough.

questions.stem: Name two things used for cleaning the teeth.
questions.explanation: A toothbrush and toothpaste are used to clean teeth.

questions.stem: What causes holes in the teeth?
options: Eating too much sweet food and not brushing
questions.explanation: Eating too much sweet food and not brushing can cause holes in teeth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think eating sweets is harmless.

questions.stem: Why should you brush gently and not too hard?
options: To make your teeth fall out
questions.explanation: You should brush gently to avoid hurting your gums.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think harder brushing is better.

questions.stem: Kofi says 'I don't need to brush my teeth because I chew gum.' Why is he wrong?
options: Chewing gum does not clean teeth like a toothbrush
Chewing gum is the same as brushing
hints: Chewing gum is not a brush.
questions.explanation: Chewing gum does not clean the teeth; you still need to brush with a toothbrush and toothpaste.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think chewing gum replaces brushing.

questions.stem: Adwoa sees her friend about to brush with soap. What should she tell her friend?
questions.explanation: Adwoa should tell her friend to use toothpaste instead of soap on her teeth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know the correct items for teeth.

questions.stem: Demonstrate to your teacher how to brush your teeth correctly.

criteria.description: Moves the brush up and down
Brushes for an appropriate time (or simulates)

questions.explanation: This tests the practical method of brushing teeth.

questions.stem: Draw the items you use for cleaning your teeth.
questions.explanation: This tests identification of dental hygiene items.

questions.stem: Write down two reasons why brushing your teeth is important.
questions.explanation: Brushing removes germs and prevents cavities.

questions.stem: Describe the steps for brushing your teeth.

criteria.description: Mentions putting toothpaste on the brush

hints: Start with the brush and paste.
questions.explanation: The steps are putting paste on the brush, brushing up and down, and rinsing.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher why you should not share your toothbrush.

criteria.description: States that it can spread germs
States that it is for personal use only

hints: Germs can pass from person to person.
questions.explanation: You should not share a toothbrush because it can spread germs.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.5.1.1: Recognise the importance of personal hygiene
indicator.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the need for and how to wash the hands

skills.description: Identify when to wash hands
Name items needed for hand-washing
Describe the steps for hand-washing
Explain why hand-washing is important
Demonstrate proper hand-washing

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Only wash hands when they look dirty.
Dipping hands in a bowl of water is enough.
Drying hands on dirty clothes is fine.
Hand-washing is only needed after using the toilet.

questions.stem: When should you wash your hands?
hints: You don't want germs on your food.
You use your hands to eat.
questions.explanation: You should wash your hands before eating to prevent germs from getting into your food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not prioritize hand-washing before meals.

questions.stem: What do you need to wash your hands properly?
questions.explanation: You need soap and running water to wash your hands properly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water alone is enough.

questions.stem: What is the first thing to do when washing your hands?
questions.explanation: The first step is to wet your hands with water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may apply soap to dry hands.

questions.stem: Why is it important to wash your hands?
questions.explanation: Washing your hands removes germs and keeps you healthy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think hand-washing is just about looks.

questions.stem: After using the toilet, what should you do?
questions.explanation: You must wash your hands with soap after using the toilet to remove germs.
questions.misconception: Pupils may skip hand-washing after the toilet.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT needed for hand-washing?
questions.explanation: A book is not needed for hand-washing.

questions.stem: How should you dry your hands after washing them?
hints: You want to keep them clean.
questions.explanation: You should dry your hands with a clean towel to keep them clean.
questions.misconception: Pupils may dry hands on dirty clothes.

questions.stem: Kofi is about to eat. What should he do first?
hints: He doesn't want germs in his food.
questions.explanation: Kofi should wash his hands with soap before eating.
questions.misconception: Pupils may forget to wash hands before eating.

questions.stem: What happens if you eat with dirty hands?
hints: You might get a stomach ache.
questions.explanation: Eating with dirty hands can make you sick because germs enter your body.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect dirty hands to sickness.

questions.stem: After applying soap, what should you do?
hints: You need to make a lather.
questions.explanation: You should rub your hands together to clean them with the soap.

questions.stem: What do you use to wash your hands?
questions.explanation: You use soap and water to wash your hands.

questions.stem: Which of these is a time you should wash your hands?
questions.explanation: You should wash your hands after playing outside because you may have touched dirt and germs.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not see playing as a dirty activity.

questions.stem: Why should you use running water to wash your hands?
options: It helps to wash germs away
questions.explanation: Running water helps to wash germs away because the dirt and germs are carried off.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a bowl of water is just as good.

questions.stem: Ama is about to cook. What should she do first?
options: Wash her hands with soap and water
questions.explanation: Ama should wash her hands before cooking to prevent germs from getting into the food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not prioritize hand-washing before cooking.

questions.stem: Demonstrate to your teacher how to wash your hands properly.

criteria.description: Applies soap and rubs hands together

questions.explanation: This tests the practical steps of hand-washing.

questions.stem: Draw pictures showing the steps of washing hands.

criteria.description: Draws at least two steps (e.g., applying soap, rinsing)

questions.explanation: This tests the understanding of the hand-washing sequence.

questions.stem: Which statement about hand-washing is TRUE?
options: You only need to wash your hands after using the toilet
You should wash your hands before eating and after using the toilet
Washing hands is a waste of water
Dirty hands are okay if you are hungry
hints: Hand-washing is important at multiple times.
questions.explanation: You should wash your hands before eating and after using the toilet, among other times.
questions.misconception: Pupils may limit hand-washing to one specific time.

questions.stem: Write two reasons why hand-washing is important.
questions.explanation: Hand-washing removes germs and prevents sickness.

questions.stem: Describe the steps you take to wash your hands properly.
questions.explanation: The steps are wet, soap, scrub, rinse, and dry.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher why you should wash your hands after playing outside.

criteria.description: States that playing outside makes hands dirty
States that washing removes germs and prevents sickness

questions.explanation: Playing outside gets dirt and germs on your hands, so washing prevents sickness.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.5.1.2: Appreciate the natural and human features of the local environment and the need for keeping the environment clean
indicator.objective: know that clean air and water are essential to human health

skills.description: Explain why clean air is important
Explain why clean water is important
Identify what happens if air or water is dirty
Identify simple actions to keep air and water clean

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Smoke is just air, so it is safe.
Dirty water is safe to drink if you cannot see the dirt.
Dust does not affect health.
Water from any source is safe to drink.

questions.stem: Why do we need clean air?
options: To breathe well and stay healthy
hints: Clean air is good for you.
questions.explanation: We need clean air to breathe well and stay healthy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize the importance of clean air.

questions.stem: Why do we need clean water?
options: To drink safely and stay healthy
To wash our hands in dirty water
questions.explanation: We need clean water to drink safely and stay healthy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any water is safe.

questions.stem: What happens if you drink dirty water?
questions.explanation: Drinking dirty water can make you sick because it contains germs.
questions.misconception: Pupils may drink from unsafe sources.

questions.stem: What happens if you breathe in a lot of smoke?
options: You can cough and get sick
questions.explanation: Breathing in smoke can make you cough and get sick.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think smoke is harmless.

questions.stem: Which of these helps to keep the air clean?
questions.explanation: Planting trees helps keep the air clean because they absorb some gases and release oxygen.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think burning rubbish cleans the air.

questions.stem: Where can we find clean air?
options: In a park with many trees
Near a busy road with many cars
questions.explanation: Clean air is found in places with many trees and less smoke, like a park.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all outdoor air is clean.

questions.stem: Which of these is a source of clean water?
options: A river with rubbish in it
hints: It is not open to rubbish.
questions.explanation: A covered well is more likely to contain clean water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all water sources are clean.

questions.stem: What should you do with rubbish to keep the environment clean?
hints: Do not throw it in water.
questions.explanation: Throwing rubbish in a bin helps keep the environment clean.

questions.stem: Ama sees a stream with rubbish in it. Is the water clean?
options: No, but it is safe to drink
questions.explanation: The water is dirty because of the rubbish.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think visible water is safe.

questions.stem: Which activity makes the air dirty?
questions.explanation: Burning rubbish produces smoke that makes the air dirty.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sweeping makes air dirty.

questions.stem: Name one thing that makes the air dirty.
questions.explanation: Smoke, dust, and fumes from cars make the air dirty.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not recognize common air pollutants.

questions.stem: Name one thing that makes water dirty.
questions.explanation: Rubbish, dirt, and waste make water dirty.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water is always clean.

questions.stem: Why is it important to keep our water sources clean?
options: So we can drink safe water and stay healthy
questions.explanation: It is important to keep water sources clean so we can drink safe water and stay healthy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect clean water to health.

questions.stem: A community wants to keep their air clean. What should they do?
options: Plant more trees and reduce burning
questions.explanation: Planting more trees and reducing burning helps keep the air clean.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know how to improve air quality.

questions.stem: Kofi has a choice between water from a tap and water from a muddy puddle. Which should he choose and why?
options: Tap water, because it is clean
Muddy puddle, because it is natural
Muddy puddle, because it is cold
Tap water, because it is colourful
questions.explanation: Kofi should choose tap water because it is clean and safe to drink.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think natural water is always safe.

questions.stem: What can happen to a person who breathes in dust every day?
questions.explanation: Breathing in dust every day can cause breathing problems.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think dust is harmless.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to throw rubbish into a river?
options: It pollutes the water and makes it unsafe for drinking and animals
It makes the river flow faster
questions.explanation: Throwing rubbish into a river pollutes the water, making it unsafe for drinking and for the animals that live in it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand the wider impact of water pollution.

questions.stem: Write two ways you can help keep your environment clean.

criteria.description: Names one correct action (e.g., throwing rubbish in a bin, planting trees, not burning rubbish)

hints: What do you do with your rubbish?
questions.explanation: You can help by throwing rubbish in a bin and planting trees, among other actions.

questions.stem: Explain why clean air is important for your health.

criteria.description: States that we need air to breathe
States that dirty air/smoke makes us sick or causes coughing

hints: We breathe air all the time.
questions.explanation: Clean air is important because we breathe it, and dirty air can make us sick.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher why you should not drink water from a dirty puddle.

criteria.description: States that the water is dirty
States that it has germs and can make you sick

questions.explanation: You should not drink from a dirty puddle because it contains germs that can make you sick.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.5.2.1: Know common diseases of humans, causes, symptoms, effects and prevention
indicator.objective: Identify some common diseases that affect the skin and their causes

skills.description: Name common skin diseases
State simple causes of skin diseases
Describe ways to prevent skin diseases
Recognise simple signs of skin diseases

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Skin diseases are caused by curses or witchcraft.
You can catch skin diseases just by looking at someone who has them.
Ringworm is caused by a worm or an insect.
Only poor people get skin diseases.
Skin diseases cannot be prevented.

questions.stem: Which of these is a common skin disease?
hints: It causes a round, itchy patch.
questions.explanation: Ringworm is a common skin disease that causes itchy, round patches on the skin.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any sickness is a skin disease.

questions.stem: What is a common sign of a skin disease?
hints: You want to scratch the spot.
questions.explanation: Itching is a common sign of a skin disease.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse skin disease symptoms with other illnesses.

questions.stem: What can cause skin diseases?
questions.explanation: Dirt and germs can cause skin diseases.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think skin diseases are caused by other actions like eating.

questions.stem: How can you prevent skin diseases?
questions.explanation: Bathing regularly with soap helps prevent skin diseases.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not link hygiene to disease prevention.

questions.stem: Which of these is a skin disease that gives red, itchy spots?
hints: It causes a rash on the skin.
questions.explanation: Measles is a disease that causes red spots on the skin.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think malaria is a skin disease.

questions.stem: Ama is wearing dirty clothes that she has not washed for days. What skin problem might she get?
hints: Dirty clothes can irritate the skin.
Sweat and dirt stay on the skin.
questions.explanation: Wearing dirty clothes can trap sweat and dirt, causing heat rashes or itching.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect dirty clothes to skin issues.

questions.stem: Why should you not share a towel with a friend who has ringworm?
options: You can catch the disease from the towel
hints: Germs can stay on the towel.
questions.explanation: You can catch skin diseases like ringworm by sharing towels because germs can spread from the infected person.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sharing is always good, without considering germs.

questions.stem: Kwame has an itchy, red patch on his arm. What type of disease is this?
questions.explanation: An itchy, red patch on the skin is a sign of a skin disease.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not identify skin conditions correctly.

questions.stem: What causes ringworm?
hints: It is caused by something you cannot see.
questions.explanation: Ringworm is caused by a fungus (germ), not a real worm, even though it is called ringworm.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think ringworm is caused by a real worm.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a skin disease?
hints: Which one is carried by mosquitoes?
It causes fever and body pain.
questions.explanation: Malaria is not a skin disease; it is caused by mosquito bites and affects the blood.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse diseases that cause fever with skin diseases.

questions.stem: Name one thing that can cause skin diseases.
hints: What happens if you don't bathe?
What do you catch if you are dirty?
questions.explanation: Dirt, germs, and poor hygiene can cause skin diseases.
questions.misconception: Pupils may answer with unrelated causes.

questions.stem: What should you do every day to prevent skin diseases?
questions.explanation: You should bathe every day with soap and water to prevent skin diseases.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say you only need to bathe when dirty.

questions.stem: Kofi sees a circular, red, itchy patch on his little brother's skin. What should he do?
options: Tell their parents to take him to a clinic
Ignore it because it is not serious
hints: A health worker can give medicine.
questions.explanation: Kofi should tell their parents so his brother can be taken to a clinic for treatment to prevent it from spreading.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think skin diseases are not serious and ignore them.

questions.stem: Why is it important to wash your clothes regularly?
options: To prevent skin diseases like heat rashes
To make the clothes change colour
questions.explanation: Washing clothes regularly prevents sweat, dirt, and germs from staying on your skin, which helps prevent skin diseases.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize dirty clothes affect skin health.

questions.stem: Which statement about skin diseases is TRUE?
options: You can catch skin diseases by looking at someone
You can prevent skin diseases by keeping your body clean
Only poor people get skin diseases
Skin diseases are caused by curses
hints: Skin diseases are caused by germs, not looks.
questions.explanation: Skin diseases can be prevented by keeping your body clean, not by looking at someone.
questions.misconception: Pupils often hold beliefs about curses or poverty causing diseases.

questions.stem: Explain why sharing personal items like towels and sponges can cause skin diseases.

criteria.description: States that germs can pass from one person to another
States that this can cause a skin infection

questions.explanation: Sharing towels and sponges can spread germs from an infected person to a healthy person, causing skin diseases.

questions.stem: Role-play a scenario showing how you can prevent a skin disease (e.g., bathing, not sharing a towel).

criteria.description: Demonstrates a valid prevention action (e.g., washing hands, bathing)
Shows understanding of why this prevents the disease

hints: What do you do before sharing?
questions.explanation: This tests the practical understanding of preventing skin diseases through hygiene.

questions.stem: Ama says 'Ringworm is caused by a worm.' Why is she wrong?
options: Ringworm is caused by germs (a fungus), not a worm
Ringworm is caused by eating too much
Ringworm is caused by a curse
hints: Can you see a worm in ringworm?
It is a germ that causes it.
questions.explanation: Ringworm is caused by a fungus (germ), not a real worm, even though the name has 'worm' in it.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think ringworm is caused by a literal worm.

questions.stem: Write down two ways you can prevent skin diseases at school.

criteria.description: Names one correct way (e.g., bathing regularly, not sharing towels, washing hands)

hints: What do you do in the bathroom?
questions.explanation: You can prevent skin diseases by bathing, washing hands, and not sharing personal items.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher what you should do if you notice an itchy rash on your skin.

criteria.description: States they should tell a parent or teacher
States they should seek medical attention or go to a clinic

questions.explanation: If you notice a rash, you should tell a trusted adult and seek medical attention to get proper treatment.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.5.3.1: Recognise the impact of science and technology on society
indicator.objective: Identify technologies in the immediate environment and describe the impact of the technology on society

skills.description: Identify technologies in the immediate environment
State what a given technology is used for
Describe a simple impact of technology on society
Explain simply what happens if a technology is absent

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Technology only means mobile phones and computers.
Technology has no effect on how people live.
A car or a radio is not technology.
Technology can solve every problem without any human effort.

questions.stem: Which of these is a technology?
questions.explanation: A mobile phone is a technology made by people to help us communicate.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think natural things are technology.

questions.stem: What is a car used for?
options: To travel from place to place
hints: It takes you to school or the market.
questions.explanation: A car is a technology used for transportation.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cars are for flying.

questions.stem: Which of these is a technology used in the home?
questions.explanation: A television is a technology used in the home for entertainment and information.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think only big machines are technology.

questions.stem: What do we use a radio for?
options: To listen to news and music
questions.explanation: A radio is used for listening to news and music.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think radios are only for music, not news.

questions.stem: How does a mobile phone help us?
options: It helps us talk to people far away
hints: You can talk to someone in another town.
questions.explanation: A mobile phone helps us communicate with people who are far away.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think phones have physical abilities.

questions.stem: Ama wants to travel from Kumasi to Accra. Which technology should she use?
questions.explanation: A car or bus is a technology used to travel between cities.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name household items instead of transport.

questions.stem: How has technology helped farmers?
options: By providing tools like tractors to farm faster
By making crops grow without water
By making the sun shine at night
hints: Think about machines on a farm.
It helps them do work faster.
questions.explanation: Technology has helped farmers by providing tools like tractors that make farming faster and easier.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think technology controls the weather.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a technology?
hints: It is found on the ground.
questions.explanation: A stone is a natural object, not a technology. Technology is made by people.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all objects are technology.

questions.stem: What would happen if there were no cars or buses?
options: It would be harder to travel long distances
hints: How would you get to another town?
questions.explanation: Without cars or buses, travelling long distances would be much harder and slower.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize the importance of transport technology.

questions.stem: Kwame wants to take a picture of his family. Which technology should he use?
questions.explanation: A camera is the technology used to take pictures.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the use of a camera with other devices.

questions.stem: Name one technology you can find in your home.
questions.explanation: There are many technologies in the home, such as a television, radio, or mobile phone.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name non-technological items like a chair.

questions.stem: Name one way a mobile phone has changed how people live.
answer: we can talk to people far away
hints: How do you contact your friends?
questions.explanation: Mobile phones have changed how we live by allowing us to communicate easily with people far away.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not see the impact of phones beyond playing games.

questions.stem: How has technology helped doctors and nurses in hospitals?
options: By providing machines to check and treat sick people
By making sick people run faster
By making medicine taste like sweets
hints: Doctors use machines to help patients.
questions.explanation: Technology has helped doctors and nurses by providing medical machines and tools to check and treat patients.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand the medical applications of technology.

questions.stem: How did people send messages to others in far places before mobile phones were invented?
options: By sending letters through the post
hints: It took a long time to arrive.
questions.explanation: Before phones, people sent letters by post, which took much longer.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think people always had phones.

questions.stem: Ama says 'Technology only means mobile phones and computers.' Is she right?
options: No, things like cars and radios are also technology
Yes, only phones and computers are technology
hints: Is a car made by people to help us?
questions.explanation: Technology includes any tool or machine made by people to help us, not just phones and computers.
questions.misconception: Pupils often limit technology to digital devices.

questions.stem: Which technology helps us to keep food cold in our homes?
questions.explanation: A fridge is the technology used to keep food cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the fridge with other home appliances.

questions.stem: Describe one technology you have seen in your community and explain how it helps people.

criteria.description: Names a valid technology (e.g., trotro, mobile phone, radio)
Explains how it helps (e.g., trotro helps people travel, phone helps communicate)

hints: What do you see in the market?
questions.explanation: This tests identifying technology and its impact in a local context.

questions.stem: Explain what would happen in your community if all mobile phones suddenly stopped working.

criteria.description: States that communication would be difficult
Gives an example of the difficulty (e.g., cannot call for help, cannot do business)

hints: How do people talk to each other?
questions.explanation: Without phones, communication would be much harder, and activities like business and calling for help would be difficult.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize how much daily life relies on phones.

questions.stem: Why is it important to learn about technology?
options: To understand how tools help us live and work better
To learn how to break machines
To make our lives more difficult
hints: Learning about it helps us use it well.
questions.explanation: Learning about technology helps us understand how tools and machines make our lives easier and how to use them properly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not see the value of learning about technology.

questions.stem: Look at a picture of a trotro (minibus) and a mobile phone. Identify which one is used for transport and which is used for communication.

criteria.description: Identifies the mobile phone as communication

questions.explanation: The trotro is used for transport, and the mobile phone is used for communication.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.1.1.1: Demonstrate understanding of the physical features and life processes of living things and use this understanding to classify them
indicator.objective: Know the basic structure of plants (roots, stem, leaves, flowers)

skills.description: Name the four basic parts of a plant
Identify plant parts from a picture, drawing, or real plant
State simply what each part does
Draw and label a plant showing the four basic parts

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Roots are not part of the plant.
Flowers are only for decoration; they have no job.
The stem is just a stick; it does not carry water.
All plants have all four parts visible at all times.
Confusing 'root' with 'stem'.

questions.stem: Which part of a plant is usually under the ground?
hints: It holds the plant in the soil.
You cannot see it above the ground.
questions.explanation: The roots are the part of the plant that grows under the ground.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the stem goes all the way underground.

questions.stem: Which part of a plant is usually green and flat?
questions.explanation: Leaves are usually green and flat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse leaves with the stem.

questions.stem: What do we call the colourful part of a plant?
hints: It can be red, yellow, or pink.
questions.explanation: The flower is the colourful part of the plant.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the flower is only for looking at.

questions.stem: Which part holds the leaves up to the sun?
hints: It connects the roots to the leaves.
questions.explanation: The stem holds the plant up, including the leaves.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the roots hold the leaves up.

questions.stem: Which part of the plant takes in water from the soil?
questions.explanation: The roots take in water from the soil.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the stem takes in water directly from the soil.

questions.stem: Kofi pulls a small plant from the ground. He sees a part with tiny hairs on it that was in the soil. What part is this?
questions.explanation: The part with tiny hairs that was in the soil is the root.
questions.misconception: Pupils may call it a stem because it looks like a thin stick.

questions.stem: Why do plants have leaves?
questions.explanation: Leaves help the plant make food using sunlight.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think leaves are only for decoration.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a basic part of a plant?
questions.explanation: A stone is not a part of a plant. Roots, stems, and leaves are plant parts.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stones are part of the plant because they are in the soil.

questions.stem: Ama sees a plant with roots, a stem, and green leaves. She does not see any flowers. Is this a plant?
options: No, it is not a plant
Yes, but it is missing a flower
hints: Does it have roots and leaves?
Can a plant live without flowers?
questions.explanation: Yes, it is still a plant. Some plants do not have flowers, or they have not grown flowers yet.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all plants must have flowers to be a plant.

questions.stem: What job does the stem do for the plant?
options: It takes in water from the soil
It carries water to the leaves
hints: It connects the roots and the leaves.
questions.explanation: The stem carries water from the roots to the leaves.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the stem only holds the plant up and does nothing else.

questions.stem: Name two parts of a plant.
hints: What is under the ground? What is green?
questions.explanation: Two parts of a plant are roots and leaves (or stem and flower).
questions.misconception: Pupils may name non-plant parts like soil.

questions.stem: What part of the plant is found under the soil?
hints: You cannot see it above the ground.
questions.explanation: The roots are found under the soil.
questions.misconception: Pupils may answer 'stem' because stems can be near the ground.

questions.stem: If you remove the roots of a plant, what will happen to the plant?
options: It will not get water and may die
It will turn into a flower
hints: Where does the plant get water?
questions.explanation: Roots take in water. Without roots, the plant cannot get water and may die.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think roots are not important.

questions.stem: Kwame is drawing a plant. He draws a line going straight up from the ground. He adds leaves to the sides. What is the line he drew?
questions.explanation: The line going straight up is the stem.
questions.misconception: Pupils may call the stem a root.

questions.stem: Why does a plant need flowers?
hints: What do we plant to grow new plants?
questions.explanation: Flowers help the plant make seeds so new plants can grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think flowers are just for beauty.

questions.stem: Adwoa has a leaf and a flower. How are they different?
options: The leaf is usually green, the flower is colourful
The leaf is usually colourful, the flower is green
The leaf is under the ground
The flower is under the ground
questions.explanation: Leaves are usually green, while flowers can be many colours like red, yellow, or pink.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not have observed flowers closely.

questions.stem: Draw a plant showing the roots, stem, and one leaf. Label the three parts.
hints: Start with the root at the bottom.
Add the stem and a leaf.
questions.explanation: This tests observation and drawing of plant parts.

questions.stem: Explain why a plant is called a living thing because of its parts.

criteria.description: Mentions that it has parts that help it grow or make food
Mentions that it takes in water or air

hints: What does the plant do with its leaves?
questions.explanation: A plant is a living thing because its parts help it grow, take in water (roots), and make food (leaves).

questions.stem: Draw a flower and label it.
questions.explanation: This tests identification and drawing of the flower.

questions.stem: A plant has roots, a stem, and leaves. It does NOT have flowers. What can we say about this plant?
options: It is a plant that may not grow flowers
hints: Are roots and leaves enough to make it a plant?
Do all plants have visible flowers all the time?
questions.explanation: Not all plants have visible flowers. As long as it has roots, a stem, and leaves, it is a plant.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all plants must have flowers.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.1.1.2: Understand the differences between living, non-living things and things which have never been alive
indicator.objective: Describe the basic structure of animals (head, limbs and trunk)

skills.description: Name the three basic parts of an animal
Identify the head, limbs, and trunk on a picture or real animal
State simply what each part does
Draw an animal and label the head, limbs, and trunk

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Animals only have a head and legs; the trunk is not a part.
Limbs are only legs; arms/wings/fins are not limbs.
The trunk is the same as the tail.
All animals have the same number of limbs.
Confusing 'trunk' with an elephant's nose.

questions.stem: What are the three main parts of an animal's body?
hints: One is the head, one is the middle.
questions.explanation: The three basic parts of an animal are the head, limbs, and trunk.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse plant parts with animal parts.

questions.stem: What do we call the main body of an animal, where the head and limbs attach?
hints: It is not the head or the legs.
questions.explanation: The trunk is the main body of the animal.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the trunk is an elephant's nose.

questions.stem: What do we call the parts of an animal used for moving, like legs or arms?
hints: Birds have wings which are also these.
questions.explanation: Limbs are the parts used for movement (legs, arms, wings, fins).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think limbs are only legs.

questions.stem: Which part of an animal contains the eyes, ears, and mouth?
questions.explanation: The head contains the eyes, ears, and mouth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the head with the trunk.

questions.stem: What do animals use their limbs for?
questions.explanation: Animals use their limbs to move from place to place.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think limbs are for seeing.

questions.stem: A goat has four legs. What part are these legs?
hints: They are not the main body.
questions.explanation: Legs are limbs.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think legs are the trunk.

questions.stem: What is the main function of an animal's head?
options: To help the animal sense its surroundings and eat
questions.explanation: The head contains the sense organs (eyes, ears, nose) and the mouth, helping the animal sense the world and eat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the head is only for eating.

questions.stem: Does a bird have limbs?
options: No, it only has a head and trunk
Yes, its wings and legs are limbs
No, birds do not have limbs
Yes, only its beak is a limb
hints: What does a bird use to fly?
What does it use to stand?
questions.explanation: A bird's wings and legs are its limbs.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think limbs are only arms and legs in humans.

questions.stem: Which part of a dog is its trunk?
hints: The head and legs are attached to it.
questions.explanation: The trunk is the main body of the dog.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the trunk is the dog's nose or tail.

questions.stem: Why do different animals have different types of limbs?
options: To help them move in their own habitat
questions.explanation: Different animals have different limbs to help them move in their specific habitats (water, air, land).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think limbs are just for decoration.

questions.stem: Name the three basic parts of an animal.
questions.explanation: The three main parts are the head, limbs, and trunk.
questions.misconception: Pupils may include the tail, which is an extension of the trunk but not one of the three main parts.

questions.stem: What do we call the middle part of an animal where the head and legs are attached?
hints: It is not the head or limbs.
questions.explanation: The trunk is the main body part.

questions.stem: Ama is looking at a picture of a fish. What are the fish's limbs?
questions.explanation: A fish's fins are its limbs, used for swimming.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think only legs and arms are limbs.

questions.stem: Kwame says 'An elephant's trunk is the same as an animal's trunk.' Is he correct?
options: Yes, they are the same thing
No, an elephant's trunk is its nose, but an animal's trunk is its main body
No, an elephant does not have a trunk
hints: What does an elephant use its trunk for?
questions.explanation: An elephant's trunk is a long nose, but in science, an animal's trunk refers to its main body.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the everyday term with the scientific term.

questions.stem: Which of these animals does NOT have limbs?
hints: Which animal slides on the ground?
questions.explanation: A snake does not have limbs; it moves by slithering.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all animals have legs.

questions.stem: Draw an animal of your choice. Label the head, trunk, and limbs.
hints: Draw a dog or a goat.
Point to the main body, the head, and the legs.
questions.explanation: This tests the ability to identify and label animal parts.

questions.stem: Explain how a dog's limbs and head work together to help it eat.

criteria.description: States the head is used to find or eat food
States the limbs are used to move the dog to the food

hints: How does the dog find food?
How does it get to the food?
questions.explanation: The dog uses its head (nose/eyes) to find food, and its limbs to move towards the food.

questions.stem: Draw a bird and label its limbs.

criteria.description: Labels the wings or legs as limbs

questions.explanation: This tests the understanding that wings are limbs.

questions.stem: Why is it important for animals to have a head, trunk, and limbs?
options: So they can survive, move, and sense their environment
hints: Think about what each part does.
The head senses, limbs move, trunk holds.
questions.explanation: These parts work together to help the animal survive, move, and interact with its environment.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think these parts are just for appearance.

questions.stem: Point to your own head, trunk, and limbs and tell your teacher what each part does.

criteria.description: Points to head and says it is for seeing/hearing/eating
Points to trunk (chest/stomach) and says it is the main body
Points to limbs (arms/legs) and says they are for moving

hints: Your arms and legs are limbs.
questions.explanation: This tests the practical understanding of the three parts.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.1.1.2: Understand the differences between living, non-living things and things which have never been alive
indicator.objective: Group things collected from the environment into living and non-living things

skills.description: Sort collected items into living and non-living things
Give a simple reason for grouping an item as living or non-living
Give examples of living and non-living things from the environment
Draw and colour some of the things collected

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Non-living things are the same as dead things.
Anything that moves is living.
Things made from plants (e.g., a wooden table) are living because they come from trees.
Things that do not move (e.g., a tree) are non-living.
Only animals are living things.

questions.stem: Is a dog living or non-living?
questions.explanation: A dog is a living thing because it eats, breathes, grows, and reproduces.
questions.misconception: Pupils may classify animals as non-living if they are thinking of a toy dog.

questions.stem: Is a stone living or non-living?
questions.explanation: A stone is a non-living thing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stones are living because they are part of the environment.

questions.stem: Which of these is a living thing?
questions.explanation: A tree is a living thing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cars are living because they move.

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-living thing?
questions.explanation: A cup is a non-living thing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think everything in the house is living.

questions.stem: Kwame collected a leaf, a stone, and a worm. Which one is living?
hints: Which one moves on its own?
questions.explanation: A worm is a living thing. A leaf from a tree is no longer living once it falls, and a stone is non-living.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a leaf is living because it came from a tree.

questions.stem: Why is a tree classified as a living thing?
hints: What does it do over time?
What does it need to survive?
questions.explanation: A tree is living because it grows, needs water and air, and reproduces.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think trees are non-living because they do not move.

questions.stem: Ama collected a stone, a leaf, a bottle, and a snail. Which group has only non-living things?
hints: Which two have never been alive?
One is from the ground, one is man-made.
questions.explanation: A stone and a bottle are non-living things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a leaf is non-living because it is no longer on the tree, but a fallen leaf is still considered living or once-living. A bottle is clearly non-living.

questions.stem: Why is a chair non-living?
options: It does not grow or eat
questions.explanation: A chair is non-living because it cannot grow, eat, breathe, or reproduce.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a wooden chair is living because it comes from a tree.

questions.stem: Is a wooden table living or non-living?
options: Living, because it comes from a tree
hints: Can a table grow new branches?
It is no longer a tree.
questions.explanation: A wooden table is non-living. Even though the wood came from a tree, the table itself cannot grow, eat, or breathe.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think wooden objects are living because they were once part of a tree.

questions.stem: Ama says 'A car is living because it moves.' Why is she wrong?
options: A car does not grow or reproduce
hints: Can a car have baby cars?
questions.explanation: A car is non-living because, although it moves, it cannot grow, eat, breathe, or reproduce.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think movement is the only sign of life.

questions.stem: Sort these items into living and non-living: dog, stone, tree, cup.
answer: living: dog, tree; non-living: stone, cup
living: dog tree, non-living: stone cup
questions.explanation: A dog and a tree are living. A stone and a cup are non-living.
questions.misconception: Pupils may group items by size or location instead of living vs non-living.

questions.stem: Name one living thing and one non-living thing you can see in your school.
answer: living: tree, grass, bird, pupil, teacher, dog; non-living: stone, desk, chair, building, car
questions.explanation: A tree is a living thing, and a desk is a non-living thing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name only animals for living things.

questions.stem: Kofi picked up a dead branch from the ground. Is it living or non-living?
options: Living, because it was once on a tree
hints: It is no longer part of a living tree.
questions.explanation: A dead branch is non-living. It was once part of a living tree, but now it is dead.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wood is always living.

questions.stem: Explain why a stone is non-living but a dog is living.

criteria.description: States a dog grows, eats, or breathes
States a stone does not grow, eat, or breathe

hints: What does the dog do that the stone cannot?
questions.explanation: A dog is living because it grows, eats, and breathes. A stone is non-living because it does none of these things.

questions.stem: Ama collected a flowing river, a bird, a stone, and grass. Which is living?
hints: A river moves but does it grow?
questions.explanation: A bird and grass are living things. A river flows but is non-living, and a stone is non-living.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a flowing river is living because it moves.

questions.stem: Why do we group things into living and non-living things?
options: To make them easier to carry
To understand the world around us
hints: Think about how scientists organise things.
It helps us learn about nature.
questions.explanation: We group things into living and non-living to help us understand and study the world around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think grouping is just for sorting objects physically.

questions.stem: Draw one living thing and one non-living thing you collected from outside.
hints: A leaf or a bug could be living.
A stone or a piece of plastic is non-living.
questions.explanation: This tests observation and classification through drawing.

questions.stem: Write two differences between a living thing and a non-living thing.

criteria.description: States living things grow, non-living do not
States living things need food/water/air, non-living do not

hints: Think about how you change as you grow.
questions.explanation: Living things grow and need food/water/air. Non-living things do not.

questions.stem: A candle flame moves and uses up fuel. Why is it NOT a living thing?
options: It does not grow or have cells
hints: Can a flame grow into a bigger flame and have baby flames?
It does not have a body like a plant or animal.
questions.explanation: A candle flame is not living because it does not grow, reproduce, or consist of cells, even though it moves and uses fuel.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think anything that moves or 'uses' something is alive.

questions.stem: Go outside and collect three things. Show them to your teacher and say whether each is living or non-living.

criteria.description: Correctly classifies at least two items as living or non-living

hints: Pick up a stone, a leaf, or a seed.
questions.explanation: This tests real-world observation and classification.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.1.2.1: Recognise materials as important resources for providing human needs
indicator.objective: Know the common properties of materials such as soft, hard, rough, smooth, opaque, transparent, bendable

skills.description: Name the common properties of materials
Identify a material's property by touching or looking at it
Sort materials based on a given property
Link a property of a material to why it is used for a particular product

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Soft means weak or easily broken.
Transparent and smooth are the same thing.
Opaque means dark-coloured.
All hard materials are heavy.
Bendable means breakable.
Confusing rough with hard.

questions.stem: What word describes a material that you can see through clearly, like a clean window?
questions.explanation: A transparent material, like clear glass, allows you to see through it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse transparent with just being clean.

questions.stem: How does a piece of cotton wool feel?
hints: You use it for a baby.
questions.explanation: Cotton wool is soft because it is fluffy and easy to squeeze.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cotton wool is hard because it is packed tightly.

questions.stem: What word describes a material that you CANNOT see through, like a brick wall?
hints: You cannot see what is behind it.
questions.explanation: An opaque material does not let light pass through, so you cannot see through it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think opaque means the material is black or dark.

questions.stem: Which of these materials is rough to touch?
hints: It is used for rubbing wood.
questions.explanation: Sandpaper has a rough surface because it is covered with tiny hard grains.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse rough with just being dirty.

questions.stem: If you can bend a material easily without it breaking, we say it is...
hints: You can change its shape with your hands.
questions.explanation: A bendable material can be bent or twisted into different shapes.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think bendable means it will break easily.

questions.stem: Which group contains only hard materials?
hints: Which group has things that are solid and difficult to squeeze?
questions.explanation: A stone, an iron nail, and wood are all hard materials.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wood is soft because it floats.

questions.stem: Kofi is sorting materials. He puts a glass cup and a clear plastic bottle in one group. What property are they sharing?
questions.explanation: Both the glass cup and the clear plastic bottle are transparent.
questions.misconception: Pupils may focus on the shape or size instead of the property.

questions.stem: Why is glass a good material for making windows?
options: Because it is transparent and lets in light
questions.explanation: Glass is used for windows because it is transparent, allowing light in and allowing people to see outside.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect the property of transparency to the use of windows.

questions.stem: Ama has two spoons: one made of metal and one made of plastic. Which one is smoother and feels colder to touch?
questions.explanation: The metal spoon is smoother and feels colder to touch than the plastic spoon.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plastic is always colder than metal.

questions.stem: Which property of a material tells you it is soft?
options: You can easily squeeze it and change its shape
It makes a loud sound when you hit it
hints: It changes shape when you press it.
questions.explanation: Soft materials are easy to squeeze and do not keep their shape when pressed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think soft means it is wet.

questions.stem: Why do we use clay for making pots?
options: Because it is bendable and can be moulded
hints: Think about how a pot is made.
Clay can be shaped by hand.
questions.explanation: Clay is used for pots because it is bendable and can be moulded into different shapes before it is baked hard.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize clay is bendable before baking.

questions.stem: Name one material that is transparent and one material that is opaque.
answer: transparent: glass, clear plastic, water; opaque: wood, stone, metal, brick
questions.explanation: Glass is transparent, while wood is opaque.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name objects instead of materials.

questions.stem: What do we call a material that you cannot see through?
questions.explanation: A material you cannot see through is opaque.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say 'dark' instead of opaque.

questions.stem: Why do we use rubber to make the wheels of a car (tyres)?
options: Because it is hard and breaks easily
Because it is rough and sticky
Because it is bendable and strong
hints: Tyres need to grip the road.
They must not break on stones.
questions.explanation: Rubber is used for tyres because it is bendable and strong, which helps it absorb shocks and not break easily.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think rubber is used because it is soft and weak.

questions.stem: Ama has a wooden block, a piece of glass, a plastic ruler, and a sheet of paper. Which group has only materials that are opaque?
questions.explanation: Wood and paper are opaque; they do not let light pass through.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think thin paper is transparent.

questions.stem: A tailor wants to make a shirt. Which material is best and why?
options: Cloth, because it is soft and bendable
questions.explanation: Cloth is the best material for a shirt because it is soft and bendable, making it comfortable to wear.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose metal for its strength without considering comfort.

questions.stem: Kofi has a material that is opaque and hard. What could it be?
hints: It does not let light through.
questions.explanation: A metal nail is both opaque and hard.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse hard with bendable.

questions.stem: Explain why glass is used to make the windshields of cars.

criteria.description: States that this allows the driver to see clearly outside

hints: The driver needs to see the road.
questions.explanation: Glass is used for car windshields because it is transparent, allowing the driver to see the road clearly.

questions.stem: A farmer needs a material to cover his crops so that sunlight can reach them but rain cannot. Which type of material should he use?
options: A transparent material like clear plastic
questions.explanation: Clear plastic is transparent (lets sunlight in) but also waterproof (keeps rain out), making it ideal for a greenhouse or crop cover.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose wood or metal because they are strong, without considering the need for sunlight.

questions.stem: Why would a metal bucket be a BAD choice for carrying water if it has a hole in it, while a plastic bucket is good?
options: Metal is always weaker than plastic
Metal is harder and cannot be moulded
hints: Can you easily fix a hole in metal without special tools?
Plastic can be melted and moulded.
questions.explanation: A metal bucket with a hole cannot be easily fixed because metal is hard and cannot be moulded by hand, whereas plastic can be moulded or welded more easily. Also, metal might rust. (Note: Focus is on metal being hard and not easily changed).
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know the difference between moulding and hammering.

questions.stem: You need a material to make a raincoat. It must not let water pass through, and it must be bendable so you can move your arms. Which material is best?
questions.explanation: A thick plastic sheet is best because it is waterproof (opaque to water) and bendable, allowing movement.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose cotton because clothes are usually made of cloth, ignoring the 'waterproof' requirement.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2. 2.1.1: Recognize that some events in our environment occur recurrently
indicator.objective: Recognise the importance of some cyclic natural phenomena such as dry and wet seasons

skills.description: Identify the dry season and wet season as cyclic natural events
Describe simple features of the dry season and the wet season
Explain why these seasons are important
Match human activities to the correct season

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: It rains every single day during the wet season.
There is no water at all during the dry season.
The seasons are the same all over the world.
We only get food during the wet season.
The dry season is bad because everything dies.

questions.stem: What are the two main seasons we experience in Ghana?
hints: One season has a lot of rain.
questions.explanation: Ghana mainly experiences the wet season and the dry season.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think we have four seasons like other countries.

questions.stem: What is the weather like during the wet season?
questions.explanation: The wet season is characterized by rain and cloudy skies.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the wet season is cold like winter.

questions.stem: During the dry season, the weather is usually...
questions.explanation: The dry season is usually sunny and hot with very little rain.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the dry season is cold because it is not raining.

questions.stem: What do farmers need to help their crops grow?
questions.explanation: Farmers need rain during the wet season to water their crops so they can grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think crops only need sunlight.

questions.stem: When do farmers usually plant their seeds?
options: In the middle of the night
hints: The ground needs to be wet.
questions.explanation: Farmers plant their seeds during the wet season so they get enough water to grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think planting happens when it is dry.

questions.stem: Which season has a lot of rain?
questions.explanation: The wet season is the time of the year when it rains a lot.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the wet season with the harmattan.

questions.stem: How does the dry season help farmers?
options: It helps them dry their crops like maize and fish
It helps them plant new seeds
hints: Think about how food is preserved.
questions.explanation: The dry season is useful for drying crops like maize, cocoa, and fish so they can be stored for a long time.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the dry season is only bad for farmers.

questions.stem: When it is raining, what do people use to keep dry?
hints: It opens up like a roof.
You hold it over your head.
questions.explanation: People use umbrellas to protect themselves from the rain.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sunglasses protect from rain.

questions.stem: Do the wet and dry seasons happen once or repeatedly?
hints: Think about the cycle of a year.
questions.explanation: The wet and dry seasons are cyclic events. They happen repeatedly, every year.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think seasons only happen once.

questions.stem: What happens to many rivers and streams during the dry season?
options: They dry up or get smaller
hints: There is no rain to fill them.
questions.explanation: During the dry season, rivers and streams often dry up or have less water because there is no rain.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think rivers always have the same amount of water.

questions.stem: Why is the wet season important for animals in the wild?
options: It gives them water to drink and plants to eat
questions.explanation: The wet season provides water for animals to drink and helps plants grow so animals have food to eat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think animals do not need rain.

questions.stem: Name one activity people do during the dry season.
hints: Think about what the sun helps us do.
How do we dry our clothes?
questions.explanation: People often dry clothes, food, and harvest crops during the dry season.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name activities that require rain, like planting.

questions.stem: What do we call the season when it rains a lot?
hints: It is the opposite of dry.
questions.explanation: The season with a lot of rain is called the wet season.

questions.stem: Why is the dry season important for drying food like gari and fish?
options: Because there is no rain and the sun is hot
Because the wind blows them away
hints: Think about what makes things dry.
The sun is out all day.
questions.explanation: The dry season is important for drying food because the hot sun and lack of rain help remove moisture, preserving the food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think drying is done in the wet season.

questions.stem: If a farmer plants his seeds in the middle of the dry season, what will likely happen?
options: The seeds will grow very fast
The seeds may not grow and could die
The seeds will turn into stones
hints: The dry season has very little water.
questions.explanation: Seeds need water to grow. Without water from the rains, they may not sprout or they might dry up and die.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the hot sun is all a seed needs.

questions.stem: Why do we say the seasons are cyclic?
options: Because they come and go every year in a pattern
Because they are always the same
Because they are caused by cars
hints: Think about a clock going round.
What happens after the wet season? And after the dry?
questions.explanation: Seasons are cyclic because they occur in a repeating pattern year after year.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'cyclic' means something is broken.

questions.stem: How does the land usually look during the wet season compared to the dry season?
options: Wet season: green and lush; Dry season: brown and dry
Wet season: brown and dry; Dry season: green and lush
Both seasons look exactly the same
Wet season: covered in snow; Dry season: covered in sand
hints: Plants grow when they get water.
What happens to grass when it is hot and dry?
questions.explanation: During the wet season, plants get plenty of water and look green. In the dry season, they dry up and turn brown.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not observe the difference in vegetation.

questions.stem: Explain why the wet season is important for providing food for the whole country.

criteria.description: States that crops need rain to grow
States that farmers can only get a good harvest if there is enough rain

questions.explanation: The wet season is important because crops need water to grow. Without rain, farmers cannot produce enough food for everyone.

questions.stem: Describe two ways people in your community change their daily activities when the dry season arrives.

criteria.description: Names one valid change (e.g., wearing lighter clothes, using fans, storing water, drying food)

hints: What do you wear when it is hot?
questions.explanation: People adapt to the dry season by wearing light clothing, using fans, storing water, and drying food.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher the names of the two main seasons in Ghana and one thing that happens in each.

criteria.description: Names the wet season and says it rains
Names the dry season and says it is sunny/hot

hints: One starts with W, one starts with D.
questions.explanation: The wet season brings rain, and the dry season brings hot, sunny weather.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2. 2.1.2: Recognize the relationship between the Earth and the Sun
indicator.objective: Identify sources of light to the earth

skills.description: Identify sources of light to the Earth
Sort sources of light into natural and artificial
Recognise the sun as the main and most important source of light to the Earth
Explain simply why we need light

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: The moon makes its own light.
Lightning and fireflies are not sources of light.
Only the sun is a source of light.
We only need light at night.
A mirror is a source of light.

questions.stem: What is the main source of light to the Earth?
hints: It is very bright and hot.
questions.explanation: The sun is the main and most important source of light to the Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon is the main source of light.

questions.stem: Which of these can give us light at night?
hints: You use it during a power outage.
questions.explanation: A torch is a source of light that we can use at night.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a mirror makes its own light.

questions.stem: Why do we need light?
hints: When it is dark, can you see well?
questions.explanation: We need light so that we can see things around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think we only need light for plants.

questions.stem: Name a source of light you use in your home.
questions.explanation: An electric bulb is a source of light used in homes.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think objects like chairs give light.

questions.stem: Is the sun a natural or artificial source of light?
questions.explanation: The sun is a natural source of light because it is not made by humans.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know the difference between natural and artificial.

questions.stem: Which of these is an artificial source of light?
hints: You light it with a match.
questions.explanation: A candle is an artificial source of light because it is made by humans.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think lightning is artificial.

questions.stem: Which of these is a natural source of light?
hints: It is very bright and comes with thunder.
questions.explanation: Lightning is a natural source of light.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not consider lightning a source of light.

questions.stem: Which of these insects produces its own light?
hints: You see them glowing at night.
They have a light on their tail.
questions.explanation: Fireflies are natural sources of light because they can produce their own light.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know that some insects can produce light.

questions.stem: Why is the sun called the main source of light?
options: Because it is the biggest and brightest source for the Earth
Because it is in the sky
Because we cannot look at it directly
hints: Is there any other light as bright as the sun?
It lights up the whole Earth during the day.
questions.explanation: The sun is the main source because it provides the most light to the Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a torch is a main source because they use it often.

questions.stem: How does light from the sun help plants?
options: It helps them grow and make food
hints: They need light to make their food.
questions.explanation: Plants need sunlight to make their own food and to grow healthy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants only need water and soil.

questions.stem: Sort these sources of light into natural and artificial: Sun, Torch, Stars, Bulb.
answer: natural: sun, stars; artificial: torch, bulb
hints: Which ones are made by humans?
Which ones are found in nature?
questions.explanation: The sun and stars are natural. A torch and a bulb are artificial (made by humans).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all bright things are natural.

questions.stem: What is the main source of light for the Earth?
hints: It comes out during the day.
questions.explanation: The sun is the main source of light for the Earth.

questions.stem: Ama says 'The moon makes its own light.' Why is she wrong?
options: Because the moon reflects light from the sun
Because the moon is too small
Because the moon only comes out at night
Because the moon is not in the sky
hints: Does the moon have fire on it?
It shines because the sun shines on it.
questions.explanation: The moon does not make its own light. It shines by reflecting light from the sun.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think the moon is a source of its own light.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a source of light?
hints: Does a mirror make its own light?
questions.explanation: A mirror is not a source of light. It only reflects light that comes from other sources.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a mirror produces light because it looks bright.

questions.stem: What would happen to the Earth if there was no source of light at all?
options: It would be completely dark and we could not see
It would be covered in ice
hints: Think about a room with no windows at night.
questions.explanation: Without any source of light, the Earth would be completely dark, and it would be impossible to see anything.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think we can see in the dark naturally.

questions.stem: Why is a candle an artificial source of light?
options: Because it is made by humans
Because it is made of wax
hints: Can you find a candle growing in a forest?
Was it made in a factory?
questions.explanation: A candle is artificial because it is manufactured by humans, not found in nature.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think anything that burns is natural.

questions.stem: Name two natural sources of light.
hints: Look up at the sky during the day.
Look up at the sky at night.
questions.explanation: The sun, stars, lightning, and fireflies are natural sources of light.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name torches or bulbs, which are artificial.

questions.stem: Explain why the sun is a more important source of light than a torch.

criteria.description: States that the sun gives light to the whole Earth
States that a torch only gives light to a small area for a short time

hints: How much of the Earth does the sun light up?
How far can a torch shine?
questions.explanation: The sun is more important because it lights up the entire Earth during the day, while a torch only provides a small amount of light for a short time.

questions.stem: Why is a mirror NOT a source of light?

criteria.description: States that a mirror only reflects light
States that it cannot produce its own light

hints: What happens if you put a mirror in a completely dark room?
questions.explanation: A mirror is not a source of light because it cannot produce its own light. It only reflects light from other sources.

questions.stem: A firefly produces its own light. Is it a natural or artificial source of light?
options: Natural, because it is a living thing found in nature
Artificial, because it has a small battery
Natural, because it is made by humans
Artificial, because it glows at night
hints: Is a firefly a living creature?
Does it come from a factory?
questions.explanation: A firefly is a natural source of light because it is a living organism that produces light naturally.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think glowing means artificial.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.3.1.1: Recognize that different parts of the human body work independently to perform a specific function
indicator.objective: Know the functions of the human body parts such as eyes, ears, mouth, nose, arms, legs and hands

skills.description: State the function of specific body parts
Match a body part to its function or identify the part used for a specific action
Explain simply what happens if a body part is missing or not working well
Draw and colour at least two body parts

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: The nose is only for breathing; it has nothing to do with smelling.
Hands are only for holding; they cannot feel.
If one part is missing, the person cannot do anything at all.
Ears are for seeing and eyes are for hearing.
The mouth is only for eating; it is not for talking.

questions.stem: Which body part do we use to see things around us?
questions.explanation: We use our eyes to see the world around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse eyes with ears.

questions.stem: Which body part do we use to hear sounds?
hints: It is on the side of your head.
questions.explanation: We use our ears to hear sounds.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think we hear with our eyes.

questions.stem: What do we use our nose for?
hints: You use it to sniff food.
It is in the middle of your face.
questions.explanation: We use our nose to smell things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the nose is only for breathing.

questions.stem: Which body parts do we use to walk and run?
questions.explanation: We use our legs to walk and run.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse legs with arms.

questions.stem: Kofi wants to pick up a pencil. Which body part will he use?
hints: You use it to hold things.
questions.explanation: We use our hands to pick up and hold objects.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think legs are used for picking up things.

questions.stem: What is the main function of the mouth?
questions.explanation: The mouth is used for eating, drinking, and speaking.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the mouth is only for eating, not speaking.
