questions.stem: Ama is listening to music. Which part of her body is she using?
questions.explanation: Ama uses her ears to listen to music.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think you listen with your eyes.

questions.stem: What do we use our hands for?
hints: You use them to catch a ball.
questions.explanation: We use our hands to hold, touch, write, and do many tasks.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think hands are only for holding.

questions.stem: What happens if a person's eyes are not working well?
hints: If they don't work, seeing is hard.
questions.explanation: If a person's eyes are not working well, they cannot see clearly or at all.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a person who cannot see also cannot hear.

questions.stem: Which body part do we use to kick a football?
hints: It is the lower part of your body.
questions.explanation: We use our legs and feet to kick a football.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say hands because they throw balls.

questions.stem: Name the body part we use to smell food.
hints: It is in the middle of your face.
questions.explanation: We use the nose to smell food.

questions.stem: What do we use our ears for?
hints: You listen to music with them.
questions.explanation: We use our ears for hearing.

questions.stem: If a person is deaf, which body part is not working well?
questions.explanation: If a person is deaf, their ears are not working well, and they cannot hear.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think deafness affects the eyes.

questions.stem: Kwame is carrying a heavy bucket. Which two body parts is he using most?
hints: He holds the bucket with one part.
questions.explanation: Kwame uses his hands to carry the bucket and his legs to walk.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect the action to the correct body parts.

questions.stem: Why is it important to take care of our body parts?
options: So they can work well and we stay healthy
hints: You want your body to work.
questions.explanation: We take care of our body parts so they keep working well and we stay healthy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not see the link between care and function.

questions.stem: Ama is blind. Which body part is not working well?
questions.explanation: A blind person's eyes are not working well, so they cannot see.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think blindness affects the ears.

questions.stem: Draw a human head and label the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth.
hints: Draw a circle for the head.
Put the eyes, nose, and mouth in the middle.
questions.explanation: This tests identifying and labelling the main parts of the face.

questions.stem: Explain how your life would change if you could not use your hands for one day.

criteria.description: States a valid difficulty (e.g., cannot write, cannot eat)

hints: What do you do with your hands every day?
How would you hold a pencil?
questions.explanation: Without hands, everyday tasks like writing, eating, and dressing would be very difficult.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher the function of the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth.
hints: What do you do with each one?
questions.explanation: This tests verbal recall of body part functions.

questions.stem: Draw a person and draw arrows pointing to the hands and legs. Write what each part does.

criteria.description: Draws a person with hands and legs
Writes a correct function for the hands
Writes a correct function for the legs

hints: Use your drawing to show how you hold and walk.
questions.explanation: This tests the connection between body parts and their functions.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.3.2.1: Show understanding of the orderliness of the sun, planets and satellites in the solar system as well as the important role of the sun in the solar system
indicator.objective: Identify the sun as the main source of light and warmth on earth

skills.description: Identify the sun as the main source of both light and warmth on Earth
Explain what we use the sun's light and warmth for
Explain simply what life would be like without the sun
Draw and colour the sun

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: The sun only gives light; it does not give warmth.
The moon gives us more warmth than the sun.
We do not need the sun because we have electric lights and heaters.
The sun is not a star; it is just a big ball of fire.
The sun only affects plants, not people or animals.

questions.stem: What is the main source of light on Earth?
hints: It comes out in the day.
questions.explanation: The sun is the main source of light on Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon is the main source of light.

questions.stem: What is the main source of warmth on Earth?
hints: When it is out, we feel hot.
It is in the sky during the day.
questions.explanation: The sun is the main source of warmth on Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon provides warmth.

questions.stem: Why do we hang wet clothes outside?
options: So the sun can dry them
So the moon can dry them
So the rain can dry them
So the wind can dry them
hints: What is in the sky outside?
questions.explanation: We hang wet clothes outside so the sun's warmth can dry them.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the wind does all the drying.

questions.stem: How does the sun help plants?
questions.explanation: The sun gives plants light and warmth, which they need to grow and make food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants only need water.

questions.stem: What would happen if there was no sun?
options: It would be very dark and cold
hints: The sun gives light and warmth.
questions.explanation: Without the sun, the Earth would be very dark and cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon would light up the Earth equally.

questions.stem: Which activity uses the warmth of the sun?
hints: You need heat to dry things.
questions.explanation: Drying fish uses the warmth of the sun to remove moisture and preserve the fish.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect warmth to drying.

questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE about the sun?
options: It gives both light and warmth
hints: You feel hot when it shines.
You can see because of it.
questions.explanation: The sun provides both light and warmth to the Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sun only provides one or the other.

questions.stem: Why do we feel warm when we stand outside on a sunny day?
options: Because the sun is giving off heat
questions.explanation: We feel warm because the sun provides heat (warmth) to the Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the wind makes them warm.

questions.stem: If the sun stopped shining, what would happen to plants?
options: They would stop growing and die
hints: Plants need light to make food.
questions.explanation: Plants need sunlight to make their food. Without the sun, they would not be able to grow and would eventually die.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants only need soil.

questions.stem: What is the main source of light and warmth on Earth?
hints: You see it in the day.
questions.explanation: The sun is the main source of light and warmth.

questions.stem: Name one thing you can do because of the sun's warmth.
hints: Think about how you feel on a sunny day.
questions.explanation: We can dry clothes or food, or keep ourselves warm thanks to the sun's warmth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name things that use light but not warmth, like reading.

questions.stem: Why is the sun important for drying our food like gari and fish?
options: Because its warmth removes water from the food
Because it makes the food wet
Because it changes the colour of the food
Because it makes the food cold
hints: Think about what happens to water in the sun.
questions.explanation: The sun's warmth causes water in the food to evaporate, which helps dry and preserve it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sun adds something to the food.

questions.stem: Why can we say the sun is a star?
options: Because it is a huge ball of burning gas that gives off light and heat
Because it is small and round
Because it is in the sky
hints: Stars give off their own light.
The sun is a big ball of gas.
questions.explanation: The sun is a star because it is a massive ball of hot, glowing gas that produces its own light and heat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stars are only the tiny dots in the night sky.

questions.stem: If the sun stopped giving warmth, what would happen to the water in rivers and oceans?
hints: Without heat, it gets very cold.
questions.explanation: Without the sun's warmth, the Earth would become very cold, and water would freeze into ice.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect the sun's warmth to the state of water.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a use of the sun's light?
options: Helping us see during the day
Cooking food directly without a stove
hints: Think about how food is cooked.
You need a fire or stove to cook.
questions.explanation: While the sun is hot, it cannot cook food directly without a stove or solar cooker; the others are direct uses of its light or warmth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sun can cook food as fast as a fire.

questions.stem: Draw the sun and colour it. Write one word to describe what it gives us.
questions.explanation: This tests recognising the sun and its primary outputs.

questions.stem: Explain what would happen to life on Earth if the sun suddenly disappeared.

criteria.description: States it would be very cold
States plants would die and animals/humans would struggle

questions.explanation: Without the sun, the Earth would be dark and freezing, plants would die, and life as we know it would not survive.

questions.stem: Why is the sun considered the most important object in the solar system for life on Earth?
options: Because it provides the light and warmth necessary for life
Because it is the smallest object
Because it is the only object in the sky
Because it revolves around the Earth
hints: What do living things need to survive?
Where does the energy come from?
questions.explanation: The sun is the most important object for life because it provides the light and warmth that plants, animals, and humans need to survive.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the Earth is the centre of the solar system.

questions.stem: Write down two ways the sun helps farmers.

criteria.description: States it helps dry harvested crops/food (warmth)

hints: What happens to maize after harvesting?
questions.explanation: The sun helps farmers by providing light for crops to grow and warmth to dry harvested produce.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher why the sun is important for both light and warmth.

criteria.description: States we need light to see
States we need warmth to stay warm/dry things

hints: What happens when it is cold?
questions.explanation: The sun gives us light to see during the day and warmth to keep us from freezing and to dry our food and clothes.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.4.1.1: Demonstrate understanding of the concept of energy, its various forms, sources and the ways in which it can be transformed and conserved
indicator.objective: Identify everyday applications of energy

skills.description: Identify everyday applications of energy
Name the source of energy for everyday activities
Explain what happens when energy is missing

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Energy is only electricity.
Only people need energy; machines and animals do not.
Food is not energy; it is just something we eat.
Energy is something you can always see.
A car at rest has no energy at all.

questions.stem: Which of these everyday activities requires energy?
hints: You move your body a lot.
You get tired after doing it.
questions.explanation: Running requires a lot of energy because your body is working hard to move.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sitting or sleeping require no energy at all.

questions.stem: Where do people get the energy to walk and work?
questions.explanation: People get energy from the food they eat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think people get energy directly from the sun like plants.

questions.stem: Which of these household items uses energy to work?
hints: It needs to be plugged in.
questions.explanation: A television uses electrical energy to work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all household items require energy.

questions.stem: What gives a car the energy to move?
hints: You buy it at a filling station.
questions.explanation: A car gets its energy from petrol (fuel).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cars run on water.

questions.stem: What happens to a person who has not eaten all day?
questions.explanation: A person who has not eaten has no energy from food and will feel weak.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think skipping food gives you energy.

questions.stem: Ama is pounding fufu. What is she using to do this work?
questions.explanation: Ama is using energy from her body (which comes from the food she eats) to pound the fufu.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect physical work to body energy.

questions.stem: What is the main source of energy for plants to make their own food?
hints: It is in the sky during the day.
questions.explanation: Plants use energy from the sun (sunlight) to make their food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants only get energy from the soil.

questions.stem: What happens to a torch when its battery runs out?
questions.explanation: A torch needs energy from the battery to give light. When the battery runs out, it stops working.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a torch can work without a battery.

questions.stem: Which of these activities does NOT use much energy?
questions.explanation: Sleeping uses much less energy than active tasks like running or playing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sleeping uses the same energy as playing.

questions.stem: Kwame plugs in an electric iron. What source of energy is he using?
hints: It comes from the wall socket.
questions.explanation: Kwame is using electrical energy from the socket to heat the iron.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think an iron uses fire.

questions.stem: Name one activity you did today that used energy.
questions.explanation: Walking, writing, and playing all require energy from your body.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name a passive activity like sleeping.

questions.stem: What gives you energy to play football?
questions.explanation: Food gives you the energy you need to play football.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say they get energy from water only.

questions.stem: Why does a fan need electricity to work?
options: To give it the energy to spin
hints: The motor makes the blades spin.
questions.explanation: A fan needs electrical energy to power its motor and make the blades spin.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fans create cold energy out of nowhere.

questions.stem: What would happen to a moving car if the driver suddenly turned off the engine (with no fuel going in)?
options: It would turn into a bicycle
hints: The engine provides the energy to move.
Without energy, it cannot keep moving.
questions.explanation: Without the engine providing energy from fuel, the car would eventually slow down and stop.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a car can move forever without fuel.

questions.stem: A farmer uses a cutlass to clear grass. What provides the energy for the cutlass to move?
questions.explanation: The farmer's muscles (body energy) provide the force and energy to swing the cutlass.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think tools have their own energy.

questions.stem: Explain how a person gets the energy to run a race.

criteria.description: Mentions the body using energy from food to run

hints: What do athletes eat before a race?
Where does body energy come from?
questions.explanation: A person eats food, which gives their body energy. The body uses this energy to run.

questions.stem: Explain what happens in a community when the electricity supply goes off for a whole day.

criteria.description: States that electrical appliances will not work
States that activities requiring electricity will stop (e.g., fridges get warm, no lights)

hints: What things in your house need electricity?
What happens to food in the fridge?
questions.explanation: When electricity goes off, appliances like fridges, fans, and lights stop working, disrupting daily life.

questions.stem: Why is the sun considered the ultimate source of energy for almost all living things?
options: Because it gives light and heat, which plants use to make food that animals and humans eat
hints: Plants use sunlight to make food.
Where does the food chain start?
questions.explanation: The sun provides light and warmth that plants need to make food. Animals and humans eat these plants (or eat animals that ate the plants), so the sun is the ultimate source of energy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand the food chain link to the sun.

questions.stem: Ama says 'My car at rest has no energy.' Why is she wrong?
options: Because the car has fuel stored in its tank which is potential energy
hints: What is in the fuel tank?
Can the car move if you start the engine?
questions.explanation: A car at rest still has stored energy (in the fuel). This stored energy can be turned into movement when the engine starts.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think only moving objects have energy.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher two ways you use energy at home and two ways you use energy at school.

criteria.description: Names a second valid home activity
Names a second valid school activity

hints: Think about sweeping, cooking, or washing.
Think about writing, running, or carrying a bag.
questions.explanation: This tests the ability to identify everyday applications of energy in different settings.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.4.1.2: Show understanding of the concept of heat in terms of its importance, effects, sources and transfer from one medium to another
indicator.objective: Understand that objects become hot or cold through the loss or gain of heat

skills.description: Understand that objects become hot by gaining heat and cold by losing heat
Name sources of heat
Describe what happens when things gain or lose heat

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Cold is a kind of energy that enters an object.
Objects become cold by gaining coldness, not by losing heat.
A fridge adds cold to food.
If something is not on fire, it has no heat.
Ice is cold because it contains cold energy.

questions.stem: How does an object become hot?
hints: Think about putting a pot on a fire.
The fire gives heat to the pot.
questions.explanation: An object becomes hot when it gains heat from a heat source.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think objects become hot on their own.

questions.stem: How does an object become cold?
hints: Think about putting water in a fridge.
questions.explanation: An object becomes cold when it loses heat. The fridge removes heat from the water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think objects become cold by gaining 'coldness'.

questions.stem: Which of these is a source of heat?
questions.explanation: A lighted stove is a source of heat used for cooking.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a fan produces heat.

questions.stem: What happens to ice when you leave it in the sun?
questions.explanation: The sun gives heat to the ice, causing it to melt into water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think ice stays solid in the sun.

questions.stem: What is the main natural source of heat on Earth?
hints: It comes out in the day.
questions.explanation: The sun is the main natural source of heat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon gives off heat.

questions.stem: Why does a spoon left in a hot cup of tea feel hot after a while?
options: The spoon makes its own heat
The heat moves from the tea to the spoon
hints: Heat moves to the cooler object.
questions.explanation: Heat transfers from the hot tea to the metal spoon, making the spoon feel hot.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the spoon generates its own heat.

questions.stem: What happens to a hot iron when you unplug it and leave it for a while?
hints: It is no longer getting electricity.
It loses heat to the air.
questions.explanation: When unplugged, the iron stops gaining heat and starts losing heat to the cooler air, so it cools down.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the iron stays hot forever.

questions.stem: Kofi wants to dry his wet clothes. What source of heat can he use?
questions.explanation: The sun provides heat that helps evaporate the water from the clothes, drying them.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a fan dries clothes by adding heat.

questions.stem: When you put a bottle of water in the fridge, what happens to the heat in the water?
options: The water loses heat to the fridge
questions.explanation: The water loses heat to the cold fridge, which is why the water becomes cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the fridge adds 'coldness' to the water.

questions.stem: Name one thing you use in your home to make heat.
hints: You use it to iron clothes.
questions.explanation: A stove, electric iron, or heater are sources of heat in the home.

questions.stem: What happens to water when you put it in a freezer?
questions.explanation: Water loses heat in the freezer and turns into solid ice.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the freezer adds cold to the water.

questions.stem: Ama holds a cold stone in her hands. Her hands feel cold. Why?
options: The stone gives cold to her hands
The stone takes heat from her hands
The stone makes her hands wet
hints: Heat moves from hot to cold.
Her hands are warmer than the stone.
questions.explanation: The stone is colder than her hands. Heat moves from her hands to the stone, making her hands feel cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cold transfers from the stone to the hands.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a source of heat?
hints: You use it to cool drinks.
questions.explanation: A block of ice is cold, not a source of heat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all solids are hot.

questions.stem: Why does a pot of water boil when you place it on a hot stove?
options: The water gains heat from the stove
The water loses heat to the stove
The water creates its own heat
The stove cools down the water
questions.explanation: The water gains heat from the hot stove, which makes it boil.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the water gains cold from the stove.

questions.stem: Ama says 'The fridge makes my food cold by adding cold to it.' Is she right?
options: No, the fridge removes heat from the food
No, the fridge adds hot air
hints: Does cold exist on its own?
The fridge takes heat away from the food.
questions.explanation: Ama is not right. A fridge does not add 'cold'; it removes heat from the food inside, which makes the food cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think cold is a substance that can be added.

questions.stem: Which two sources of heat are commonly used in a Ghanaian home for cooking?
options: A charcoal stove and a gas cooker
questions.explanation: A charcoal stove and a gas cooker are common sources of heat for cooking.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name electrical items that do not produce heat.

questions.stem: Explain why a metal spoon feels hot when placed in a cup of hot tea.

criteria.description: States that heat moves from the tea to the spoon
States that the spoon gains heat and becomes hot

hints: Does heat stay in the tea or move?
questions.explanation: The spoon feels hot because it gains heat from the hot tea.

questions.stem: Explain why an ice cube melts when you hold it in your hand.

criteria.description: States that the hand is warmer than the ice
States that heat moves from the hand to the ice, causing it to melt

questions.explanation: Your hand is warmer than the ice. Heat moves from your hand to the ice, causing it to gain heat and melt.

questions.stem: A student puts a cold metal spoon in a cup of hot tea. After a while, the tea becomes slightly cooler and the spoon becomes warmer. Why?
options: The spoon added cold to the tea
Heat moved from the tea to the spoon until they reached a similar temperature
The tea lost heat to the air only
The spoon gained cold from the tea
hints: Heat moves from hot to cold.
The tea is hot, the spoon is cold.
questions.explanation: Heat moves from the hot tea to the cold spoon. The tea loses heat (so it cools slightly) and the spoon gains heat (so it warms up).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cold transfers from the spoon to the tea.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher what happens to an object when it gains heat and what happens when it loses heat.

criteria.description: States it becomes hot when it gains heat
States it becomes cold when it loses heat

hints: Think about a pot on a fire.
Think about water in a fridge.
questions.explanation: An object becomes hot when it gains heat and cold when it loses heat.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.4.2.1: Demonstrate knowledge of generation of electricity, its transmission and transformation into other forms of energy
indicator.objective: Recognise the importance of safety when using electricity

skills.description: Identify safe practices when using electricity
Identify unsafe practices
Explain simply why an action is unsafe
Recognise why electrical gadgets are covered with plastic or rubber

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: You can touch a socket if your hands are only a little wet.
Plastic covers are just for decoration.
Only naked wires are dangerous; covered wires are always safe.
Electricity is safe to play with if it is from a battery.
Wood and rubber are dangerous because they burn.

questions.stem: Which of these is a safe way to use electricity?
options: Touching a socket with wet hands
Keeping your hands dry before touching a switch
Pulling a plug by its wire
hints: Water and electricity are dangerous together.
questions.explanation: You should always keep your hands dry before touching electrical switches or sockets.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wet hands are fine if the water is clean.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT safe?
options: Using a dry cloth to hold a plug
Sticking your fingers into a socket
Turning off the light before changing a bulb
Using a wooden stick to push a switch
hints: Never put your fingers where electricity flows.
questions.explanation: Sticking your fingers into a socket is very dangerous and can cause a severe electric shock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize how dangerous sockets are.

questions.stem: Why are electrical wires covered with plastic or rubber?
options: To protect people from getting a shock
hints: Plastic does not let electricity pass through.
questions.explanation: Plastic and rubber are insulators. They stop electricity from flowing into your body and giving you a shock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the covering is just for decoration or to keep the wire clean.

questions.stem: Kwame sees a wire with the plastic covering peeled off. What should he do?
options: Touch it to see if it works
questions.explanation: A wire with the covering peeled off (naked wire) is dangerous. Kwame should not touch it and should tell an adult.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it is safe to touch wires if they want to check them.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to touch a switch with wet hands?
options: Water can conduct electricity and cause a shock
hints: Water and electricity do not mix.
You could get an electric shock.
questions.explanation: Water can conduct (carry) electricity. Touching a switch with wet hands can cause an electric shock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water protects you from electricity.

questions.stem: Ama wants to unplug the television. What is the safest way to do it?
options: Pull the plug itself with dry hands
hints: Hold the plastic part of the plug.
questions.explanation: You should always hold the plug itself with dry hands, not pull the wire, to avoid damaging the wire or getting a shock.
questions.misconception: Pupils often pull the wire because it is faster.

questions.stem: Which of these is a dangerous thing to do near a live electric wire?
hints: The kite string can touch the wire.
questions.explanation: Flying a kite near electric wires is dangerous because the string can touch the wires and cause a shock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize string can conduct electricity.

questions.stem: Why is it safer to use a wooden stick to push a fallen electric wire away from you than to use your hand?
options: Wood is heavier than your hand
Wood is an insulator and does not carry electricity well
Wood is colder than your hand
hints: Wood does not let electricity pass through easily.
questions.explanation: Wood is an insulator (or a poor conductor), so it helps protect you from getting a shock when moving a live wire.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any solid object protects them.

questions.stem: If you see someone getting an electric shock, why should you NOT touch them with your bare hands?
options: They will be too heavy to pull
The electricity can pass into your body too
hints: You could get shocked as well.
questions.explanation: Touching someone who is being shocked can allow the electricity to flow into your body as well. You should turn off the power source first.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they can just pull the person away.

questions.stem: Why is it important to wear shoes (especially with rubber soles) when dealing with electricity?
options: Because shoes make you run faster
Because rubber is an insulator and protects you from shocks
Because shoes make you look good
Because shoes keep your feet warm
hints: It stops electricity from going into your feet.
questions.explanation: Rubber-soled shoes act as insulators, helping to protect you from electric shocks by stopping electricity from reaching the ground through your body.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know rubber is an insulator.

questions.stem: Ama is playing with a broken electric socket. Is it safe?
options: Yes, if you use a stick
Yes, it is just a game
hints: Broken sockets can have naked wires.
questions.explanation: Playing with a broken socket is very dangerous. It might still have power and could cause a shock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a broken item is safe to play with.

questions.stem: Which of these materials would be best to make the handle of an electric iron?
questions.explanation: Rubber is an insulator, so it is safe to use for the handle of an iron to prevent the user from getting a shock.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think metals are good for handles.

questions.stem: Kofi sees an electric fire starting in his house. What should he do FIRST?
options: Tell an adult and try to turn off the main power switch safely
Touch the fire with his hands
hints: Water and electricity are dangerous together.
Get help and stop the power.
questions.explanation: You should never throw water on an electrical fire. The best step is to tell an adult and safely cut off the electricity supply.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water can put out any fire.

questions.stem: Why is overloading a socket (plugging too many appliances into one socket) dangerous?
options: It can cause the wires to overheat and start a fire
It makes the appliances run faster
hints: Too much electricity through one wire.
questions.explanation: Plugging too many appliances into one socket pulls too much electricity, which can overheat the wires and cause a fire.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand the limits of a socket.

questions.stem: Which of these is an unsafe electrical practice?
options: Using a dry cloth to clean a switch
Using a fork to get bread out of a plugged-in toaster
Turning off the lights before leaving the room
hints: The toaster is still plugged in.
questions.explanation: Using a metal object like a fork in a plugged-in appliance is very dangerous because you could easily touch live parts and get shocked.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize everyday actions can be dangerous.

questions.stem: Why are power lines outside usually covered with thick plastic or rubber, and sometimes hung high up?
options: To protect birds and people from getting shocked
hints: They are out in the open.
questions.explanation: Covering them with insulators and hanging them high helps protect people and animals from accidental contact and shocks.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not think about safety in outdoor power lines.

questions.stem: Why is it important to have a qualified electrician do wiring in a house?
options: Because they are the only ones who can buy wires
Because they know how to do it safely and avoid dangerous mistakes
hints: A mistake can cause a fire.
questions.explanation: Electricians are trained to install wiring safely. Poor wiring can lead to electric shocks or fires.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think anyone can fix wires.

questions.stem: Look at pictures of these scenarios: (1) touching a socket with wet hands, (2) pulling a plug by the wire, (3) turning off a switch with dry hands. Show your teacher which one is safe and explain why.

criteria.description: Identifies turning off the switch with dry hands as the safe option
Explains that water and pulling wires are dangerous

questions.explanation: This tests identifying safe and unsafe electricity practices.

questions.stem: Explain why it is dangerous to use a metal spoon to unplug a faulty electric kettle.

criteria.description: States that it can cause an electric shock

hints: What is the spoon made of?
What does metal do with electricity?
questions.explanation: Metal is a good conductor of electricity. Using a metal spoon can cause the electricity to flow into your body, giving you a severe shock.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher three rules for staying safe with electricity.

criteria.description: States one valid safety rule (e.g., dry hands)
States a second valid rule (e.g., don't pull wires)
States a third valid rule (e.g., don't climb poles)

hints: What should your hands be like?
Should you put things in sockets?
questions.explanation: Rules include: keep hands dry, never stick objects into sockets, don't pull plugs by the wire, and tell an adult about broken wires.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.4.2.2: Know the functions and assemblage of basic electronics components
indicator.objective: Investigate the function of batteries in electronic devices

skills.description: Understand that a battery stores and provides electrical energy to make a device work
Identify common devices that use batteries
Describe what happens when a battery is removed or dead
Understand that a battery must be connected in a complete loop to work

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Batteries make electricity forever.
Any battery can work in any device.
A wire alone can light a bulb without a battery.
Batteries are only found in phones.
If a device doesn't work, it is always broken; it never just needs a new battery.

questions.stem: Which of these devices needs a battery to work?
options: A television plugged into the wall
questions.explanation: A torch uses batteries to work, making it portable.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all devices need wall sockets.

questions.stem: What is the job of a battery in a device?
options: To provide energy for the device to work
To change the colour of the device
hints: Without it, the device won't work.
questions.explanation: A battery stores and provides electrical energy to make the device work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know what a battery actually does.

questions.stem: What happens to a torch when you take out its batteries?
questions.explanation: Without the batteries, the torch has no source of energy and will not light up.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a torch can work without a battery.

questions.stem: Which of these common household items uses a battery?
hints: You use it to change TV channels.
It is small and you hold it.
questions.explanation: A remote control uses batteries to send signals to the TV.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not think of small devices as using batteries.

questions.stem: What do we call a device that stores electrical energy?
hints: You put it in a torch.
It has positive and negative ends.
questions.explanation: A battery stores electrical energy for use in devices.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wires store energy.

questions.stem: Ama has a toy car that won't move. She checks inside and sees it needs batteries. What should she do?
questions.explanation: The toy car needs batteries to get energy to move. Putting in new batteries should make it work.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the toy is permanently broken.

questions.stem: Why does a torch stop shining after a long time of use?
options: The battery runs out of energy
questions.explanation: The battery stores a limited amount of energy. After it runs out, the torch stops shining.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the bulb itself 'wears out' instantly.

questions.stem: To make a bulb light up using a battery and a wire, what must you do?
options: Connect only one end of the wire
Make a complete loop connecting the battery and bulb
Just place the wire on the table
hints: The loop must go all the way around.
questions.explanation: Electricity must flow in a complete loop (circuit) from the battery to the bulb and back again for it to light up.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think one connection is enough.

questions.stem: Which of these devices does NOT use a battery?
options: A television plugged into the wall
hints: It is plugged into a wall socket.
It is large and not portable.
questions.explanation: A television plugged into the wall uses electricity from the mains, not a battery.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all electronics use batteries.

questions.stem: Why do we put batteries in a flashlight instead of plugging it into a wall?
options: Because it needs to be portable and used anywhere
hints: You might need it when there is no wall socket.
questions.explanation: Batteries make a flashlight portable so you can carry it anywhere, even without a power outlet.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand the concept of portability.

questions.stem: What is needed to make electricity flow in a simple circuit?
hints: It must be a full circle.
questions.explanation: Electricity needs a complete, unbroken loop to flow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think broken circuits work.

questions.stem: Name one device in your home that uses batteries.
hints: What small device do you carry around?
questions.explanation: Common devices include torches, remote controls, watches, and radios.

questions.stem: Ama puts a battery into a torch the wrong way round. The torch does not light. Why?
options: The battery must be inserted correctly for the circuit to complete
The torch is afraid of the dark
hints: Batteries have positive and negative ends.
questions.explanation: Batteries must be placed in the correct direction to connect the circuit properly and let electricity flow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think you can put a battery in any way.

questions.stem: Why does a bulb go off if you cut the wire in a simple circuit?
options: Because the electricity can no longer flow in a complete loop
Because the wire is too long
hints: A cut wire breaks the path.
questions.explanation: Cutting the wire breaks the circuit, stopping the flow of electricity, so the bulb goes off.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cutting the wire destroys the electricity.

questions.stem: What does it mean when we say a battery is 'flat'?
options: It is physically flat in shape
It has run out of stored electrical energy
It is too big for the device
hints: It cannot power the device anymore.
You need to recharge or replace it.
questions.explanation: A 'flat' or 'dead' battery has used up its stored energy and cannot power the device.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think flat refers to the shape.

questions.stem: Which two components would you need to make a simple flashlight?
options: A battery, a bulb, and a wire (to make a circuit)
A bulb and a wire only
hints: You need power, a light, and a path.
The electricity needs to flow from one to the other.
questions.explanation: You need a battery (power), a bulb (light), and a wire (to make the complete circuit for electricity to flow).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think you just need a battery and a bulb touching.

questions.stem: Explain why a toy car will not move if the batteries are removed.

criteria.description: States that the batteries provide the energy
States that without batteries, the circuit is broken and electricity cannot flow

hints: What is the job of the batteries?
questions.explanation: Batteries provide the energy for the toy car. Without them, there is no source of electricity to complete the circuit and power the motor.

questions.stem: A student connects a wire to the positive end of a battery, then touches the other end of the wire to the same positive end. Will the bulb light up?
options: No, because the circuit is not complete (it bypasses the bulb and goes back to the same end)
Yes, if the battery is new
It depends on the colour of the wire
hints: The electricity needs to go through the bulb.
Connecting both ends to the same side does not make a complete loop through the bulb.
questions.explanation: The circuit is not complete. To light the bulb, the wire must go from one end of the battery, through the bulb, and back to the other end of the battery.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think touching a wire to a battery is enough.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to leave dead batteries in a device for a very long time?

criteria.description: States that dead batteries can leak acid or chemicals
States that this can damage the device or be harmful to the user

hints: It is not good to leave them inside.
questions.explanation: Old batteries can leak corrosive chemicals, which can ruin the device and be harmful if touched.

questions.stem: Using a battery, a bulb, and a wire, show your teacher how to make the bulb light up.

criteria.description: Connects one end of the wire to one end of the battery
Connects the other end of the wire to the other end of the battery
Successfully creates a complete circuit and lights the bulb

hints: Make sure the wire touches the metal parts.
questions.explanation: This demonstrates understanding of a simple circuit and the function of a battery as a power source.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.4.3.1: Know that movement is caused by applied forces due to the release of stored energy
indicator.objective: Discover the effects of forces on objects

skills.description: Describe the effects of forces on objects (making them move, stopping them, changing shape, changing direction, changing speed)
Identify everyday actions that apply force to an object
Demonstrate a force changing the shape, movement, or direction of an object
Explain simply why an object moved, stopped, or changed shape

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Forces only make things move; they cannot change shape.
If an object stops, no force was involved.
Only humans can apply force.
Pushing and pulling are the only forces.
A moving object has no force acting on it.

questions.stem: What happens to a ball when you kick it?
hints: You use your foot to push it.
questions.explanation: Kicking a ball applies a force that makes the ball move.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think kicking only changes the shape of the ball.

questions.stem: When you squeeze a sponge, what happens to its shape?
hints: You press it with your hands.
questions.explanation: Squeezing applies a force that changes the shape of the sponge.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think forces only cause movement, not shape changes.

questions.stem: Which of these actions applies a force to an object?
questions.explanation: Pushing a wheelbarrow applies a force that moves it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think looking at an object applies a force.

questions.stem: Which action involves pulling?
hints: You drag it along the ground.
questions.explanation: Dragging a bag involves pulling it towards you.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse pulling with pushing.

questions.stem: What happens to a moving toy car when you put your hand in front of it?
questions.explanation: Your hand applies a force that stops the moving toy car.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the car will go through the hand.

questions.stem: Ama squeezes a tube of toothpaste. What effect does her force have?
options: It changes the shape of the tube
It changes the colour of the tube
questions.explanation: Squeezing applies a force that changes the shape of the tube.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think squeezing changes the temperature.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a force changing the direction of a moving object?
options: Kicking a moving ball to the left
hints: You change where it is going.
questions.explanation: Kicking a moving ball to the left changes its direction.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize forces can change direction, not just start movement.

questions.stem: Kwame pushes a box on the floor. It starts to move. What effect did his push have?
questions.explanation: Kwame's push applied a force that made the stationary box move.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think you have to pull to make something move.

questions.stem: Which of these actions does NOT apply a force?
hints: Which action only uses your eyes?
questions.explanation: Watching a bird does not apply a force because you are not pushing or pulling anything.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think seeing something applies a force.

questions.stem: Why does a rolling ball eventually stop on its own?
options: Because the ground applies a friction force that slows it down
hints: The ground is not perfectly smooth.
There is rubbing between the ball and the floor.
questions.explanation: The ball stops because friction (a force from the ground and air) slows it down.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the ball stops because it runs out of energy completely.

questions.stem: Ama pushes a door, but it does not move. Why?
options: She is not applying a force
The door is too heavy or locked and resists her force
She is pulling instead of pushing
questions.explanation: The door does not move because another force (like friction or a lock) is pushing back against Ama's force. If the door is just too heavy, her force is not enough to overcome it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think no movement means no force was applied.

questions.stem: What happens to the shape of a rubber band when you stretch it?
hints: You pull it from both ends.
questions.explanation: Stretching applies a force that changes the shape of the rubber band, making it longer.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the rubber band breaks immediately.

questions.stem: Name one action that involves pushing an object.
hints: You move it away from you.
questions.explanation: Pushing a door or a box applies a force away from you.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name a pulling action.

questions.stem: Kofi is playing with a lump of clay. He presses it with his thumb. What effect does his force have?
options: It changes the shape of the clay
It turns the clay into stone
questions.explanation: The force from Kofi's thumb changes the shape of the clay.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not associate force with changing the shape of soft materials.

questions.stem: Why is it easier to move a chair by pushing it on a smooth floor than on a rough, sandy floor?
options: Because the chair is lighter on smooth floors
Because there is less friction force on the smooth floor
Because sand helps the chair move faster
hints: Think about rubbing your hands on sand.
questions.explanation: There is less friction (a resisting force) on a smooth floor, so it is easier to push the chair.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the chair changes weight.

questions.stem: Ama throws a ball up into the air. What force causes the ball to fall back down to the ground?
hints: It pulls things towards the Earth.
questions.explanation: Gravity is the force that pulls the ball back down to the Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the wind blows it down.

questions.stem: Show your teacher how you can use a force to change the shape of a piece of paper.

criteria.description: Performs an action that changes the shape of the paper (e.g., crumpling, folding, tearing)
Explains that they applied a force

questions.explanation: Crushing or folding the paper applies a force that changes its shape.

questions.stem: Explain why a moving bicycle slows down when the rider applies the brakes.

criteria.description: States that the brakes apply a force
States that this force causes the bicycle to slow down or stop

hints: What do the brakes do to the wheel?
They stop the wheel from turning.
questions.explanation: The brakes apply a friction force to the wheels, which slows down and eventually stops the bicycle.

questions.stem: Show your teacher how you can use a force to change the direction of a moving object.

criteria.description: Performs an action that changes direction (e.g., hitting a ball to the side)
Explains that they applied a force

hints: Roll a ball and hit it with a stick.
Kick a ball slightly to the side.
questions.explanation: Hitting or kicking a moving ball to the side applies a force that changes its direction.

questions.stem: A car is moving fast. The driver applies the brakes hard. What happens to the car and why?
options: It speeds up because of the force
It stops because the brakes apply a force opposing the motion
It changes colour because of heat
questions.explanation: The brakes apply a force that opposes the car's movement, causing it to slow down and stop.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stopping requires no force.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.4.3.2: Recognise some simple machines and their advantages of making work easier
indicator.objective: Identify simple machines used for specific work

skills.description: Identify simple machines used for specific work
Match a simple machine to the specific task it performs
Demonstrate or describe how to use a simple machine safely to complete a specific task
Explain why a specific simple machine is the right tool for a specific job

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Any tool can do any job.
A screwdriver can be used as a hammer.
Simple machines do the work for you without you doing anything.
Scissors are only for cutting paper; they cannot cut cloth.
Only complex machines (like cars or computers) are machines.

questions.stem: Which of these is a simple machine used for cutting paper?
questions.explanation: Scissors are a simple machine used for cutting paper, cloth, and other materials.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a spoon can cut paper.

questions.stem: Which simple machine is used to open a bottle of soft drink?
hints: You use it in the kitchen.
questions.explanation: A bottle opener is a simple machine specifically designed to remove bottle caps.
questions.misconception: Pupils may try to use a spoon or their teeth.

questions.stem: Which simple machine is used to sweep the floor?
questions.explanation: A broom is a simple machine used for sweeping.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not consider a broom a machine.

questions.stem: Ama wants to remove a nail from a piece of wood. Which tool should she use?
questions.explanation: A claw hammer is used for removing nails.
questions.misconception: Pupils may try to use scissors.

questions.stem: Which simple machine is used for cutting cloth?
questions.explanation: Scissors are used for cutting cloth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think scissors are only for paper.

questions.stem: Kofi is using a bottle opener. How should he hold it to open the bottle safely?
options: Point the sharp edge at his face
Hold it firmly and place it on the cap, then lift
hints: You need to grip the cap.
Do not point it at yourself.
questions.explanation: You should hold the opener firmly, place it correctly on the cap, and lift to remove the cap safely.
questions.misconception: Pupils may use tools incorrectly if not shown.

questions.stem: Why is a wheelbarrow useful for carrying heavy loads?
options: It has a wheel that helps it roll, making it easier to move heavy things
questions.explanation: A wheelbarrow has a wheel that reduces friction, making it easier to move heavy loads with less effort.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the wheelbarrow magically reduces the weight.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a simple machine?
hints: Which one is an electronic device?
It has a screen and needs electricity.
questions.explanation: A television is an electronic device, not a simple machine.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all tools are simple machines.

questions.stem: Which simple machine would you use to tighten a screw into a piece of wood?
hints: It has a shaped tip for screws.
questions.explanation: A screwdriver is used to turn and tighten screws.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a hammer is for screws.

questions.stem: Ama is using scissors to cut a piece of cloth. What is the safest way to hold the scissors?
hints: You put your fingers through loops.
questions.explanation: You should hold scissors by the handles to keep your fingers away from the sharp blades.
questions.misconception: Pupils may hold the blades, which is dangerous.

questions.stem: Why do we use a spoon rather than a fork to eat fufu?
options: A spoon can scoop and hold the soft fufu better than a fork
hints: A spoon has a bowl shape.
questions.explanation: A spoon is the right tool for eating fufu because its shape can scoop and hold the soft food, while a fork would just pierce it and let it fall.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any tool can eat any food.

questions.stem: Name the simple machine you would use to cut paper.
questions.explanation: Scissors are used to cut paper.

questions.stem: Name one simple machine you can find in a kitchen.
hints: You use it to open bottles.
You use it to cut or peel food.
questions.explanation: A bottle opener or a knife are simple machines found in the kitchen.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name an electronic device like a microwave.

questions.stem: Ama wants to open a tin of tomatoes. She only has a spoon, a hammer, a bottle opener, and a tin cutter. Which is the right tool and why?
options: A tin cutter, because it is made to cut metal tins safely
A hammer, because it can smash the tin
A spoon, because it is small
A bottle opener, because it is metal
hints: Which tool is designed for tins?
Using a hammer would be dangerous and messy.
questions.explanation: A tin cutter is the correct simple machine designed to safely open metal tins.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose dangerous improvised tools.

questions.stem: Why does a broom make sweeping easier than using your bare hands?
options: The broom handle reaches further and the bristles gather dirt better
hints: Think about the length of the handle.
questions.explanation: A broom makes sweeping easier because the long handle lets you reach the floor without bending, and the bristles gather dirt efficiently.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not think about the physical advantage of the tool.

questions.stem: Kofi is trying to pull a nail out of a piece of wood using a hammer. He holds the hammer by the head and tries to pull. Why is this wrong?
options: He should hold the handle to get leverage and use the claw part
He should use the flat part
hints: You need to grip the handle.
questions.explanation: Kofi should hold the hammer by the handle to get a good grip and leverage, and use the claw part to grip and pull the nail.
questions.misconception: Pupils may use tools incorrectly without understanding leverage.

questions.stem: Which simple machine would a tailor use to remove a stubborn button from a shirt?
hints: They need to cut the thread.
questions.explanation: A tailor would use scissors to cut the thread holding the button.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose a tool that would damage the shirt.

questions.stem: Explain why it is better to use a wheelbarrow to carry stones than to carry them in your hands.

criteria.description: States that the wheelbarrow holds more stones
States that the wheel helps roll the load, reducing the effort needed

hints: How many stones can you carry in your hands?
questions.explanation: A wheelbarrow carries more stones and the wheel reduces the effort needed to move the heavy load.

questions.stem: Show your teacher how to safely use a pair of scissors to cut a straight line on a piece of paper.

criteria.description: Keeps fingers away from the blades

hints: Put your fingers in the loops.
questions.explanation: This tests the safe and correct use of a simple machine.

questions.stem: Ama says 'I can use a spoon to cut my meat.' Why is this a bad idea?
options: A spoon is not sharp and cannot cut meat; a knife is the right tool
A spoon is made of metal
A spoon is for soup only
hints: Spoons are for scooping, not cutting.
questions.explanation: A spoon is not designed to cut. It would squash the meat instead of cutting it. A knife is the correct simple machine for cutting meat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may try to use the wrong tool for a job.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.5.1.1: Recognise the importance of personal hygiene
indicator.objective: Explain how to keep the body clean and describe why it is important

skills.description: Describe ways to keep the body clean
Explain why keeping the body clean is important
Explain why we trim our finger nails and hair
Explain why we should not share personal items
Demonstrate or describe how to use items for trimming hair and nails correctly

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: You only need to keep your body clean when you are visibly dirty.
Trimming nails and hair is only for looking good, not for health.
Sharing combs and towels is fine because they are just for grooming.
Bathing once a week is enough.
Germs only live in dirt you can see.
Wearing clean clothes is not part of personal hygiene.

questions.stem: Which of these is a good way to keep your body clean?
questions.explanation: Bathing with soap and water is one of the best ways to keep your body clean.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think playing in the mud is a way to clean.

questions.stem: What should you use to clean your teeth?
hints: You use it in your mouth.
questions.explanation: A toothbrush and toothpaste are used to clean your teeth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse items used for different hygiene routines.

questions.stem: Why is it important to keep your body clean?
questions.explanation: Keeping your body clean prevents germs from making you sick.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not see the link between hygiene and health.

questions.stem: How often should you take a bath?
questions.explanation: You should bathe every day to remove dirt and germs.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think bathing once a week is enough.

questions.stem: Should you share your toothbrush with a friend?
options: Yes, if they are your best friend
questions.explanation: You should not share your toothbrush because it can spread germs from one person to another.
questions.misconception: Pupils may share personal items with friends without knowing the risks.

questions.stem: Why should you cut your finger nails regularly?
options: To keep them clean and prevent dirt from hiding under them
To make them sharp like a knife
hints: Dirt gets stuck under long nails.
questions.explanation: Cutting your nails keeps them short and clean, preventing dirt and germs from hiding underneath.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think long nails are just a style choice.

questions.stem: Why do we wear clean clothes?
options: To stay clean and avoid skin diseases
questions.explanation: Wearing clean clothes helps keep your skin clean and prevents skin diseases.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think clothes only need washing when visibly dirty.

questions.stem: Ama and her sister use the same comb. Why is this a bad idea?
options: They can spread germs like lice or ringworm
hints: What is on the comb after use?
questions.explanation: Sharing a comb can spread germs, lice, or skin diseases like ringworm from one person to another.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sharing is always good without considering germs.

questions.stem: Which of these is part of keeping your body clean?
questions.explanation: Washing your hands before eating is an important part of personal hygiene.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not see hand-washing as part of body cleanliness.

questions.stem: What can happen if you do not keep your body clean?
options: You can get skin diseases and fall sick
questions.explanation: Not keeping your body clean allows germs to grow, which can cause skin diseases and other sicknesses.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect poor hygiene to illness.

questions.stem: What should you use to cut your finger nails?
questions.explanation: A nail cutter or nail clipper is the correct tool for trimming finger nails.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say teeth or a knife, which are dangerous.

questions.stem: Name two things you need to bathe.
questions.explanation: You need water and soap (and a sponge and towel) to bathe.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to bite your finger nails?
options: It can damage your teeth and allow germs into your body
It makes your nails grow faster
It is good for your health
hints: Teeth are not for biting nails.
questions.explanation: Biting your nails can damage your teeth and allow germs from under the nails to enter your body, making you sick.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think biting nails is harmless.

questions.stem: Why should you not share a towel with someone who has a skin disease?
options: The towel might be too small
The germs from their skin can transfer to you
questions.explanation: Sharing a towel with an infected person can transfer germs to your skin, causing you to catch the disease.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize diseases can spread through shared items.

questions.stem: Why is it important to keep your finger nails clean?
options: Because you use your fingers to eat and touch your face, and germs can enter your body
hints: What do you do with your fingers?
How do germs get into your body?
questions.explanation: You use your fingers for many tasks, including eating. If your nails are dirty, germs can enter your body and make you sick.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think nail hygiene is only about appearance.

questions.stem: Show your teacher how to correctly use a nail cutter to trim your nails.
hints: Do not cut too close to the skin.
questions.explanation: This tests the safe and correct use of a nail cutter.

questions.stem: Describe how you keep your body clean each day. Write at least three things you do.

criteria.description: Mentions washing hands or wearing clean clothes

hints: What do you do in the bathroom?
questions.explanation: A daily routine includes bathing, brushing teeth, and washing hands.

questions.stem: Explain why keeping your body clean is important for your health.

criteria.description: States that it prevents germs from entering the body
States that it prevents sickness or skin diseases

hints: What do germs do to your body?
questions.explanation: Keeping clean removes germs and prevents sickness.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher two personal items you should not share and explain why.

criteria.description: Names a personal item (e.g., toothbrush, towel, comb)
Explains that sharing can spread germs or diseases

hints: What do you use on your body only?
Why is it bad to share?
questions.explanation: Items like toothbrushes, towels, and combs should not be shared because they can spread germs.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2. 5.2.1: Know common diseases of humans, causes, symptoms, effects and prevention
indicator.objective: Identify causes and prevention of ringworm

skills.description: Identify the causes of ringworm
Identify ways to prevent ringworm
Recognise the signs of ringworm
Address common misconceptions about ringworm

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Ringworm is caused by a real worm.
Ringworm is caused by a curse or witchcraft.
You can only get ringworm if you are visibly dirty.
Sharing a towel or comb is safe because it is just for grooming.
Ringworm will go away on its own without any treatment.

questions.stem: What causes ringworm?
questions.explanation: Ringworm is caused by a fungus (germ), not a real worm.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think ringworm is caused by a real worm.

questions.stem: What does ringworm look like on the skin?
hints: It is shaped like a ring.
questions.explanation: Ringworm appears as a red, circular, itchy patch on the skin.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it looks like a worm.

questions.stem: How can you prevent ringworm?
options: Keep your skin clean and dry
questions.explanation: Keeping your skin clean and dry helps prevent ringworm.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not link hygiene to ringworm prevention.

questions.stem: Which of these can cause ringworm to spread?
options: Sharing a towel with an infected person
questions.explanation: Sharing a towel or comb with an infected person can spread the ringworm fungus.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize skin diseases spread through shared items.

questions.stem: What should you do if you think you have ringworm?
options: Tell a parent and go to a clinic
hints: A health worker can give medicine.
questions.explanation: You should tell a parent and go to a clinic for treatment.

questions.stem: Ama says 'Ringworm is caused by a real worm.' Is she right?
options: No, it is caused by a germ (fungus)
Yes, it is a small insect
No, it is caused by a curse
hints: Do you see a worm in the patch?
questions.explanation: Ama is not right. Ringworm is caused by a fungus, not a real worm.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think ringworm is a literal worm.

questions.stem: Kwame has a round, red, itchy patch on his arm. What might it be?
questions.explanation: A round, red, itchy patch on the skin is a common sign of ringworm.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse ringworm with other diseases.

questions.stem: Why should you not share your towel with a friend who has ringworm?
options: The towel might be too small
The germs can transfer from their skin to the towel and then to you
questions.explanation: Sharing a towel with an infected person can spread the ringworm fungus to you.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sharing is always safe.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a cause of ringworm?
hints: Which one does not affect the skin?
Sugar is food, not a skin germ.
questions.explanation: Eating too much sugar does not cause ringworm. Ringworm is caused by a fungus and spreads through poor hygiene and shared items.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think food causes skin diseases.

questions.stem: Ama has ringworm. What should she do with her towel and clothes?
options: Wash them separately with hot water and soap
questions.explanation: Ama should wash her towel and clothes separately with hot water and soap to kill the fungus and prevent spreading.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know how to prevent spreading.

questions.stem: What type of germ causes ringworm?
hints: It grows in warm, moist places.
questions.explanation: Ringworm is caused by a fungus.

questions.stem: Describe what ringworm looks like on the skin.
questions.explanation: Ringworm appears as a round, red, itchy patch on the skin.
questions.misconception: Pupils may describe it as a worm.

questions.stem: Why is it important to dry your body properly after bathing to prevent ringworm?
options: Because the fungus grows well in warm, wet places
hints: Dry skin is less welcoming to fungus.
questions.explanation: Ringworm fungus thrives in warm, moist areas. Drying your body properly removes moisture and helps prevent infection.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize moisture encourages fungal growth.

questions.stem: A student says 'Only poor people get ringworm.' Why is this statement wrong?
options: Ringworm is caused by a fungus, not by poverty; anyone can get it if they come into contact with the germ
Ringworm is not a real disease
questions.explanation: Ringworm is caused by a fungus, and anyone can get it regardless of wealth if they come into contact with the germ.
questions.misconception: Pupils may associate diseases with poverty.

questions.stem: Write down two ways to prevent ringworm.

criteria.description: States keeping the skin clean and dry
States not sharing personal items like towels or combs

hints: What should your skin be like?
questions.explanation: Prevention includes keeping skin clean and dry, and not sharing personal items.

questions.stem: Explain how ringworm spreads from one person to another.

criteria.description: States that the fungus can be on shared items like towels, combs, or clothes
States that touching these items or the infected person's skin can pass the germ on

questions.explanation: Ringworm spreads when a person touches the infected skin or shares items like towels, combs, or clothes that have the fungus on them.

questions.stem: A family shares one towel in the bathroom. One child gets ringworm. What is the BEST action to stop it from spreading?
options: Give each person their own towel and wash them separately
Use the same towel but wash it once a month
Ignore it because it will go away
questions.explanation: Giving each person their own towel and washing them separately prevents the fungus from spreading to others.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize shared items spread disease.

questions.stem: Explain why ringworm is NOT caused by a worm, even though it is called 'ringworm'.

criteria.description: States that it is caused by a fungus (germ)
States that the name comes from the ring-shaped rash, not a worm

hints: Look at the shape of the rash.
It is a germ, not an animal.
questions.explanation: Ringworm is caused by a fungus, not a worm. It is called ringworm because the rash forms a ring shape on the skin.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher what you would do if you saw a round, itchy patch on your skin.

criteria.description: States they would tell a parent or teacher
States they would go to a clinic for treatment

questions.explanation: You should tell an adult and seek medical treatment for the rash.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.5.3.1: Recognize the impact of science and technology in society
indicator.objective: Identify the technological devices used in the community and describe their impact

skills.description: Identify technological devices used in the community
Describe the impact of technology on society
Compare how things were done in the past without technology
Draw a technological device and describe how it helps the community

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Technology only means mobile phones and computers.
Life was exactly the same before these technologies were invented.
Technology has no effect on how people live.
A sewing machine or a car is not technology.
Technology can solve every problem without any human effort.

questions.stem: Which of these is a technological device used in the community?
questions.explanation: A mobile phone is a technological device used for communication in the community.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think natural things are technology.

questions.stem: Which of these technologies helps people travel from one town to another?
questions.explanation: A car is a technology used for transportation.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name household items instead of transport.

questions.stem: How does a mobile phone help people?
options: It helps them talk to people far away
hints: You can talk to someone in another town.
questions.explanation: A mobile phone helps people communicate with others who are far away.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think phones have physical abilities.

questions.stem: How did people send messages to far places before mobile phones were invented?
options: By sending letters through the post
hints: It took a long time to arrive.
questions.explanation: Before phones, people sent letters by post, which took much longer.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think people always had phones.

questions.stem: Which of these is a technology used in hospitals?
questions.explanation: A thermometer is a technological device used in hospitals to check body temperature.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not think of medical tools as technology.

questions.stem: How has technology helped farmers?
options: By providing tools like tractors to farm faster
By making crops grow without water
By making the sun shine at night
hints: Think about machines on a farm.
It helps them do work faster.
questions.explanation: Technology has helped farmers by providing tools like tractors that make farming faster and easier.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think technology controls the weather.

questions.stem: How has technology helped doctors and nurses in hospitals?
options: By providing machines to check and treat sick people
By making sick people run faster
By making medicine taste like sweets
hints: Doctors use machines to help patients.
questions.explanation: Technology has helped doctors and nurses by providing medical machines and tools to check and treat patients.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand the medical applications of technology.

questions.stem: How did people travel long distances before cars and buses were invented?
options: By walking or using animals like horses
hints: What did people use before engines?
They used their feet or animals.
questions.explanation: Before cars and buses, people walked or used animals like horses and donkeys for long journeys.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think modern transport always existed.

questions.stem: Which of these is a technological device used in a market?
hints: Traders use it to sell food.
questions.explanation: A weighing scale is a technological device used in markets to measure the weight of goods.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not think of simple tools as technology.

questions.stem: What impact has the mobile phone had on how people do business in Ghana?
options: Traders can call customers and arrange deliveries easily
Traders can no longer sell goods
Traders have to walk to every customer
hints: They can call or send mobile money.
questions.explanation: Mobile phones allow traders to communicate quickly with customers, arrange deliveries, and even receive payments through mobile money, making business easier.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not see the business impact of phones.

questions.stem: Name one technological device used in your community.
hints: What helps people communicate or travel?
questions.explanation: Common devices include mobile phones, cars, radios, and televisions.

questions.stem: Name one way a mobile phone has changed how people live.
answer: we can talk to people far away
hints: How do you contact your friends?
questions.explanation: Mobile phones have changed how we live by allowing us to communicate easily, send money, and access information.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not see the impact of phones beyond playing games.

questions.stem: How has technology changed the way people get water in many communities?
options: People can use boreholes and pumps instead of walking to rivers
People use stones to get water
questions.explanation: Technology like boreholes and pumps has made it easier to get clean water without walking long distances to rivers.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect water access to technology.

questions.stem: Ama says 'Technology only means mobile phones and computers.' Is she right?
options: No, things like cars and radios are also technology
Yes, only phones and computers are technology
hints: Is a car made by people to help us?
questions.explanation: Technology includes any tool or machine made by people to help us, not just phones and computers.
questions.misconception: Pupils often limit technology to digital devices.

questions.stem: How did people preserve food before refrigerators were invented?
options: By drying, smoking, or salting it
By putting it in the freezer
By using ice blocks from shops
hints: The sun and fire were used.
questions.explanation: Before fridges, people preserved food by drying it in the sun, smoking it over a fire, or salting it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think people always had fridges.

questions.stem: What is one negative impact of technology on the environment?
questions.explanation: Technology can cause pollution from factories, cars, and electronic waste, which harms the environment.
questions.misconception: Pupils may only see the positive side of technology.

questions.stem: Draw one technological device used in your community. Write a sentence to describe how it helps people.

criteria.description: Writes a correct description of how it helps

hints: Think of a car or a phone.
questions.explanation: This tests identification of technology and its impact.

questions.stem: Explain how technology has changed the way people communicate in Ghana over the past 50 years.

criteria.description: States that people used to send letters, which took a long time
States that people now use mobile phones to call, text, and use the internet instantly

hints: How did people communicate before phones?
questions.explanation: In the past, people relied on letters that took days or weeks. Now, mobile phones allow instant communication across the country and the world.

questions.stem: Write down one positive and one negative impact of technology on society.

criteria.description: States a positive impact (e.g., faster communication, easier travel)
States a negative impact (e.g., pollution, job loss)

questions.explanation: Positive: faster communication. Negative: pollution from factories and cars.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher about one technological device you use at home and explain how it has changed your life.

criteria.description: Explains how it has changed their life

hints: Think about your phone or TV.
What can you do now that you couldn't before?
questions.explanation: This tests the ability to identify technology and its personal impact.

indicator.subject: Science
