indicator.content_standard: B2.5.3.2: Exhibit knowledge of food processing and preservation
indicator.objective: Know the ways foods are processed for consumption

skills.description: Explain why food must be processed before it is consumed
Name ways food is processed
Match a raw food to the correct processing method
Present a sample of raw food and describe how it can be processed for consumption

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Food processing means adding chemicals.
Raw food is always better than processed food.
Processing and preservation are exactly the same thing.
Food only needs to be processed if it is dirty.
You can eat all foods raw.

questions.stem: Which of these is a way of processing food?
hints: You do it in a pot.
questions.explanation: Boiling is a common method of processing food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know the word 'processing'.

questions.stem: Why do we process food before eating it?
options: To make it safe and easier to eat
questions.explanation: Processing food makes it safe to eat by killing germs and makes it easier to chew and digest.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think processing is just for taste.

questions.stem: What do we do to maize before we can eat it as kenkey or banku?
questions.explanation: Maize is ground into flour and cooked to make kenkey or banku.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect the raw maize to the final food.

questions.stem: Why do we wash vegetables before cooking them?
hints: They can have dirt on them.
questions.explanation: Washing vegetables removes dirt, sand, and germs before cooking.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think washing is just for appearance.

questions.stem: Which method is used to process cassava into gari?
hints: Gari is made from grated cassava.
It is fried in a pan.
questions.explanation: Cassava is grated, fermented, and fried to make gari.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think gari is made by boiling.

questions.stem: Which of these is a method of processing food?
questions.explanation: Frying is a method of processing food using hot oil.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know frying is a processing method.

questions.stem: Why do we dry food like fish and maize in the sun?
options: To remove water and preserve it for a long time
questions.explanation: Drying food in the sun removes moisture, which helps preserve it so it doesn't spoil quickly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think drying makes food taste better only.

questions.stem: Which processing method is used to make bread?
hints: It is cooked in an oven.
questions.explanation: Bread is made by baking dough in an oven.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a food processing method?
hints: Which one is for walls, not food?
questions.explanation: Painting is not a food processing method.

questions.stem: Why is it important to cook meat properly before eating it?
options: To kill germs and make it safe to eat
questions.explanation: Cooking meat properly kills harmful germs, making it safe to eat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand the health risk of undercooked meat.

questions.stem: What processing method is used to make fufu?
questions.explanation: Fufu is made by boiling cassava or plantain and then pounding it into a soft dough.

questions.stem: Name two ways food can be processed for eating.
questions.explanation: Boiling and frying are two common ways to process food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name only one method.

questions.stem: Ama says 'Raw food is always better than cooked food.' Is she right?
options: No, some raw foods have germs and need to be cooked to be safe
Yes, raw food is always healthier
No, cooked food has no nutrients
hints: Raw meat can make you sick.
questions.explanation: Ama is not right. While some foods can be eaten raw, many foods like meat, fish, and some vegetables must be cooked to kill germs and be safe to eat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think raw is always better.

questions.stem: What happens to rice when you process it by boiling?
options: It becomes hard like a stone
questions.explanation: Boiling rice makes it absorb water, becoming soft and edible.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think rice can be eaten raw.

questions.stem: Why do we preserve food like fish by smoking it?
options: Smoking removes moisture and adds flavour, making it last longer
questions.explanation: Smoking dries the fish and adds flavour, which helps preserve it for a longer time.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know smoking preserves food.

questions.stem: Bring a raw food item (e.g., maize, cassava, or plantain) to class. Show your teacher how it can be processed for eating and explain the steps.

criteria.description: Describes or demonstrates a correct processing method
Explains why the processing is needed

hints: What do you do with it before eating?
questions.explanation: This tests knowledge of food processing methods and their importance.

questions.stem: Describe how you would process a raw cassava tuber to make it safe to eat.
questions.explanation: Cassava must be peeled and cooked (boiled or fried) to remove harmful substances and make it safe to eat.

questions.stem: Which of these foods is usually eaten raw without processing?
hints: You peel it and eat it.
questions.explanation: A banana is usually eaten raw because it is safe and soft, while chicken, maize, and cassava must be cooked.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all foods must be cooked.

questions.stem: Explain why food processing is important for keeping us healthy.

criteria.description: States that it makes food safe to eat and easier to digest

hints: What do germs do to your body?
questions.explanation: Food processing kills germs and makes food safe and easier to digest, which keeps us healthy.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher the steps you would take to process a raw egg before eating it.

criteria.description: States that the egg must be cooked (boiled or fried)
Explains that cooking kills germs and makes it safe to eat

hints: Can you eat a raw egg?
What happens when you boil it?
questions.explanation: Eggs must be cooked (boiled or fried) to kill germs and make them safe to eat.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.1.1: Show understanding of the physical features and life processes of living things and use this understanding to classify them
indicator.objective: Classify living things into plants and animals by their life processes

skills.description: Identify a given living thing as a plant or an animal
Recognise key features/life processes used to classify them
Choose the best reason why a living thing is classified as a plant or an animal based on its life processes
Sort a small group of living things into plants and animals

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Anything that moves is an animal, and anything that does not move is a plant.
All animals live on land.
Plants are not living things because they do not eat food like us.
Seaweed and water lilies are animals because they live in water.
Trees are not plants; they are just wood.

questions.stem: Which of these living things is a plant?
questions.explanation: A mango tree is a plant because it has roots, a stem, and leaves, and it makes its own food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think anything green is just a decoration, not a living plant.

questions.stem: Which of these living things is an animal?
hints: It moves around and eats food.
It has four legs and gives milk.
questions.explanation: A cow is an animal because it moves, eats food, and breathes.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think animals must be wild.

questions.stem: Is a fish a plant or an animal?
hints: It does not have roots or leaves.
questions.explanation: A fish is an animal because it moves, eats, and breathes (using gills).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fish are not animals because they live in water.

questions.stem: Which of these features is usually found in plants but NOT in animals?
questions.explanation: Roots are a feature of plants that help them take in water and stay in the soil.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think animals have roots.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an animal?
hints: It does not move from place to place.
questions.explanation: A rose plant is a plant, not an animal. It has roots, leaves, and flowers.
questions.misconception: Pupils may classify a rose as an animal because it is colourful.

questions.stem: Which life process helps us tell that a plant is a living thing?
hints: Plants use sunlight to make food.
questions.explanation: Plants are living things because they make their own food, grow, and reproduce, even though they do not run or talk.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants are non-living because they do not move.

questions.stem: Why is a dog classified as an animal?
options: Because it can move and eat food
hints: Think about what it does to stay alive.
questions.explanation: A dog is an animal because it moves, eats food, breathes, and reproduces.
questions.misconception: Pupils may classify by colour or size instead of life processes.

questions.stem: Which group has ONLY plants?
hints: Which group has things that grow in the soil and have leaves?
questions.explanation: Maize, grass, and a pawpaw tree are all plants.
questions.misconception: Pupils may put a goat in the plant group because it eats grass.

questions.stem: Ama says 'A stone is a plant because it does not move.' Why is she wrong?
options: A stone cannot grow or make food; it is non-living, not a plant
A stone is a type of plant
A stone is a living thing
questions.explanation: A stone is non-living, not a plant. Plants are living things that grow and make food.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think anything that does not move is a plant.

questions.stem: Which of these life processes is common to BOTH plants and animals?
options: They both make their own food
hints: Do both get bigger over time?
questions.explanation: Both plants and animals grow. They are both living things.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants do not grow.

questions.stem: Sort these into plants and animals: goat, maize, fish, orange tree.
answer: plants: maize, orange tree; animals: goat, fish
hints: Which two have leaves and roots?
questions.explanation: Maize and the orange tree are plants. The goat and fish are animals.
questions.misconception: Pupils may struggle with the fish because it lives in water.

questions.stem: Give one reason why a mango tree is a plant and not an animal.
answer: it does not move from place to place
hints: Where does it get its food?
questions.explanation: A mango tree is a plant because it has roots, makes its own food, and does not move from place to place.
questions.misconception: Pupils may focus on what it produces (mangoes) rather than its features.

questions.stem: Why is a frog classified as an animal, even though it can live in water?
options: It moves, eats food, and breathes
hints: Think about what makes an animal an animal.
questions.explanation: A frog is an animal because it is a living thing that moves, eats food, and breathes, regardless of where it lives.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water-dwelling creatures are not animals.

questions.stem: Which of these sets of features best describes an animal?
options: Has roots, makes food, stays in one place
Has leaves, grows tall, needs sunlight
Has a stem, flowers, and roots
hints: Think about how animals get their food.
questions.explanation: Animals move around, eat food, and breathe. The other options describe plants.
questions.misconception: Pupils may mix up plant and animal features.

questions.stem: Kofi finds an organism that grows in the soil, has green leaves, and does not move from place to place. How should he classify it?
hints: It has leaves and grows in the soil.
These are features of a plant.
questions.explanation: Organisms that grow in the soil, have green leaves, and do not move are classified as plants.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it is non-living because it does not move.

questions.stem: Ama has four pictures: a dog, a seaweed, a cow, and a water lily. Which are the plants?
hints: Which ones make their own food and have roots/leaves?
Which ones live in water but are still plants?
questions.explanation: Seaweed and water lilies are plants, even though they live in water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all water-dwelling things are animals.

questions.stem: Write down two features that tell you a living thing is a plant.

criteria.description: States a correct plant feature (e.g., has roots, leaves, makes its own food)
States a second correct plant feature

questions.explanation: Plants have roots, stems, leaves, and make their own food using sunlight.

questions.stem: Ama says 'A moving car is an animal because it moves.' Why is she wrong?
options: A car cannot grow, eat, or breathe
hints: Can a car make baby cars?
questions.explanation: A car is non-living. Even though it moves, it cannot grow, eat, breathe, or reproduce like an animal.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think movement is the only sign of life.

questions.stem: Explain why a fish is an animal even though it lives in water.

criteria.description: States that it moves and eats food
States that it breathes (using gills) and is a living thing

questions.explanation: A fish is an animal because it is a living thing that moves, eats, and breathes, even though it lives in water.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher one plant and one animal you can see in your community, and explain how you know which is which.

criteria.description: Names a plant and an animal
Explains a correct feature for each (e.g., plant has leaves/roots, animal moves/eats)

hints: Does it move? Does it have leaves?
questions.explanation: This tests the ability to classify using observable features.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.2.1: Recognize materials as important resources for providing human needs
indicator.objective: Identify the uses of everyday materials and link the uses to their properties

skills.description: Identify the uses of everyday materials
Link a property of a material to its use
Match an object to the material it is made from and explain why
Choose the best explanation of why a material is used for a specific purpose

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Glass is used because it is pretty, not because it is transparent.
Metal is used for pots because it is shiny, not because it conducts heat.
Any material can be used for any purpose.
Plastic is always better than wood.
Clay is used for pots because it is soft, not because it can be moulded and baked hard.

questions.stem: What is wood commonly used for?
options: Making furniture like tables and chairs
questions.explanation: Wood is commonly used to make furniture like tables and chairs.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wood is only used for burning.

questions.stem: What is glass commonly used for?
questions.explanation: Glass is commonly used for window panes because it lets light in.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse glass with plastic.

questions.stem: Why is metal used for making cooking pots?
hints: The heat needs to reach the food.
questions.explanation: Metal is used for cooking pots because it conducts heat well, allowing the food to cook.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think metal is used just because it is shiny.

questions.stem: Why is clay used for making pots?
options: Because it is bendable and can be moulded
Because it is waterproof when dry
hints: Clay is soft and wet at first.
You can shape it with your hands.
questions.explanation: Clay is used for pots because it can be moulded into shapes before it is baked hard.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think clay is used because it is hard.

questions.stem: Which material is best for making a raincoat because it keeps water out?
hints: It must not soak up water.
questions.explanation: Plastic is used for raincoats because it is waterproof and keeps the rain out.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any cloth keeps water out.

questions.stem: Which property of glass makes it suitable for windows?
questions.explanation: Glass is transparent, allowing light to enter the room and people to see outside.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say glass is used because it is smooth.

questions.stem: Ama wants to make a bucket to carry water. Which material should she use?
hints: It must not tear or break easily.
questions.explanation: Plastic is a good material for a bucket because it is strong and waterproof.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose glass because it holds water, but it breaks easily.

questions.stem: Kwame needs to cut a piece of paper. Which material is best for making a tool to cut it?
hints: The tool needs to be sharp.
questions.explanation: Metal is used for cutting tools like scissors because it can be made sharp and hard.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose wood because it is hard, but it cannot be made sharp enough easily.

questions.stem: Why is cloth used for making clothes?
hints: You need to move your body.
questions.explanation: Cloth is used for clothes because it is soft and bendable, making it comfortable to wear.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not link comfort to the property of being soft.

questions.stem: Which material is used to make a tyre for a car?
hints: It must be strong and bendable.
questions.explanation: Rubber is used for tyres because it is strong, bendable, and grips the road well.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think metal is best because it is strong, but metal would be too hard and slippery.

questions.stem: Why is plastic commonly used for making water bottles?
options: Because it is light and waterproof
questions.explanation: Plastic is used for water bottles because it is light (easy to carry) and waterproof (holds liquid).
questions.misconception: Pupils may not consider weight as a property.

questions.stem: Name one use of metal in the home.
hints: What are your spoons made of?
questions.explanation: Metal is used for cooking pots, spoons, and many other items in the home.

questions.stem: Why is a sponge used for bathing? (Hint: Think about its property)
hints: What happens when you put it in water?
questions.explanation: A sponge is used for bathing because it is soft on the skin and absorbs water and soap.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say it is used because it is colourful.

questions.stem: Ama wants to buy a cup that will not break if she drops it. Which material should she choose?
questions.explanation: Plastic is a better choice than glass or clay because it is less likely to break when dropped.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all cups are made of glass.

questions.stem: Why is wood a better material for a cooking spoon than metal?
options: Wood does not get as hot as metal, so it is safer to hold
questions.explanation: Wood is a poor conductor of heat, so the handle of a wooden spoon does not get as hot as a metal one, making it safer to use.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think metal is better for all kitchen tools.

questions.stem: Why do we use glass for car windshields instead of wood?
options: Glass is transparent, allowing the driver to see the road
hints: The driver needs to see clearly.
questions.explanation: Glass is used because it is transparent and lets the driver see the road, whereas wood is opaque.
questions.misconception: Pupils may focus on strength rather than visibility.

questions.stem: Explain why clay is a good material for making a water pot.

criteria.description: States that clay can be moulded into shape
States that when baked, it becomes hard and can hold water

hints: Can you shape clay with your hands?
What happens when it is baked in a fire?
questions.explanation: Clay is mouldable when wet, so it can be shaped into a pot. When baked, it becomes hard and waterproof enough to hold water.

questions.stem: A tailor needs to make a school bag. Write down one material the tailor could use and explain why its properties make it suitable.

criteria.description: Names a suitable material (e.g., cloth, leather, plastic)
Explains a property that makes it suitable (e.g., strong, bendable, waterproof)

hints: Does it need to be strong?
questions.explanation: Cloth is suitable because it is strong and bendable, allowing it to hold books without tearing.

questions.stem: Why would a metal bucket be BAD for carrying hot water, while a plastic bucket might also be bad?
options: Metal conducts heat (gets hot quickly) and plastic might melt or soften
Metal is too heavy and plastic is too light
Metal is transparent and plastic is opaque
hints: Think about holding a hot metal pot.
questions.explanation: Metal conducts heat quickly, making it dangerous to hold. Plastic may soften or melt when in contact with very hot water. Both have drawbacks for hot water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not consider the effect of heat on plastic.

questions.stem: A company wants to make a cheap, light, and waterproof raincoat. Which material is most suitable?
hints: It must be light to wear.
questions.explanation: A thin plastic sheet is cheap, light, and waterproof, making it ideal for a cheap raincoat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think leather is best, but it is heavy and expensive.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.2.1: Recognize materials as important resources for providing human needs
indicator.objective: Demonstrate understanding that an object is made of one or more materials

skills.description: Recognise that an object can be made of one material or more than one material
Identify the materials that make up a given object
Give examples of objects made of one material and objects made of more than one material
Explain why some objects need to be made of more than one material

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Every object is made of only one material.
A computer is made of only plastic.
If an object has different parts, they must all be made of the same material.
Glass and plastic are the same because they can both be clear.

questions.stem: Is a wooden spoon made of one material or more than one material?
questions.explanation: A simple wooden spoon is made of just one material: wood.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all objects are made of many materials.

questions.stem: Is a mobile phone made of one material or more than one material?
hints: Look at the screen and the case.
questions.explanation: A mobile phone is made of more than one material, such as plastic, glass, and metal.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a phone is just one solid block of material.

questions.stem: Which materials are used to make a simple wooden pencil?
hints: What is the dark part inside?
questions.explanation: A pencil is made of wood (the outside) and graphite (the dark writing part inside).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a pencil is only wood.

questions.stem: Which of these objects is made of just one material?
hints: Which one is natural and solid all the way through?
questions.explanation: A stone is made of one material (rock).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think simple objects are made of many materials.

questions.stem: A ruler is made of one material. What is it likely to be?
questions.explanation: Many simple rulers are made of just one material, like plastic or wood.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think rulers have multiple parts.

questions.stem: Kofi has a school bag. It has a main body, a zip, and straps. What materials is it likely made of?
questions.explanation: A school bag is made of multiple materials: cloth for the body, metal for the zip, and sometimes plastic for the straps.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the whole bag is just one material.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of an object made of more than one material?
hints: Are the blades and handles the same material?
questions.explanation: Scissors are made of metal (blades) and plastic or metal (handles).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think scissors are just metal.

questions.stem: What is a glass window made of?
hints: Look at the part that holds it.
questions.explanation: A window is made of glass (the pane) and wood or metal (the frame).
questions.misconception: Pupils may say it is only glass.

questions.stem: Why is a computer made of more than one material (plastic, glass, metal)?
options: Because different parts need different properties
Because it is a big object
Because it is made in a factory
hints: What is the screen made of?
What is the case made of?
questions.explanation: Different materials are used because they have different properties: glass is transparent for the screen, plastic is mouldable for the case, and metal conducts electricity for the wires.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think objects are made of multiple materials just because they look complex.

questions.stem: Ama has a pair of shoes. The top is leather and the bottom is rubber. What are the materials?
questions.explanation: The shoes are made of leather (the top) and rubber (the sole).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think shoes are only one material.

questions.stem: Name one object in your classroom made of more than one material.
hints: Does it have different parts made of different things?
questions.explanation: A chair is often made of wood (seat) and metal (legs).
questions.misconception: Pupils may name an object that is just one material.

questions.stem: Name the two main materials used to make a pencil.
questions.explanation: A pencil is made of wood and graphite.

questions.stem: Why is a car made of metal, glass, rubber, and plastic?
options: Because each material has properties suited for specific parts (e.g., glass for seeing, rubber for tyres)
Because the factory has many materials
Because it is a large object
questions.explanation: Different parts of a car require different properties. Glass is transparent, rubber is strong and flexible, and metal is hard, so multiple materials are needed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think materials are chosen randomly.

questions.stem: Ama says 'All objects are made of only one material.' Is she right?
options: No, some objects like phones and cars are made of more than one material
Yes, all objects are just one material
No, all objects are made of plastic
hints: Think about a pen or a phone.
questions.explanation: Ama is not right. Many objects, especially complex ones, are made of multiple materials.
questions.misconception: Pupils may oversimplify how objects are made.

questions.stem: A bicycle has a metal frame and rubber tyres. Why is rubber better than metal for the tyres?
options: Rubber is bendable and grips the road, while metal would be too hard and slippery
hints: Metal wheels would not be smooth.
questions.explanation: Rubber is better for tyres because it is bendable, providing a smooth ride and good grip, whereas a metal tyre would be hard and slippery.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not think about the function of tyres.

questions.stem: Which of these is made of only one material?
hints: Which one is a simple, single-piece object?
questions.explanation: A simple clay pot is made of just one material (clay).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all large objects are multi-material.

questions.stem: Choose an object in your home (e.g., a chair, a shoe, a pot) and write down the materials it is made of.

criteria.description: Lists the correct materials it is made of (at least two if applicable)

hints: What are the different parts made of?
questions.explanation: For example, a shoe can be made of leather and rubber.

questions.stem: Explain why a cooking pot needs to be made of metal and not just plastic.

criteria.description: States that metal conducts heat well for cooking
States that plastic would melt or burn on a fire

hints: What happens to plastic on a fire?
How does food cook in a pot?
questions.explanation: Metal conducts heat to cook the food and can withstand high temperatures. Plastic would melt or burn on a stove.

questions.stem: A student says 'A wooden door is made of one material.' Is this completely true?
options: No, it also has metal hinges, screws, and a handle
No, it is made of glass
hints: What is the handle made of?
questions.explanation: A wooden door is mostly wood, but it also includes metal hinges, screws, and often a metal or plastic handle, making it a multi-material object.
questions.misconception: Pupils may overlook the small components that make up an object.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher two materials used to make a car and explain why each is used.

criteria.description: Names two valid materials (e.g., metal, glass, rubber)
Gives a valid reason for each material's use

questions.explanation: Glass is used for windows to see through. Rubber is used for tyres for grip and flexibility.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.2.2: Understand mixtures, types, formation, uses and ways of separating them into their components
indicator.objective: Describe a solid-liquid mixture and explain how to separate the components

skills.description: Describe a solid-liquid mixture
Explain ways to separate a solid-liquid mixture
Give examples of solid-liquid mixtures from everyday life
Demonstrate or describe how to separate a given solid-liquid mixture

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Salt and water is not a mixture because the salt disappears.
You can separate sand and water by simply picking the sand out with your hands.
Filtering works for separating salt from water.
Evaporation is the same as boiling.
All mixtures can be separated the same way.

questions.stem: What is a solid-liquid mixture?
options: A solid mixed with another solid
A solid mixed with a liquid
A liquid mixed with a gas
hints: One part is solid, one is wet.
questions.explanation: A solid-liquid mixture is formed when a solid and a liquid are put together.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a mixture is only when two liquids are mixed.

questions.stem: Which of these is a solid-liquid mixture?
questions.explanation: Sand and water is a solid-liquid mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse solid-liquid mixtures with liquid-liquid mixtures.

questions.stem: How can you separate sand from water?
hints: Use a filter or a sieve.
questions.explanation: Sand can be separated from water by filtering, which traps the sand while the water passes through.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think you can just let it sit (settling/decanting is also valid, but filtering is the standard answer for separating an insoluble solid).

questions.stem: When you mix gari and water, what type of mixture do you get?
questions.explanation: Gari and water form a solid-liquid mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it is a liquid-liquid mixture because it looks wet.

questions.stem: Which of these is a solid-liquid mixture?
hints: It is a solid mixed with a liquid.
questions.explanation: Sugar and water is a solid-liquid mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it is not a mixture because the sugar dissolves.

questions.stem: Ama mixes sand and water. She wants to separate them. What should she use?
questions.explanation: A filter traps the solid sand particles while allowing the liquid water to pass through.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a spoon can separate them completely.

questions.stem: Kwame mixes salt and water. How can he get the salt back?
options: By picking it out with his hands
hints: The water can turn into gas.
questions.explanation: Salt is dissolved in the water, so filtering will not work. The water must be evaporated to leave the salt crystals behind.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think filtering works for dissolved substances.

questions.stem: Which of these describes a solid-liquid mixture?
options: A solid that dissolves or floats in a liquid
Two liquids that do not mix
A gas mixed with a solid
Two solids that are stuck together
hints: One part is solid, one is liquid.
questions.explanation: A solid-liquid mixture contains a solid and a liquid combined, whether the solid dissolves or not.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think mixing only refers to things that don't dissolve.

questions.stem: Give one example of a solid-liquid mixture you can make in the kitchen.
hints: Do you mix a powder with a liquid?
questions.explanation: Salt and water or sugar and water are common solid-liquid mixtures.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name a solid-solid mixture like salt and pepper.

questions.stem: What method can you use to separate sand from water?
questions.explanation: Filtering or settling/decanting can be used to separate sand and water.

questions.stem: Show your teacher how you would separate a mixture of sand and water using a filter.

criteria.description: Pours the mixture through the filter
Observes the sand trapped in the filter and the water passing through

hints: Put the filter in a funnel.
questions.explanation: This demonstrates filtering as a separation method for an insoluble solid-liquid mixture.

questions.stem: Why does filtering NOT separate salt from water?
options: Because the salt dissolves and passes through the filter with the water
Because water is thicker than salt
hints: Can you see the salt in the water?
Does it stay on the filter?
questions.explanation: Salt dissolves into tiny particles that pass through the filter along with the water. It does not get trapped.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think filtering separates all mixtures.

questions.stem: Ama has a mixture of sand and water. She leaves it in a cup for a long time. The sand settles at the bottom. What is this process called?
hints: The solid falls to the bottom.
questions.explanation: When a solid settles to the bottom of a liquid over time, it is called settling or sedimentation.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know the term for this.

questions.stem: Which of these is true about a solid-liquid mixture?
options: The solid and liquid keep their own properties
They always form a new substance
The liquid always turns into a solid
questions.explanation: In a mixture, the original solid and liquid keep their own properties.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a mixture creates a new substance.

questions.stem: Write down two solid-liquid mixtures and state one way to separate each.

criteria.description: States a correct separation method for each

hints: Sand and water, salt and water.
questions.explanation: Sand and water can be separated by filtering. Salt and water can be separated by evaporation.

questions.stem: Describe how you would separate a mixture of salt and water in the classroom.

criteria.description: States that the mixture should be heated or left in the sun
States that the water will evaporate, leaving salt crystals behind

questions.explanation: Heating or leaving the mixture in the sun causes the water to evaporate, leaving the solid salt behind.

questions.stem: Explain why you would use a different method to separate salt and water than the method used for sand and water.

criteria.description: States that sand does not dissolve, so it can be filtered out
States that salt dissolves in water, so evaporation is needed to separate it

hints: Can you see the sand in the water?
Can you see the salt in the water?
questions.explanation: Sand is insoluble and can be trapped by a filter. Salt is soluble and passes through the filter, so evaporation is needed to recover it.

questions.stem: A student filters a mixture of salt and sand in water. What is on the filter paper and what is in the water that passes through?
options: Sand on the filter, salt water passes through
Salt on the filter, sand water passes through
Both salt and sand on the filter
hints: Which one passes through the holes?
questions.explanation: The sand is trapped on the filter paper because it does not dissolve. The salt dissolves in the water and passes through the filter.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think filtering separates everything.

questions.stem: A farmer has muddy water and wants clear water. Which two processes can he use?
questions.explanation: Settling allows the mud to fall to the bottom, and filtering removes the remaining fine particles to make the water clearer.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think boiling makes water clear.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher what a solid-liquid mixture is and give one example.

criteria.description: States it is a solid mixed with a liquid
Gives a valid example (e.g., sand and water)

hints: Think about a mixture where one part is wet and one part is dry.
questions.explanation: A solid-liquid mixture is a solid combined with a liquid, like sand and water.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.2.3: Know that substances can exist in different physical state (solid, liquid, Gas). Many substances can be changed from one state to another by heating or cooling
indicator.objective: Explain how substances change state between solid, liquid and gas

skills.description: Explain that substances can change state when heated or cooled
Give examples of substances changing state
Explain simply why a substance changes state
Demonstrate or describe an observation of a substance changing state

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Melting and freezing are the same thing.
Steam is not water; it is smoke.
When water boils, it disappears completely.
Ice is a different substance from water.
Condensation is when water turns into ice.

questions.stem: What happens to ice when it is left in the sun?
questions.explanation: Heating ice causes it to melt and change from a solid to a liquid (water).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think ice stays solid.

questions.stem: What happens to water when you put it in a freezer?
questions.explanation: Cooling water causes it to freeze and change from a liquid to a solid (ice).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the freezer boils the water.

questions.stem: What do we call water when it is in the form of a gas?
hints: It comes from a boiling kettle.
questions.explanation: Water in its gaseous state is called steam or water vapour.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think steam is smoke.

questions.stem: Which of these is a solid form of water?
questions.explanation: Ice is the solid form of water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think rain is solid.

questions.stem: What causes water to turn into steam?
hints: You put it on a fire.
questions.explanation: Heating water to its boiling point causes it to turn into steam (a gas).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think adding cold causes steam.

questions.stem: When water vapour (steam) hits a cold window, it turns into liquid water droplets. What is this change called?
hints: You see drops on the glass.
questions.explanation: Condensation is the change of state from a gas to a liquid.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse it with melting.

questions.stem: Butter changes from solid to liquid when you put it in a hot pan. What is this process called?
questions.explanation: The change from a solid to a liquid is called melting.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it is boiling.

questions.stem: Why does a puddle of water dry up on a hot day?
options: The water evaporates into the air
The water turns into a solid
The water hides in the ground
hints: It goes into the air as a gas.
questions.explanation: The heat from the sun causes the liquid water to evaporate into water vapour (a gas) in the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the water just vanishes.

questions.stem: Ice is a solid. Water is a liquid. What is the process of ice turning into water?
hints: It happens when it gets warm.
questions.explanation: Ice melts into water when it gains heat.

questions.stem: Name one example of a gas changing into a liquid.
answer: steam turning to water on a cold glass
questions.explanation: Steam condensing on a cold surface is a gas-to-liquid change.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know the word condensation.

questions.stem: What do we call the process when a liquid turns into a solid?
questions.explanation: The process of a liquid turning into a solid is called freezing.

questions.stem: Why do we put water in the fridge to make it cold?
options: The fridge removes heat from the water
The fridge adds cold to the water
The fridge makes the water evaporate
questions.explanation: The fridge removes heat from the water, lowering its temperature.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the fridge adds 'cold' to the water.

questions.stem: Which of these changes happens when a gas is cooled?
options: It turns into a solid directly (always)
questions.explanation: Cooling a gas causes it to condense into a liquid.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cooling a gas always makes a solid.

questions.stem: Why does a water bottle left in the sun become warm?
options: It gains heat from the sun
It loses heat to the sun
hints: The sun is a source of heat.
Heat moves from hot to cold.
questions.explanation: The sun transfers heat to the water bottle, raising its temperature.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the bottle creates heat.

questions.stem: A substance changes from a solid to a liquid and then to a gas. What must happen for these changes to occur?
options: It must stay in the dark
questions.explanation: Both melting and boiling require the substance to gain heat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cooling causes these changes.

questions.stem: Explain what happens to the water particles when ice melts.

criteria.description: States that the ice gains heat
States that the solid ice turns into liquid water

questions.explanation: When ice melts, it gains heat, causing the solid ice to change into liquid water.

questions.stem: Show your teacher how you can change a piece of ice into water.

criteria.description: Places the ice in a warm area or holds it
Observes and explains that the solid ice melts into liquid water due to heat

hints: What happens if you hold ice in your hand?
questions.explanation: The heat from the hand or room causes the ice to melt into water.

questions.stem: Describe an experiment you can do at home to see water change from liquid to gas.

criteria.description: States boiling water in a kettle or pot

hints: What happens when you boil water?
What comes out of the kettle?
questions.explanation: Boiling water produces steam, which is water changing from a liquid to a gas.

questions.stem: Which of these statements is TRUE?
options: Water can exist as a solid (ice), liquid (water), and gas (steam)
Water only exists as a liquid
Ice is a different substance from water
hints: Can you freeze water? Can you boil it?
questions.explanation: Water is the same substance in all three states: solid (ice), liquid (water), and gas (steam).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think ice and steam are different substances.

questions.stem: Explain why a glass of cold water gets wet on the outside on a hot day.

criteria.description: States that water vapour in the air cools when it touches the cold glass
States that the vapour condenses into liquid water droplets

hints: Is the glass colder than the air?
What happens to gas when it cools?
questions.explanation: The cold glass cools the water vapour in the air, causing it to condense into liquid water droplets on the outside of the glass.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher the difference between melting and freezing.

criteria.description: States melting is solid to liquid
States freezing is liquid to solid

questions.explanation: Melting is changing from solid to liquid. Freezing is changing from liquid to solid.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.1.1: Recognize that some events in our environment occur recurrently
indicator.objective: Describe some cyclic events like day and night, wet and dry seasons and their intervals/periods

skills.description: Identify day and night and wet and dry seasons as cyclic events that repeat
Describe the features of each cyclic event
Recognise the approximate intervals/periods
Explain why these cyclic events are important

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Day and night happen only once.
Wet and dry seasons happen every week.
There is no pattern to the seasons.
Night is just a dark day; the cycle doesn't matter.

questions.stem: Which of these is a cyclic event?
questions.explanation: Day and night is a cyclic event because it repeats every 24 hours.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse everyday one-time events with cycles.

questions.stem: What do we see in the sky during the night?
questions.explanation: At night, we see the moon and stars because it is dark and the sun is on the other side of the Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sun is still visible at night.

questions.stem: Why do we need the wet season?
questions.explanation: The wet season brings rain that waters crops and fills rivers, which is essential for farming and life.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the wet season is only for playing in puddles.

questions.stem: Do the wet and dry seasons happen once or repeatedly?
hints: Think about the cycle of a year.
questions.explanation: The wet and dry seasons are cyclic events. They happen repeatedly, every year.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think seasons only happen once.

questions.stem: How would you describe the dry season?
questions.explanation: The dry season is usually sunny and dry with very little rain.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the dry season with the harmattan.

questions.stem: About how long does one full cycle of day and night take?
hints: From morning to the next morning.
questions.explanation: One full cycle of day and night takes about 24 hours, which is one day.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it takes 12 hours (just one part of the cycle).

questions.stem: About how often do the wet and dry seasons occur?
questions.explanation: The wet and dry seasons occur once a year as part of the annual weather cycle.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think seasons change every month.

questions.stem: What happens to most trees during the dry season?
options: They may lose their leaves and look dry
questions.explanation: During the dry season, many trees lose their leaves or look dry because of the lack of water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think trees grow fastest in the dry season.

questions.stem: Why do farmers often prefer to plant during the wet season?
options: Because the rain provides water for the seeds to grow
Because they have more free time
questions.explanation: Farmers plant in the wet season because the rain provides the water that seeds need to germinate and grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think planting is done in the dry season.

questions.stem: Which statement about day and night is TRUE?
options: Day and night happen in a repeating pattern
Night happens only once a year
The pattern of day and night is random
questions.explanation: Day and night follow a regular, repeating pattern (cycle).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the pattern is random.

questions.stem: Name one thing you see during the day and one thing you see at night.
answer: day: sun, clouds, blue sky; night: moon, stars, dark sky
questions.explanation: We see the sun, clouds, and blue sky during the day; we see the moon, stars, and dark sky at night.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say they see the moon during the day (sometimes true, but night is the primary answer).

questions.stem: How many hours are there in a full day and night cycle?
questions.explanation: A full day and night cycle is 24 hours.

questions.stem: What would happen if the Earth stopped experiencing the day and night cycle (e.g., if one side was always day and the other always night)?
options: One side would be too hot and the other too cold, making life very difficult
questions.explanation: Without the cycle, the side facing the sun would be extremely hot, and the dark side would be freezing, which would make it hard for life to survive.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not consider the extreme temperature changes.

questions.stem: Why are the wet and dry seasons described as 'cyclic' events?
options: Because they come and go in a repeating pattern
Because they are always the same length
Because they depend on the moon
hints: Think about a circle or a wheel.
What happens after the dry season?
questions.explanation: They are cyclic because they occur in a repeating pattern every year.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think 'cyclic' means something is broken.

questions.stem: Which of these events completes its cycle in the shortest time?
options: The movement of the Earth around the sun
hints: The others take months or a year.
questions.explanation: Day and night takes 24 hours, which is much shorter than the yearly cycle of seasons.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not have a clear sense of the timescales.

questions.stem: Describe the differences between the wet season and the dry season.

criteria.description: States that the wet season has rain and the dry season has little rain
States another difference (e.g., plants are green vs dry; weather is cool vs hot)

questions.explanation: The wet season is rainy and plants are green. The dry season is sunny and dry, and plants may wither.

questions.stem: Explain why the day and night cycle is important for living things.

criteria.description: States that day provides light for plants to grow and for people to work
States that night provides rest and sleep

hints: What do we do during the day?
What do we do at night?
questions.explanation: The day provides light and warmth for activity and growth. Night provides a time for rest and sleep for many living things.

questions.stem: A student says 'The wet and dry seasons are exactly the same every year.' Is this completely true?
options: No, the exact start and amount of rain can vary from year to year
Yes, it is always exactly the same
No, there are no seasons anymore
Yes, it rains every day in the wet season
hints: Does it rain the same amount every year?
Are the start dates always the same?
questions.explanation: While the pattern is cyclic, the exact timing and amount of rainfall can vary from year to year.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cycles are rigid and identical every time.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher about your favourite season and describe two things you do during that season.

criteria.description: Describes two activities suited to that season

hints: What do you do when it is hot?
questions.explanation: This tests the ability to relate daily activities to the seasons.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.1.2: Recognise the relationship between the Earth and the Sun
indicator.objective: Know the importance of the sun to the earth

skills.description: State the importance of the sun
Give examples of everyday uses of the sun
Explain what would happen without the sun

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: The sun only gives light; it doesn't help plants grow.
We could live without the sun because we have electric lights.
The sun is only important in the dry season.
The moon is more important than the sun.

questions.stem: What does the sun give us that helps us see?
questions.explanation: The sun gives us light, which helps us see during the day.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sun only gives heat.

questions.stem: What does the sun give us that keeps us warm?
hints: You feel it on a hot day.
questions.explanation: The sun gives us heat (warmth), which keeps the Earth warm enough for life.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sun only gives light.

questions.stem: How does the sun help us dry our clothes?
options: It gives heat that evaporates the water
questions.explanation: The sun's heat evaporates the water from the clothes, drying them.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the wind does all the drying.

questions.stem: How does the sun help farmers dry their harvested crops like maize?
options: By providing heat to remove moisture
hints: Farmers spread crops in the sun.
questions.explanation: The sun's heat dries the crops, helping to preserve them so they can be stored for a long time.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sun makes the crops wet.

questions.stem: What would happen if the sun stopped shining?
options: It would become dark and cold
hints: The sun gives light and heat.
questions.explanation: Without the sun, the Earth would be dark and cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think electric lights could completely replace the sun.

questions.stem: Why is the sun important for plants?
options: It helps them make their own food
hints: They make food in their leaves.
questions.explanation: Plants use the sun's light to make their own food (photosynthesis), which helps them grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants get all their food from the soil.

questions.stem: Which of these is an everyday use of the sun's warmth?
options: Bathing in warm water from a sun-heated tank
Reading a book under a lamp
hints: People use it to stay warm.
questions.explanation: The sun's warmth can heat water (e.g., in black tanks on roofs), which is then used for bathing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not think of the sun as a source of hot water.

questions.stem: Why is the sun important for animals?
options: It provides warmth and helps plants grow, which animals eat
questions.explanation: The sun provides warmth and helps plants grow. Animals depend on these plants for food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not link the sun to the animal food chain.

questions.stem: What would happen to plants if they did not get sunlight?
options: They would not be able to make food and would die
hints: Plants need light to make food.
questions.explanation: Without sunlight, plants cannot make their own food and will eventually die.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants can grow in the dark.

questions.stem: Name one way the sun helps us at home every day.
questions.explanation: The sun helps us dry clothes, dry food, and provides natural light during the day.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name things that require electricity.

questions.stem: What two things does the sun give to the Earth?
questions.explanation: The sun gives both light and heat (warmth) to the Earth.

questions.stem: Why is the sun called the main source of energy for life on Earth?
options: Because it provides light and heat that plants and animals need to survive
Because it is very far away
Because it is the biggest object in the sky
Because it moves around the Earth
hints: What do plants use to make food?
Where does the energy come from?
questions.explanation: The sun is the main source of energy because it provides the light and heat that drive almost all life processes on Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect the sun to the energy chain.

questions.stem: If the sun stopped providing heat, what would happen to the water in rivers and oceans?
hints: Without heat, it gets very cold.
Water freezes when it is cold.
questions.explanation: Without the sun's heat, the Earth would become very cold, and water would freeze into ice.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect the sun's heat to the state of water.

questions.stem: Ama wants to dry fish quickly. What should she do?
options: Spread it out in the hot sun
hints: The sun is hottest in the open.
questions.explanation: Spreading the fish out in the hot sun allows it to dry quickly because the sun's heat evaporates the moisture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the shade is better for drying.

questions.stem: Explain why the sun is important for providing food for people.

criteria.description: States that the sun helps plants grow
States that people eat these plants (or animals that eat the plants) for food

hints: Where does the food chain start?
What do plants need to grow?
questions.explanation: The sun helps plants grow. People eat these plants, or eat animals that feed on the plants, so the sun is ultimately the source of our food.

questions.stem: Describe what a day would be like if the sun never came out.

criteria.description: States that it would be completely dark
States that it would be very cold and plants would die

hints: Would it be warm or cold?
questions.explanation: Without the sun, it would be permanently dark and freezing, and plants would die, making life on Earth impossible.

questions.stem: Kwame says 'We don't need the sun because we have electricity.' Why is he wrong?
options: Because electricity is generated using resources that ultimately depend on the sun, and without the sun, life itself would not exist
Because electricity is better than the sun
Because the sun is not real
hints: Where do fossil fuels come from?
questions.explanation: Even with electricity, we need the sun for food, warmth, and the environment. Most energy sources are ultimately linked to the sun.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think technology replaces all natural needs.

questions.stem: List three daily activities that depend on the sun.

criteria.description: Names one valid activity (e.g., drying clothes)
Names a second valid activity (e.g., farming)
Names a third valid activity (e.g., providing light)

questions.explanation: Daily activities include drying clothes, drying food, farming, and seeing during the day.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher what would happen to you if the sun stopped giving heat.

criteria.description: States that it would be very cold
States that it would be difficult to stay warm and survive

hints: What do you wear when it is cold?
Would it be easy to live?
questions.explanation: Without the sun's heat, it would be freezing, and humans would struggle to survive in such extreme cold.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.1.3: Show understanding of the roles of condensation, evaporation, transpiration and precipitation in the hydrological (water) cycle
indicator.objective: Identify the types of precipitation (rain, snow, hail, sleet) and describe the differences among them

skills.description: Name the types of precipitation
Describe the differences among them
Match a description to the correct type of precipitation
Give examples of when each type might occur

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Snow and hail are the same thing.
Sleet is just heavy rain.
It snows in Ghana all the time.
Hail is frozen rain.
All precipitation is liquid water.

questions.stem: Which of these is a type of precipitation?
questions.explanation: Rain is a common type of precipitation that falls from clouds.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wind is precipitation.

questions.stem: Which of these falls as small hard pieces of ice during a storm?
hints: It is ice that falls like stones.
questions.explanation: Hail is precipitation in the form of small, hard balls of ice that fall during thunderstorms.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse hail with snow.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between rain and snow?
options: Rain is liquid water and snow is soft white ice crystals
Rain is cold and snow is hot
Rain falls up and snow falls down
hints: What happens to rain when it hits the ground?
questions.explanation: Rain is liquid water, while snow is frozen water vapour that forms soft, white ice crystals.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they are identical.

questions.stem: What type of precipitation is most common in Ghana?
hints: It happens during the wet season.
questions.explanation: Rain is the most common type of precipitation in Ghana because of its tropical climate.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think snow falls in Ghana.

questions.stem: What is sleet?
options: Ice pellets or a mixture of rain and snow
hints: It falls like rain but is icy.
questions.explanation: Sleet is precipitation consisting of ice pellets or a mixture of rain and snow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sleet is just heavy rain.

questions.stem: Which type of precipitation consists of soft, white ice crystals?
hints: It falls in very cold places.
questions.explanation: Snow is made of soft, white ice crystals.
questions.misconception: Pupils may match this description to hail.

questions.stem: How is hail different from snow?
options: Hail is hard ice pellets, while snow is soft ice crystals
Hail is soft and snow is hard
Hail is liquid and snow is solid
hints: Hail can hurt if it hits you.
questions.explanation: Hail is made of hard ice pellets, while snow consists of soft ice crystals.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think hail and snow are identical.

questions.stem: Which type of precipitation is liquid water drops falling from clouds?
questions.explanation: Rain consists of liquid water drops falling from clouds.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it is sleet.

questions.stem: When is hail most likely to occur?
hints: There is usually thunder and lightning.
questions.explanation: Hail forms in strong thunderstorm clouds (cumulonimbus clouds) when updrafts carry raindrops high where it is freezing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think hail occurs on sunny days.

questions.stem: In which type of climate would you expect to see snow?
questions.explanation: Snow occurs in very cold climates where the temperature in the clouds is below freezing.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think snow occurs in hot climates.

questions.stem: Name two types of precipitation.
questions.explanation: Common types of precipitation include rain, snow, hail, and sleet.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name non-precipitation items like wind.

questions.stem: What is the difference between rain and hail?
answer: rain is liquid water, hail is hard ice pellets
questions.explanation: Rain is liquid water, while hail is hard ice pellets.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think hail is just frozen rain.

questions.stem: Ama says 'Sleet is just heavy rain.' Is she right?
options: No, sleet contains ice pellets or a mix of rain and snow
hints: Does sleet feel like rain or ice?
questions.explanation: Ama is not right. Sleet is not just heavy rain; it contains ice pellets or a mixture of rain and snow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may simplify sleet as heavy rain.

questions.stem: Why does snow fall in some countries but not in Ghana?
options: Because those countries are much colder, so the water freezes in the clouds
Because Ghana is closer to the moon
Because snow only falls on mountains
questions.explanation: Snow forms when water freezes in cold clouds. Countries that have very cold temperatures at cloud level experience snow, while Ghana's tropical climate is too warm.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think snow is random.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between rain, snow, and hail.

criteria.description: States snow is soft ice crystals and hail is hard ice pellets

questions.explanation: Rain is liquid. Snow is soft ice crystals. Hail is hard ice pellets.

questions.stem: Name the four main types of precipitation and briefly describe one.
questions.explanation: The four types are rain, snow, hail, and sleet.

questions.stem: A farmer hears thunder and sees dark clouds. It starts to rain, but soon hard ice pellets start falling. What type of precipitation is this?
questions.explanation: The hard ice pellets falling during a thunderstorm are hail.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse it with sleet (which is softer and mixed with rain).

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to walk outside during a heavy hailstorm?
options: Hailstones can be hard and large enough to cause injury
questions.explanation: Hailstones can be hard and large, and falling ice can cause injuries to people and damage to property.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think hail is harmless like snow.

questions.stem: Show your teacher how you can create 'artificial rain' in the classroom (e.g., using a watering can or a sieve with water).

criteria.description: Performs the activity to simulate rain
Explains that the water drops represent rain

hints: Let the water fall like drops.
questions.explanation: This demonstrates the concept of rain as liquid drops falling from above.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.1.4: Recognise water and air as important natural resources
indicator.objective: Identify things that make water impure

skills.description: Identify things that make water impure
Describe the effect of impure water on health
Suggest ways to keep water clean
Give an example of how water becomes impure in the community

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Water is only impure if it is visibly dirty.
Water from a well is always clean.
Chemicals in water are harmless if you cannot see them.
Littering in a river is fine because the water washes it away.

questions.stem: Which of these makes water impure?
hints: It adds dirt to the water.
questions.explanation: Throwing rubbish into water makes it impure (dirty).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water is always clean.

questions.stem: Ama sees a river with rubbish floating in it. Is the water clean?
questions.explanation: The water is impure (dirty) because of the rubbish.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think flowing water cleans itself immediately.

questions.stem: What can happen if you drink impure water?
questions.explanation: Drinking impure water can make you sick because it may contain harmful germs.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all water is safe to drink.

questions.stem: What should you do with rubbish to keep water clean?
hints: Put rubbish in the right place.
Do not throw it in water.
questions.explanation: Throwing rubbish in a bin keeps it out of water sources and helps keep water clean.

questions.stem: Which of these can make water impure?
questions.explanation: Chemicals from factories can pollute water and make it impure.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not consider invisible chemicals.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to drink water from a stream where animals drink and bathe?
options: The water may contain germs from the animals' waste
hints: Their waste can get into the water.
questions.explanation: Animal waste can contaminate the water with germs, making it unsafe for humans to drink.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think natural water is always safe.

questions.stem: Ama wants to keep her well water clean. What should she do?
options: Cover the well and keep animals away
hints: Covering stops dirt from falling in.
questions.explanation: Covering the well and keeping animals away prevents dirt and germs from getting into the water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know how to protect a well.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a cause of water pollution?
questions.explanation: Filtering is a way to clean water, not pollute it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse cleaning methods with pollution.

questions.stem: How can farming activities make water impure?
options: Fertilizers and pesticides can wash into rivers
hints: Rain can wash them into water.
questions.explanation: Chemicals like fertilizers and pesticides can be washed by rain into rivers and streams, polluting the water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not link farming to water pollution.

questions.stem: Name one sickness you can get from drinking impure water.
questions.explanation: Drinking impure water can cause diseases like cholera, typhoid, or diarrhoea.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say malaria (which is from mosquitoes).

questions.stem: Name one thing that can make water impure.
hints: Think about what people throw away.
questions.explanation: Rubbish, chemicals, and animal waste can all make water impure.

questions.stem: A factory is dumping waste into a river. What is the effect on the community?
options: The water becomes unsafe for drinking and fish may die
questions.explanation: Dumping industrial waste pollutes the water, making it unsafe for drinking and harming aquatic life.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think rivers can absorb any waste.

questions.stem: Which of these is the BEST way to protect a community's water source?
options: Fencing the area and stopping people from dumping waste there
Allowing animals to graze near the water
Throwing rubbish far from the source
questions.explanation: Fencing and preventing dumping protects the water source from contamination.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not think about protecting the area around the source.

questions.stem: Why is it important to keep water sources clean in the community?
options: To prevent the spread of diseases
To make the water taste better
To help the water flow faster
questions.explanation: Keeping water sources clean prevents germs and diseases from spreading in the community.
questions.misconception: Pupils may focus on appearance rather than health.

questions.stem: Write down two ways you can help keep water clean in your community.

criteria.description: States one method (e.g., not throwing rubbish in rivers, using bins)
States a second method (e.g., preventing animals from entering water sources)

questions.explanation: Ways to keep water clean include proper waste disposal and protecting water sources from animals and chemicals.

questions.stem: Describe one way water in your community can become impure.

criteria.description: Gives a valid example (e.g., flooding carries waste into wells, mining pollutes rivers)
Explains how it makes the water impure

questions.explanation: Flooding can wash dirt and waste into water sources, making them impure.

questions.stem: A community gets its water from a stream upstream, and a new factory opens upstream and dumps waste. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The community's water will become polluted and unsafe
The factory will clean the water
questions.explanation: The factory's waste will flow downstream to the community, making their water polluted and unsafe.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand the flow of water.

questions.stem: What is the BEST way to prevent water pollution from household chemicals?
options: Dispose of them safely at designated collection points
hints: Do not put them in water.
questions.explanation: Household chemicals should be disposed of safely at designated collection points to prevent them from entering water sources.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think pouring chemicals down the drain is safe.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher one thing that makes water impure in your area and what can be done about it.

criteria.description: Names a valid cause (e.g., rubbish dumping)
Suggests a valid solution (e.g., using bins)

hints: What can be done to stop it?
questions.explanation: This tests identifying local water pollution issues and solutions.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.1.4: Recognise water and air as important natural resources
indicator.objective: Describe the properties of air

skills.description: Name the properties of air
Describe simple demonstrations that show these properties
Explain why air is important for life
Demonstrate or describe one property of air using simple materials

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Air is nothing because it is invisible.
Air only exists outside.
A balloon has no air when it is not blown up.
Air has no weight or mass.

questions.stem: Does air take up space?
questions.explanation: Air takes up space, which is why a balloon gets bigger when you blow into it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air has no volume.

questions.stem: Why do we need air?
questions.explanation: We need air to breathe. All living things need oxygen from the air to stay alive.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not prioritize breathing as an air use.

questions.stem: Which of these is a property of air?
options: It is hard like a stone
questions.explanation: Air has mass (weight), even though it is very light.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air has no mass.

questions.stem: Can we see air?
hints: You can feel it but not see it.
questions.explanation: Air is invisible (colourless and transparent).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they can see air.

questions.stem: Which of these shows that air is present?
options: A flag waving in the wind
questions.explanation: A flag waving shows that moving air (wind) is present.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect wind to air.

questions.stem: Ama blows into a balloon and it gets bigger. What property of air does this show?
questions.explanation: The balloon gets bigger because the air you blow in takes up space inside it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the balloon fills with nothing.

questions.stem: Kwame waves a piece of paper in front of his face. What does he feel?
questions.explanation: Waving the paper moves the air, and Kwame feels it as a breeze on his face.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize they are feeling air.

questions.stem: Air is made up of...
hints: We need oxygen, but it's not the only gas.
questions.explanation: Air is a mixture of gases, including oxygen, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air is just oxygen.

questions.stem: Why does a deflated balloon have less mass (weight) than an inflated one?
options: Because the inflated one contains extra air, which has mass
questions.explanation: An inflated balloon weighs more because it contains air, which has mass.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think air has no weight at all.

questions.stem: How do plants use air?
options: They take in carbon dioxide from the air to make food
hints: Plants make food in their leaves.
They need a gas from the air.
questions.explanation: Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air, along with sunlight and water, to make their own food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants do not interact with air.

questions.stem: Is air a solid, liquid, or gas?
hints: It fills the space around us.
It is not hard or wet.
questions.explanation: Air is a gas.

questions.stem: Name one way you can show that air takes up space.
answer: put a glass upside down in water
hints: Think about pushing air into something.
questions.explanation: Blowing up a balloon shows that air takes up space.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name a demonstration that doesn't clearly show space.

questions.stem: A glass is pushed upside down into a bowl of water. The water does not fill the glass. Why?
options: Because the glass is already full of air, which takes up space
Because the glass is too small
questions.explanation: The air trapped inside the glass takes up space, preventing the water from filling it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the glass is empty (containing nothing).

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to burn things in a closed room without ventilation?
options: Because the fire uses up oxygen from the air, leaving less for you to breathe
Because the fire makes the room too bright
Because the fire makes the air wet
Because it makes the room too clean
hints: Without fresh air, you will struggle to breathe.
questions.explanation: Burning consumes oxygen. In a closed room without fresh air, oxygen levels drop, making it hard to breathe.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know that fire uses oxygen.

questions.stem: A paper fan is waved, creating a breeze. What is happening to the air?
options: The fan is moving the air, showing that air can be pushed
The fan is creating new air
The fan is turning air into water
hints: You can feel the air move.
It is being pushed by the fan.
questions.explanation: The fan pushes the air, creating a breeze. This shows that air can be moved (it has mass and takes up space).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fans create air from nothing.

questions.stem: Explain why air is important for both humans and plants.

criteria.description: States that humans need air to breathe
States that plants use a gas from the air to make food

questions.explanation: Humans need air to breathe. Plants take in carbon dioxide from air to make food.

questions.stem: Show your teacher one demonstration that proves air exists.

criteria.description: Performs a valid demonstration (e.g., waving paper, blowing a balloon)
Explains what they observed to prove air is present

hints: What can you see or feel?
questions.explanation: This tests the practical understanding of air's existence.

questions.stem: Describe how you would show that air has mass (weight).

criteria.description: States that an inflated balloon weighs more than a deflated one
Explains that the extra weight is the air inside

hints: What happens if you add air?
questions.explanation: An inflated balloon has more mass than a deflated one because air has mass.

questions.stem: Why does a hot air balloon rise when the air inside is heated?
options: Heating air makes it expand and become lighter, so it rises
hints: Warm air is lighter than cool air.
questions.explanation: Heating the air inside the balloon makes it expand and become less dense (lighter), causing the balloon to rise.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know the relationship between heat and air density.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher two properties of air and give an example of each.

criteria.description: Names a property (e.g., takes up space) and gives an example (e.g., balloon)
Names another property (e.g., has mass) and gives an example

hints: What happens when you blow a balloon?
How do you know air is there?
questions.explanation: Air takes up space (balloon) and has mass (weighs something).

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.2.1: Demonstrate understanding of life cycle of a plant
indicator.objective: Observe the germination of maize and bean seeds

skills.description: Understand that germination is the process of a seed sprouting and beginning to grow into a new plant
Identify the conditions seeds need to germinate (water/moisture, air, warmth)
Compare seeds in wet conditions vs. dry conditions to see which germinate
Describe the steps of setting up the germination experiment
Record or predict what happens to the seeds over time

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Seeds need soil to germinate.
Seeds need sunlight to germinate.
Dry seeds are dead and can never grow.
All seeds sprout at the same time.
A seed turns into a fully grown plant immediately after sprouting.

questions.stem: What is the process called when a seed begins to sprout and grow?
hints: It happens when a seed comes to life.
questions.explanation: Germination is the process where a seed sprouts and begins to grow into a new plant.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse plant growth processes with physical changes of matter.

questions.stem: What do seeds need to germinate?
questions.explanation: Seeds need water, air, and warmth to germinate. Sunlight is not required initially.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think seeds only need soil and sunlight.

questions.stem: If you put a bean seed in wet cotton wool and another in dry cotton wool, which one will sprout?
