options: The one in wet cotton wool
The one in dry cotton wool
hints: Dry cotton wool has no water.
questions.explanation: The seed in wet cotton wool will sprout because it has the moisture it needs to germinate.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think seeds can sprout without water.

questions.stem: What will you first observe when a bean seed starts to germinate?
options: The seed turning into a stone
questions.explanation: The first visible sign of germination is usually the tiny root emerging from the seed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a full leaf appears first.

questions.stem: In the germination experiment, what is the cotton wool used for?
options: To hold water and keep the seed moist
To make the seed grow faster
questions.explanation: The cotton wool acts as a bed that holds water and keeps the seed moist.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the cotton wool is food for the seed.

questions.stem: Why do we keep the cotton wool moist (damp) and not completely flooded with water?
options: Seeds need air, and too much water might block the air
Seeds can only drink a little water
Flooding makes the seeds too cold
The water will wash the seed away
hints: Too much water drowns the seed.
questions.explanation: Seeds need air to germinate. If the cotton wool is flooded, it blocks the air from reaching the seed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think more water is always better.

questions.stem: After one week, the seed in the dry container has not sprouted. Why?
hints: What was missing from the dry cotton wool?
questions.explanation: Without water, the seed cannot begin the germination process.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the lack of soil is the problem.

questions.stem: After the tiny root appears, what grows next from the seed?
questions.explanation: After the root emerges, the shoot (stem and small leaves) grows upwards towards the light.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a mature fruit appears next.

questions.stem: When setting up the experiment, where should you place the seeds in the container?
options: Between the cotton wool and the side of the glass
At the very bottom under all the cotton wool
Floating on top of the water
hints: You want to see them clearly.
questions.explanation: Placing the seeds against the side of the glass allows you to observe them clearly as they germinate.
questions.misconception: Pupils may bury the seeds too deep to see.

questions.stem: Do seeds need sunlight to begin germinating in the cotton wool experiment?
options: No, they can germinate in the dark
Yes, they must be in direct sunlight
Yes, but only for one hour a day
hints: Think about seeds buried in soil.
They sprout before reaching the surface.
questions.explanation: Most seeds do not need sunlight to germinate. They need water, air, and warmth. They only need light after the leaves appear.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think seeds need sunlight to sprout.

questions.stem: What is the name of the process when a seed sprouts?
questions.explanation: The process is called germination.

questions.stem: Name two things a seed needs to germinate.
questions.explanation: Seeds need water and air (and warmth) to germinate.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say soil or sunlight.

questions.stem: Ama sets up her germination experiment but forgets to add water to the cotton wool. What will happen?
options: The seeds will grow into huge plants
The seeds will turn into soil
hints: Water is a basic need for germination.
questions.explanation: Without water, the seeds cannot germinate and will remain dormant or dry up.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think seeds can grow without water.

questions.stem: Why did the seeds in the cotton wool without soil still germinate?
options: Because seeds only need water, air, and warmth at this stage; soil is not necessary for germination
Because cotton wool is a type of soil
Because soil is not needed by plants at all
hints: What did the cotton wool provide?
Do seeds need soil to sprout?
questions.explanation: Seeds carry their own food for the initial stage. They only need water, air, and warmth to germinate, which the cotton wool provided.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think soil is absolutely required from day one.

questions.stem: You set up two containers: Container A has seeds in wet cotton wool, and Container B has seeds in dry cotton wool. After one week, describe what you will see in each container.

criteria.description: States Container A will have sprouted seeds (roots/shoots)
States Container B will have unsprouted/dry seeds

hints: What happens to a dry seed?
questions.explanation: Container A will show germination because it has water. Container B will show no germination because it lacks water.

questions.stem: Describe what a bean seed looks like 5 days after it has been placed in wet cotton wool.

criteria.description: Mentions the seed coat has split open
Mentions a small root and/or a tiny green shoot has appeared

hints: Does the outer skin stay whole?
questions.explanation: After 5 days, the seed coat should be split, and a small white root and a tiny green shoot should be visible.

questions.stem: Show your teacher how to set up a germination experiment for a maize seed using a transparent container and cotton wool.

criteria.description: Places cotton wool in the container
Puts the seed between the cotton wool and the glass
Adds a little water to moisten the cotton wool

hints: Make sure you can see the seed.
Do not flood it with water.
questions.explanation: This tests the practical steps of setting up the experiment.

questions.stem: In your experiment, the roots grow downwards into the cotton wool, and the shoot grows upwards. Why does the shoot grow upwards?
options: To reach the light it needs for making food later
Because the seed wants to escape
hints: What does a green plant need?
questions.explanation: After germination, the shoot grows upwards towards the light so the plant can make its own food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think roots and shoots grow randomly.

questions.stem: A farmer plants maize seeds but the weather is very cold and there is no rain. What will likely happen to the seeds?
options: They will not germinate because they lack water and warmth
They will germinate in one hour
hints: Cold and dry conditions are not good for sprouting.
questions.explanation: Without water and sufficient warmth, the maize seeds will remain dormant and not germinate.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think seeds germinate in any weather.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher what you observed happening to your seed over the week.

criteria.description: States that the seed swelled up/split open
States that a root emerged and then a small shoot

questions.explanation: This tests the ability to accurately describe observations of germination.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.3.1.1: Recognise that different parts of the human body work independently to perform a specific function
indicator.objective: Explain that the external parts of the human body work interdependently to perform a function

skills.description: Explain that different body parts work together (interdependently) to perform a task
Give examples of how parts work together
Explain why it is important for body parts to work together
Describe how specific parts cooperate in a given scenario

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Body parts work completely alone and do not need each other.
Only the legs are needed to play football.
The eyes are not needed for walking.
If one part is missing, the others cannot do anything at all.

questions.stem: Which body parts work together when you clap your hands?
hints: They are at the end of your arms.
questions.explanation: When you clap, both of your hands work together to make a sound.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think you clap with your legs.

questions.stem: Which parts of your body work together to help you walk?
questions.explanation: Your legs and feet work together to help you walk, run, and jump.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think eyes are the most important for walking, but legs and feet do the movement.

questions.stem: When you read a book, which two body parts work together most closely?
hints: You think about what they mean.
questions.explanation: Your eyes see the words, and your brain helps you understand them.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the mouth is needed for reading.

questions.stem: When you smell a flower, your nose sends messages to your...
hints: It helps you understand the smell.
questions.explanation: Your nose detects the smell, and your brain helps you recognise it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the nose does all the work alone.

questions.stem: Which body parts work together to help you eat a bowl of rice?
hints: You use a spoon with one part.
questions.explanation: Hands hold the spoon, the mouth takes in food, and teeth chew it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may forget the role of hands in eating.

questions.stem: Kofi is kicking a football. Which body parts are working together?
questions.explanation: Kofi's eyes help him see the ball, and his legs help him kick it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may only think of the legs.

questions.stem: Ama is sweeping the floor. Which parts of her body are she using together?
questions.explanation: Ama uses her hands to hold the broom and her eyes to see where to sweep.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not consider the eyes as part of physical chores.

questions.stem: When you are listening to a story on the radio, what parts are working together?
questions.explanation: Your ears hear the sound, and your brain helps you understand the story.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think listening only involves the ears.

questions.stem: Kwame is riding a bicycle. His hands are steering, and his legs are...
questions.explanation: Kwame's hands steer the bike while his legs pedal to make it move.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the hands and legs do the same job.

questions.stem: Why is it important for your eyes and hands to work together when you catch a ball?
options: Your eyes see the ball and your hands catch it
hints: You need to see where the ball is.
questions.explanation: Eyes track the ball's movement, and hands move to catch it. They must work together.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think catching is only about hands.

questions.stem: Why do your ears and eyes work together when you cross a busy road?
options: You see the cars and hear them coming
questions.explanation: You use your eyes to see oncoming traffic and your ears to hear vehicles approaching, helping you cross safely.
questions.misconception: Pupils may rely only on sight.

questions.stem: Why do your nose and mouth work together when you have a cold?
options: They both help you breathe when your nose is blocked
hints: When you are sick, you cannot breathe well through your nose.
questions.explanation: When your nose is blocked, your mouth helps you breathe, showing how they work together for survival.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think only the nose is for breathing.

questions.stem: Ama says 'I only use my legs to play football.' Why is she wrong?
options: She also uses her eyes, arms, and brain to play
She actually uses only her arms
hints: How does she see the goal?
How does she keep her balance?
questions.explanation: Playing football requires many parts: legs to run and kick, eyes to see, arms for balance, and the brain to make decisions.
questions.misconception: Pupils may oversimplify physical activities to one body part.

questions.stem: When you hold a hot cup of tea, your hand feels the heat and you quickly pull it away. Which parts work together here?
hints: The brain tells the hand to move.
questions.explanation: The hand senses the heat and sends a message to the brain, which tells the hand to pull away.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize the brain's role in reflex actions.

questions.stem: Kofi is carrying a bucket of water on his head. Which parts of his body are working together to keep him balanced and moving?
hints: He uses his neck to balance the bucket.
He uses his legs to walk.
He uses his eyes to see the path.
questions.explanation: The neck supports the bucket, legs provide movement, and eyes guide the way.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not consider the neck's role in carrying loads.

questions.stem: How do your mouth and nose work together when you are eating a delicious meal?
options: Your nose smells the food while your mouth tastes and chews it
hints: You smell the food before eating.
You taste it when you eat.
questions.explanation: The nose detects the aroma, and the mouth tastes and breaks down the food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think taste and smell are completely separate.

questions.stem: To write a sentence on the board, which body parts work together?
hints: Your brain thinks of the words.
questions.explanation: Eyes guide the hand, the hand writes, and the brain forms the sentence.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think writing is only about the hand.

questions.stem: If a person loses their eyesight, which other body parts might they use more to help them navigate their environment?
hints: They might touch things to feel them.
They might listen carefully for sounds.
questions.explanation: People who are blind often rely more on their hands to feel their surroundings and their ears to listen for cues.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think losing sight means all other senses stay the same without adaptation.

questions.stem: If you break your leg, how do your other body parts work together to help you move around?
options: Arms and hands help you use crutches or a wheelchair
Your ears help you balance on one leg
hints: You might hold onto something for support.
questions.explanation: When one leg is injured, the arms and hands take on extra work to support the body using crutches or a wheelchair.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think losing the use of one part stops all movement.

questions.stem: Ama broke her right arm. How does her left arm work interdependently to help her eat?
options: The left arm holds the food or spoon for her
The left arm chews the food
The left arm helps her see
The left arm helps her hear
hints: She can still use her good arm.
It takes over the work of the injured arm.
questions.explanation: Body parts can adapt and compensate for an injured part, showing how they work together to achieve a goal (eating).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think an injured arm stops all eating activities.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.3.3.1: Show understanding and appreciation of the interactions and interdependencies of organisms in an ecosystem
indicator.objective: Identify organisms in a habitat and describe why they live in a particular place

skills.description: Identify organisms in a given habitat
Identify observable features that help organisms live there
Explain why an organism lives in a particular place
Give examples of organisms and their habitats

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: All animals can live in any habitat.
A fish can live on land if it is wet.
Plants are not part of a habitat.
Birds live only in the air and never on land.
A frog is a fish because it lives in water.

questions.stem: Where does a fish live?
questions.explanation: A fish lives in water (a water habitat).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fish can live on land.

questions.stem: Where does a bird usually live?
questions.explanation: Birds live in trees (land habitat) and fly in the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think birds only live in the air.

questions.stem: Where does a goat live?
questions.explanation: A goat lives on land.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all animals live in water.

questions.stem: Where do grasshoppers usually live?
questions.explanation: Grasshoppers live in grassy areas on land.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think grasshoppers live in water.

questions.stem: What feature helps a fish swim in water?
hints: They are on the side of its body.
They help it move through water.
questions.explanation: Fins are the features that help a fish swim and balance in water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fish use legs to move.

questions.stem: What feature helps a bird fly in the air?
questions.explanation: Wings are the features that allow a bird to fly in the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think birds fly using fins.

questions.stem: What feature helps a frog swim in water?
hints: It has skin between its toes.
questions.explanation: A frog has webbed feet, which act like paddles to help it swim.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think frogs swim like fish with fins.

questions.stem: What feature helps a cow eat grass?
questions.explanation: Cows have flat teeth suitable for grinding grass and plants.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cows have sharp teeth like lions.

questions.stem: Why does a fish live in water?
options: It needs water to breathe and swim
It is afraid of the land
questions.explanation: A fish lives in water because it uses gills to breathe and fins to swim. It cannot survive on land.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fish just prefer water but could live on land.

questions.stem: Why do birds live in trees?
options: Trees provide shelter, safety, and a place to build nests
They are afraid of the ground
hints: Where do they lay their eggs?
Trees keep them safe from some predators.
questions.explanation: Birds live in trees because trees offer shelter, a safe place for their nests, and protection.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think birds live in trees because they are made of wood.

questions.stem: Why do grasshoppers live in grass?
options: The grass provides food and camouflage (hiding)
questions.explanation: Grasshoppers live in grass because they eat it and their green colour helps them hide from predators.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they live in grass for no reason.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a habitat?
hints: It is a natural place where living things live.
questions.explanation: A pond is an example of a natural habitat where fish, frogs, and water plants live.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any place is a habitat.

questions.stem: Why can a fish NOT live on land?
options: It does not have legs to walk, and it cannot breathe air
questions.explanation: A fish lacks legs for walking and uses gills to breathe in water. It cannot survive out of water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a fish can breathe on land if it is wet.

questions.stem: A tilapia has fins and gills. How are these features suited to its habitat?
options: Fins help it swim, and gills help it breathe in water
Fins help it fly, and gills help it eat
Fins help it walk, and gills help it run
Fins help it climb, and gills help it jump
hints: How does it move? How does it breathe?
questions.explanation: Tilapia lives in water; its fins help it swim, and its gills extract oxygen from the water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse the function of fins and gills.

questions.stem: Why does a frog live near a pond or stream?
options: It needs water to lay eggs, but also land to catch insects
It needs to drink water every minute
hints: Frogs start their lives as tadpoles in water.
Adult frogs catch insects on land.
questions.explanation: Frogs need water for breeding and laying eggs, but as adults, they live on land to catch insects.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think frogs are completely aquatic like fish.

questions.stem: After heavy rain, earthworms often come to the surface of the soil. Why do they live in the soil?
options: The soil is moist, and they can burrow for safety
They come up to drink water
They want to see the sun
hints: Where do they make their homes?
questions.explanation: Earthworms live in soil because it provides moisture and protection. When it rains, the soil gets too wet, forcing them up.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think worms come up because they like the light.

questions.stem: What feature helps a bird to catch insects in the air?
hints: It uses this to grab food.
questions.explanation: Birds have beaks adapted for catching and eating their specific types of food (e.g., insects).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think feet are used for catching food in the air.

questions.stem: Why can a camel survive in a hot desert, but not in a rainforest?
options: It is adapted to survive with very little water and extreme heat, which it would not find in a rainforest
It is too big for the rainforest
questions.explanation: Camels are adapted to dry, hot conditions. In a wet rainforest, they would suffer from the moisture and different environment.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any animal can survive anywhere.

questions.stem: Why do different organisms live in different habitats?
options: Because they have different features adapted to survive in specific conditions
Because they are afraid of each other
questions.explanation: Organisms live in habitats where their physical features and needs (food, water, shelter) are best met.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think habitat choice is random.

questions.stem: A frog has webbed feet and a fish has fins. Explain how BOTH features are suited to living in water.
options: Both features act like paddles to help them move through water
They are not suited to water
questions.explanation: Webbed feet and fins both increase the surface area, acting as paddles to propel the animals through water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not see the analogy between a frog's foot and a fish's fin.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.4.1.1: Demonstrate understanding of the concept of energy, its various forms and sources and the ways in which it can be transformed and conserved
indicator.objective: Know that light is a form of energy

skills.description: Understand that light is a form of energy that helps us see
Identify sources of light
Explain why light is important
Describe what happens when there is no light

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Light is not energy; it just makes things bright.
The moon is a source of light energy.
We can see in the dark without any light.
Light energy is only needed during the day.

questions.stem: What is light?
options: A form of energy that helps us see
questions.explanation: Light is a form of energy that enables us to see things around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think light is just brightness, not a form of energy.

questions.stem: Which of these is a natural source of light?
questions.explanation: The sun is a natural source of light because it is not made by humans.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon is a source of light.

questions.stem: Why do we need light?
hints: When it is dark, can you see well?
questions.explanation: We need light to see things around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think we only need light for plants.

questions.stem: Which of these is an artificial source of light?
questions.explanation: A flashlight is an artificial source of light made by humans.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all bright things are natural.

questions.stem: What happens when there is no light?
options: It is dark and we cannot see
questions.explanation: Without light, it is dark and our eyes cannot see objects around us.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think they can see in the dark naturally.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a source of light?
hints: Does a mirror make its own light?
questions.explanation: A mirror is not a source of light; it only reflects light from other sources.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a mirror produces light because it looks bright.

questions.stem: Why is light considered a form of energy?
options: Because it helps us do work like seeing and helps plants make food
Because it comes from the sun
hints: It helps plants and humans function.
questions.explanation: Light is energy because it enables us to see and helps plants make their own food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think energy only means electricity.

questions.stem: Why do plants need light?
hints: Plants use sunlight in their leaves.
questions.explanation: Plants need light to make their own food through photosynthesis.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants only need water.

questions.stem: Is the moon a source of light?
options: Yes, it makes its own light
No, it reflects light from the sun
hints: Does the moon have fire on it?
It shines because the sun shines on it.
questions.explanation: The moon does not make its own light; it reflects light from the sun.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think the moon produces its own light.

questions.stem: If you are in a dark room and you switch on a torch, what happens?
options: The light energy helps you see the objects in the room
questions.explanation: The torch emits light energy, which travels to the objects and allows you to see them.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think light just makes things look pretty.

questions.stem: Name one source of light you can find in your home.
questions.explanation: Common sources of light in the home include electric bulbs, candles, and torches.

questions.stem: What form of energy helps us to see?
hints: It helps you see in the dark with a torch.
questions.explanation: Light is the form of energy that helps us see.

questions.stem: Why is light energy important for animals?
options: It helps them find food and see danger
hints: Animals need to see to hunt.
They need to avoid being eaten.
questions.explanation: Light energy allows animals to see their surroundings, which helps them find food and avoid predators.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize animals depend on light for survival.

questions.stem: What would happen to plants if there was no light for many days?
options: They would stop making food and eventually die
questions.explanation: Without light, plants cannot perform photosynthesis and will eventually die.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants only need water.

questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE about light?
options: Light is a form of energy that travels and allows us to see
hints: It can be blocked by a wall.
questions.explanation: Light is a form of energy that travels in waves and enables vision.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think light is a physical object.

questions.stem: A firefly glows in the dark. Is it a natural or artificial source of light?
options: Natural, because it is a living thing that produces light
Natural, because it is made by humans
Artificial, because it is a bug
questions.explanation: A firefly is a natural source of light because it produces light through a chemical reaction in its body.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think anything that glows is artificial.

questions.stem: Explain why light is considered a form of energy.

criteria.description: States that light helps us see
States that it helps plants make food or is necessary for life

hints: What does light allow you to do?
questions.explanation: Light is energy because it enables us to see and helps plants make food.

questions.stem: Describe what your day would be like if there were no light from the sun or electricity.

criteria.description: States it would be very dark
States that activities like reading, walking, or finding things would be difficult

questions.explanation: Without light, it would be extremely difficult to perform daily activities like walking, reading, or working.

questions.stem: Why is the sun the most important source of light energy on Earth?
options: It provides the vast majority of light that supports life and ecosystems
It is the only source of light
It is the closest star to the Earth
hints: How much of the Earth does it light up?
Do we need it to live?
questions.explanation: The sun provides the primary light and energy for Earth, driving photosynthesis and maintaining life.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think artificial lights can replace the sun.

questions.stem: A student says 'Light and heat are the same thing.' Why is this not entirely true?
options: While they often come from the same sources (like the sun), light helps us see, while heat makes things warm
hints: What does light do to your eyes?
What does heat do to your skin?
questions.explanation: Light and heat are different forms of energy. Light allows vision, while heat changes temperature, although both can come from the sun or a fire.
questions.misconception: Pupils may conflate light and heat because they often occur together.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher the difference between a natural source of light and an artificial source of light, and give one example of each.

criteria.description: Explains that natural sources are found in nature and artificial sources are made by humans
Gives a correct example for each

hints: Think about the sun vs a torch.
questions.explanation: Natural sources exist in nature (e.g., the sun), while artificial sources are made by humans (e.g., a bulb).

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.4.1.2: Show understanding of the concept of heat in terms of its sources, effects, importance, and transfer from one medium to another
indicator.objective: Know heat as a form of energy and identify some sources of heat

skills.description: Understand that heat is a form of energy that makes things warm or hot
Identify sources of heat
Describe simple ways heat is produced
Explain why heat is important

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Heat is only produced by fire.
Cold is a form of energy.
Rubbing your hands together makes them cold.
Electric devices do not produce heat.

questions.stem: What is heat?
options: A form of energy that makes things warm or hot
questions.explanation: Heat is a form of energy that raises the temperature of objects, making them warm or hot.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think heat is a physical object.

questions.stem: Which of these is a natural source of heat?
questions.explanation: The sun is the main natural source of heat for the Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon gives heat.

questions.stem: Which of these produces heat in the home?
questions.explanation: A stove is a source of heat used for cooking in the home.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all household items produce heat.

questions.stem: What happens when you rub your hands together quickly?
questions.explanation: Rubbing your hands together creates friction, which produces heat, making them warm.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think rubbing makes them cold.

questions.stem: Why do we need heat?
options: To cook food and stay warm
hints: You wear a coat when it is cold.
questions.explanation: Heat is essential for cooking food and keeping our bodies warm.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think heat is only for cooking.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a source of heat?
questions.explanation: A block of ice is cold, not a source of heat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all solids are hot.

questions.stem: How is heat produced when you burn a piece of wood?
options: The burning process releases heat energy
The wood absorbs heat from the air
questions.explanation: Burning wood is a chemical reaction that releases heat energy.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the fire just appears.

questions.stem: Why is heat important for drying clothes?
options: Heat helps water evaporate from the clothes
Heat adds water to the clothes
Heat makes the clothes change colour
hints: Wet clothes dry in the sun.
The water goes into the air.
questions.explanation: Heat energy helps water evaporate, which dries the clothes.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not link heat to evaporation.

questions.stem: Which of these is an artificial source of heat?
options: A campfire started by a match
hints: It is used for warmth or cooking.
questions.explanation: A campfire is an artificial source of heat because it is started by humans.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think fire is always natural.

questions.stem: Ama touches a metal spoon left in a hot pot. What happens to the spoon?
options: The spoon becomes hot because heat moves from the pot to the spoon
hints: The pot is hotter than the spoon.
questions.explanation: Heat transfers from the hot pot to the cooler spoon, making the spoon hot.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand heat transfer.

questions.stem: Name one source of heat you use at home.
hints: You use it to warm up.
questions.explanation: Common sources of heat at home include stoves, fires, and electric heaters.

questions.stem: What form of energy makes things hot?
questions.explanation: Heat is the form of energy that makes things hot.

questions.stem: Why does a light bulb get hot after it has been on for a long time?
options: Because it converts electrical energy into light and heat energy
Because it absorbs cold from the room
Because it is painted with heat
hints: Some of the energy is lost as heat.
questions.explanation: Light bulbs convert electrical energy into light, but some of the energy is also transformed into heat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think bulbs only produce light.

questions.stem: Why is heat important for life on Earth?
options: It keeps the planet warm enough for living things to survive
It gives us light to see
hints: What would happen if the Earth was freezing?
questions.explanation: Heat from the sun keeps the Earth at a temperature suitable for life. Without it, the planet would be too cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect heat to survival.

questions.stem: Kwame wants to boil water. Which source of heat is best?
questions.explanation: A stove or fire provides enough heat to boil water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a fan can boil water.

questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE about heat?
options: Heat is a form of energy that transfers from a hotter object to a colder one
hints: The heat moves to your hand.
questions.explanation: Heat is energy that transfers from hotter objects to cooler ones.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think heat is static.

questions.stem: Explain how friction produces heat when you rub two sticks together.

criteria.description: States that friction converts movement energy into heat

hints: What happens when you rub your hands?
questions.explanation: The friction between the sticks converts kinetic energy into heat, making them warm.

questions.stem: Write down two ways heat is useful in our daily lives.

criteria.description: States a second valid use (e.g., drying clothes, keeping warm)

hints: What do you do in the kitchen?
What do you do when you are cold?
questions.explanation: Heat is useful for cooking food, keeping us warm, drying clothes, and generating electricity.

questions.stem: A student says 'Cold is a form of energy.' Why is this incorrect?
options: Cold is just the absence of heat; it is not a form of energy itself
Cold is a type of solid
hints: Objects get cold by losing heat.
questions.explanation: Cold is not an energy form; it is simply the state of having low heat. Objects become cold by losing heat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cold is an entity that can be added or removed.

questions.stem: Explain how the sun provides heat to the Earth.

criteria.description: States that the sun is a very hot object
States that it radiates heat energy across space to the Earth

hints: How does the heat reach us?
questions.explanation: The sun is extremely hot and radiates heat energy, which travels through space to warm the Earth.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher two sources of heat and explain why they are useful.

criteria.description: Explains a valid use for each

hints: Think about fire and the sun.
What do you use them for?
questions.explanation: For example, fire (for cooking) and the sun (for drying clothes and warming the Earth).

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.4.3.2: Recognise some simple machines used for making work easier, analyse their advantages and know their uses. e.g. levers, inclined planes and pulleys
indicator.objective: Demonstrate how to maintain and care for simple machines

skills.description: Identify ways to maintain simple machines
Explain why maintenance is important
Demonstrate a basic maintenance practice
Describe safe storage and handling of simple machines

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Machines don't need care; they are strong.
Water helps all machines work better.
Rust makes machines work better.
Oiling a machine is just for making it look shiny.
You can store any tool anywhere.

questions.stem: What is one way to care for a pair of scissors?
options: Clean them after use and keep them dry
questions.explanation: Cleaning and drying scissors prevents rust and keeps them working well.
questions.misconception: Pupils may leave tools in wet areas.

questions.stem: How can you care for a bicycle chain?
options: Apply oil to keep it moving smoothly
Leave it outside in the rain
questions.explanation: Oiling the bicycle chain keeps it lubricated, prevents rust, and ensures smooth movement.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water helps the chain.

questions.stem: Why is it important to maintain simple machines?
options: To make them last longer and work better
hints: You want to use them for a long time.
questions.explanation: Maintenance keeps machines in good condition so they last longer and function correctly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not see the value in maintenance.

questions.stem: Where should you store a sharp knife after using it?
options: In a safe, dry place away from children
questions.explanation: Sharp tools should be stored safely away from children to prevent accidents.
questions.misconception: Pupils may leave sharp tools lying around.

questions.stem: What happens to a metal tool if it is left in the rain?
questions.explanation: Leaving metal tools in the rain causes them to rust and become weak.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think rain cleans the tool.

questions.stem: Why should you oil a door hinge that is squeaking?
options: To reduce friction and stop the noise
hints: The squeak is caused by friction.
questions.explanation: Oil lubricates the hinge, reducing friction and stopping the squeaking sound.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect noise to friction.

questions.stem: Ama wants to clean her father's hammer. What should she use?
options: A dry cloth to wipe off dirt
questions.explanation: Wiping the hammer with a dry cloth removes dirt and prevents rust without damaging the tool.
questions.misconception: Pupils may wash metal tools with water.

questions.stem: Why is it important to use a tool for its correct purpose?
options: To prevent damage to the tool and avoid injury
hints: Do not use a screwdriver as a hammer.
It could break or hurt you.
questions.explanation: Using a tool for the wrong job can damage it and cause injury. Tools are designed for specific tasks.

questions.stem: Where should you keep a pair of scissors in the classroom?
options: In a drawer or a safe container
On the edge of the table
hints: Keep sharp things away from edges.
questions.explanation: Storing scissors in a safe place prevents them from falling or being played with dangerously.
questions.misconception: Pupils may leave tools on the floor.

questions.stem: What is the best way to prevent a metal tool from rusting?
options: Keep it dry and wipe it after use
questions.explanation: Keeping the tool dry and wiping off moisture prevents the rusting process.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think leaving it outside is good.

questions.stem: What should you apply to a machine to make its moving parts smooth?
hints: It comes in a bottle or tin.
questions.explanation: Applying oil or grease lubricates the moving parts, making them smooth.

questions.stem: Why should you keep your tools clean?
hints: You want them to work well.
questions.explanation: Clean tools last longer, work better, and are safer to use.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cleaning is just for appearance.

questions.stem: A bicycle chain is squeaking. What is the BEST solution?
hints: The squeak is due to friction.
questions.explanation: Cleaning the chain removes dirt, and applying oil lubricates it to stop the friction and noise.
questions.misconception: Pupils may try to force it.

questions.stem: If a farmer does not clean and oil his cutlass after using it, what will happen?
options: It will rust and become blunt or weak
questions.explanation: Without care, the metal cutlass will rust, making it weaker and less effective for cutting.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think tools stay sharp forever.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to use a hammer with a loose head?
options: The head can fly off and hurt someone
hints: The metal part could come off.
It could hit you or someone else.
questions.explanation: A loose hammer head can detach during use, causing serious injury. It should be repaired or replaced.

questions.stem: What is the correct way to maintain a wooden spoon?
options: Wash it, dry it thoroughly, and keep it in a dry place
Leave it soaking in water overnight
hints: Too much water can cause it to rot.
questions.explanation: Washing and drying a wooden spoon prevents it from cracking or growing mold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may leave wooden tools soaking.

questions.stem: Explain why a sewing machine needs to be oiled regularly.

criteria.description: States that oil reduces friction between moving parts
States that this keeps the machine running smoothly and prevents wear

questions.explanation: Oiling reduces friction between the moving parts, preventing wear and tear and ensuring the machine runs smoothly.

questions.stem: Show your teacher how to clean and oil a simple metal tool (e.g., a pair of scissors or a hinge).

criteria.description: Wipes the tool with a dry cloth to remove dirt
Applies a small amount of oil to the moving part

questions.explanation: This demonstrates the basic maintenance of a simple machine.

questions.stem: Describe how you would clean and store a kitchen knife safely.

criteria.description: States washing and drying the knife thoroughly
States storing it safely in a knife block or drawer

hints: Keep it dry to prevent rust.
Do not leave it on the counter.
questions.explanation: Washing, drying, and storing the knife safely prevents rust and accidents.

questions.stem: A worker is using a chisel with a mushroomed (flattened and jagged) head. Why is this dangerous?
options: The metal can shatter and fly into the eyes or skin
It makes the tool too light
It makes the chisel cut too fast
It turns the tool into a lever
questions.explanation: A mushroomed head is a sign of damaged, weakened metal that can shatter under impact, causing serious injury.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not recognize tool damage.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher two important maintenance practices for a bicycle.

criteria.description: Names one valid practice (e.g., oiling the chain)
Names a second valid practice (e.g., checking tire pressure, cleaning dirt)

questions.explanation: Oiling the chain and checking the tires are important maintenance practices for a bicycle.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.5.1.1: Recognise the importance of personal hygiene
indicator.objective: Describe ways of keeping the environment clean

skills.description: Describe ways to keep the environment clean
Explain why keeping the environment clean is important
Identify cleaning tools and materials and their uses
Demonstrate or describe cleaning a specific area safely

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Cleaning the environment is only about sweeping.
You can clean without any tools.
Dust from sweeping is harmless.
Weeding is not part of keeping the environment clean.
Only adults can clean the environment.

questions.stem: Which of these is a way to keep your school environment clean?
options: Leaving empty bottles on the desk
questions.explanation: Sweeping the compound removes dirt and leaves, keeping the environment clean.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cleaning only happens inside the classroom.

questions.stem: How can you help keep your classroom clean?
options: Eating in class and dropping crumbs
questions.explanation: Putting rubbish in the bin keeps the classroom tidy and prevents pests.
questions.misconception: Pupils may litter if they think someone else will clean it.

questions.stem: Why is it important to keep our environment clean?
questions.explanation: A clean environment reduces germs and pests, helping to prevent sickness.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect cleanliness to health.

questions.stem: Which tool is used for sweeping the floor?
hints: You use it on the floor.
questions.explanation: A broom is the tool used for sweeping floors and compounds.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse a broom with a mop.

questions.stem: What should you do with weeds in the school garden?
questions.explanation: Weeding (pulling out unwanted plants) keeps the garden clean and helps crops grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not consider weeding as cleaning.

questions.stem: Ama is going to dust the shelves. What should she use?
questions.explanation: A duster or clean cloth is used to wipe dust off shelves and surfaces.
questions.misconception: Pupils may use wet tools for dusting.

questions.stem: What happens if rubbish is left to pile up in the school compound?
options: It attracts flies and can cause diseases
It makes the school look beautiful
questions.explanation: Piled-up rubbish rots, attracts flies and pests, and can spread diseases.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize the health hazards of litter.

questions.stem: How can you keep the school toilet clean?
options: Flush after use and wash the floor
Leave dirty water on the floor
Do not clean it at all
questions.explanation: Flushing after use and washing the floor keeps the toilet clean and hygienic.

questions.stem: Why should you wear a nose mask when sweeping a very dusty area?
hints: Dust is bad for your lungs.
A mask covers your nose and mouth.
questions.explanation: Wearing a nose mask protects you from inhaling dust, which can cause coughing or breathing problems.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not see the health risk of dust.

questions.stem: Why is a clean environment important for children's health?
options: It reduces the spread of germs and diseases
questions.explanation: A clean environment reduces the presence of germs, which helps prevent diseases in children.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not link environment to health.

questions.stem: Name one way you can keep your home clean.
hints: What do you do with a broom?
What do you do with a mop?
questions.explanation: Sweeping, mopping, dusting, and throwing rubbish in a bin are ways to keep the home clean.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name a non-cleaning activity.

questions.stem: What tool is used for scrubbing the floor?
hints: You use it with soap and water.
questions.explanation: A scrubbing brush is used with soap and water to scrub floors.

questions.stem: How does keeping the environment clean help prevent the spread of diseases?
options: It removes breeding grounds for germs, flies, and mosquitoes
It increases the amount of dust
questions.explanation: Cleaning removes stagnant water and rubbish that mosquitoes and flies use to breed, reducing disease spread.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not understand how diseases spread.

questions.stem: What is the correct way to dispose of rubbish in school?
options: Put it in the bin and empty the bin regularly
Throw it over the school wall
questions.explanation: The correct way is to use a rubbish bin and ensure it is emptied and disposed of properly.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose unsafe methods like burning inside.

questions.stem: A community organizes a clean-up day. Which of these activities would help keep the environment clean?
options: Sweeping the streets and clearing gutters
hints: Sweeping and clearing gutters remove dirt.
Burning and throwing create more pollution.
questions.explanation: Sweeping streets and clearing gutters removes waste, making the environment cleaner and healthier.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think burning is a good way to clean up.

questions.stem: Ama needs to clean a dusty table. Which tools should she use?
options: A duster and a clean cloth
hints: Dust is best removed with a dry cloth.
You do not need water for dust.
questions.explanation: A duster or clean cloth is appropriate for wiping dust off a table.
questions.misconception: Pupils may use a broom on a table.

questions.stem: Describe the steps you would take to sweep a classroom.

criteria.description: Mentions clearing the floor of items
Mentions sweeping from the corners to the door
Mentions disposing of the dust in a bin

hints: Put the dust in a bin.
questions.explanation: Clearing items, sweeping from corners, and disposing of dust properly are the steps to clean a classroom.

questions.stem: Explain why it is important to keep the school environment clean.

criteria.description: States that it keeps the environment looking neat and free of pests

hints: What happens if it is dirty?
How do you feel in a clean place?
questions.explanation: A clean school environment is safer, healthier, and more pleasant for learning.

questions.stem: Show your teacher how to clean a designated area of the school environment (e.g., sweep a small section of the compound).

criteria.description: Shows proper handling of the tool

questions.explanation: This demonstrates the practical application of cleaning skills.

questions.stem: A school's clean-up club noticed that stagnant water in old cans was breeding mosquitoes. Which action is the BEST solution?
options: Emptying the cans and removing all stagnant water
Adding more water to the cans
hints: Remove the water to stop them.
questions.explanation: Removing stagnant water eliminates mosquito breeding sites, reducing the spread of malaria.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think covering the water is enough.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher two ways you can help keep your community clean.
hints: Think about where you throw rubbish.
questions.explanation: Proper waste disposal and participating in clean-up efforts help keep the community clean.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.5.2.1: Know common diseases of humans, causes, symptoms, effects and prevention
indicator.objective: Know how common skin diseases can be prevented

skills.description: Identify ways to prevent skin diseases
Name common skin diseases
Explain why prevention is important
Demonstrate or role-play a prevention scenario

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Skin diseases cannot be prevented.
You only need to bathe when you are dirty.
Sharing towels is fine as long as you are friends.
Skin diseases go away on their own without treatment.

questions.stem: How can you prevent skin diseases?
options: Bathe regularly with soap and water
questions.explanation: Bathing regularly with soap and water removes dirt and germs, helping prevent skin diseases.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not link bathing to disease prevention.

questions.stem: Why should you not share your towel with a friend?
options: The towel might be too small
questions.explanation: Sharing a towel can spread germs that cause skin diseases like ringworm.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sharing is always safe.

questions.stem: Which of these is a common skin disease?
hints: It causes a round, itchy patch.
questions.explanation: Ringworm is a common skin disease caused by a fungus.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse skin diseases with other illnesses.

questions.stem: Why is it important to prevent skin diseases?
hints: Skin diseases can be itchy and painful.
questions.explanation: Preventing skin diseases keeps you healthy and avoids discomfort.

questions.stem: What should you do after playing in the sand to prevent skin problems?
options: Wipe your hands on your clothes
questions.explanation: Washing your hands and bathing after playing in the sand removes dirt and prevents skin irritation.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not clean up after play.

questions.stem: Ama has ringworm. What should she do to prevent spreading it to her sister?
options: Not share her towel or clothes and wash them separately
questions.explanation: Not sharing personal items and washing them separately prevents the fungus from spreading.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize how contagious ringworm is.

questions.stem: Which of these is a common skin disease in children?
hints: It causes red spots on the skin.
questions.explanation: Measles is a viral disease that causes a red rash on the skin.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse measles with non-skin diseases.

questions.stem: Why is it important to keep your skin dry after bathing?
options: Fungus grows well in warm, wet places
questions.explanation: Drying your skin removes moisture, making it harder for fungi that cause skin diseases to grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not see the link between wet skin and fungal infections.

questions.stem: What can you do to prevent heat rashes?
options: Wear light, clean clothes and bathe regularly
Wear heavy clothes in the sun
hints: Heat rashes happen when you sweat.
questions.explanation: Wearing light, clean clothes and bathing regularly helps prevent sweat from irritating the skin.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know what causes heat rashes.

questions.stem: If you notice a red, itchy patch on your skin, what should you do?
options: Tell a parent or teacher and go to a clinic
hints: It might be a skin disease.
questions.explanation: Telling an adult and seeking medical help ensures proper treatment and prevents spreading.

questions.stem: Name one way to prevent skin diseases.
hints: What do you do in the bathroom?
questions.explanation: Bathing regularly and not sharing personal items are ways to prevent skin diseases.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say 'taking medicine' (prevention is about hygiene).

questions.stem: Name one common skin disease.
questions.explanation: Ringworm, measles, and eczema are common skin diseases.

questions.stem: Why is it important to wash your clothes regularly to prevent skin diseases?
options: Dirty clothes can trap sweat and dirt, causing skin irritation or infections
hints: Sweat and dirt stay on clothes.
questions.explanation: Dirty clothes trap sweat and dirt against the skin, creating an environment where germs and fungi can grow.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think clothes only need washing when visibly dirty.

questions.stem: How does keeping your finger nails short and clean help prevent skin diseases?
options: It stops dirt and germs from collecting under the nails and spreading to your skin
It makes your nails grow faster
hints: Short nails are easier to clean.
questions.explanation: Short, clean nails prevent dirt and germs from accumulating and causing skin infections.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think nail care is only cosmetic.

questions.stem: Role-play a scenario where you show a younger sibling how to bathe properly to prevent skin diseases.

criteria.description: Demonstrates correct bathing steps (wet, soap, scrub, rinse, dry)
Explains why each step is important for preventing skin diseases

questions.explanation: This tests the practical understanding of hygiene practices.

questions.stem: Act out how you would explain to a friend why they should not share their comb.

criteria.description: States that sharing combs can spread skin diseases or lice
Suggests a safer alternative (e.g., using your own comb)

hints: Think about what stays on a comb.
questions.explanation: This tests communication about preventing the spread of skin infections.

questions.stem: Write down two ways to prevent ringworm from spreading in a household.

criteria.description: States not sharing towels, clothes, or combs
States keeping the skin clean and dry

hints: What items should not be shared?
What should the skin be like?
questions.explanation: Not sharing personal items and keeping the skin dry prevent the spread of ringworm.

questions.stem: Explain why good personal hygiene is the best way to prevent skin diseases.

criteria.description: States that hygiene removes germs and dirt
States that it stops the conditions that allow skin diseases to spread

questions.explanation: Good hygiene removes the dirt and germs that cause skin diseases and prevents them from spreading.

questions.stem: A family shares one bar of soap for bathing. One child has a skin infection. What is the BEST advice?
options: Use separate soaps or liquid soap to prevent spreading the infection
Use the soap only on the infected child
hints: Soap can carry germs from one person to another.
questions.explanation: Using separate soaps prevents the infection from spreading via the shared bar of soap.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not think soap can transmit germs.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher three things you do every day to keep your skin healthy and prevent diseases.

criteria.description: Names a second action (e.g., wearing clean clothes)
Names a third action (e.g., not sharing personal items)

hints: What do you do in the morning?
What do you do after playing?
questions.explanation: Daily habits like bathing, wearing clean clothes, and not sharing personal items keep the skin healthy.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.5.4.1: Know that climate change is one of the most important environmental issues facing the world today and is a long-term change in the pattern of average weather of a specific region of the earth
indicator.objective: Identify human activities that pollute the atmosphere

skills.description: Identify human activities that pollute the atmosphere
Describe how these activities pollute the air
Explain how air pollution affects life
Suggest ways to reduce air pollution

spec.difficultyPlan: 5x D1, 7x D2, 5x D3, 3x D4
misconceptions: Burning rubbish is safe because it disappears.
Smoke from cars is harmless.
Air pollution only happens in cities.
Cutting down trees helps the atmosphere.
Climate change is not related to human activities.

questions.stem: Which of these human activities pollutes the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Burning rubbish releases smoke and harmful gases into the air, polluting the atmosphere.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think burning is safe.

questions.stem: Which of these releases harmful gases into the air?
questions.explanation: Car exhaust fumes release harmful gases like carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide, polluting the atmosphere.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not consider cars as polluters.

questions.stem: What happens to the air when people burn bushes?
questions.explanation: Bush burning releases smoke and harmful particles into the air, causing air pollution.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think burning cleans the air.

questions.stem: How does air pollution affect people's health?
hints: Dirty air goes into the lungs.
questions.explanation: Air pollution can cause coughing, asthma, and other breathing problems.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not link air pollution to health.

questions.stem: Which of these helps reduce air pollution?
questions.explanation: Planting trees helps clean the air by absorbing carbon dioxide and releasing oxygen.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know trees improve air quality.

questions.stem: How does smoke from factories pollute the atmosphere?
options: It releases harmful gases and particles into the air
It removes oxygen from the air
It turns the air into water
questions.explanation: Factory smoke releases pollutants like carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide, and particulate matter into the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think factory smoke is harmless.

questions.stem: Why is it harmful to burn rubbish in the open air?
options: It releases toxic smoke that pollutes the air and can make people sick
It makes the rubbish disappear safely
questions.explanation: Burning rubbish releases toxic fumes and particles that pollute the air and can cause health problems.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think burning is a safe way to dispose of waste.

questions.stem: How does air pollution affect plants?
options: It can damage leaves and slow down growth
questions.explanation: Air pollutants can damage plant leaves and reduce their ability to make food, slowing growth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think pollution only affects humans.

questions.stem: What can a community do to reduce air pollution from vehicles?
options: Encourage walking, cycling, and using public transport
Cut down trees along the road
questions.explanation: Walking, cycling, and using public transport reduce the number of vehicles on the road, lowering air pollution.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think more cars are better.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a cause of air pollution?
questions.explanation: Planting trees is not a cause of air pollution; it helps reduce it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all human activities pollute.

questions.stem: Name one human activity that pollutes the atmosphere.
hints: It comes from vehicles or factories.
questions.explanation: Burning rubbish, driving cars, and factory smoke are activities that pollute the atmosphere.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name a clean activity.

questions.stem: Name one way to reduce air pollution.
questions.explanation: Planting trees and reducing the burning of waste help reduce air pollution.

questions.stem: Why is air pollution a serious problem in big cities?
options: There are many cars and factories, leading to high levels of harmful gases
People in cities do not breathe
questions.explanation: High concentrations of vehicles and factories in cities release large amounts of pollutants into the air.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cities have cleaner air.

questions.stem: How does air pollution contribute to climate change?
options: Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere, causing the Earth to warm up
It has no effect on climate
hints: Gases like carbon dioxide trap heat.
questions.explanation: Pollutants like carbon dioxide are greenhouse gases that trap heat, contributing to global warming and climate change.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect air pollution to climate change.

questions.stem: Why is burning fossil fuels (like petrol) bad for the atmosphere?
options: It releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change
hints: Fossil fuels release gases when burned.
questions.explanation: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, which traps heat in the atmosphere and contributes to climate change.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know what fossil fuels are.

questions.stem: Write down two ways you can help reduce air pollution in your community.

criteria.description: States one action (e.g., planting trees, not burning rubbish)

questions.explanation: Planting trees and avoiding burning rubbish both help reduce air pollution.

questions.stem: Explain how smoke from vehicles and factories affects the atmosphere.

criteria.description: States that smoke releases harmful gases into the air
States that these gases pollute the air and can affect health and climate

hints: What comes out of exhaust pipes?
What does it do to the air?
questions.explanation: Smoke from vehicles and factories releases harmful gases that pollute the air and contribute to climate change.

questions.stem: A community is planning to reduce air pollution. Which strategy would be most effective?
options: Promoting the use of clean energy sources like solar power
Encouraging more people to burn their waste
Increasing the number of old vehicles on the road
hints: Solar power does not produce smoke.
It is a clean energy source.
questions.explanation: Using clean energy like solar power reduces the burning of fossil fuels, significantly lowering air pollution.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know about renewable energy.

questions.stem: Explain why cutting down trees can make air pollution worse.

criteria.description: States that trees absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen
States that fewer trees mean less carbon dioxide is removed from the air

hints: What do trees do with gases?
Why are trees important for clean air?
questions.explanation: Trees absorb carbon dioxide. Without them, more of this greenhouse gas remains in the atmosphere, worsening pollution and climate change.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher three human activities that pollute the atmosphere.
questions.explanation: Burning rubbish, car exhaust, and factory smoke are common sources of air pollution.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.1.1 Understand the physical features and life processes of living things and use this understanding to classify them
indicator.objective: Classify animals into insects, birds, mammals and reptiles

skills.description: Recognise the main observable features of insects, birds, mammals and reptiles (body covering, limbs, young ones, where they live).
Place a named Ghanaian animal into the correct group: insect, bird, mammal or reptile.
Give a simple reason for a classification using an observable feature, not just the animal's name.
Identify whether an animal is an example or non-example of a named group.

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: All animals that fly are birds.
Bats are birds.
Spiders are insects.
All small crawling animals are insects.
Mammals are only large land animals.
Reptiles are insects because they crawl.

questions.stem: Which of these is a feature of all insects?
options: They feed their young with milk.
They have scales on their body.
hints: Think about how many legs a cockroach or housefly has.
Count the legs on an ant.
questions.explanation: Insects have six legs. Feathers belong to birds, milk-feeding belongs to mammals, and scales belong to reptiles.
questions.misconception: Some learners think any small crawling animal is an insect.

questions.stem: A dog is best classified as which of these?
hints: Think about how a dog's body is covered.
Does a dog feed its puppies with milk?
questions.explanation: A dog has hair, gives birth to live young, and feeds its puppies with milk. These are features of mammals.
questions.misconception: Some learners think only wild animals are mammals.

questions.stem: A butterfly belongs to which group of animals?
hints: How many legs does a butterfly have?
Look at the body of a butterfly — is it in three parts?
questions.explanation: A butterfly has six legs and a body divided into three parts. These are features of insects.
questions.misconception: Some learners think butterflies are birds because they have wings.

questions.stem: Which group of animals has feathers covering their bodies?
hints: Think about the animals you see in a poultry farm.
What covers the body of a hen?
questions.explanation: Birds are the only group of animals among these that have feathers.
questions.misconception: Some learners think all flying animals have feathers.

questions.stem: Which of these animals is a reptile?
hints: Reptiles have dry skin covered with scales.
Think of an animal that crawls on its belly.
questions.explanation: A snake has dry, scaly skin and crawls on its belly. It is a reptile.
questions.misconception: Some learners think all crawling animals are insects.

questions.stem: A parrot is best classified as which of these?
hints: Think about what covers a parrot's body.
questions.explanation: A parrot has feathers, wings, and a beak. It is a bird.
questions.misconception: Some learners think parrots are mammals because they can talk.

questions.stem: A snake belongs to which group of animals?
hints: What covers the body of a snake?
questions.explanation: A snake has dry, scaly skin and no legs. These features show it is a reptile.
questions.misconception: Some learners think snakes are insects because they crawl.

questions.stem: Why is a bat grouped as a mammal and not a bird, even though it flies?
options: It has feathers on its body.
It has six legs and a three-part body.
It has hair and feeds its young with milk.
It has dry scales on its skin.
hints: Look at what covers a bat's body.
Think about how a bat feeds its babies.
questions.explanation: A bat has hair on its body and feeds its young with milk. These are mammal features. Flying alone does not make an animal a bird.
questions.misconception: All animals that fly are birds.

questions.stem: Which of these animals is NOT a mammal?
hints: Mammals have hair or fur and feed their young with milk.
Which of these animals has scales?
questions.explanation: A crocodile has scales and lays eggs. It is a reptile, not a mammal. The cow, goat and dog all have hair and feed their young with milk.
questions.misconception: Some learners think all four-legged animals are mammals.

questions.stem: Which group of animals has dry skin covered with scales?
hints: Think of the skin of a lizard.
questions.explanation: Reptiles such as lizards, snakes, and crocodiles have dry, scaly skin.
questions.misconception: Some learners think fish and reptiles are the same because both have scales.

questions.stem: A grasscutter belongs to which group of animals?
hints: Does a grasscutter have hair or fur?
Does it feed its young with milk?
questions.explanation: A grasscutter has fur and feeds its young with milk. It is a mammal.
questions.misconception: Some learners think grasscutters are reptiles because they live in holes.

questions.stem: A learner says a spider is an insect because it has many legs. What is the best correction?
options: A spider is not an insect because it has eight legs, not six.
A spider is a mammal because it has hair.
A spider is a reptile because it has scales.
A spider is a bird because it can climb trees.
hints: Count the legs on a spider.
How many legs do insects have?
questions.explanation: Insects have six legs. A spider has eight legs, so it is not an insect.

questions.stem: Give one reason why a lizard is classified as a reptile.
answer: it has dry skin covered with scales
hints: Think about the skin of a lizard.
Does a lizard have feathers or scales?
questions.explanation: A lizard has dry skin covered with scales. This is a feature of reptiles.
questions.misconception: Some learners think lizards are insects because they crawl.

questions.stem: Why is a whale classified as a mammal and not a fish?
options: It lives in water and has fins.
It has scales and lays eggs.
It breathes air and feeds its young with milk.
hints: Think about how a whale breathes.
Does a whale feed its baby with milk?
questions.explanation: A whale breathes air and feeds its young with milk. These are mammal features, even though it lives in water.
questions.misconception: All animals that live in water are fish.

questions.stem: Name two mammals that live in water.
hints: Think of large animals in the sea that breathe air.
They feed their babies with milk.
questions.explanation: Whales and dolphins are mammals that live in water. They breathe air and feed their young with milk.
questions.misconception: All animals in water are fish.

questions.stem: A millipede has many legs. Is it an insect? Explain your answer.
answer: no, it has more than six legs
no, it is not an insect because it has many legs, not six
hints: How many legs does an insect have?
Count the legs on a millipede — is it six?
questions.explanation: A millipede is not an insect because it has many more than six legs. Insects have exactly six legs.
questions.misconception: All small crawling animals are insects.

questions.stem: State one difference between birds and reptiles.
answer: birds have feathers but reptiles have scales
birds have feathers, reptiles have scales
birds have feathers and reptiles do not
hints: What covers the body of a bird?
What covers the body of a reptile?
questions.explanation: Birds have feathers on their bodies, while reptiles have dry scales.
questions.misconception: Some learners think all animals with wings are birds.

questions.stem: A learner finds a small animal with six legs, wings, and a body in three parts. Which group does it belong to and why?
options: Insect, because it has six legs and a three-part body.
hints: How many body parts does it have?
questions.explanation: Six legs and a body in three parts are insect features. Wings alone are not enough to make it a bird because it has no feathers.
questions.misconception: All animals that fly are birds.

questions.stem: A friend says, 'All animals that fly are birds.' Name two flying animals that are NOT birds and state their groups.
answer: butterfly is an insect and bat is a mammal
bat is a mammal, butterfly is an insect
hints: Think of an animal that flies at night and has fur.
Think of an insect with colourful wings.
questions.explanation: A bat is a mammal that flies, and a butterfly is an insect that flies. Flying alone does not make an animal a bird.
questions.misconception: All animals that fly are birds.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly explains why a cow is a mammal?
options: It has four legs and lives on land.
It eats grass and chews cud.
It has a tail and horns.
It has hair, gives birth to live young, and feeds its calf with milk.
hints: How does a cow feed its calf?
questions.explanation: A cow has hair, gives birth to live young, and feeds its calf with milk. These are the key features of mammals.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B4.1.2.2 Understand mixtures, their types, formation, uses and ways of separating them into their components
indicator.objective: Identify a liquid-liquid mixture and describe how to separate its components

skills.description: Recognise that a liquid-liquid mixture is formed when two or more liquids are combined.
Distinguish between liquids that mix uniformly (miscible) and those that do not mix uniformly (immiscible).
Give or identify everyday examples of miscible liquid pairs (e.g. water and vinegar, water and soft drink).
Give or identify everyday examples of immiscible liquid pairs (e.g. water and cooking oil, water and kerosene).
Describe how to separate immiscible liquids using a separating funnel or improvised version.
Explain simply why immiscible liquids can be separated by a separating funnel (they form layers).

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: All liquids mix together.
Oil and water form one uniform liquid when stirred.
You can separate oil and water by stirring them well.
A separating funnel works because it heats the liquids.
Miscible liquids can be separated with a separating funnel.
Kerosene and water are miscible because both are liquids.

questions.stem: What is a liquid-liquid mixture?
options: When two solids are mixed together
When two or more liquids are combined
When a liquid is mixed with a gas
hints: Think about what is being mixed — are they solids or liquids?
A liquid-liquid mixture has two liquids.
questions.explanation: A liquid-liquid mixture is formed when two or more liquids are combined, such as water and vinegar.
questions.misconception: Some learners think any mixture is a liquid-liquid mixture.

questions.stem: When you pour water and vinegar into the same cup and stir, what have you made?
hints: Are both water and vinegar liquids?
questions.explanation: Water and vinegar are both liquids. Mixing them makes a liquid-liquid mixture.
questions.misconception: Some learners think mixing liquids creates a solid.

questions.stem: What do we call liquids that mix uniformly without forming separate layers?
hints: Think of water and vinegar — they mix completely.
questions.explanation: Miscible liquids mix uniformly and do not form separate layers.
questions.misconception: Some learners confuse miscible with immiscible.

questions.stem: Which of these is a miscible liquid pair?
hints: Which pair mixes completely without layers?
questions.explanation: Water and vinegar mix uniformly. Cooking oil, kerosene and palm oil do not mix with water — they form layers.

questions.stem: Which of these liquid pairs does NOT mix uniformly?
questions.explanation: Water and cooking oil do not mix uniformly — they form separate layers. The other pairs mix uniformly.

questions.stem: A learner mixes water and cooking oil in a bottle and shakes it well. After some time, what will the learner observe?
options: One uniform liquid with no layers
Two separate layers with oil on top
The oil will turn into a solid
questions.explanation: Water and cooking oil are immiscible. They do not mix uniformly, so they form two separate layers with oil on top.
questions.misconception: Oil and water form one uniform liquid when stirred.

questions.stem: Why do water and palm oil form separate layers when mixed?
hints: They form layers instead of mixing.
questions.explanation: Water and palm oil are immiscible. They do not mix uniformly and form separate layers.
questions.misconception: Stirring makes immiscible liquids mix permanently.

questions.stem: Which tool is best used to separate a mixture of cooking oil and water?
hints: Oil and water form two layers.
A separating funnel lets you drain one layer at a time.
questions.explanation: A separating funnel is used to separate immiscible liquids like oil and water because they form two layers.
questions.misconception: You can separate oil and water by stirring them well.

questions.stem: Give one example of two liquids that mix uniformly (miscible liquids).
hints: Think of two liquids you can mix without them forming layers.
questions.explanation: Water and vinegar mix uniformly. They are miscible liquids.
questions.misconception: All liquids form layers when mixed.

questions.stem: Which of these is an immiscible liquid pair?
hints: Which pair does not mix and forms layers?
Kerosene is like oil — it floats on water.
questions.explanation: Water and kerosene do not mix uniformly. They are immiscible and form separate layers.
questions.misconception: Kerosene and water are miscible because both are liquids.

questions.stem: When using a separating funnel to separate a mixture of oil and water, which liquid comes out first when the tap is opened?
hints: Which liquid is heavier — water or oil?
The heavier liquid settles at the bottom.
questions.explanation: Water is denser than oil and settles at the bottom of the funnel, so it comes out first when the tap is opened.
questions.misconception: Oil comes out first because it is on top.

questions.stem: Why can a separating funnel separate a mixture of oil and water?
options: Because oil and water are miscible liquids
Because oil and water form two separate layers, with water at the bottom
Because the separating funnel heats the liquids
Because the separating funnel changes oil into water
hints: Do oil and water form layers?
