Which liquid settles at the bottom?
questions.explanation: Oil and water are immiscible, so they form two layers. Water is denser and settles at the bottom, allowing it to be drained out first.
questions.misconception: A separating funnel works because it heats the liquids.

questions.stem: Describe how you would separate a mixture of kerosene and water using a separating funnel.
answer: pour the mixture into a separating funnel and let it settle into two layers, then open the tap to let the water out first
pour it into a separating funnel, let it settle, then open the tap to drain the water
hints: First let the mixture settle into two layers.
Which liquid is denser — water or kerosene?
questions.explanation: Pour the kerosene-water mixture into a separating funnel. Let it settle into two layers. Open the tap to let the denser water flow out first, then close the tap to keep the kerosene.
questions.misconception: You can separate kerosene and water by stirring.

questions.stem: A learner says, 'You can separate water and vinegar by using a separating funnel.' Is the learner correct?
options: Yes, because all liquid mixtures can be separated by a separating funnel
No, because water and vinegar are miscible and do not form separate layers
Yes, because vinegar is heavier than water
No, because vinegar is a solid
hints: Do water and vinegar form layers?
A separating funnel works only when layers form.
questions.explanation: Water and vinegar are miscible — they mix uniformly and do not form layers. A separating funnel works only for immiscible liquids that form layers.
questions.misconception: Miscible liquids can be separated with a separating funnel.

questions.stem: A learner mixes two liquids in a cup. After some time, they form two layers. What type of mixture is this?
hints: Layers mean the liquids did not mix uniformly.
What do we call liquids that do not mix uniformly?
questions.explanation: When two liquids form separate layers, they are immiscible. The mixture is an immiscible liquid-liquid mixture.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between miscible and immiscible liquids.
answer: miscible liquids mix uniformly while immiscible liquids do not mix uniformly and form layers
miscible liquids mix completely, immiscible liquids form separate layers
questions.explanation: Miscible liquids mix uniformly without forming layers (e.g. water and vinegar). Immiscible liquids do not mix uniformly and form separate layers (e.g. water and oil).

questions.stem: Give two examples of immiscible liquid pairs.
answer: water and cooking oil, water and kerosene
cooking oil and water, kerosene and water
water and palm oil, water and kerosene
hints: Think of two liquids that do not mix and form layers.
Oil and water is one example.
questions.explanation: Water and cooking oil, and water and kerosene, are immiscible pairs. They do not mix uniformly and form separate layers.

questions.stem: Why can you separate oil and water with a separating funnel but not water and vinegar?
answer: oil and water are immiscible and form two layers so the denser water can be drained out first, but water and vinegar are miscible and mix uniformly so they cannot be separated this way
oil and water form layers but water and vinegar mix completely
hints: Do oil and water form layers?
Do water and vinegar form layers?
questions.explanation: Oil and water are immiscible — they form two layers, and the denser water can be drained out first. Water and vinegar are miscible — they mix uniformly and do not form layers, so a separating funnel cannot separate them.
questions.misconception: Miscible liquids can be separated with a separating funnel.

questions.stem: A pupil has a mixture of cooking oil and water. They want to separate the two liquids. Which method will work best?
options: Pouring the mixture through a sieve
Heating the mixture until one liquid boils
Pouring the mixture into a separating funnel and letting it settle
hints: Stirring does not separate immiscible liquids.
Oil and water form layers — how can you drain one layer off?
questions.explanation: Pouring the mixture into a separating funnel allows the oil and water to settle into two layers. The water can then be drained out from the bottom.
questions.misconception: You can separate oil and water by stirring them well.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to make a miscible liquid mixture for a class activity. Which pair of liquids should they choose?
hints: Which pair mixes completely without forming layers?
Cooking oil, kerosene and palm oil all float on water.
questions.explanation: Water and vinegar are miscible and mix uniformly. The other pairs are immiscible and form separate layers.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.1.1 Recognise that some events in our environment occur recurrently
indicator.objective: Demonstrate understanding of cyclic movements in the environment

skills.description: Recognise that a movement or event that repeats in a regular pattern is called a cycle.
Identify examples of cyclic movements in the environment (e.g. swinging pendulum, clock hands, merry-go-round, walking limbs).
Describe the back-and-forth (to-and-fro) swinging of a pendulum as a cyclic movement.
Describe the repeating movement of the second hand on an analogue clock.
Describe how parts of the body move in a repeating pattern during walking.
State the common feature of cyclic movements (they repeat after a regular time or pattern).

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: A cycle is any movement, even if it does not repeat.
A pendulum moves in only one direction.
Clock hands move randomly.
Walking is not a cycle because we can stop.
Merry-go-round is not cyclic because it does not go back and forth.
Cyclic movements never stop.

questions.stem: What is a cyclic movement?
options: A movement that happens only once
A movement that changes direction randomly
A movement that repeats in a regular pattern
A movement that stops and never starts again
hints: Think about the word 'cycle' — like a bicycle wheel going round and round.
Does a cyclic movement happen once or many times?
questions.explanation: A cyclic movement is a movement that repeats in a regular pattern. The word 'cycle' means going round and round or repeating.
questions.misconception: A cycle is any movement, even if it does not repeat.

questions.stem: Which of these is a cyclic movement?
options: A car moving from Accra to Kumasi
A stone falling once to the ground
A girl walking straight to the market and stopping
hints: A pendulum swings back and forth many times.
questions.explanation: A pendulum keeps swinging back and forth in a regular pattern. That is a cyclic movement.
questions.misconception: A cycle is any movement, even if it does not repeat.

questions.stem: What does the second hand of an analogue clock do?
options: It only moves when someone pushes it
It moves randomly in any direction
It moves round the clock face again and again
hints: Watch a clock for one minute.
Does the second hand keep moving?
questions.explanation: The second hand moves round the clock face again and again in a regular pattern. This is a cyclic movement.

questions.stem: A pendulum is a small ball hanging on a string. When you pull the ball to one side and let it go, what does it do?
hints: Think about a swing in a playground.
It moves from one side to the other.
questions.explanation: When you let go, the ball swings from one side to the other and back again. This back-and-forth movement is cyclic.
questions.misconception: A pendulum moves in only one direction.

questions.stem: When you walk, your legs move in a pattern. What kind of pattern is this?
options: A pattern that happens only once
hints: Think about the steps you take when walking.
Left, right, left, right — does the pattern repeat?
questions.explanation: When we walk, our legs move left, right, left, right in a repeating pattern. This repeating pattern makes walking a cyclic movement.
questions.misconception: Walking is not a cycle because we can stop.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a cyclic movement?
options: It repeats after a regular time or pattern
It happens once and never again
hints: Does it happen once or many times?
questions.explanation: A cyclic movement repeats after a regular time or pattern. Examples include a clock's second hand and a swinging pendulum.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a cyclic movement?
options: The hands of a clock moving
A ball rolling once down a hill
hints: Which movement happens only once and does not repeat by itself?
A ball rolling down a hill stops at the bottom.
questions.explanation: A ball rolling once down a hill does not repeat by itself. The other three movements repeat in a regular pattern.
questions.misconception: A cycle is any movement, even if it does not repeat.

questions.stem: Ama set up a pendulum and watched it. What describes the movement of the pendulum?
options: It moves forward and never comes back
It moves back and forth many times
It spins in a full circle
hints: Think about how a pendulum hangs.
Does it swing from side to side?
questions.explanation: A pendulum swings from one side to the other and back again, many times. This is a back-and-forth cyclic movement.
questions.misconception: A pendulum moves in only one direction.

questions.stem: Why is the movement of the second hand on an analogue clock called a cyclic movement?
options: Because it moves only when the clock is wound
Because it only moves during the day
Because it moves in a straight line
Because it goes round the clock face again and again
hints: Watch the second hand for one minute.
Does it return to where it started?
questions.explanation: The second hand goes round the clock face and returns to the same position again and again. This regular repeating is what makes it cyclic.

questions.stem: What is the common feature of a swinging pendulum, the second hand of a clock and a merry-go-round?
options: They all move in a repeating pattern
They all move in straight lines
They all stop after one round
They all only move at night
hints: Think about what happens after each movement.
Do they keep doing the same movement?
questions.explanation: All three movements repeat in a regular pattern. That is the common feature of cyclic movements.
questions.misconception: A cycle is any movement, even if it does not repeat.

questions.stem: Which of these is a cyclic movement?
options: A kite flying once across the sky
A boy running in a straight line
A stone thrown into a river
hints: Which one keeps going round and round?
A merry-go-round goes round again and again.
questions.explanation: A merry-go-round turns round and round, returning to the same position repeatedly. This is a cyclic movement.
questions.misconception: Merry-go-round is not cyclic because it does not go back and forth.

questions.stem: Name one movement of your body that is cyclic.
hints: Think of something you do again and again.
Walking uses your legs in a repeating pattern.
questions.explanation: Walking, breathing, blinking and chewing are all movements that repeat. They are cyclic movements of the body.

questions.stem: Pupil A says a pendulum is cyclic. Pupil B says a merry-go-round is cyclic. What makes both movements cyclic?
options: They both happen again and again in a regular pattern
They both happen only at night
hints: Think about what happens after one round.
questions.explanation: Both movements happen again and again in a regular pattern. Repeating regularly is what makes a movement cyclic.
questions.misconception: A cycle is any movement, even if it does not repeat.

questions.stem: A pupil notices that the sun rises every morning and sets every evening. Why is this a cyclic movement?
options: Because it happens every day in a regular pattern
Because it happens only in Kumasi
Because the sun moves in a straight line
hints: Think about how often the sun rises.
questions.explanation: The sun rises and sets every day in a regular pattern. This repeated daily pattern is a cycle.
questions.misconception: A cycle is any movement, even if it does not repeat.

questions.stem: Describe the movement of a pendulum in one sentence.
answer: a pendulum swings back and forth in a regular pattern
it swings from side to side and back again
hints: It is a ball on a string.
It moves from one side to the other and back.
questions.explanation: A pendulum swings from side to side and back again in a regular pattern. This back-and-forth movement repeats, so it is cyclic.
questions.misconception: A pendulum moves in only one direction.

questions.stem: A pupil watches the second hand of an analogue clock. The hand passes the 12 at 10:00:00 am and again at 10:01:00 am. What does this show?
options: The hand stops after one round
The hand repeats its movement every 60 seconds
The hand only moves once a day
hints: How many seconds are in one minute?
Does the hand come back to the same place after 60 seconds?
questions.explanation: The second hand passes the 12 once every 60 seconds. So its movement repeats every 60 seconds in a regular pattern — that is a cycle.

questions.stem: A pupil lists movements they see at home. Which list contains ONLY cyclic movements?
options: A window being opened once, a door being closed once, a pot boiling
A cup falling off a table, a stone thrown into a river, a match being lit
A girl running to school, a boy jumping once, a goat eating once
A mother stirring soup round and round, a fan spinning, a child swinging on a swing
hints: Which list has movements that keep repeating?
Stirring, spinning and swinging all repeat.
questions.explanation: Stirring soup, a spinning fan and a child swinging all repeat in a regular pattern. The other lists contain one-time movements.
questions.misconception: A cycle is any movement, even if it does not repeat.

questions.stem: Explain why walking is a cyclic movement.
answer: because the legs move in a repeating pattern like left, right, left, right
because the legs keep moving in the same repeating pattern
because the legs keep alternating left and right in a pattern
hints: What pattern do your legs make when walking?
questions.explanation: When we walk, our legs move left, right, left, right in a repeating pattern. This repeating pattern makes walking a cyclic movement.
questions.misconception: Walking is not a cycle because we can stop.

questions.stem: What do all cyclic movements have in common?
answer: they repeat in a regular pattern
hints: Do they happen once or many times?
questions.explanation: All cyclic movements repeat in a regular pattern. A pendulum, a clock's second hand and a merry-go-round all do this.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'The movement of a fan is NOT cyclic because the fan can be switched off.' Is this correct?
options: Yes, because a movement must never stop to be cyclic
No, because a movement can stop and still be cyclic while it is happening
Yes, because only pendulums are cyclic
No, because a fan does not move
hints: Does stopping later mean the movement was never cyclic?
Think about the movement WHILE the fan is on.
questions.explanation: A cyclic movement can stop, but while it is happening, it repeats in a regular pattern. A fan blade turning round and round is cyclic while the fan is on.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.1.2 Recognise the relationship between the earth and the sun
indicator.objective: Identify the objects in the sky during day and night

skills.description: Identify objects seen in the daytime sky (e.g. sun, clouds, birds, sometimes moon).
Identify objects seen in the night-time sky (e.g. moon, stars, darkness).
Compare similarities and differences between the day sky and the night sky.
Recognise objects that can be seen in both day and night skies (e.g. moon, clouds, sometimes stars).
Explain simply that day and night follow each other in a 24-hour cycle.

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: The sun disappears at night because it goes behind a hill.
Stars only exist at night.
The moon is only in the night sky.
Day and night happen at the same time everywhere.
The sky is always blue at night.
The sun and moon cannot be seen on the same day.

questions.stem: Which of these is found in the daytime sky?
hints: What lights up the sky in the morning?
What do you see above you at noon?
questions.explanation: The sun and clouds are seen in the daytime sky. Stars usually appear at night.
questions.misconception: The sun disappears at night because it goes behind a hill.

questions.stem: Which of these is found in the night-time sky?
hints: What do you see when it is dark?
Think of the moon and twinkling lights.
questions.explanation: The moon and stars are seen in the night-time sky.

questions.stem: What gives light to the earth during the day?
hints: What is very bright in the sky at noon?
It rises in the morning and sets in the evening.
questions.explanation: The sun gives light during the day. The moon and stars give some light at night.
questions.misconception: The sun disappears at night because it goes behind a hill.

questions.stem: What can you see in the sky on a clear night?
hints: What twinkles in the sky at night?
questions.explanation: The moon and stars are seen in the night sky on a clear night.

questions.stem: How long does it take for day and night to follow each other once?
hints: How many hours are in a day and a night together?
A day and a night make one full cycle.
questions.explanation: Day and night together take 24 hours. This is one full day.
questions.misconception: Day and night happen at the same time everywhere.

questions.stem: What is ONE difference between the day sky and the night sky?
options: The day sky is dark and the night sky is bright
The night sky is dark and the day sky is bright
hints: What colour is the sky at noon?
What colour is the sky at midnight?
questions.explanation: The day sky is bright, mostly lit by the sun. The night sky is dark, lit only by the moon and stars.
questions.misconception: The sky is always blue at night.

questions.stem: Which of these can sometimes be seen in BOTH the day sky and the night sky?
hints: Is the moon only visible at night?
Sometimes you can see the moon before sunset.
questions.explanation: The moon can sometimes be seen during the day and also at night. It is not only a night-time object.
questions.misconception: The moon is only in the night sky.

questions.stem: Name two things you can see in the daytime sky.
hints: What is very bright in the sky?
What white shapes float in the sky?
questions.explanation: The sun, clouds, birds, and sometimes the moon can be seen in the daytime sky.
questions.misconception: Only the sun is visible during the day.

questions.stem: Name two things you can see in the night sky.
hints: What is bright in the sky at night?
questions.explanation: The moon and stars are common objects in the night sky.
questions.misconception: Only the moon is in the night sky.

questions.stem: What happens to the sky in a 24-hour cycle?
options: Day and night follow each other
The sky stays bright for 24 hours
The sky stays dark for 24 hours
The sky turns green and red
questions.explanation: In 24 hours, day and night follow each other once. This is the 24-hour cycle.
questions.misconception: Day and night happen at the same time everywhere.

questions.stem: Why are the sun and moon often seen at different times?
options: Because the sun shines only at noon
Because the moon runs away from the sun
Because the sun is afraid of the moon
Because the sun gives light while the moon is usually brighter at night
hints: When do we usually see the moon clearly?
questions.explanation: The sun lights the day. The moon is often seen more clearly at night because the sky is darker. The moon is sometimes seen during the day too.
questions.misconception: The moon is only in the night sky.

questions.stem: Which object can be seen in the sky during the day and sometimes at night?
hints: It is round and gives some light at night.
Sometimes you can see it in the afternoon too.
questions.explanation: The moon can be seen at night and sometimes in the daytime too.
questions.misconception: The moon is only in the night sky.

questions.stem: Which of these correctly compares the day and night skies?
options: Both skies have the same objects all the time
The day sky is bright and mostly lit by the sun, while the night sky is dark and lit by the moon and stars
The day sky is dark and the night sky is bright
hints: What lights the sky at midday?
What lights the sky at midnight?
questions.explanation: The day sky is bright because of the sun. The night sky is dark and lit by the moon and stars.
questions.misconception: The sky is always blue at night.

questions.stem: In which of these ways are the day and night skies SIMILAR?
options: Both can show the moon at some time
hints: Is the moon seen only at night?
The moon can appear in the day as well.
questions.explanation: The moon can appear in both the day and night skies, though it is usually clearer at night. This is one similarity.
questions.misconception: The moon is only in the night sky.

questions.stem: What happens to the sky in a 24-hour cycle?
answer: day and night follow each other
the sky changes from day to night and back to day
day follows night and night follows day
hints: Think about what comes after daytime.
questions.explanation: In 24 hours, daytime follows night-time and then night-time follows daytime again. This repeating pattern is the 24-hour cycle.
questions.misconception: The sky stays the same for 24 hours.

questions.stem: Ama says, 'The sun goes behind a hill at night.' What is a better explanation?
options: The sun is switched off by people
The sun moves to another country
The earth turns so that the sun is hidden from our side until morning
hints: Why does the sun seem to leave at night?
Is the sun hidden from view while the earth turns?
questions.explanation: The earth turns (rotates). At night, our side of the earth faces away from the sun, so we cannot see it. In the morning, our side faces the sun again.
questions.misconception: The sun disappears at night because it goes behind a hill.

questions.stem: Why do stars seem to disappear in the daytime?
options: The stars go away during the day
The stars turn into the sun
The bright light of the sun makes it hard to see the stars
hints: Do stars go away or do we just see them less?
questions.explanation: Stars are still there in the daytime, but the sun's bright light makes it hard to see them from the earth. They are easier to see at night.

questions.stem: Describe one difference and one similarity between the day sky and the night sky.
answer: difference: the day sky is bright and the night sky is dark; similarity: the moon can be seen in both skies
difference: the sun lights the day while the moon and stars light the night; similarity: clouds can be seen in both skies
hints: Think of what lights the day and the night.
Is there anything that can be seen in both?
questions.explanation: Difference: the day sky is bright (from the sun) while the night sky is dark (lit by the moon and stars). Similarity: both skies can show the moon or clouds at some time.
questions.misconception: The day and night skies are exactly the same.

questions.stem: Which of these can be seen in the sky during both the day and the night?
hints: Think of white or grey shapes in the sky.
Do clouds only appear in the daytime?
questions.explanation: Clouds can be seen in the sky during both the day and the night. They are not only a daytime object.
questions.misconception: Only the sun and stars are in the sky.

questions.stem: Why do day and night follow each other every 24 hours?
options: Because the sun goes around the earth once every 24 hours
Because the earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours
Because the moon covers the sun
Because the sky changes its mind
hints: What does the earth do every 24 hours?
Think about one side of the earth facing the sun while the other side is dark.
questions.explanation: The earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours. The side facing the sun has day, and the side facing away has night. As it spins, day and night follow each other.
questions.misconception: The sun moves around the earth.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.1.3 Show understanding of the roles of condensation, evaporation, transpiration and precipitation in the hydrological (water) cycle
indicator.objective: Demonstrate the process of evapotranspiration

skills.description: State simply that evapotranspiration is water vapour leaving plants and animals/the ground into the air.
Describe transpiration as the loss of water vapour from plant leaves.
Recognise evaporation as water changing into vapour from surfaces like soil, rivers and puddles.
Describe how breathing out onto a surface shows water vapour leaving the body.
Explain what happens when a plastic bag is tied over a leafy plant (water droplets form inside).
State one reason evapotranspiration is important in the water cycle.

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: Plants do not release water.
Evapotranspiration is only about evaporation from rivers.
Water droplets in the bag come from outside the bag.
Only animals breathe out water vapour.
Transpiration is the same as respiration.
Evapotranspiration happens only at night.

questions.stem: What is evapotranspiration?
options: When water vapour leaves plants and the ground into the air
When rain falls from the sky
When water is poured into a bottle
hints: Both processes send water vapour into the air.
questions.explanation: Evapotranspiration is when water vapour leaves plants (transpiration) and the ground (evaporation) and goes into the air.
questions.misconception: Evapotranspiration is only about evaporation from rivers.

questions.stem: What is transpiration in plants?
options: When plants lose water vapour from their leaves
hints: Does a plant release water into the air?
The water comes out through the leaves.
questions.explanation: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plant leaves into the air.

questions.stem: When a puddle dries up after the rain, what has happened to the water?
options: It has changed into vapour and gone into the air
It has been drunk by ants
hints: Does the water disappear or change into vapour?
questions.explanation: The water changes into vapour (evaporation) and goes into the air. This is part of evapotranspiration when it happens from the ground.
questions.misconception: Evapotranspiration is only about evaporation from rivers.

questions.stem: When you breathe out onto a mirror or glass, what appears on the surface?
hints: Vapour turns into droplets when it hits a cool surface.
questions.explanation: Your breath contains water vapour. When it touches a cool surface, the vapour changes into tiny water droplets.
questions.misconception: Only animals breathe out water vapour.

questions.stem: Why is evapotranspiration important in the water cycle?
options: It adds water vapour to the air
It removes oxygen from the air
hints: What does evapotranspiration put into the air?
Water vapour in the air helps form clouds.
questions.explanation: Evapotranspiration puts water vapour into the air, which helps form clouds and leads to rain in the water cycle.
questions.misconception: Evapotranspiration has nothing to do with the water cycle.

questions.stem: Which part of a plant loses most of its water through transpiration?
hints: Leaves have tiny holes called stomata.
questions.explanation: Most water vapour is lost from plant leaves through tiny openings called stomata.
questions.misconception: Plants lose water mainly through the roots.

questions.stem: A learner ties a clear plastic bag over a young plant for one hour. What will be seen inside the bag after some time?
hints: When vapour cools, it forms droplets.
questions.explanation: The plant releases water vapour through transpiration. The vapour collects inside the bag, cools, and forms tiny water droplets.

questions.stem: In the plastic bag experiment, where do the water droplets inside the bag come from?
options: They come from the plant through transpiration
They come from outside the bag through the plastic
They come from the learner's hands
They are already inside the bag before the plant is covered
hints: The plant is inside the bag.
The plant loses water through its leaves.
questions.explanation: The water droplets come from the plant. The plant loses water vapour through transpiration, and the vapour condenses on the inside of the bag.
questions.misconception: Water droplets in the bag come from outside the bag.

questions.stem: Evapotranspiration is made up of which two processes?
hints: Look at the word — what two words are combined?
One process is from the ground; the other is from plants.
questions.explanation: Evapotranspiration combines evaporation (water from the ground and surfaces) and transpiration (water from plants).
questions.misconception: Evapotranspiration is the same as condensation.

questions.stem: On a hot day, a wet towel dries quickly outside. Which process explains this?
hints: The heat of the sun helps the water dry.
questions.explanation: The heat of the sun causes water in the towel to change into vapour. This is evaporation, a part of evapotranspiration.
questions.misconception: Water disappears completely when it dries.

questions.stem: What appears on a cool glass surface when you breathe out on it?
hints: Breath has water vapour in it.
Vapour turns into droplets on a cool surface.
questions.explanation: When you breathe on a cool surface, the water vapour in your breath changes into tiny water droplets on the surface.

questions.stem: How does evapotranspiration help the water cycle?
options: It puts water vapour into the air, which can form clouds
It removes water from the ocean
It causes the sun to shine
hints: Where does the water vapour go?
What forms from water vapour in the sky?
questions.explanation: Evapotranspiration releases water vapour into the air. This vapour rises, cools and helps form clouds, which eventually produce rain.
questions.misconception: Evapotranspiration has nothing to do with the water cycle.

questions.stem: Explain how transpiration happens in plants.
answer: plants lose water vapour through tiny openings in their leaves
water in the plant leaves the plant as vapour from the leaves
questions.explanation: Plants take up water through their roots. Some of this water travels to the leaves, where it is released as water vapour through tiny openings. This is transpiration.

questions.stem: In the plastic bag experiment, why are the water droplets inside the bag?
answer: because the plant releases water vapour that condenses into droplets inside the bag
the plant transpires and the water vapour condenses
hints: The plant gives off water vapour.
Why does the vapour turn into droplets?
questions.explanation: The plant releases water vapour through transpiration. The vapour cannot escape through the plastic, so it cools and condenses into droplets inside the bag.
questions.misconception: The droplets come from outside the bag.

questions.stem: In the plastic bag experiment, why should the learner mop off any water droplets on the plant leaves before starting?
answer: so that any water droplets found later come from the plant's transpiration and not from the water already on the leaves
to ensure that the water droplets inside the bag come only from the plant
hints: Where could the water in the bag come from if the leaves are wet?
We want to prove that the plant itself releases water.
questions.explanation: If the leaves are already wet, we cannot tell whether water in the bag came from the wet leaves or from transpiration. Mopping the leaves first makes the experiment more reliable.
questions.misconception: It does not matter if the leaves are wet at the start.

questions.stem: What is evapotranspiration?
answer: it is the release of water vapour from plants and the ground into the air
the loss of water vapour from plants and the ground into the air
water vapour leaving plants and the ground into the air
hints: It involves plants and the ground.
questions.explanation: Evapotranspiration is the combined process of water vapour leaving plants (transpiration) and the ground (evaporation) into the air.
questions.misconception: Evapotranspiration is only about evaporation from rivers.

questions.stem: On a sunny day, water evaporates from a pond. Which statement explains this in the context of evapotranspiration?
options: Water from the pond changes into vapour and goes into the air
Fish in the pond drink all the water
The pond is turned into land
hints: What happens to water when the sun heats it?
questions.explanation: Water from the pond changes into vapour (evaporation) when heated by the sun. This adds water vapour to the air and is part of evapotranspiration.
questions.misconception: Evapotranspiration is only about evaporation from rivers.

questions.stem: Why does water form on a cool glass when you breathe on it, but not on a warm glass?
options: Because the cool glass warms the breath
Because the water in the breath changes to vapour on the warm glass
Because the breath contains more water vapour than the warm glass
Because the water vapour in the breath changes into droplets faster when it meets a cool surface
hints: What happens to water vapour when it cools?
Does vapour condense faster on a cool or warm surface?
questions.explanation: Water vapour in your breath condenses into droplets faster on a cool surface because the cool surface causes the vapour to lose heat and change into liquid.
questions.misconception: Water vapour is only in warm breath.

questions.stem: Give one reason why evapotranspiration is important for the water cycle.
answer: it adds water vapour into the air which helps form clouds and brings rain
it supplies water vapour that forms clouds and rain
it puts water vapour in the air that cools and forms rain
hints: What does evapotranspiration add to the air?
How does this lead to rain?
questions.explanation: Evapotranspiration adds water vapour to the air. This vapour rises, cools and condenses to form clouds, which later release rain.
questions.misconception: Evapotranspiration has nothing to do with the water cycle.

questions.stem: A learner says, 'Transpiration is when a plant breathes out carbon dioxide.' Is this correct?
options: Yes, transpiration is the same as respiration
No, transpiration is the loss of water vapour, not carbon dioxide
Yes, plants only release carbon dioxide
No, transpiration is about taking in water, not releasing it
hints: Is water vapour released or carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plant leaves. It is different from respiration, which involves gases like carbon dioxide and oxygen.
questions.misconception: Transpiration is the same as respiration.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.1.5 Recognise water and air as important natural resources
indicator.objective: Demonstrate ways of making water safe for use

skills.description: Identify common sources of water in the community (river, well, borehole, pond, standpipe, lagoon).
State simple qualities of good drinking water (clear, odourless, free from germs).
Identify ways of making water safe (boiling, filtering, chlorination, adding iodine tablets, using alum, water filters).
Explain simply why boiling makes water safe (it kills germs).
Explain simply how filtering removes dirt particles from water.
State one danger of drinking unsafe water (e.g. sickness, diarrhoea, cholera).

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: Clear water is always safe to drink.
Filtering water kills all germs.
Boiling water adds medicine to it.
Water from a borehole never needs treatment.
Adding alum makes water taste better, not cleaner.
Only dirty-looking water can make you sick.

questions.stem: Which of these is a common source of water in a Ghanaian community?
hints: Think of places where people fetch water.
A borehole is dug deep into the ground for water.
questions.explanation: A borehole is a common source of water in many Ghanaian communities. Others include rivers, wells, ponds, lagoons and standpipes.
questions.misconception: Only bottled water is a water source.

questions.stem: Which quality shows that water is good for drinking?
options: It is clear and has no smell
hints: Would you drink water with a bad smell?
Good drinking water should be clear and odourless.
questions.explanation: Good drinking water is clear and has no bad smell. It should also be free from germs.
questions.misconception: Clear water is always safe to drink.

questions.stem: Where does water from a standpipe come from?
options: A pipe supplied by the water company
hints: A standpipe has a tap connected to a pipe.
questions.explanation: A standpipe is a public tap connected to a water supply pipe. It is a common source of water in many communities.

questions.stem: Which of these makes water safe to drink?
options: Stirring the water with a spoon
hints: Heat can kill germs in water.
What does your family do to make water safe?
questions.explanation: Boiling water kills germs, making it safe to drink. Adding sand, sugar or stirring does not make water safe.
questions.misconception: Boiling water adds medicine to it.

questions.stem: What can happen if you drink unsafe water?
options: You may become sick with diarrhoea or cholera
questions.explanation: Drinking unsafe water can make you sick with diseases like diarrhoea, cholera or typhoid.
questions.misconception: Only dirty-looking water can make you sick.

questions.stem: Ama fetches water from a well. The water looks clear but has a slight smell. Is this water safe to drink?
options: No, because it has a smell and may contain germs
Yes, because it comes from a well
hints: Good drinking water should have no smell.
Clear water can still contain germs.
questions.explanation: Water with a smell may contain germs. It should be treated (e.g. by boiling) before drinking, even if it looks clear.
questions.misconception: Clear water is always safe to drink.

questions.stem: Which of these is used to make water safe by killing germs?
hints: Chlorine is added to water in some treatment plants.
questions.explanation: Adding chlorine kills germs in water. Alum helps particles settle, and filtering with a cloth removes some dirt but does not kill germs.

questions.stem: Why does boiling make water safe to drink?
options: It adds flavour to the water
It changes the water into vapour
It kills harmful germs in the water
It makes the water look clear
hints: Heat can kill tiny living things.
What happens to germs at high heat?
questions.explanation: Boiling water to a high temperature kills harmful germs. This makes the water safe to drink.
questions.misconception: Boiling water adds medicine to it.

questions.stem: What does filtering water do?
options: It removes dirt particles from the water
It kills all germs in the water
It adds minerals to the water
hints: What gets trapped in the filter?
questions.explanation: Filtering removes dirt and solid particles from water. It does not kill germs, so filtered water may still need boiling.

questions.stem: Name two sources of water in your community.
hints: Think of a river and a well.
questions.explanation: Common water sources include rivers, wells, boreholes, ponds, lagoons and standpipes.
questions.misconception: Water only comes from one source.

questions.stem: What is alum used for when making water safe?
options: To help dirt settle to the bottom
To change the colour of the water
hints: The clumps settle at the bottom.
questions.explanation: Alum helps tiny dirt particles clump together and settle at the bottom, making the water clearer. It does not kill germs.
questions.misconception: Adding alum makes water completely safe to drink.

questions.stem: Why should you boil water before drinking it?
answer: to kill germs in the water
to make the water safe by killing germs
hints: What happens to germs when water is boiled?
questions.explanation: Boiling water kills harmful germs. This makes the water safe to drink and helps prevent diseases.
questions.misconception: Boiling water adds medicine to it.

questions.stem: State one disease you can get from drinking unsafe water.
hints: One disease is often linked to dirty water in Ghana.
questions.explanation: Drinking unsafe water can cause diseases such as cholera, diarrhoea or typhoid fever.
questions.misconception: Unsafe water does not cause disease.

questions.stem: A family collects rainwater in a barrel. Which is the best way to make it safe before drinking?
options: Boil the water and let it cool
Leave the water in the sun
Stir the water with a clean spoon
questions.explanation: Boiling the rainwater kills germs. Letting it cool before drinking makes it safe.
questions.misconception: Rainwater is always safe to drink.

questions.stem: Kojo boiled water for drinking. His friend said, 'Boiling removes the dirt from the water.' Is the friend correct?
options: Yes, boiling turns dirt into gas
No, boiling kills germs but does not remove dirt
No, boiling makes the water taste bad
questions.explanation: Boiling water kills germs, but it does not remove dirt particles. Dirt is usually removed by filtering or letting the water settle.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes filtering water?
options: It removes all germs from the water
It removes dirt particles but not all germs
It adds chemicals to the water
questions.explanation: Filtering removes dirt particles from water, but it does not kill germs. Germs are too small to be trapped by most simple filters.

questions.stem: State two qualities of good drinking water.
answer: it is clear and has no smell
it is clear and free from germs
hints: Should drinking water have a smell?
questions.explanation: Good drinking water should be clear, free from bad smell and free from germs.
questions.misconception: Clear water is always safe to drink.

questions.stem: Explain why clear water from a stream may still be unsafe to drink.
answer: because it may contain germs that cannot be seen with the eyes
because germs are too small to see, so the water can look clear but still have germs
hints: Can you see germs with your eyes?
questions.explanation: Water can look clear but still contain germs that are too small to see. These germs can cause diseases, so the water should be treated (e.g. boiled) before drinking.
questions.misconception: Clear water is always safe to drink.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes a simple way to make water safe from a river?
options: Boil the water, let it cool, then drink
Filter the water with a cloth, then drink
Let the water settle, then drink
hints: Filtering and settling do not kill germs.
questions.explanation: Boiling kills germs. Filtering, adding alum or letting water settle only removes dirt; boiling is needed to make it safe from germs.

questions.stem: A pupil has three water samples: river water, well water and borehole water. Which is the most important step to make ALL of them safe to drink?
options: Pour each sample into a bottle
hints: Which method works for all water sources?
Heat kills germs in any water.
questions.explanation: Boiling kills germs in any water sample, whether from a river, well or borehole. It is the most reliable way to make water safe.
questions.misconception: Water from a borehole never needs treatment.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B4.2.2.1 Demonstrate understanding of the life cycle of plants
indicator.objective: Observe, identify and give functions of the parts of a plant

skills.description: Name the main parts of a plant: root, stem, leaf, flower.
State the function of the root (absorbs water and mineral salts; holds the plant in the soil).
State the function of the stem (supports the plant; carries water and food between root and leaves).
State the function of the leaf (makes food for the plant using sunlight).
State the function of the flower (produces seeds/fruits; helps in reproduction).
Link a part's position on the plant to its function (e.g. roots are underground because they absorb water from soil).

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: Roots only hold the plant; they do not take in water.
Leaves only make the plant look green.
The stem is only for beauty.
Flowers are only for decoration; they have no job.
All parts of a plant do the same work.
Roots are always the biggest part of the plant.

questions.stem: Which part of a plant is usually found under the ground?
hints: Which part holds the plant in the soil?
It grows downwards into the ground.
questions.explanation: The root is usually found under the ground. It holds the plant in place and takes in water from the soil.
questions.misconception: All parts of a plant grow above the ground.

questions.stem: Which part of a plant is usually green and flat?
hints: It grows out from the stem.
questions.explanation: The leaf is usually green and flat. It catches sunlight to make food for the plant.
questions.misconception: Leaves only make the plant look green.

questions.stem: Which part of a plant is often colourful and produces seeds?
questions.explanation: The flower is often colourful and produces seeds and fruits. It helps the plant reproduce.

questions.stem: What is the main job of the root?
options: To make food for the plant
To absorb water from the soil
hints: They take in water from the soil.
questions.explanation: The main job of the root is to absorb water and mineral salts from the soil. It also holds the plant in place.
questions.misconception: Roots only hold the plant; they do not take in water.

questions.stem: What is the main job of the leaf?
options: To hold the plant in the soil
To absorb water from the soil
To make food for the plant using sunlight
To carry water to the roots
hints: Green leaves use sunlight to make food.
questions.explanation: The leaf makes food for the plant using sunlight. The green colour in leaves helps trap sunlight.
questions.misconception: Leaves only make the plant look green.

questions.stem: What is the main job of the stem?
options: To support the plant and carry water between roots and leaves
To absorb water from the soil
To make food for the plant
hints: It connects the roots to the leaves.
questions.explanation: The stem supports the plant and carries water and food between the roots and the leaves.
questions.misconception: The stem is only for beauty.

questions.stem: What is the main job of the flower?
options: To absorb water from the soil
To carry water to the leaves
To produce seeds and fruits for reproduction
hints: Flowers produce something that can grow into new plants.
questions.explanation: The flower produces seeds and fruits. This helps the plant to reproduce.

questions.stem: A farmer pulls a plant from the ground and finds many thin roots spread out in the soil. What are these roots doing?
options: They are making food for the plant
They are absorbing water and holding the plant in the soil
hints: They take in water and hold the plant.
questions.explanation: The roots spread out in the soil to absorb water and minerals and to hold the plant firmly in the ground.
questions.misconception: Roots only hold the plant; they do not take in water.

questions.stem: Why is the root found under the ground?
options: So that it can catch sunlight
So that it can absorb water from the soil and hold the plant in place
So that it can produce flowers
So that it can carry food to the leaves
hints: The root holds the plant down.
questions.explanation: The root is under the ground so it can absorb water from the soil and hold the plant firmly in place.

questions.stem: Name two parts of a plant.
hints: Think of what you see above and below the ground.
One part is green and flat; another is under the soil.
questions.explanation: The main parts of a plant are the root, stem, leaf and flower.

questions.stem: What does the stem do for the plant?
answer: it supports the plant and carries water and food
it holds the plant upright and carries water between the roots and the leaves
hints: It connects the root to the leaf.
questions.explanation: The stem supports the plant and carries water and food between the roots and the leaves.
questions.misconception: The stem is only for beauty.

questions.stem: Which TWO jobs does the root do for the plant?
options: Absorbs water and holds the plant in the soil
Catches sunlight and carries water to leaves
hints: The root is under the ground.
questions.explanation: The root absorbs water from the soil and holds the plant firmly in place.
questions.misconception: Roots only hold the plant; they do not take in water.

questions.stem: Why are leaves important to a plant?
answer: they make food for the plant using sunlight
leaves make food for the plant
they use sunlight to make food
questions.explanation: Leaves make food for the plant using sunlight. Without leaves, the plant cannot make its own food.
questions.misconception: Leaves only make the plant look green.

questions.stem: Why are most leaves found at the top of the plant, spread out?
options: So that they can catch as much sunlight as possible
So that they can absorb water from the soil
So that they can hold the plant in the soil
So that they can produce seeds
hints: Leaves need sunlight to make food.
questions.explanation: Leaves are spread out at the top of the plant to catch as much sunlight as possible for making food.

questions.stem: What is the main function of a flower?
answer: it produces seeds and fruits for the plant to reproduce
hints: Flowers produce something that grows into new plants.
questions.explanation: The flower produces seeds and fruits. This helps the plant to reproduce.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes why the stem is important?
options: It is the only green part of the plant
It makes food for the plant
It supports the plant and carries water and food between parts
It absorbs water from the soil
hints: What would happen if the stem were removed?
The stem is like a pipe.
questions.explanation: The stem supports the plant and carries water and food between the roots and the leaves. Without the stem, the plant would fall over and food and water could not move around.
questions.misconception: The stem is only for beauty.

questions.stem: Why do you think the roots are underground and not above the ground?
answer: because roots absorb water from the soil and hold the plant in place underground
because the roots need to take water from the soil
so they can absorb water and hold the plant firmly in the soil
questions.explanation: Roots are underground because they need to absorb water from the soil and hold the plant firmly in place.

questions.stem: Draw a simple plant. Label the root, stem, leaf and flower. Write one function of each part next to its label.

criteria.description: Drew a plant showing all four parts: root, stem, leaf and flower
Wrote a correct function for the root (absorbs water and holds plant)
Wrote a correct function for the stem (supports and carries water/food)
Wrote a correct function for the leaf (makes food using sunlight)
Wrote a correct function for the flower (produces seeds/fruits)

questions.answer: Teacher-assessed using the rubric. Expected drawing: a plant with roots below the soil line, a stem going up, leaves attached to the stem, and a flower at the top.
hints: Think about what you see above and below the ground.
Each part has a special job.
questions.explanation: This is a drawing task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: All parts of a plant do the same work.

questions.stem: A plant's leaves are shaded by a taller tree. What is likely to happen to the plant?
options: It will grow faster because it has shade
It will make less food because it cannot get enough sunlight
It will produce more flowers immediately
The roots will stop absorbing water
hints: What do leaves need to make food?
Without sunlight, can leaves work well?
questions.explanation: Leaves need sunlight to make food. If the leaves are shaded, the plant gets less sunlight and makes less food, so its growth will slow down.
questions.misconception: Leaves can make food without sunlight.

questions.stem: A gardener plants a flower in a pot with very little soil and no room for the roots to spread. What problem will the plant most likely have?
options: It will not be able to absorb enough water
It will produce too many flowers
The leaves will turn to stone
hints: What do roots need to spread and absorb?
Very little soil means less water and minerals.
questions.explanation: Roots need space in the soil to spread and absorb water. With very little soil, the plant cannot absorb enough water and may die or grow poorly.
questions.misconception: Roots can absorb water without soil space.

questions.stem: A farmer notices that one of his maize plants has no flowers. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The plant will grow taller than others
The roots will absorb more water
The plant will not produce seeds or fruits
hints: Seeds are needed for the plant to reproduce.
questions.explanation: Flowers produce seeds and fruits. A plant without flowers will not produce seeds or fruits, so it cannot reproduce.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.1.1 Recognize that different parts of the human body work independently to perform a specific function
indicator.objective: Know the organs of the digestive system and their functions

skills.description: Name or recognise the main organs of the digestive system: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, anus.
State the simple function of each organ (e.g. mouth chews food, stomach breaks down food, small intestine absorbs nutrients, large intestine absorbs water).
Arrange the organs in the correct order that food passes through the digestive system.
Match a described function to the correct organ.
Explain simply why the digestive system is important (breaks down food, helps the body get nutrients).
Identify an organ from a simple description of its position in the body (e.g. “the tube that connects the mouth to the stomach”).

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: Food goes straight to the stomach after swallowing.
The large intestine comes before the small intestine.
The stomach is where most food is absorbed into the blood.
The mouth only chews food; it does not start breaking it down.
The oesophagus stores food.
The anus is part of the small intestine.

questions.stem: Which organ is the first part of the digestive system that food enters?
hints: Where does food go when you start eating?
questions.explanation: The mouth is the first part of the digestive system. Food enters the mouth and is chewed.
questions.misconception: Food goes straight to the stomach.

questions.stem: Which organ is a long tube that connects the mouth to the stomach?
hints: Food travels down it to reach the stomach.
questions.explanation: The oesophagus is the tube that connects the mouth to the stomach. Food travels down it after swallowing.

questions.stem: Which organ is like a bag where food is mixed and broken down?
hints: Food stays here for a while after leaving the oesophagus.
questions.explanation: The stomach is a bag-like organ where food is mixed and broken down further.
questions.misconception: The stomach absorbs most food into the blood.

questions.stem: Which of these is the last part of the digestive system where waste leaves the body?
hints: It is at the end of the digestive system.
Waste leaves the body through it.
questions.explanation: The anus is the last part of the digestive system. Waste leaves the body through it.
questions.misconception: The anus is part of the small intestine.

questions.stem: Why is the digestive system important?
options: It breaks down food so the body can use it.
It pumps blood around the body.
hints: What happens to food after you eat it?
The body needs nutrients from food.
questions.explanation: The digestive system breaks down food into nutrients the body can use for energy and growth.
questions.misconception: The digestive system is not important.

questions.stem: What does the mouth do in the digestive system?
options: It chews food and mixes it with saliva
questions.explanation: The mouth chews food into smaller pieces and mixes it with saliva. This starts the digestion process.
questions.misconception: The mouth only chews food; it does not start breaking it down.

questions.stem: What is the job of the small intestine?
options: To absorb nutrients from food into the blood
To carry food to the mouth
hints: It is a long, coiled tube.
questions.explanation: The small intestine absorbs nutrients from digested food into the blood. This is where most absorption happens.
questions.misconception: The stomach is where most food is absorbed into the blood.

questions.stem: What does the large intestine do?
options: It absorbs water from undigested food
hints: Water is removed from the waste here.
questions.explanation: The large intestine absorbs water from the undigested food, turning it into solid waste.
questions.misconception: The large intestine comes before the small intestine.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order that food passes through the digestive system?
options: Mouth → stomach → oesophagus → small intestine → large intestine
Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine
Stomach → mouth → oesophagus → large intestine → small intestine
Mouth → large intestine → stomach → small intestine → oesophagus
hints: It goes down a tube before reaching the stomach.
questions.explanation: Food passes: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → anus.
questions.misconception: Food goes straight to the stomach after swallowing.

questions.stem: Which organ is described as the tube that connects the mouth to the stomach?
questions.explanation: The oesophagus connects the mouth to the stomach.

questions.stem: Which organ pushes waste out of the body?
hints: It is at the end of the digestive system.
questions.explanation: The anus is the opening at the end of the digestive system through which waste leaves the body.
questions.misconception: The anus is part of the small intestine.

questions.stem: Which organ matches this function: 'absorbs water from undigested food'?
hints: Water is removed from waste here.
It is wider than the small intestine.
questions.explanation: The large intestine absorbs water from undigested food. This makes the waste solid.
questions.misconception: The small intestine absorbs water from undigested food.

questions.stem: List the organs of the digestive system in the correct order that food passes through them, starting from the mouth.
answer: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, anus
mouth oesophagus stomach small intestine large intestine anus
questions.explanation: The order is: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → anus.
questions.misconception: Food goes straight to the stomach after swallowing.

questions.stem: What would happen if the digestive system did not break down food?
options: The body would get more nutrients
The body would not get the nutrients it needs from food
Food would stay in the mouth forever
hints: The body needs nutrients from food.
If food is not broken down, can the body use it?
questions.explanation: If food is not broken down, the body cannot absorb the nutrients it needs for energy and growth.
questions.misconception: Digestion is not needed for the body to get nutrients.

questions.stem: Which TWO organs absorb substances from food into the blood?
questions.explanation: The small intestine absorbs nutrients, and the large intestine absorbs water. Both absorb substances from food.
questions.misconception: The stomach is the only organ that absorbs substances.

questions.stem: Which organ is a long, coiled tube found after the stomach?
questions.explanation: The small intestine is a long, coiled tube that comes after the stomach. It absorbs nutrients from food.
questions.misconception: The large intestine comes before the small intestine.

questions.stem: Why does the body need the digestive system?
answer: to break down food so the body can get nutrients and energy
to break down food into nutrients the body can use
it breaks down food for the body to use
hints: Food needs to be broken down.
The body needs nutrients and energy.
questions.explanation: The body needs the digestive system to break down food into nutrients that can be absorbed and used for energy, growth and repair.
questions.misconception: The body can use food without breaking it down.

questions.stem: Match the organ to its function: stomach, small intestine, large intestine. Write the correct function next to each.
answer: stomach breaks down food, small intestine absorbs nutrients, large intestine absorbs water
stomach: breaks down food; small intestine: absorbs nutrients; large intestine: absorbs water
hints: The stomach is a bag that mixes food.
One intestine absorbs nutrients; the other absorbs water.
questions.explanation: Stomach: breaks down food. Small intestine: absorbs nutrients. Large intestine: absorbs water.

questions.stem: Draw a simple diagram of the digestive system. Label the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine.

criteria.description: Drew a simple diagram showing the digestive system organs

questions.answer: Teacher-assessed using the rubric. Expected diagram: mouth at top, oesophagus as a tube, stomach as a bag, small intestine as a coiled tube, large intestine as a wider tube around the small intestine.
hints: Start at the top with the mouth.
The small intestine is long and coiled; the large intestine is wider.
questions.explanation: This is a drawing task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: The large intestine comes before the small intestine.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'The stomach is where most food is absorbed into the blood.' What is the best correction?
options: The small intestine absorbs most nutrients into the blood
hints: Most absorption happens in a long, coiled tube.
questions.explanation: The stomach breaks down food, but most nutrients are absorbed into the blood in the small intestine.
questions.misconception: The stomach is where most food is absorbed into the blood.

questions.stem: In your group, role-play the organs of the digestive system. One learner acts as the mouth, another as the oesophagus, another as the stomach, another as the small intestine, and another as the large intestine. Each learner should say one sentence describing what their organ does as 'food' passes through.

criteria.description: Learner correctly acted as an organ of the digestive system
Learner stated at least one correct function of their organ
Learner participated in the correct sequence when 'food' passed through

questions.answer: Teacher-assessed using the rubric. Expected responses: mouth — chews food; oesophagus — carries food to the stomach; stomach — breaks down food; small intestine — absorbs nutrients; large intestine — absorbs water.
hints: Think about what each organ does.
Remember the order food passes through.
questions.explanation: This is a role-play task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: Food goes straight to the stomach after swallowing.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B4.3.2.1 Show an understanding of the orderliness of the sun, planets and satellites in the solar system, as well as the important role of the sun in the existence of the solar system
indicator.objective: Explain that the sun is at the centre of the solar system

skills.description: State that the sun is at the centre of the solar system.
Recognise that planets move around the sun.
State simple benefits of the sun to the solar system (light, heat, energy for life).
Identify the main bodies in the solar system: sun, planets, satellites.
Interpret a simple diagram or model showing the sun at the centre with planets around it.

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: The earth is at the centre of the solar system.
The sun moves around the earth.
The moon is a planet.
The sun is a planet.
Satellites are only man-made objects.
The sun has no effect on life on earth.

questions.stem: What is at the centre of the solar system?
hints: It is the biggest and brightest object in the solar system.
questions.explanation: The sun is at the centre of the solar system. All the planets move around the sun.
questions.misconception: The earth is at the centre of the solar system.

questions.stem: Which of these is a planet?
hints: Is the moon a planet? No, it moves around the earth.
questions.explanation: Earth is a planet. It moves around the sun. The sun is a star, and the moon is a satellite of the earth.
questions.misconception: The earth is at the centre of the solar system.

questions.stem: What does the sun give to the earth?
hints: The sun makes you feel warm.
The sun lights up the day.
questions.explanation: The sun gives light and heat to the earth. These are important for life on earth.
questions.misconception: The sun has no effect on life on earth.

questions.stem: What do the planets do in the solar system?
hints: The sun is at the centre.
Planets travel in paths around the sun.
questions.explanation: Planets move around the sun. The sun is at the centre of the solar system.
questions.misconception: The sun moves around the earth.

questions.stem: Which of these is a satellite of the earth?
questions.explanation: The moon is a satellite of the earth. It moves around the earth.

questions.stem: A learner says, 'The earth is at the centre of the solar system.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, the earth is at the centre
No, the sun is at the centre of the solar system
No, the moon is at the centre
No, the stars are at the centre
hints: Which object is the biggest in the solar system?
Everything else moves around the sun.
questions.explanation: The sun is at the centre of the solar system. The earth is one of the planets that move around the sun.
questions.misconception: The earth is at the centre of the solar system.

questions.stem: What path does a planet follow?
options: It moves in a straight line away from the sun
It moves in a curved path around the sun
It moves towards the sun and stops
hints: Planets do not move in straight lines.
They go round and round the sun.
questions.explanation: Planets move in curved paths around the sun. This regular movement keeps them in the solar system.

questions.stem: Why is the sun important to plants on earth?
options: It gives them light to make food
hints: Plants need sunlight to make food.
questions.explanation: Plants need sunlight to make food. Without the sun, plants would not be able to grow.
questions.misconception: The sun has no effect on life on earth.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly identifies the bodies in the solar system?
options: The sun is a planet and the earth is a star
The sun is a star and the earth is a planet
The sun is a satellite and the moon is a star
The earth is a satellite and the moon is a planet
hints: The sun gives its own light — that makes it a star.
The earth moves around the sun — that makes it a planet.
questions.explanation: The sun is a star because it produces its own light. The earth is a planet because it moves around the sun.

questions.stem: What is at the centre of the solar system?
questions.explanation: The sun is at the centre of the solar system.
questions.misconception: The earth is at the centre of the solar system.

questions.stem: In a model of the solar system, where should the sun be placed?
hints: The sun is the centre of the solar system.
questions.explanation: In a model of the solar system, the sun should be placed at the centre, with the planets arranged around it.
questions.misconception: The earth should be at the centre of the model.

questions.stem: Give one reason why the sun is important to life on earth.
answer: it gives energy for plants to make food
it provides heat and light for living things
questions.explanation: The sun provides light and heat. It also helps plants make food, which supports life on earth.
questions.misconception: The sun has no effect on life on earth.

questions.stem: A diagram shows a big yellow ball in the middle and smaller balls arranged in circles around it. What does the big yellow ball represent?
options: A star that is not the sun
questions.explanation: The big yellow ball in the centre represents the sun. The smaller balls moving around it represent the planets.
questions.misconception: The earth is at the centre of the solar system.

questions.stem: Why do planets stay in the solar system as they move?
options: Because they are tied to the sun with strings
Because the sun's pull keeps them moving around it
Because they are afraid to leave
hints: The sun is very big and heavy.
questions.explanation: The sun is very large and has a strong pull that keeps the planets moving around it. This is why they stay in the solar system.

questions.stem: Name the three main types of bodies found in the solar system.
questions.explanation: The three main types of bodies in the solar system are the sun, planets and satellites.

questions.stem: In a model of the solar system made with a football at the centre and small balls around it, what does the football represent?
questions.explanation: The football at the centre represents the sun. The small balls around it represent the planets.
questions.misconception: The earth is at the centre of the solar system.

questions.stem: What would happen to life on earth if the sun stopped giving light and heat?
options: There would be no light or warmth, and living things would struggle to survive
The moon would take over the sun's job
hints: The sun gives heat and light.
questions.explanation: Without the sun's light and heat, plants could not make food, the earth would become cold and dark, and most living things would not survive.
questions.misconception: The sun has no effect on life on earth.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the sun is at the centre of the solar system?
options: Because it is the biggest object and its pull keeps the planets moving around it
Because it is smaller than the planets
Because it moves around the earth
Because the moon pushes it there
hints: The sun is the largest object in the solar system.
Its strong pull keeps planets in their paths.
questions.explanation: The sun is at the centre because it is the largest object in the solar system, and its strong pull keeps the planets moving around it.
questions.misconception: The earth is at the centre of the solar system.

questions.stem: Draw a simple diagram of the solar system. Show the sun at the centre and at least four planets around it. Label the sun, one planet, and one satellite.

criteria.description: Drew the sun at the centre of the diagram
Drew at least four planets around the sun

questions.answer: Teacher-assessed using the rubric. Expected diagram: a large circle in the centre labeled 'sun', smaller circles arranged around it labeled with planet names, and at least one smaller circle near a planet labeled 'moon' or 'satellite'.
hints: Put the sun in the middle.
The moon is a satellite of the earth.
questions.explanation: This is a drawing task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: The earth is at the centre of the solar system.

questions.stem: In groups, use clay, blu tack, or balls of paper to build a simple model of the solar system. Place the sun at the centre and arrange the planets around it. Show where the moon (satellite) is.

criteria.description: Placed the sun at the centre of the model
Arranged at least four planets around the sun
Showed the moon as a satellite of the earth
Explained the model to the class

questions.answer: Teacher-assessed using the rubric. Expected model: a large central ball for the sun, smaller balls around it for planets, and a tiny ball near one planet for the moon.
hints: The sun is the biggest and should be in the middle.
Planets are smaller and go around the sun.
The moon is a satellite of the earth.
questions.explanation: This is a practical task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: The earth is at the centre of the solar system.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B4.4.1.1 Demonstrate understanding of the concept of energy, its various forms, sources and how to transform and conserve it
indicator.objective: Identify the effect of heat on the change of state of substances

skills.description: Recognise that heating can change a substance from one state to another (e.g. solid to liquid, liquid to gas).
Identify everyday examples of melting caused by heat (e.g. candle wax, shea butter, ice).
Distinguish between evaporation (slow change of liquid to vapour) and boiling (fast change with bubbles when heated).
Recognise that cooling can change a gas back to a liquid (condensation) — e.g. vapour from boiling water changes to water droplets when cooled.
Explain simply that the amount of water decreases after boiling because some water changes to vapour.
Predict what will happen when heat is applied to or removed from a substance (e.g. shea butter in the sun, water in a fridge).

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: Boiling destroys water; it disappears completely.
Melting and boiling are the same thing.
Cooling makes water hotter.
Evaporation only happens when water boils.
Condensation happens when water is heated.
When water boils, its amount stays exactly the same.

questions.stem: What happens to ice when it is left in the sun?
hints: Ice is a solid. What happens to it when warmed?
questions.explanation: Heat from the sun changes solid ice into liquid water. This is called melting.
questions.misconception: Ice disappears completely when it melts.

questions.stem: When a solid is heated enough, it can change into which state?
hints: Ice is a solid. What does it become when it melts?
questions.explanation: When a solid is heated, it melts into a liquid. If heated further, it can change into a gas.
questions.misconception: Heating a solid makes it harder.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of melting?
options: Shea butter becoming liquid in the sun
hints: Shea butter starts as a solid.
questions.explanation: Shea butter is solid at room temperature. When left in the sun, heat melts it into a liquid.
questions.misconception: Shea butter becomes hard in the sun.

questions.stem: What do we see when water is boiling?
questions.explanation: When water boils, bubbles form and steam (water vapour) rises. Boiling is a fast change from liquid to gas.

questions.stem: What will happen if you put a piece of shea butter in the hot sun?
hints: Shea butter is a solid that melts easily.
questions.explanation: Shea butter is a solid fat. When placed in the hot sun, heat melts it into a liquid.
questions.misconception: Shea butter becomes harder in the sun.

questions.stem: A pupil holds a candle near a flame. The candle wax changes from solid to liquid. What is this process called?
questions.explanation: Melting is when heat changes a solid into a liquid. The candle wax melted because of the heat from the flame.
questions.misconception: Melting and boiling are the same thing.

questions.stem: When water is heated and turns into steam, what change of state has happened?
questions.explanation: When water turns into steam, it changes from a liquid to a gas. This is evaporation or boiling, depending on how fast it happens.
questions.misconception: Boiling destroys water; it disappears completely.

questions.stem: What is the difference between evaporation and boiling?
options: Evaporation is fast; boiling is slow
Evaporation happens slowly; boiling happens fast with bubbles
Evaporation and boiling are the same
hints: Wet clothes dry slowly — is that evaporation or boiling?
questions.explanation: Evaporation happens slowly (like wet clothes drying). Boiling happens fast with bubbles when water is very hot.
questions.misconception: Evaporation only happens when water boils.

questions.stem: Steam from a boiling pot touches a cold plate and forms water droplets. What is this process called?
hints: The droplets form on a cold surface.
questions.explanation: Condensation is the change from gas (vapour) to liquid (water droplets) when the gas is cooled.
questions.misconception: Condensation happens when water is heated.

questions.stem: Give one example of a solid that melts when heated.
hints: Think of something you put in the sun that turns to liquid.
questions.explanation: Ice, candle wax, shea butter, chocolate and butter all melt when heated.

questions.stem: Ama left a piece of ice on a plate in the sun. After some minutes, what will she see?
options: The ice will turn into water
The ice will turn into stone
questions.explanation: The heat from the sun melts the ice into liquid water.
questions.misconception: Ice does not change in the sun.

questions.stem: A pupil boiled a cup of water for a long time. What will be left in the cup?
hints: The vapour escapes into the air.
questions.explanation: When water boils, some of it changes to vapour and escapes into the air. So there is less water left in the cup.
questions.misconception: When water boils, its amount stays exactly the same.

questions.stem: Water droplets form on the inside of a cold bottle of water. What caused this?
options: Vapour from the air cooled and changed to water droplets
The water inside the bottle melted
hints: Vapour in the air touches a cold surface.
questions.explanation: Water vapour in the air cooled on contact with the cold bottle and changed into water droplets. This is condensation.

questions.stem: What happens to water vapour when it cools?
answer: it changes into liquid water droplets
questions.explanation: When water vapour cools, it condenses and changes back into liquid water droplets.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares evaporation and boiling?
options: Evaporation happens only when water boils
Evaporation happens at the surface and is slow; boiling happens throughout the liquid and is fast
Evaporation and boiling are the same process
questions.explanation: Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid and is slow. Boiling happens throughout the liquid, with bubbles, and is fast.
questions.misconception: Evaporation only happens when water boils.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Melting and boiling are the same process.' What is the best correction?
options: Melting is solid to liquid; boiling is liquid to gas
Melting is liquid to gas; boiling is solid to liquid
hints: What does ice become when heated?
What does water become when boiled?
