questions.explanation: Melting changes a solid to a liquid. Boiling changes a liquid to a gas. They are different changes of state.
questions.misconception: Melting and boiling are the same thing.

questions.stem: Why does the amount of water in a pot decrease after boiling for a long time?
answer: because some water changes into vapour and escapes into the air
some water turns into vapour and goes into the air
the water evaporates and escapes as vapour
hints: What do you see rising from a boiling pot?
questions.explanation: Some of the water changes into water vapour and escapes into the air, so the amount of water left in the pot decreases.

questions.stem: A learner puts a cup of water in a fridge. What will likely happen to the water if the fridge is very cold?
options: It will turn into shea butter
hints: Very cold water changes into what solid?
questions.explanation: If the fridge is cold enough, the water loses heat and changes into ice (freezes).

questions.stem: Explain why wet clothes dry even when the sun is not very hot.
answer: because water evaporates slowly from the clothes into the air
the water in the clothes evaporates into the air
hints: Does water need to boil to evaporate?
Wet clothes dry at room temperature.
questions.explanation: Wet clothes dry because water evaporates slowly from the cloth into the air. Boiling is not needed for evaporation to happen.
questions.misconception: Evaporation only happens when water boils.

questions.stem: A learner measured 200 ml of water and boiled it for a long time. After boiling, only 150 ml of water was left. How much water changed into vapour?
hints: Subtract the water left from the water at the start.
questions.explanation: 200 ml − 150 ml = 50 ml. So 50 ml of water changed into vapour and escaped into the air.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B4.4.2.1 Demonstrate knowledge of generation of electricity, its transmission and transformation into other forms
indicator.objective: Identify the uses of electricity

skills.description: Recognise common appliances that use electricity (e.g. bulb, television, iron, fan, phone charger).
State simple uses of electricity: lighting, heating, cooling, entertainment, communication.
Match an appliance to its main use (e.g. iron → pressing clothes; bulb → light).
Recognise electricity as a form of energy that makes appliances work.
Give examples of electricity use at home and at school.

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: Electricity is only for lighting.
A television works without electricity.
Electricity is not a form of energy.
Only bulbs use electricity.
Electricity is only used in cities.

questions.stem: Which of these uses electricity to work?
hints: Which one has a plug or needs power?
questions.explanation: A television uses electricity to work. Brooms, buckets and chairs do not need electricity.

questions.stem: Which of these is a use of electricity?
hints: What happens when you switch on a bulb?
questions.explanation: Electricity is used to make light. Other uses include heating, cooling, entertainment and communication.

questions.stem: What is an electric iron used for?
questions.explanation: An electric iron is used for pressing clothes to make them smooth.
questions.misconception: Electric iron is used for cooking.

questions.stem: Electricity is a form of what?
hints: It can be changed into light and heat.
questions.explanation: Electricity is a form of energy. It can be changed into light, heat, sound and movement.
questions.misconception: Electricity is not a form of energy.

questions.stem: Which of these uses electricity at school?
hints: What gives light in the classroom?
questions.explanation: A classroom bulb uses electricity to give light. Chalkboards, desks and books do not use electricity.
questions.misconception: Electricity is only used at home.

questions.stem: Which of these appliances does NOT use electricity?
hints: Which one is made of wood and has no plug?
A wooden spoon is used for cooking.
questions.explanation: A wooden spoon does not use electricity. Fans, kettles and phone chargers need electricity.

questions.stem: Ama uses an electric fan in her room. What is the fan used for?
hints: What does a fan do to the air?
questions.explanation: An electric fan is used to cool the room by moving air around.

questions.stem: Which appliance is used for communication?
hints: You can call and send messages with it.
It uses electricity and has a screen.
questions.explanation: A mobile phone is used for communication. It uses electricity to work.
questions.misconception: Mobile phones do not use electricity.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of electricity use at home?
options: Using an electric kettle to boil water
hints: Which activity needs a plug or power?
questions.explanation: Using an electric kettle to boil water is an example of electricity use at home.
questions.misconception: Electricity is only used at school.

questions.stem: Why does a television stop working when there is no electricity?
options: Because it needs electricity to work
Because it does not like darkness
questions.explanation: A television needs electricity to work. When there is no electricity, it cannot function.
questions.misconception: A television can work without electricity.

questions.stem: Name two appliances in your home that use electricity.
hints: Think of things that need to be plugged in.
One gives light; one keeps food cold.
questions.explanation: Common appliances that use electricity include televisions, fans, bulbs, irons, kettles, fridges and phone chargers.

questions.stem: State two uses of electricity.
questions.explanation: Electricity is used for lighting, heating, cooling, entertainment, communication and many other purposes.

questions.stem: Match the appliance to its use: which pair is correct?
hints: A fan makes you feel cool.
questions.explanation: A fan is used for cooling the room by moving air. The other pairs are mismatched.
questions.misconception: Bulbs are used for pressing clothes.

questions.stem: Give one example of how electricity is used at school and one example of how it is used at home.
answer: at school: lights in the classroom; at home: watching television
at school: bulb; at home: iron
at school: computer; at home: fan
hints: Think of a light at school.
Think of an appliance at home.
questions.explanation: At school, electricity is used for lighting classrooms, powering computers, etc. At home, it is used for lighting, cooking, ironing, entertainment, etc.
questions.misconception: Electricity is only used in one place.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes electricity?
options: It is a type of food
It is a form of energy that makes appliances work
hints: What does electricity do to a bulb?
It is a form of energy.
questions.explanation: Electricity is a form of energy. It makes appliances like bulbs, fans and televisions work.
questions.misconception: Electricity is not a form of energy.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a use of electricity?
hints: Plants grow using sunlight, not electricity.
Which one is a natural process?
questions.explanation: Making a plant grow is not a use of electricity. Plants grow using sunlight and water. Electricity is used for heating, cooling and lighting.

questions.stem: A pupil lists four items: a torch, a book, a radio, a pencil. Which two items use electricity?
questions.explanation: A torch and a radio use electricity. A book and a pencil do not.

questions.stem: A family wants to cook food faster using electricity. Which appliance should they use?
hints: Which appliance is made for cooking?
A kettle boils water, but a cooker cooks food.
questions.explanation: An electric cooker is designed for cooking food using electricity. Fans cool, irons press clothes, and kettles boil water.
questions.misconception: Any electric appliance can cook food.

questions.stem: Explain why electricity is important in our homes.
answer: it is used for lighting, cooking, cooling and entertainment
it powers appliances we use every day
it helps us do many things like lighting, cooking and ironing
hints: Think of what you use at home that needs electricity.
What would happen if there was no electricity?
questions.explanation: Electricity is important because it powers many appliances we use daily for lighting, cooking, cooling, entertainment, communication and more.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B4.4.2.1 Demonstrate knowledge of generation of electricity, its transmission and transformation into other forms
indicator.objective: Describe ways of conserving electricity

skills.description: Explain simply what conserving electricity means (using less and avoiding waste).
List ways to conserve electricity (switching off lights, using energy-efficient bulbs, unplugging appliances).
Recognise actions that waste electricity (leaving lights on, appliances on standby).
State why conserving electricity is important (saves money, reduces waste).
Suggest conservation actions for home and school.

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: Leaving appliances on standby does not waste electricity.
Turning off lights does not save electricity.
Only big appliances use electricity.
Conserving electricity means not using it at all.
Electricity is free, so there is no need to conserve it.

questions.stem: What does conserving electricity mean?
options: Using electricity wisely and avoiding waste
hints: You still use electricity, but you do not waste it.
questions.explanation: Conserving electricity means using it wisely and avoiding waste. It does not mean never using electricity.
questions.misconception: Conserving electricity means not using it at all.

questions.stem: Which of these helps to conserve electricity?
options: Switching off lights when leaving a room
Turning on all appliances at once
Leaving the television on when nobody is watching
hints: Switching off unused lights saves power.
questions.explanation: Switching off lights when leaving a room conserves electricity. Leaving them on wastes electricity.
questions.misconception: Leaving lights on does not waste electricity.

questions.stem: Which of these actions wastes electricity?
options: Switching off the fan when leaving the room
Unplugging the phone charger after use
Leaving the television on when nobody is watching
Turning off the light during the day
hints: Which action uses electricity for no reason?
If nobody is watching, the TV is wasting power.
questions.explanation: Leaving the television on when nobody is watching wastes electricity. The other actions conserve electricity.
questions.misconception: Leaving appliances on does not waste electricity.

questions.stem: Why should we conserve electricity?
options: To save money and reduce waste
questions.explanation: Conserving electricity saves money on electricity bills and reduces waste of energy.
questions.misconception: Electricity is free, so there is no need to conserve it.

questions.stem: What can pupils do at school to conserve electricity?
options: Leave classroom lights on after school
Switch off lights when leaving the classroom
Turn on all fans and leave them on
hints: What should you do when you leave a room?
questions.explanation: Switching off classroom lights when leaving helps conserve electricity at school.

questions.stem: Which of these is a good way to conserve electricity at home?
options: Leaving the iron on after use
Keeping all lights on at night
hints: They save electricity compared to ordinary bulbs.
questions.explanation: Energy-efficient bulbs use less electricity than ordinary bulbs. They help conserve electricity.
questions.misconception: All bulbs use the same amount of electricity.

questions.stem: Ama leaves her phone charger plugged in even after her phone is fully charged. Is this a good practice?
options: Yes, it charges the phone faster
No, it makes the phone cold
hints: Does a charger use electricity when the phone is full?
questions.explanation: Leaving a charger plugged in when the phone is fully charged wastes electricity. Unplugging it helps conserve electricity.
questions.misconception: Leaving appliances on standby does not waste electricity.

questions.stem: What should you do to conserve electricity when you are the last person to leave the classroom?
options: Switch off the lights and fans
hints: What uses electricity in the classroom?
Turn off what is not needed.
questions.explanation: Switching off the lights and fans when leaving the classroom conserves electricity.
questions.misconception: Lights and fans do not need to be switched off.

questions.stem: Which of these should a family do to conserve electricity at home?
options: Leave the television on all night
Use natural light during the day instead of electric lights
Keep all lights on in every room
hints: The sun gives light during the day.
Why use electric lights when the sun is shining?
questions.explanation: Using natural light from the sun during the day reduces the need for electric lights, conserving electricity.
questions.misconception: Electric lights should be on all day.

questions.stem: What does it mean to conserve electricity?
answer: to use electricity wisely and avoid wasting it
to use less electricity and not waste it
using electricity carefully without wasting it
questions.explanation: Conserving electricity means using it wisely and avoiding waste. It does not mean never using electricity.
questions.misconception: Conserving electricity means not using it at all.

questions.stem: Which is a reason for conserving electricity?
questions.explanation: Conserving electricity reduces electricity bills because less power is used.
questions.misconception: Electricity is free, so there is no need to conserve it.

questions.stem: Give one example of an action that wastes electricity.
answer: leaving lights on when leaving a room
leaving the television on when nobody is watching
leaving the fan on when not in the room
leaving the charger plugged in after the phone is charged
hints: Think of something left on with no one using it.
Leaving lights on is one example.
questions.explanation: Actions like leaving lights on, leaving the TV on when nobody is watching, or leaving appliances on standby all waste electricity.
questions.misconception: Leaving lights on does not waste electricity.

questions.stem: State two reasons why conserving electricity is important.
answer: it saves money and reduces waste
it saves money and helps protect the environment
it reduces electricity bills and prevents waste of energy
questions.explanation: Conserving electricity saves money on bills and reduces waste of energy resources, which is good for the environment.

questions.stem: List two ways of conserving electricity at home.
answer: switch off lights when leaving a room and unplug appliances when not in use
use energy-efficient bulbs and switch off unused appliances
turn off lights during the day and unplug chargers after use
hints: What should you do with lights when leaving a room?
What should you do with appliances not in use?
questions.explanation: Ways to conserve electricity include switching off lights when leaving a room, unplugging appliances when not in use, using energy-efficient bulbs, and using natural light during the day.
questions.misconception: There is no way to conserve electricity.

questions.stem: Suggest one way pupils can help conserve electricity at school.
answer: switch off lights and fans when leaving the classroom
turn off lights when not needed
unplug appliances when not in use
hints: What uses electricity in the classroom?
Turn them off when not needed.
questions.explanation: Pupils can help conserve electricity by switching off lights and fans when leaving the classroom or when they are not needed.

questions.stem: Which of these actions conserves electricity?
options: Leaving the TV on standby all night
Using natural light during the day
Keeping all lights on in the house
Leaving the iron on after use
hints: The sun gives light during the day.
questions.explanation: Using natural light during the day conserves electricity. The other actions waste electricity.
questions.misconception: Using natural light does not save electricity.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Conserving electricity means never using electricity at all.' What is the best correction?
options: No, conserving means using electricity wisely without wasting it
No, conserving means using more electricity
No, conserving means buying more appliances
hints: Can you live without electricity entirely?
Conserving is about avoiding waste, not avoiding use.
questions.explanation: Conserving electricity means using it wisely and avoiding waste. It does not mean never using electricity.
questions.misconception: Conserving electricity means not using it at all.

questions.stem: A family leaves all their lights, fans, and television on even when they go out. What is the effect of this?
options: It wastes electricity and increases their bill
hints: If nobody is home, are the appliances needed?
questions.explanation: Leaving appliances on when nobody is home wastes electricity and increases the electricity bill.
questions.misconception: Leaving appliances on does not waste electricity.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to help their family conserve electricity. Which plan is BEST?
options: Leave all lights on at night
Switch off unused lights and unplug appliances not in use
Leave the fridge door open to keep the kitchen cool
hints: Switching off and unplugging saves electricity.
questions.explanation: Switching off unused lights and unplugging appliances not in use is the best plan for conserving electricity at home.
questions.misconception: Leaving appliances on does not waste electricity.

questions.stem: Why is conserving electricity important for the whole country, not just for one family?
options: It helps the country save energy resources and reduces the cost of electricity for everyone
It stops people from using electricity
hints: If everyone conserves, less energy is wasted.
questions.explanation: Conserving electricity helps the whole country save energy resources and reduces the cost of generating and supplying electricity, which benefits everyone.
questions.misconception: Conserving electricity only benefits one person.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B4.4.2.2 Know the functions and assemblage of basic electronics components
indicator.objective: Identify the basic components of electronic circuits

skills.description: Name basic components: battery/dry cell, connecting wire, switch, bulb/LED.
State the simple function of each component (battery supplies energy, wire carries current, switch opens/closes circuit, bulb/LED lights).
Match a component to its description or picture.
Draw a simple circuit showing battery, wire, switch and bulb.
Connect components to make a bulb/LED light (practical).
Recognise a complete circuit versus an incomplete circuit.

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: A bulb can light without a battery.
Any wire can be used in a circuit.
A switch is not needed in a circuit.
A bulb lights even if the circuit is broken.
The battery is not part of the circuit.

questions.stem: Which of these is a basic component of an electric circuit?
hints: Which one stores energy for the circuit?
It has two ends, positive and negative.
questions.explanation: A battery is a basic component of an electric circuit. It supplies energy to make the circuit work.
questions.misconception: The battery is not part of the circuit.

questions.stem: What is the component that lights up in a simple circuit?
questions.explanation: The bulb (or LED) is the component that lights up when the circuit is complete.

questions.stem: Name one basic component of an electric circuit.
questions.explanation: Basic components include the battery (dry cell), bulb (or LED), switch, and connecting wires.
questions.misconception: Only the bulb is part of a circuit.

questions.stem: When will a bulb in a simple circuit light up?
hints: A complete circuit lets electricity flow.
questions.explanation: A bulb lights up only when the circuit is complete, allowing electricity to flow through it.
questions.misconception: A bulb lights even if the circuit is broken.

questions.stem: What happens if the connecting wire in a circuit is cut?
questions.explanation: If the wire is cut, the circuit is broken. Electricity cannot flow, so the bulb does not light.
questions.misconception: A bulb lights even with a broken wire.

questions.stem: What is the function of the battery in an electric circuit?
options: It opens and closes the circuit
questions.explanation: The battery supplies energy to the circuit. This energy makes the bulb light and the components work.

questions.stem: Which set lists only basic components of an electric circuit?
hints: Which set has parts used in a real circuit?
A switch, bulb, wire and battery all belong in a circuit.
questions.explanation: The basic components of an electric circuit are the battery, bulb, connecting wire and switch.
questions.misconception: Any object can be part of an electric circuit.

questions.stem: Name two basic components of an electric circuit.
questions.explanation: Two basic components are the battery and the bulb. Other components include the switch and connecting wires.
questions.misconception: Only the battery matters in a circuit.

questions.stem: What is the function of the switch in an electric circuit?
options: It opens and closes the circuit
hints: A switch can be on or off.
questions.explanation: The switch opens and closes the circuit. When the switch is closed, electricity flows; when open, the circuit is broken.
questions.misconception: A switch is not needed in a circuit.

questions.stem: What is the function of the connecting wire in an electric circuit?
options: It carries electricity around the circuit
questions.explanation: The connecting wire carries electricity around the circuit, linking the battery, switch and bulb.
questions.misconception: Wires are not important in a circuit.

questions.stem: Which component matches this description: 'supplies energy to the circuit'?
hints: You put it in a torch.
questions.explanation: The battery supplies energy to the circuit. It is the source of power.
questions.misconception: The battery is not part of the circuit.

questions.stem: Which component matches this description: 'opens and closes the circuit'?
hints: You press it to turn a light on.
It has an on and off position.
questions.explanation: The switch opens and closes the circuit, controlling whether electricity flows.
questions.misconception: The switch is the same as the bulb.

questions.stem: Draw a simple electric circuit with a battery, a bulb, and connecting wires.

criteria.description: Drew a battery in the circuit
Drew a bulb in the circuit
Drew connecting wires linking the components
The drawing forms a complete loop (closed circuit)

questions.answer: Teacher-assessed using the rubric. Expected drawing: a rectangle or loop showing a battery, a bulb, and wires connecting them in a continuous path.
hints: Connect the bulb to the battery with wires.
questions.explanation: This is a drawing task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: The circuit does not need to form a complete loop.

questions.stem: In which situation will the bulb light?
options: When the switch is closed and all wires are connected
hints: A closed switch lets electricity flow.
questions.explanation: The bulb lights when the switch is closed and the circuit is complete, allowing electricity to flow.
questions.misconception: The bulb lights even when the switch is open.

questions.stem: Match the component to its function. Which pair is correct?
options: Wire → opens and closes the circuit
hints: Think about what each part does.
questions.explanation: The battery supplies energy. The bulb gives light, the switch opens/closes the circuit, and the wire carries electricity.

questions.stem: A pupil builds a circuit with a battery, wire and bulb, but forgets the switch. What is the effect?
options: The bulb will not light at all
The bulb will light but cannot be turned off easily
hints: Without a switch, the circuit stays closed.
questions.explanation: Without a switch, the circuit stays closed and the bulb lights, but there is no easy way to turn it off. The switch is used to control the circuit.
questions.misconception: A switch is not needed in a circuit.

questions.stem: Draw a simple circuit that includes a battery, a switch, a bulb and connecting wires. Label all four components.

criteria.description: Drew a battery and labeled it
Drew a switch and labeled it
Drew a bulb and labeled it
Drew connecting wires and labeled them
The components form a complete closed loop

questions.answer: Teacher-assessed using the rubric. Expected drawing: a closed loop containing all four labeled components.
questions.explanation: This is a drawing task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: Some components can be left out of the drawing.

questions.stem: In groups, use a battery, connecting wires, a switch and a bulb. Connect them to make the bulb light. Show your working circuit to your teacher.

criteria.description: Connected the battery, wires, switch and bulb correctly
Used the switch to turn the bulb on and off
Worked safely and cooperatively in the group

questions.answer: Teacher-assessed using the rubric. Expected outcome: a working circuit where the bulb lights when the switch is closed.
hints: Make sure all connections are tight.
The switch must be closed for the bulb to light.
questions.explanation: This is a practical task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: The bulb can light even if the circuit is not complete.

questions.stem: A pupil connects a battery, wire and bulb, but the bulb does not light. What is the most likely reason?
questions.explanation: The most likely reason is that the circuit is not complete. A loose connection or a gap in the circuit stops electricity from flowing.
questions.misconception: The bulb lights even if the circuit is broken.

questions.stem: Draw a circuit diagram using symbols for a battery, a switch and a bulb. Show the switch in the open position and in the closed position.

criteria.description: Used correct symbols for battery, switch and bulb
Drew the switch in the open position
Drew the switch in the closed position
Both diagrams form complete loops (except at the open switch)

questions.answer: Teacher-assessed using the rubric. Expected diagrams: two circuit diagrams with standard symbols, one with an open switch and one with a closed switch.
hints: Use simple symbols for each component.
Open switch = gap in the circuit.
questions.explanation: This is a drawing task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: Open and closed switches look the same in a diagram.

questions.stem: In groups, build a circuit with a battery, wire, switch and bulb. Test what happens when you use different materials (e.g. a metal spoon, a plastic ruler, a piece of paper) in place of the switch. Record which materials let the bulb light and which do not.

criteria.description: Built a working circuit with battery, wire, switch and bulb
Tested at least three different materials
Correctly recorded which materials let the bulb light (conductors)
Correctly recorded which materials did not let the bulb light (insulators)

questions.answer: Teacher-assessed using the rubric. Expected findings: metal spoon lets the bulb light (conductor); plastic ruler and paper do not (insulators).
hints: Plastics and paper usually do not.
questions.explanation: This is a practical task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B4.5.1.1 Recognise the importance of personal hygiene
indicator.objective: Know how to care for one's self and the environment

skills.description: Name personal hygiene practices (bathing, brushing teeth, cutting nails, washing clothes/towels).
Explain simply why each hygiene practice matters (e.g. bathing removes dirt and germs, brushing prevents tooth decay).
State what can happen if personal hygiene is neglected (body odour, sickness, germs).
Identify materials used for hygiene (soap, toothbrush, toothpaste, water, nail cutter, towel).
Give examples of caring for the environment (sweeping classroom, disposing of waste properly).
Describe a simple daily hygiene routine (e.g. bath twice daily, brush teeth morning and night).

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions total — Difficulty 1: 5; Difficulty 2: 7; Difficulty 3: 5; Difficulty 4: 3.
misconceptions: Bathing once a week is enough.
Brushing teeth once a day is enough.
Dirty fingernails are not a health problem.
Personal hygiene is only about looking good.
Sweeping the classroom is not part of hygiene.
Washing towels is not necessary.

questions.stem: Which of these is a personal hygiene practice?
hints: Which activity keeps your body clean?
questions.explanation: Bathing regularly is a personal hygiene practice. It removes dirt and germs from the body.
questions.misconception: Personal hygiene is only about looking good.

questions.stem: Which materials are used for brushing teeth?
hints: You use them in your mouth.
questions.explanation: A toothbrush and toothpaste are used for brushing teeth. They help remove food particles and prevent tooth decay.
questions.misconception: Brushing teeth once a day is enough.

questions.stem: Why do we bathe?
hints: What does soap and water remove?
Dirt and germs collect on the body.
questions.explanation: We bathe to remove dirt and germs from our bodies. This helps us stay clean and healthy.
questions.misconception: Bathing is only for looking good.

questions.stem: How often should you brush your teeth?
options: Twice a day, morning and night
hints: Think about morning and before bed.
Brushing twice a day keeps teeth healthy.

questions.misconception: Bathing once a week is enough.

questions.stem: Which materials are used to clean the armpit?

questions.stem: Which materials are used to wash clothes?

questions.misconception: Bathing once a week is enough.

questions.stem: Which of these is a hygiene practice at school?

questions.stem: Why should you wash your towels regularly?

questions.stem: What can happen if you do not cut your fingernails?

questions.stem: Why should you sweep your classroom?

questions.misconception: Sweeping the classroom is not part of hygiene.

questions.stem: Why is caring for the environment part of personal hygiene?

It is not about daily weather.
questions.explanation: Climate change means long-term changes in weather patterns, such as hotter days or changes in rainfall.
questions.misconception: Climate change means the weather changes from morning to evening.

questions.stem: Which of these is a cause of climate change?
questions.explanation: Burning of waste and vegetation produces smoke that contributes to climate change.
questions.misconception: Climate change is caused only by factories.

questions.stem: What does burning produce that dirties the air?
hints: You can see it rising from a fire.
questions.explanation: Burning produces smoke, which dirties the air and can harm health.

questions.stem: What can bush burning do to plants and animals?
options: Kill them and destroy their homes
questions.explanation: Bush burning kills plants and animals and destroys their homes.
questions.misconception: Bush burning helps plants grow better.

questions.stem: Which of these helps reduce burning?
options: Disposing of waste properly in bins
questions.explanation: Disposing of waste properly in bins helps reduce burning and its harmful effects.
questions.misconception: Burning waste is always good because it removes rubbish.

questions.stem: Why is burning considered a cause of climate change?
options: It produces smoke and gases that trap heat
hints: Smoke and gases go into the air.
questions.explanation: Burning produces smoke and gases that trap heat in the atmosphere, contributing to climate change.
questions.misconception: Burning does not affect the climate.

questions.stem: Which statement about smoke from burning is correct?
options: It dirties the air and can harm health
hints: Smoke is not good to breathe.
questions.explanation: Smoke from burning dirties the air and can harm the health of people and animals.

questions.stem: A farmer sets fire to a bush. What effect can this have on the farmer's property?
options: It can destroy crops and buildings
hints: It can burn houses and farms.
questions.explanation: Bush burning can spread and destroy crops, buildings, and other property.
questions.misconception: Burning only affects the person who starts the fire.

questions.stem: What will happen if people continue to burn waste and vegetation?
options: There will be more smoke and the environment will get hotter
questions.explanation: Continuous burning will produce more smoke, dirty the air, and contribute to a hotter environment.
questions.misconception: Burning waste is harmless in the long run.

questions.stem: What is climate change?
answer: changes in the weather over many years
long-term changes in the earth's weather
hints: Think about changes over a long time.
questions.explanation: Climate change is long-term change in weather patterns, like hotter days or changes in rainfall.
questions.misconception: Climate change means daily weather changes.

questions.stem: Give one reason why burning causes climate change.
answer: it produces smoke and gases that trap heat
smoke and gases from burning trap heat
it releases smoke that warms the earth
questions.explanation: Burning produces smoke and gases that trap heat in the atmosphere, leading to climate change.

questions.stem: What does burning produce that makes the air dirty?
hints: You can see it rising from a fire.
questions.explanation: Burning produces smoke, which makes the air dirty.

questions.stem: Which of these is an effect of bush burning on humans?
options: It can cause health problems from smoke
hints: Smoke is not good to breathe.
questions.explanation: Bush burning produces smoke that can cause breathing problems and other health issues.

questions.stem: A learner says, 'Burning waste is good because it removes rubbish.' What is the best correction?
options: No, burning produces smoke that harms the environment
No, burning makes the rubbish disappear completely
hints: There are better ways to manage waste.
questions.explanation: Burning waste is not good because it produces smoke that dirties the air and contributes to climate change.
questions.misconception: Burning waste is always good because it removes rubbish.

questions.stem: Suggest one way to reduce burning in your community.
answer: dispose of waste in bins instead of burning
compost food waste instead of burning
hints: Do not set fire to bushes.
questions.explanation: Ways to reduce burning include avoiding bush burning, disposing of waste in bins, and recycling or composting instead of burning.
questions.misconception: Burning waste is the only way to manage it.

questions.stem: Which of these shows an effect of burning on animals?
options: They lose their homes and can be killed
questions.explanation: Burning destroys vegetation and habitats, and can kill animals.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes climate change?
options: It is a change in weather from day to night
It is a change in the colour of the sky
It is long-term change in weather patterns over many years
It is a change in the time of sunrise each day
questions.explanation: Climate change refers to long-term changes in weather patterns over many years.
questions.misconception: Climate change means daily weather changes.

questions.stem: Explain how burning can affect humans, plants, and animals.
answer: burning produces smoke that harms human health, kills plants, and destroys animal homes
smoke from burning harms humans, fire kills plants, and destroys animals' habitats
burning harms humans through smoke, kills plants, and destroys animal habitats
questions.explanation: Burning harms humans through smoke (breathing problems), kills plants, and destroys the homes of animals.

questions.stem: Design a poster that shows the effects of burning on climate change. Include at least two effects, such as smoke and dirty air, and write a short message encouraging people to stop burning waste.

criteria.description: Showed at least two effects of burning on climate change
Used drawings to show smoke and dirty air
Included a short message encouraging people not to burn waste

hints: Include a picture of a clean environment.
questions.explanation: This is a drawing task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.1.1 Understand the physical features and life processes of living things and use this understanding to classify them
indicator.objective: Know the life processes of living things (growth, sensitivity to the environment, respiration and excretion)

questions.stem: Which of these is a life process of living things?
hints: Think about what all living things do.
It is one of the four life processes you learned.
questions.explanation: Growth is a life process. The four life processes in this lesson are growth, sensitivity, respiration and excretion.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT one of the four life processes of living things?
hints: Think about the four processes you learned.
Dancing is an activity, not a life process.
questions.explanation: The four life processes are growth, sensitivity, respiration and excretion. Dancing is not a life process.
questions.misconception: Any activity is a life process.

questions.stem: What does growth mean in living things?
hints: Think about a seed becoming a plant.
questions.explanation: Growth means increasing in size over time. A seedling grows into a mature plant.

questions.stem: What is sensitivity in living things?
options: The ability to respond to changes in the environment
hints: Think about the mimosa plant closing when touched.
It is about responding to changes.
questions.explanation: Sensitivity is the ability of living things to respond to changes in their environment.

questions.stem: What is respiration?
options: The process of breathing in and out to get energy
hints: You do this all the time without thinking.
questions.explanation: Respiration is the process of breathing in and out to get energy from food.
questions.misconception: Respiration and breathing are exactly the same thing.

questions.stem: Ama plants a bean seed. After two weeks, the plant is taller and has more leaves. Which life process is this?
questions.explanation: The plant is growing. Growth is the increase in size over time.

questions.stem: When you touch the leaves of a mimosa plant, they fold up. What life process is the plant showing?
hints: The plant is responding to touch.
It is reacting to a change.
questions.explanation: The mimosa plant is responding to touch. This is sensitivity — responding to changes in the environment.

questions.stem: A pupil breathes in and out quickly after running. Which life process is this?
questions.explanation: The pupil is respiring. Respiration is breathing in and out to get energy.
questions.misconception: Respiration only happens when we sleep.

questions.stem: What is excretion?
options: The process of removing waste products from the body
The process of responding to touch
hints: Think about what the body removes as waste.
questions.explanation: Excretion is the removal of waste products from the body, such as urine and sweat.
questions.misconception: Excretion is the same as eating.

questions.stem: Why is respiration important for living things?
options: It gives them energy to live and work
It helps them respond to touch
hints: What does breathing give the body?
questions.explanation: Respiration gives living things energy to live, grow and work.
questions.misconception: Respiration is only for making noise.

questions.stem: What is growth in living things?
hints: Think about a seed becoming a plant.
questions.explanation: Growth is the increase in size of a living thing over time.

questions.stem: What is respiration?
answer: breathing in and out to get energy
the process of breathing to get energy
hints: You do it all the time.
questions.explanation: Respiration is the process of breathing in and out to get energy from food.
questions.misconception: Respiration and breathing are not related.

questions.stem: A pupil touches a snail and it quickly pulls back into its shell. What does this show?
hints: The snail is responding to touch.
It is reacting to a change.
questions.explanation: The snail is responding to touch by pulling back. This is sensitivity.

questions.stem: Why is excretion important for living things?
options: It removes waste products that can harm the body
It helps them respond to touch
hints: What happens if waste stays in the body?
questions.explanation: Excretion removes waste products that would harm the body if they stayed inside.

questions.stem: A pupil observes a seedling and a mature plant of the same kind. Which difference shows growth?
options: The mature plant is taller and has more leaves
The mature plant is a different colour
The mature plant is in a different pot
The mature plant has a different smell
hints: What happens to size over time?
questions.explanation: The mature plant is taller and has more leaves, showing it has grown.

questions.stem: Give an example of a plant showing sensitivity.
answer: the mimosa plant folds its leaves when touched
hints: Think about a plant that moves when touched.
questions.explanation: The mimosa plant folds its leaves when touched. This is an example of sensitivity in plants.

questions.stem: Why is sensitivity important for living things?
answer: it helps them respond to danger and changes in their environment
it helps them react to changes around them
hints: It helps them react to the environment.
questions.explanation: Sensitivity helps living things respond to changes and danger in their environment, helping them survive.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of excretion in humans?
questions.explanation: Passing out urine is an example of excretion. The body removes waste products.
questions.misconception: Excretion is the same as eating.

questions.stem: Explain how a seedling shows growth over time.
answer: it gets taller and develops more leaves as it grows
the seedling increases in size and grows more leaves
it grows bigger and taller over time
hints: What happens to the number of leaves?
questions.explanation: A seedling shows growth by getting taller and developing more leaves over time.

questions.stem: Explain why living things need respiration.
answer: respiration gives the body energy to live and work
it provides energy for life processes
hints: What does breathing give the body?
questions.explanation: Living things need respiration to get energy from food. This energy is used for growth, movement and other life processes.
questions.misconception: Respiration is not needed for energy.

questions.stem: A pupil lists four life processes: growth, sensitivity, respiration and excretion. Which statement about these processes is correct?
options: Only animals show all four processes
Only humans show all four processes
Plants show only growth and respiration
questions.explanation: Plants show all four life processes: growth, sensitivity, respiration and excretion. They grow, respond to touch, respire and excrete waste.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.1.2 Demonstrate understanding of the differences between living things, non-living things, and things which have never been alive
indicator.objective: Compare the differences among things that are living, dead and things that have never been alive

questions.stem: What makes something a living thing?
options: It carries out life processes like growth and respiration
questions.explanation: Living things carry out life processes such as growth, respiration, sensitivity and excretion.
questions.misconception: Things that move are always living.

questions.stem: What does 'dead' mean?
options: Something that was once alive but no longer carries out life processes
hints: It was part of a tree but is no longer alive.
questions.explanation: Dead things were once alive but no longer carry out life processes.
questions.misconception: A dead tree was never alive.

questions.stem: What does 'never alive' mean?
options: Something that was never living and does not carry out life processes
questions.explanation: Things that have never been alive do not carry out life processes and never did.

questions.stem: Which of these is a living thing?
hints: Which one grows and carries out life processes?
questions.explanation: A growing plant is a living thing because it carries out life processes.
questions.misconception: Things that move are always living.

questions.stem: Which statement compares a living plant and a dead plant correctly?
options: The living plant grows, but the dead plant does not
The dead plant grows, but the living plant does not
hints: Dead things do not carry out life processes.
questions.explanation: A living plant grows, but a dead plant does not. This is one difference between living and dead things.

questions.stem: A pupil says a fire is living because it moves and grows. What is the best correction?
options: No, fire does not carry out life processes like respiration and excretion
questions.explanation: Fire is not living because it does not carry out life processes such as respiration and excretion.
questions.misconception: A fire is living because it moves and grows.

questions.stem: A pupil finds a dry leaf on the ground. How should the pupil classify it?
hints: It was once part of a living plant.
questions.explanation: The dry leaf was once part of a living plant but is no longer alive. It is dead.

questions.stem: Why is a rock classified as 'never alive'?
options: Because it does not carry out life processes and never did
questions.explanation: A rock is never-alive because it does not carry out life processes and never did.

questions.stem: Which of these is a difference between a living thing and a dead thing?
options: Living things move, but dead things do not
Living things carry out life processes, but dead things do not
Living things are always bigger than dead things
hints: Living things carry out life processes.
questions.explanation: Living things carry out life processes, while dead things do not. This is a key difference.
questions.misconception: Dead things still carry out life processes.

questions.stem: Which of these was never alive?
hints: Was it ever part of a living thing?
questions.explanation: A rock was never alive. Dry sticks, dead insects and fallen leaves were once part of living things.

questions.stem: What makes something a living thing?
answer: it carries out life processes like growth and respiration
hints: Living things carry out life processes.
questions.explanation: A living thing carries out life processes such as growth, respiration, sensitivity and excretion.

questions.stem: What does it mean when something is dead?
answer: it was once alive but no longer carries out life processes
it was once living but is no longer alive
it was alive but is not now
questions.explanation: Dead things were once alive but no longer carry out life processes.
questions.misconception: A dead thing was never alive.

questions.stem: A pupil classifies a car as 'never alive'. Which reason is correct?
options: It moves, so it is living
It does not carry out life processes and was never alive
It is made of metal, so it is dead
It has wheels, so it is living
questions.explanation: A car is never-alive because it does not carry out life processes and was never alive.
questions.misconception: A car is living because it moves.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares living and dead things?
options: Living things grow and respire, but dead things do not
Dead things grow, but living things do not
Both living and dead things respire
Neither living nor dead things grow
hints: Living things carry out life processes.
questions.explanation: Living things grow and respire, but dead things do not carry out life processes.

questions.stem: Classify a rock as living, dead, or never alive.
answer: never alive because it was never living
hints: It does not carry out life processes.
questions.explanation: A rock is never alive because it does not carry out life processes and never did.

questions.stem: Give one reason why a dry stick is classified as dead.
answer: it was once part of a living tree but no longer carries out life processes
it was once alive but is no longer alive
it was part of a living plant but is now dead
hints: Was it ever part of a living thing?
questions.explanation: A dry stick was once part of a living tree but no longer carries out life processes, so it is dead.

questions.stem: What does 'never alive' mean?
answer: something that was never living and does not carry out life processes
questions.explanation: Never alive means something was never living and does not carry out life processes.

questions.stem: A pupil has four things: a growing bean plant, a dry leaf, a stone, and a dead insect. Which list correctly classifies them?
options: Living: growing bean plant; Dead: dry leaf and dead insect; Never alive: stone
Living: growing bean plant and dry leaf; Dead: stone; Never alive: dead insect
Living: stone; Dead: growing bean plant; Never alive: dry leaf and dead insect
Living: dead insect; Dead: growing bean plant; Never alive: stone and dry leaf
hints: Which ones were once alive but are not now?
questions.explanation: The growing bean plant is living. The dry leaf and dead insect were once alive but are now dead. The stone was never alive.

questions.stem: Explain one difference between a living plant and a dead plant.
answer: a living plant grows and carries out life processes, but a dead plant does not
the living plant grows, but the dead plant does not
living plants respire, dead plants do not
questions.explanation: A living plant grows and carries out life processes, while a dead plant does not.

questions.stem: Explain why a car is not a living thing, even though it moves.
answer: because it does not carry out life processes like growth and respiration
it moves but it does not grow or breathe, so it is not living
a car is never alive because it does not carry out life processes
questions.explanation: A car is not living because it does not carry out life processes such as growth and respiration, even though it moves.
questions.misconception: Things that move are always living.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.2.1 Recognise materials as important resources for providing human needs
indicator.objective: Classify everyday materials based on their properties (soft, hard, rough, smooth, opaque, transparent and bendable)

questions.stem: Which of these is a property of a material?
hints: Properties describe how a material feels or behaves.
questions.explanation: Bendable is a property of a material. It describes whether the material can be bent without breaking.
questions.misconception: Any word can describe a material.

questions.stem: Which material is soft?
hints: Which one feels gentle to touch?
questions.explanation: Cotton wool is soft. Iron nails, stones and wood are hard.

questions.stem: Which material is transparent?
hints: Which one can you see through?
questions.explanation: Clear glass is transparent because you can see through it. Wood, metal and cardboard are opaque.

questions.stem: Which material is bendable?
hints: Which one can you bend without breaking?
questions.explanation: Rubber is bendable. Glass, stone and iron are not easily bendable and may break if forced.

questions.stem: What do we call a material that you cannot see through?
questions.explanation: A material you cannot see through is called opaque.

questions.stem: A pupil is sorting materials into 'hard' and 'soft'. Which group is correct?
options: Hard: stone, iron; Soft: cotton wool, sponge
Hard: sponge, cotton wool; Soft: stone, iron
Hard: sponge, stone; Soft: iron, cotton wool
Hard: cotton wool, iron; Soft: stone, sponge
hints: Which materials cannot be easily squeezed?
questions.explanation: Stone and iron are hard materials. Cotton wool and sponge are soft materials.

questions.stem: Ama touches a piece of sandpaper and a piece of glass. Which statement correctly describes their textures?
options: Sandpaper is smooth, glass is rough
Sandpaper is rough, glass is smooth
questions.explanation: Sandpaper is rough because it has a bumpy surface. Glass is smooth because it has an even surface.

questions.stem: Which set contains only transparent materials?
options: Clear plastic, clear glass, clean water
hints: Which materials can you see through?
questions.explanation: Clear plastic, clear glass and clean water are transparent materials. You can see through them.

questions.stem: Which of these materials is NOT bendable?
hints: Which one will snap if you try to bend it?
questions.explanation: An iron nail is not bendable. It is a hard metal. Clay, rubber bands and raffia can be bent or moulded.

questions.stem: Why is clay used for making pots?
options: Because it can be moulded when wet and becomes hard when baked
hints: Clay can be shaped when wet.
questions.explanation: Clay is used for pots because it can be moulded into shape when wet and becomes hard when baked.
questions.misconception: Any material can be used for any purpose.

questions.stem: Which material is best for making a window pane?
options: Clear glass because it is transparent
Cotton wool because it is soft
hints: You need to see through a window.
questions.explanation: Clear glass is best for a window pane because it is transparent and lets light through.
questions.misconception: Any material can be used for any purpose.

questions.stem: Why is raffia palm used for making baskets?
answer: because it is bendable and can be woven easily
it bends easily so it can be woven into baskets
it is flexible and easy to weave
questions.explanation: Raffia palm is used for baskets because it is bendable and can be woven easily.
questions.misconception: Any material can be used for baskets.

questions.stem: Name three properties of materials.
hints: Think about whether you can see through them or bend them.
questions.explanation: Properties of materials include soft, hard, rough, smooth, opaque, transparent and bendable.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'All plastics are transparent.' Is the pupil correct?
options: No, some plastics are opaque, like black plastic bowls
hints: Think about a black plastic bucket.
questions.explanation: Not all plastics are transparent. Some plastics are opaque, like black plastic bowls or buckets.

questions.stem: Why are cooking pots usually made of metal rather than cloth?
options: Metal is soft and cloth is hard
Metal is hard and can withstand heat, while cloth burns
Cloth is bendable and metal is not
Metal is transparent and cloth is opaque
questions.explanation: Metal is hard and can withstand the high heat of cooking. Cloth is soft and would burn on a fire.
questions.misconception: Any material can be used for any purpose.

questions.stem: Sort these materials into 'transparent' and 'opaque': clear glass, wood, clear plastic, cardboard.
answer: transparent: clear glass and clear plastic; opaque: wood and cardboard
transparent: clear glass, clear plastic; opaque: wood, cardboard
clear glass and clear plastic are transparent; wood and cardboard are opaque
hints: Which ones can you see through?
Wood and cardboard are not see-through.
questions.explanation: Clear glass and clear plastic are transparent because you can see through them. Wood and cardboard are opaque because you cannot see through them.
questions.misconception: All materials are either completely transparent or completely opaque.

questions.stem: Why is cotton wool used for making pillows?
answer: because it is soft and comfortable to rest on
it is soft and makes the pillow comfortable
cotton wool is soft, so it is good for pillows
hints: You rest your head on it.
questions.explanation: Cotton wool is used for pillows because it is soft and comfortable.
questions.misconception: Any material can be used for pillows.

questions.stem: Name one material that is bendable and one that is not bendable.
answer: bendable: rubber band; not bendable: iron nail
hints: Think of something you can bend.
Think of something that would break if you tried to bend it.
questions.explanation: Rubber and raffia are bendable. Glass, iron and stone are not bendable.

questions.stem: Design a simple raincoat for a farmer in Ghana. Choose a material that is suitable. Draw your design and write one sentence explaining why you chose that material.

criteria.description: Drew a simple design of a raincoat
Chose a suitable material (e.g. plastic, waterproof fabric)
Explained that the material is waterproof/does not let water through

hints: What happens when rain falls on the farmer?
The material should keep water out.
questions.explanation: This is a drawing task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: Any material can be used for a raincoat.

questions.stem: A learner needs a material to make a transparent container to store water. Which material is best and why?
options: Wood, because it is hard and strong
Clear plastic, because it is transparent and does not let water through
Cotton wool, because it is soft
Rough stone, because it is heavy
hints: The container needs to be see-through.
It must hold water without leaking.
questions.explanation: Clear plastic is best because it is transparent (you can see through it) and it does not let water pass through.
questions.misconception: Any material can be used for any purpose.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.2.2 Know that substances can exist in different physical states (solid, liquid, gas). Many substances can be changed from one state to another by heating or cooling
indicator.objective: Know that some changes are reversible, while others cannot be reversed

questions.stem: What is a reversible change?
options: A change that cannot be undone
A change that can be undone
A change that makes a new substance
hints: You can go back to the original form.
questions.explanation: A reversible change is one that can be undone. The original substance can be recovered.

questions.stem: What is an irreversible change?
options: A change that can be undone
A change that cannot be undone
hints: You cannot go back to the original form.
questions.explanation: An irreversible change is one that cannot be undone. You cannot get the original substance back easily.

questions.stem: Which of these is a reversible change?
hints: Can you freeze melted ice back into ice?
questions.explanation: Melting ice is a reversible change. If you freeze the water, it becomes ice again.

questions.stem: In an irreversible change, what usually happens?
hints: Ash and smoke are new things.
questions.explanation: In an irreversible change, a new substance is usually formed. For example, burning paper produces ash and smoke.
questions.misconception: Irreversible changes do not form new substances.

questions.stem: Which of these is an irreversible change?
hints: Can you turn a fried egg back into a raw egg?
questions.explanation: Frying an egg is an irreversible change. You cannot turn a fried egg back into a raw egg.

questions.stem: A pupil melts some candle wax, then lets it cool and harden again. Is the change reversible or irreversible?
options: Reversible, because the wax can be melted and hardened again
Irreversible, because the wax changed colour
hints: Can you go from solid wax to liquid and back again?
questions.explanation: Melting and hardening candle wax is a reversible change. The wax can be melted and solidified again.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about a reversible change is correct?
options: A new substance is always formed
The original substance can be recovered
hints: Can you get the ice back?
questions.explanation: In a reversible change, the original substance can be recovered. For example, melted ice can be frozen again.

questions.stem: Which change forms a new substance?
questions.explanation: Burning paper forms a new substance (ash and smoke). Freezing, melting and crumpling do not form new substances.
questions.misconception: Burning is reversible because you can put out the fire.

questions.stem: Which of these is an irreversible change?
hints: Which one produces smoke and ash?
You cannot change ash back into wood.
questions.explanation: Burning wood is an irreversible change. You cannot turn the ash and smoke back into a piece of wood.

questions.stem: Which of these is a reversible change?
hints: Can you melt the ice back into water?
questions.explanation: Freezing water is a reversible change. The ice can melt back into water.

questions.stem: What is an irreversible change?
answer: a change that cannot be undone
a change that cannot be changed back
hints: You cannot get the original back.
questions.explanation: An irreversible change is a change that cannot be undone to get the original substance back.

questions.stem: What is a reversible change?
answer: a change that can be undone
a change that can be reversed
a change where you can get the original substance back
questions.explanation: A reversible change is a change that can be undone, and the original substance can be recovered.
questions.misconception: A reversible change cannot be undone.

questions.stem: A pupil crumples a piece of paper into a ball. Is this change reversible or irreversible?
options: Irreversible, because the paper has changed forever
Reversible, because you can unfold the paper back to a flat sheet
Irreversible, because the paper is now smaller
Reversible, because the paper changed colour
questions.explanation: Crumpling paper is a reversible change. You can unfold the paper to make it flat again.

questions.stem: A learner burns a piece of paper. They collect the ash. Can they turn the ash back into paper?
options: No, burning is an irreversible change
questions.explanation: No, burning is an irreversible change. The ash cannot be turned back into paper.

questions.stem: Which of these changes does NOT form a new substance?
questions.explanation: Melting ice does not form a new substance. Ice is water in a solid state; it simply changes to liquid water.
questions.misconception: Any change forms a new substance.

questions.stem: Give one example of a reversible change and one example of an irreversible change.
answer: reversible: melting ice; irreversible: burning paper
reversible: freezing water; irreversible: frying an egg
reversible: melting wax; irreversible: burning wood
hints: Think of something you can undo.
Think of something you cannot undo.
questions.explanation: Melting ice is reversible. Burning paper is irreversible.

questions.stem: A learner melts some chocolate. Can the chocolate become solid again? Explain.
answer: yes, if it is cooled it will become solid again
questions.explanation: Yes, melted chocolate can become solid again if it is cooled. This is a reversible change.

questions.stem: Classify these changes as reversible or irreversible: (a) melting ice, (b) burning paper, (c) freezing water, (d) frying an egg.
answer: reversible: melting ice, freezing water; irreversible: burning paper, frying an egg
reversible: a, c; irreversible: b, d
hints: Burning and frying cannot be undone.
questions.explanation: Melting ice and freezing water are reversible. Burning paper and frying an egg are irreversible.
questions.misconception: All changes involving heat are irreversible.

questions.stem: Explain why burning is an irreversible change.
answer: because new substances like ash and smoke are formed and cannot be turned back into the original material
burning produces ash and smoke which cannot be reversed
you cannot get the original substance back after burning
hints: What new things are formed when you burn something?
Can you turn ash back into wood?
questions.explanation: Burning is irreversible because it forms new substances (ash and smoke) that cannot be turned back into the original material.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between a reversible change and an irreversible change in terms of new substances.
answer: reversible changes do not form new substances while irreversible changes form new substances
in a reversible change no new substance is formed, but in an irreversible change a new substance is formed
reversible: no new substance; irreversible: new substance formed
questions.explanation: Reversible changes do not form new substances; the original substance can be recovered. Irreversible changes form new substances that cannot be easily changed back.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B5.1.2.3 Understand mixtures, the types, formation, uses and ways of separating them into their components
indicator.objective: Demonstrate formation and separation of mixtures (solid-liquid and liquid-liquid mixtures)

questions.stem: What type of mixture is formed when salt is added to water?
hints: Salt is a solid and water is a liquid.
So the mixture is solid and liquid.
questions.explanation: Salt and water form a solid-liquid mixture because salt is a solid and water is a liquid.

questions.stem: What type of mixture is formed when cooking oil is mixed with water?
hints: Both oil and water are liquids.
questions.explanation: Cooking oil and water form a liquid-liquid mixture because both are liquids.
questions.misconception: Oil and water form a solid-liquid mixture.

questions.stem: How do you form a mixture of sand and water?
options: Heat the sand, then add water
Add sand to water and stir
questions.explanation: To form a mixture of sand and water, simply add sand to water and stir.
questions.misconception: You need heat to form a mixture.

questions.stem: In which mixture does the solid dissolve completely?
questions.explanation: Salt dissolves completely in water to form a solution. Sand and stones do not dissolve.

questions.stem: Which method is used to separate sand from water?
hints: Sand is solid and does not dissolve.
You can pour the mixture through a filter.
questions.explanation: Filtration is used to separate sand from water. The filter traps the sand while the water passes through.

questions.stem: A pupil adds salt to water and stirs. The salt disappears. What has happened?
options: The salt has dissolved in the water to form a solution
The salt has turned into water
The salt has sunk to the bottom
hints: The salt is still there but you cannot see it.
questions.explanation: The salt has dissolved in the water to form a solution. It is still there, just mixed evenly.

questions.stem: Which method is best for separating a mixture of salt and water?
hints: Salt is dissolved in the water.
If you boil the water away, the salt is left behind.
questions.explanation: Evaporation is used to separate salt from water. When the water evaporates, the salt is left behind.

questions.stem: Which of these pairs forms a mixture where the solid does NOT dissolve?
hints: Which solid stays visible in the water?
questions.explanation: Sand does not dissolve in water. It forms a mixture where the solid can be seen.

questions.stem: Which method is used to separate a mixture of cooking oil and water?
hints: A separating funnel lets you drain one layer at a time.
questions.explanation: A separating funnel is used to separate cooking oil and water because they are immiscible and form layers.

questions.stem: What type of mixture is formed when sugar is added to water?
questions.explanation: Sugar and water form a solid-liquid mixture.
questions.misconception: Sugar and water form a liquid-liquid mixture.

questions.stem: How do you form a mixture of sugar and water?
answer: add sugar to water and stir
put sugar into water and mix
hints: Put the solid into the liquid.
questions.explanation: To form a sugar-water mixture, add sugar to water and stir until it dissolves.
questions.misconception: You need heat to form a sugar-water mixture.

questions.stem: Which method would you use to separate stones from sand?
hints: A sieve can catch the big stones.
questions.explanation: Sieving is used to separate stones from sand. The sieve catches the stones while the sand passes through.

questions.stem: Match the mixture to the best separation method: sand and water, salt and water, oil and water.
options: Sand + water → evaporation; Salt + water → filtration; Oil + water → sieving
Sand + water → filtration; Salt + water → evaporation; Oil + water → separating funnel
Sand + water → separating funnel; Salt + water → sieving; Oil + water → filtration
Sand + water → sieving; Salt + water → separating funnel; Oil + water → evaporation
hints: Sand is solid and does not dissolve.
questions.explanation: Sand + water is separated by filtration. Salt + water is separated by evaporation. Oil + water is separated by a separating funnel.
questions.misconception: Any method works for any mixture.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between a mixture of sand and water and a mixture of salt and water.
answer: salt dissolves in water to form a solution, but sand does not dissolve and can be seen in the water
in salt and water the salt dissolves, but in sand and water the sand does not dissolve
salt dissolves but sand does not
hints: Which solid can still be seen?
questions.explanation: Salt dissolves completely in water to form a solution. Sand does not dissolve and can still be seen in the water.

questions.stem: How can you recover salt from a salt solution?
options: By boiling or evaporating the water
hints: What happens if you remove the water?
questions.explanation: You can recover salt from a salt solution by evaporating the water. The salt is left behind.
questions.misconception: Filtering recovers salt from a solution.

questions.stem: What type of mixture is formed when kerosene is mixed with water?
hints: Kerosene and water are both liquids.
questions.explanation: Kerosene and water form a liquid-liquid mixture because both are liquids.
questions.misconception: Kerosene and water form a solid-liquid mixture.

questions.stem: Explain how you would recover sand from a mixture of sand and water.
answer: pour the mixture through a filter so the sand is trapped and the water passes through
use filtration to trap the sand in the filter paper
filter the mixture to separate the sand
hints: Sand is solid and does not dissolve.
questions.explanation: Pour the mixture through a filter. The sand is trapped by the filter, while the water passes through.
questions.misconception: You can recover sand by evaporation.

questions.stem: Which separation method would you use to separate a mixture of cooking oil and water?
hints: Use a funnel that lets one layer out at a time.
questions.explanation: A separating funnel is used to separate cooking oil and water because they form separate layers.

questions.stem: In groups, you are given a mixture of sand and water. Plan and carry out an experiment to separate the sand from the water using a filter (or improvised filter). Describe what you did and what you observed.

criteria.description: Correctly observed that sand was trapped in the filter
Correctly observed that clear water passed through

hints: Use a filter paper or cloth in a funnel.
Look at what remains on the filter and what passes through.
questions.explanation: This is a practical task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to make a mixture where the solid can be easily separated by filtration. Which mixture should the pupil make?
questions.explanation: Sand and water make a mixture where the solid does not dissolve and can be separated by filtration. Salt, sugar and soft drink powder dissolve in water.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B5.2.1.1 Recognise that some events in our environment occur recurrently
indicator.objective: Know how day and night are formed

questions.stem: What does the earth do that causes day and night?
questions.explanation: The earth spins on its axis. This spinning causes day and night.

questions.stem: What causes day and night?
options: The moon moving around the earth
The earth rotating on its axis
The sun going behind a hill
hints: One side faces the sun while the other is dark.
questions.explanation: Day and night are caused by the earth rotating on its axis.
questions.misconception: The sun moves around the earth.

questions.stem: Which side of the earth has day?
options: The side facing away from the sun
hints: Day is when it is bright.
questions.explanation: The side of the earth facing the sun has day.
questions.misconception: The side facing away from the sun has day.

questions.stem: How long does it take the earth to complete one rotation?
hints: A day and a night together.
questions.explanation: The earth takes about 24 hours to complete one rotation.
questions.misconception: The earth rotates once a year.

questions.stem: When is it usually dark outside?
hints: When do you see the moon and stars?
questions.explanation: It is usually dark at night because the side of the earth you are on is facing away from the sun.
questions.misconception: It is dark during the day.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Day and night happen because the sun goes behind a hill.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, the sun goes behind a hill
No, day and night are caused by the earth rotating on its axis
No, the moon causes day and night
No, day and night happen at the same time everywhere
hints: The sun does not move around the earth.
questions.explanation: Day and night are caused by the earth rotating on its axis, not by the sun going behind a hill.
questions.misconception: Day and night happen because the sun goes behind a hill.

questions.stem: Why is it night on one side of the earth while it is day on the other side?
options: Because the sun shines on only one side at a time
Because the moon blocks the sun
Because the stars are brighter at night
hints: The sun can only light the side facing it.
The other side is in shadow.
questions.explanation: The sun shines on the side of the earth facing it, making it day there. The other side is in shadow, so it is night there.
questions.misconception: Day and night happen at the same time everywhere.

questions.stem: In a model using a globe and a torch, what does the torch represent?
hints: What gives light to the earth?
questions.explanation: In the model, the torch represents the sun because it gives light to the globe (earth).

questions.stem: What is the imaginary line that the earth spins around called?
hints: It goes through the North and South Poles.
questions.explanation: The earth spins on its axis, an imaginary line passing through the North and South Poles.
questions.misconception: The earth spins on its orbit.

questions.stem: How long does the earth take to complete one rotation?
questions.explanation: The earth takes about 24 hours (one day) to complete one rotation.
questions.misconception: The earth rotates once a year.

questions.stem: Give one thing you do during the day and one thing you do at night.
answer: day: go to school; night: sleep
hints: When do you go to school?
questions.explanation: We usually go to school and play during the day, and sleep at night.
questions.misconception: Day and night have no effect on activities.

questions.stem: Explain how day and night are formed.
answer: the earth rotates on its axis, so the side facing the sun has day and the side facing away has night
the earth spins on its axis, causing day on the side facing the sun and night on the other side
as the earth rotates, one side faces the sun (day) and the other side faces away (night)
hints: One side faces the sun, the other does not.
questions.explanation: Day and night are formed because the earth rotates on its axis. The side facing the sun has day, and the side facing away has night.
questions.misconception: The sun moves around the earth.

questions.stem: In a model, a lamp is placed in the middle of a dark room and a globe is placed near it. Half of the globe is bright and half is dark. What does the dark half represent?
hints: The dark half is facing away from the lamp.
questions.explanation: The dark half of the globe represents night because it faces away from the light source (the sun).

questions.stem: Why is it day on the side of the earth facing the sun?
answer: because the sun shines light on that side
the side facing the sun receives sunlight
that side is lit by the sun
questions.explanation: It is day on the side facing the sun because that side receives sunlight.
questions.misconception: The sun shines on all sides of the earth at once.

questions.stem: What is the earth's axis?
answer: the imaginary line the earth spins around
an imaginary line through the earth that it rotates on
the line through the North and South Poles that the earth spins on
questions.explanation: The earth's axis is the imaginary line passing through the North and South Poles that the earth spins on.
questions.misconception: The axis is a real stick through the earth.

questions.stem: In groups, use a globe (or a ball) and a torch to show how day and night are formed. One learner holds the torch (sun) and another slowly turns the globe (earth). Describe what you observe.

criteria.description: Held the torch to represent the sun
Turned the globe slowly to represent the earth rotating
Observed that the side facing the torch is bright (day) and the other side is dark (night)
Explained how day and night are formed

hints: Watch the light and dark areas.
questions.explanation: This is a practical task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: The sun moves around the earth.

questions.stem: Explain why we have day and night every 24 hours.
answer: because the earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours, so each side faces the sun and then turns away
the earth spins once every 24 hours, causing day and night to alternate
the earth's rotation takes 24 hours, so day and night follow each other
hints: What happens to the side facing the sun after some hours?
questions.explanation: The earth rotates once every 24 hours. As it turns, the side facing the sun has day, and then turns away to have night, so day and night follow each other every 24 hours.
questions.misconception: Day and night happen at the same time everywhere.

questions.stem: A learner in Accra is experiencing daytime. What is happening on the opposite side of the earth?
hints: The sun cannot light the whole earth at once.
questions.explanation: If it is daytime in Accra, the opposite side of the earth is facing away from the sun, so it is nighttime there.
questions.misconception: Day and night happen at the same time everywhere.

questions.stem: Explain why the earth's rotation is important for life.
answer: it causes day and night, which gives living things light and darkness for activities and rest
