options: They take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen
They release carbon dioxide and take in oxygen
questions.explanation: Trees take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen, which helps keep the air clean for living things.

questions.stem: How does deforestation contribute to climate change?
options: Fewer trees mean less carbon dioxide is absorbed, making the environment hotter
More trees grow and cool the earth
Trees stop the rain from falling
Cutting trees makes the air cleaner
hints: Less trees mean more carbon dioxide in the air.
questions.explanation: Deforestation reduces the number of trees that absorb carbon dioxide, so more carbon dioxide stays in the air and the environment gets hotter.
questions.misconception: Cutting trees has no effect on climate.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Cutting trees has nothing to do with climate change.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, cutting trees does not affect climate
No, cutting trees reduces the number of trees that absorb carbon dioxide, contributing to climate change
No, cutting trees makes the climate cooler
No, cutting trees only affects animals
hints: Less trees mean more carbon dioxide in the air.
questions.explanation: Cutting trees reduces the number of trees that absorb carbon dioxide, which contributes to climate change.
questions.misconception: Cutting trees has no effect on climate.

questions.stem: Explain how deforestation leads to climate change.
answer: cutting down trees reduces the number of trees that absorb carbon dioxide, so more carbon dioxide stays in the air and the earth gets hotter
fewer trees mean less carbon dioxide is absorbed and the environment gets hotter
deforestation increases carbon dioxide in the air, leading to a hotter climate
hints: Less trees mean more carbon dioxide in the air.
questions.explanation: Deforestation reduces the number of trees that absorb carbon dioxide. With fewer trees, more carbon dioxide remains in the air, which traps heat and contributes to climate change.
questions.misconception: Cutting trees has no effect on climate.

questions.stem: Which of these best explains why deforestation makes the environment hotter?
options: Fewer trees means less shade and less carbon dioxide absorption
questions.explanation: Deforestation makes the environment hotter because there are fewer trees to provide shade and absorb carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: What can happen to animals when trees are cut down?
hints: Trees are homes for many animals.
questions.explanation: When trees are cut down, animals lose their homes and habitats.

questions.stem: Which of these is an effect of deforestation?
hints: Without tree roots, soil can wash away.
Trees hold the soil in place.
questions.explanation: Deforestation can lead to soil erosion because tree roots are no longer there to hold the soil in place.

questions.stem: State one effect of deforestation.
questions.explanation: Effects of deforestation include loss of animal habitats, soil erosion, less rain and a hotter climate.

questions.stem: How does deforestation affect rainfall?
options: It can reduce rainfall because fewer trees release water vapour
It increases rainfall because trees block clouds
It has no effect on rainfall
It makes rain fall only at night
hints: Less trees mean less vapour for rain.
questions.explanation: Deforestation can reduce rainfall because fewer trees release water vapour into the air, which is needed for cloud formation and rain.
questions.misconception: Trees do not help produce rain.

questions.stem: Which of these helps reduce deforestation?
hints: Planting trees is the opposite of cutting them.
questions.explanation: Planting trees helps reduce deforestation by replacing trees that have been cut down.

questions.stem: Give one way to reduce deforestation.
questions.explanation: Ways to reduce deforestation include planting trees, avoiding unnecessary cutting, and protecting forests.

questions.stem: A community wants to reduce deforestation. Which plan is BEST?
options: Plant new trees and protect existing forests
Cut down all trees for farming
hints: Cutting and burning make it worse.
questions.explanation: The best plan is to plant new trees and protect existing forests, which helps reduce deforestation.
questions.misconception: Planting one tree will not help.

questions.stem: In groups, plant a tree seedling in your school compound or a nearby area. Describe the steps you took and explain why planting trees helps fight climate change.

criteria.description: Planted a tree seedling correctly (dug a hole, placed the seedling, covered with soil, watered)
Explained that trees absorb carbon dioxide
Explained that trees help cool the environment and produce oxygen

hints: Dig a hole, place the seedling, cover it with soil, and water it.
Trees absorb carbon dioxide and give out oxygen.
questions.explanation: This is a practical task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: Planting one tree will not help.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.1.1 Show understanding of the physical features and life processes of living things and use this understanding to classify them
indicator.objective: Classify plants based on their root system

questions.stem: Which two main root systems are used to classify plants?
hints: One has a single main root.
The other has many thin roots.
questions.explanation: Plants are classified by their root systems into tap roots and fibrous roots.
questions.misconception: All plants have the same root system.

questions.stem: What is a tap root system?
options: One main root with smaller side roots
Many thin roots of the same size
Roots that grow above the ground
Roots that only grow in water
hints: Think about a carrot or a mango seedling.
It has one thick main root.
questions.explanation: A tap root system has one main root with smaller side roots growing from it.
questions.misconception: Tap roots have many equal-sized roots.

questions.stem: Name the two main types of root systems.
hints: The other is many thin roots.
questions.explanation: The two main root systems are tap root and fibrous root.
questions.misconception: Plants only have one type of root.

questions.stem: Which of these plants has a tap root?
hints: Which one has one main root?
Grass and maize have many thin roots.
questions.explanation: A mango plant has a tap root — one main root with smaller side roots.

questions.stem: Which description best fits a tap root?
options: Many thin roots of similar size spreading out
One thick main root with smaller side roots
Roots that grow from the leaves
hints: Tap roots have one main root.
questions.explanation: A tap root is one thick main root with smaller side roots growing from it.
questions.misconception: Tap roots are many thin roots.

questions.stem: Describe a tap root system.
answer: one main root with smaller side roots
one thick main root and smaller side roots
a single main root with side roots
questions.explanation: A tap root system has one main root with smaller side roots growing from it.
questions.misconception: Tap roots are many thin roots.

questions.stem: A pupil uproots a bean plant and sees one main root with smaller roots branching from it. What type of root system is this?
questions.explanation: The bean plant has a tap root system — one main root with smaller side roots.

questions.stem: Which of these plants has a fibrous root?
hints: Which one has many thin roots?
Mango and cassava have one main root.
questions.explanation: Grass has a fibrous root system — many thin roots of similar size spreading out.

questions.stem: Which description best fits a fibrous root?
options: One thick main root with side roots
Many thin roots of similar size spreading out
Roots that do not absorb water
hints: Fibrous roots are many and thin.
They are all about the same size.
questions.explanation: A fibrous root system has many thin roots of similar size spreading out from the base of the stem.
questions.misconception: Fibrous roots are one main root.

questions.stem: Describe a fibrous root system.
answer: many thin roots of similar size spreading out
many thin roots of the same size
many fine roots spreading out from the stem
hints: They are all about the same size.
questions.explanation: A fibrous root system has many thin roots of similar size spreading out from the base of the stem.
questions.misconception: Fibrous roots are one main root.

questions.stem: A pupil uproots a maize plant and sees many thin roots of the same size. What type of root system is this?
hints: They are all the same size.
questions.explanation: The maize plant has a fibrous root system — many thin roots of similar size.

questions.stem: Which group correctly lists plants with tap roots?
hints: Which plants have one main root?
Mango, cassava and bean all have one main root.
questions.explanation: Mango, cassava and bean have tap roots.

questions.stem: Which group correctly lists plants with fibrous roots?
hints: Which plants have many thin roots?
Grass, maize and rice all have many thin roots.
questions.explanation: Grass, maize and rice have fibrous roots.

questions.stem: Classify these plants into tap roots and fibrous roots: mango, grass, cassava, maize.
answer: tap roots: mango, cassava; fibrous roots: grass, maize
mango and cassava are tap roots; grass and maize are fibrous roots
tap: mango, cassava; fibrous: grass, maize
questions.explanation: Mango and cassava have tap roots. Grass and maize have fibrous roots.
questions.misconception: All plants have the same root type.

questions.stem: A pupil classifies a plant as having a fibrous root because it has many thin roots. Which plant could it be?
hints: Which plant has many thin roots?
Rice has a fibrous root system.
questions.explanation: Rice has many thin roots of similar size, so it has a fibrous root system.

questions.stem: Why is a cassava plant classified as having a tap root?
options: It has one main root with smaller side roots
It has roots that grow above the ground
questions.explanation: Cassava is classified as having a tap root because it has one main root with smaller side roots.

questions.stem: Give one reason why a maize plant is classified as having a fibrous root.
answer: it has many thin roots of similar size
it has many thin roots spreading out
it has many fine roots of the same size
hints: Think about the number of roots.
They are all thin and similar.
questions.explanation: Maize is classified as having a fibrous root because it has many thin roots of similar size spreading out from the base of the stem.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'A plant with a tap root must be bigger than a plant with a fibrous root.' Is the pupil correct?
options: Yes, tap root plants are always bigger
No, root type does not determine plant size
Yes, fibrous root plants are always smaller
No, only the roots are different
hints: Can a small plant have a tap root?
Root type and plant size are not the same.
questions.explanation: No, root type does not determine plant size. Small plants can have tap roots, and large plants can have fibrous roots.
questions.misconception: Tap roots are always bigger than the whole plant.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares tap roots and fibrous roots?
options: Tap roots have one main root; fibrous roots have many thin roots of similar size
Tap roots have many thin roots; fibrous roots have one main root
hints: One has a single main root.
The other has many equal-sized roots.
questions.explanation: Tap roots have one main root with smaller side roots, while fibrous roots have many thin roots of similar size.
questions.misconception: Tap roots and fibrous roots are the same.

questions.stem: Explain one difference between a tap root and a fibrous root.
answer: a tap root has one main root with side roots, while a fibrous root has many thin roots of similar size
tap root: one main root; fibrous root: many thin roots of the same size
tap roots have one main root, fibrous roots have many equal-sized roots
hints: Think about the number of main roots.
One has one main root; the other has many.
questions.explanation: A tap root has one main root with smaller side roots, while a fibrous root has many thin roots of similar size.
questions.misconception: Tap roots and fibrous roots are the same.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.2.1 Recognise materials as important resources for providing human needs
indicator.objective: Know the general properties of metals such as lustre, malleability, conductivity and ductility

questions.stem: What is lustre?
hints: Think about how shiny a new coin looks.
questions.explanation: Lustre is the shiny appearance of metals.
questions.misconception: Lustre means a material is heavy.

questions.stem: Which of these best describes lustre?
options: The ability of a metal to be drawn into wires
The shiny appearance of a metal
The ability of a metal to conduct electricity
The ability of a metal to be hammered into sheets
hints: It is about how shiny the metal looks.
questions.explanation: Lustre is the shiny appearance of a metal.

questions.stem: What does lustre mean when describing a metal?
questions.explanation: Lustre means the shiny appearance of a metal.

questions.stem: What is malleability?
options: The ability of a metal to be hammered into thin sheets
The ability of a metal to be drawn into wires
The shiny appearance of a metal
The ability of a metal to conduct heat
questions.explanation: Malleability is the ability of a metal to be hammered or pressed into thin sheets without breaking.

questions.stem: Which property allows a metal to be hammered into a flat sheet?
questions.explanation: Malleability is the property that allows a metal to be hammered or pressed into thin sheets.
questions.misconception: Ductility allows metals to be hammered into sheets.

questions.stem: What is malleability?
answer: the ability of a metal to be hammered or pressed into thin sheets
the ability of a metal to be shaped into thin sheets
metals can be hammered into flat sheets
hints: It can be made into sheets.
questions.explanation: Malleability is the ability of a metal to be hammered or pressed into thin sheets without breaking.
questions.misconception: Malleability and ductility are the same.

questions.stem: A metalsmith hammers a piece of gold into a very thin sheet. Which property of metals does this show?
hints: The metal is being made into a sheet.
It is not being drawn into a wire.
questions.explanation: Hammering gold into a thin sheet shows malleability.

questions.stem: What is conductivity in metals?
options: The ability to carry heat or electricity
The ability to be hammered into sheets
The ability to be drawn into wires
hints: Think about how wires carry electricity.
Metals can pass heat and electricity.
questions.explanation: Conductivity is the ability of metals to carry heat or electricity.

questions.stem: Which property allows copper to be used for electrical wires?
questions.explanation: Copper is used for electrical wires because of its conductivity — it can carry electricity.
questions.misconception: Copper is used for wires because it is shiny.

questions.stem: What is conductivity?
answer: the ability of a metal to carry heat or electricity
the ability to conduct electricity or heat
hints: Think about metal pots on fire.
questions.explanation: Conductivity is the ability of metals to carry heat or electricity.

questions.stem: Why are cooking pots made of metals?
hints: Pots need to get hot on the fire.
questions.explanation: Cooking pots are made of metals because metals conduct heat, allowing food to cook evenly.
questions.misconception: Pots are made of metals because they are shiny.

questions.stem: What is ductility?
options: The ability of a metal to be drawn into thin wires
The ability of a metal to be hammered into sheets
The shiny appearance of a metal
The ability of a metal to carry heat
questions.explanation: Ductility is the ability of a metal to be drawn into thin wires.
questions.misconception: Ductility means being hammered into sheets.

questions.stem: Which property allows copper to be drawn into thin wires?
questions.explanation: Ductility is the property that allows copper to be drawn into thin wires.
questions.misconception: Malleability allows metals to be drawn into wires.

questions.stem: What is ductility?
answer: the ability of a metal to be drawn into thin wires
metals can be drawn into wires
the ability to be made into wires
questions.explanation: Ductility is the ability of a metal to be drawn into thin wires.
questions.misconception: Ductility and malleability are the same.

questions.stem: A copper wire is used in a circuit. Which property of copper is being used?
hints: Which property allows electricity to flow?
questions.explanation: The copper wire carries electricity, showing the conductivity of copper.
questions.misconception: Copper wire works because of lustre.

questions.stem: Aluminium foil is used to wrap food. It can be pressed into a thin sheet. Which property does aluminium show?
hints: The metal is pressed into a sheet.
questions.explanation: Aluminium foil shows malleability because it is pressed into a thin sheet.

questions.stem: A pupil observes that a metal spoon shines in the light. Which property of metals is this?
questions.explanation: The shiny appearance of the metal spoon is lustre.

questions.stem: A pupil stretches a piece of copper into a thin wire and hammers another piece into a flat sheet. Which two properties are shown?
questions.explanation: Drawing copper into a wire shows ductility. Hammering copper into a sheet shows malleability.
questions.misconception: Ductility and malleability are the same.

questions.stem: A pupil tests four materials by trying to hammer them into sheets. Which material is a metal?
hints: Which material can be shaped by hammering?
questions.explanation: A copper coin is a metal and is malleable. Plastic, chalk and rubber are not metals.

questions.stem: A pupil has a metal nail and a plastic spoon. Which one conducts electricity? Explain your answer.
answer: the metal nail conducts electricity because it is a metal
the nail conducts electricity; plastic does not
the metal nail, because metals are conductors
questions.explanation: The metal nail conducts electricity because metals have conductivity. The plastic spoon is an insulator and does not conduct.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.2.1 Recognise materials as important resources for providing human needs
indicator.objective: Investigate the uses of metals in everyday life and link the uses to their properties

questions.stem: Which of these objects is made from metal?
hints: Which one is shiny and hard?
questions.explanation: A metal nail is made from metal. It is shiny, hard and strong.
questions.misconception: Metals are only used for jewellery.

questions.stem: Which of these farm tools is made from metal?
hints: Which part is hard and shiny?
questions.explanation: A cutlass blade is made from metal. It needs to be strong and sharp for cutting.
questions.misconception: Farm tools are only made of wood.

questions.stem: Name two objects in your home that are made from metal.
questions.explanation: Common metal objects at home include spoons, cooking pots, knives, door handles and nails.
questions.misconception: Metals are only used for jewellery.

questions.stem: Why is copper used to make electrical wires?
questions.explanation: Copper is used for electrical wires because it conducts electricity.
questions.misconception: Copper is used for wires because it is shiny.

questions.stem: Why is aluminium used to make roofing sheets?
options: Because it is malleable and can be pressed into thin sheets
Because it is ductile and can be drawn into wires
hints: Roofing sheets are thin and flat.
Aluminium can be pressed into sheets.
questions.explanation: Aluminium is malleable, so it can be pressed into thin sheets for roofing.
questions.misconception: Aluminium is used for roofing because it is heavy.

questions.stem: Why is copper used for electrical wires?
answer: it is a good conductor of electricity
questions.explanation: Copper is used for electrical wires because it conducts electricity.
questions.misconception: Copper is used for wires because it is shiny.

questions.stem: Why are cooking pots made from metals like aluminium?
hints: Pots need to get hot on the fire.
questions.explanation: Cooking pots are made from metals because metals conduct heat well, allowing food to cook evenly.
questions.misconception: Pots are made of metal because they are shiny.

questions.stem: Why is aluminium used for making cooking pots?
answer: aluminium is a good conductor of heat
it allows heat to pass through for cooking
questions.explanation: Aluminium is used for cooking pots because it is a good conductor of heat, allowing food to cook evenly.
questions.misconception: Pots are made of aluminium because it is shiny.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches a metal property to its use?
hints: Wires are made by drawing metal.
questions.explanation: Ductility allows metals to be drawn into wires, so it is linked to electrical wires.
questions.misconception: Lustre is used for cooking pots.

questions.stem: Which property of metals makes them suitable for making jewellery?
questions.explanation: Lustre (shininess) makes metals suitable for jewellery.
questions.misconception: Jewellery is made of metals because they are ductile.

questions.stem: Match the property to its use: ductility, malleability, conductivity.
answer: ductility - wires; malleability - sheets; conductivity - electrical wires or cooking pots
ductility: wires, malleability: sheets, conductivity: electrical wires
ductility for wires, malleability for sheets, conductivity for electrical wires and pots
questions.explanation: Ductility is used for wires, malleability for sheets, and conductivity for electrical wires and cooking pots.
questions.misconception: All metal properties have the same use.

questions.stem: Which of these correctly links a metal property to an everyday object?
questions.explanation: Lustre (shininess) is linked to jewellery. Ductility is for wires, malleability is for sheets, and conductivity is for wires and pots.

questions.stem: Why is copper used for electrical wires while aluminium is used for roofing sheets?
options: Copper conducts electricity; aluminium is malleable for sheets
Copper is malleable; aluminium conducts electricity
Both are used for the same reason
Copper is shiny; aluminium is heavy
hints: Each metal is used for a different property.
Copper conducts electricity; aluminium can be pressed into sheets.
questions.explanation: Copper is used for wires because it conducts electricity. Aluminium is used for roofing sheets because it is malleable and can be pressed into thin sheets.
questions.misconception: All metals are used for the same reason.

questions.stem: Compare why copper is used for wires and aluminium is used for cooking pots.
answer: copper conducts electricity for wires, while aluminium conducts heat for cooking pots
copper is used for wires because it conducts electricity; aluminium is used for pots because it conducts heat
copper: electrical conductivity; aluminium: heat conductivity
hints: Think about what wires and pots need to do.
Both need conductivity, but of different types.
questions.explanation: Copper is used for wires because it conducts electricity. Aluminium is used for cooking pots because it conducts heat well.
questions.misconception: All metals are used for the same purpose.

questions.stem: Two metals are available for making a cooking pot and an electrical wire. Metal A conducts heat well and is malleable. Metal B conducts electricity well and is ductile. Which metal is better for each use?
options: Metal A for pots, Metal B for wires
Metal A for wires, Metal B for pots
hints: Wires need electrical conduction and ductility.
questions.explanation: Metal A is better for cooking pots because it conducts heat and is malleable. Metal B is better for wires because it conducts electricity and is ductile.
questions.misconception: Any metal is suitable for any purpose.

questions.stem: Which metal object is used at school?
hints: Which one is made of metal?
questions.explanation: A metal scissors is used at school for cutting paper.
questions.misconception: Metals are not used at school.

questions.stem: Give two examples of metals used in the community and state their uses.
answer: metal roofs for buildings, metal tools for farming
aluminium for roofing, iron for tools
copper for wires, iron for bridges
questions.explanation: Metals are used in the community for roofs (aluminium), tools (iron), bridges (steel), and electrical wires (copper).

questions.stem: A bridge is built using steel. Which property makes steel suitable for this use?
questions.explanation: Steel is used for bridges because it is strong and hard, allowing it to support heavy loads.
questions.misconception: Bridges are built with soft metals.

questions.stem: Why are metals important in everyday life?
options: They are used to make tools, utensils and buildings
They are only used for decoration
They are only found in labs
hints: Think about cooking utensils and tools.
questions.explanation: Metals are important because they are used to make tools, utensils, buildings, wires and many other things we use daily.

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (3–4 sentences) explaining why metals are important in everyday life. Include at least two examples and one property linked to a use.

criteria.description: Stated that metals are important for making tools/utensils/buildings
Gave at least two correct examples of metal uses
Linked one metal property to a specific use

hints: Think about cooking pots, wires, or tools.
Link a property like conductivity to wires.
questions.explanation: This is a written task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.2.2 Understand mixtures, the types of formation, uses and ways of separating them into their components
indicator.objective: Examine some uses of mixtures in everyday life

questions.stem: Which of these is an everyday example of a mixture?
hints: A mixture has two or more substances combined.
questions.explanation: Salt solution is a mixture of salt and water.
questions.misconception: Salt solution is not a mixture.

questions.stem: Which of these is a mixture used for building?
hints: It is used to build houses.
It is made from cement, sand and water.
questions.explanation: Concrete is a mixture used for building.

questions.stem: Name two everyday examples of mixtures.
answer: sugar solution and sand and water
hints: One is food, one is for building.
questions.explanation: Everyday mixtures include salt solution, sugar solution, concrete, sand and water, and gari and beans.

questions.stem: A pupil mixes gari and beans in a bowl. What type of mixture is this?
hints: Both gari and beans are solids.
questions.explanation: Gari and beans form a solid-solid mixture because both are solids.
questions.misconception: Gari and beans is not a mixture.

questions.stem: What are the components of a salt solution?
hints: What two things are mixed together?
questions.explanation: A salt solution is made of salt and water.

questions.stem: Name the components of concrete.
hints: It is made from cement and other materials.
questions.explanation: Concrete is made from cement, sand, gravel and water.

questions.stem: What are the components of gari and beans?
hints: The mixture is named after its components.
questions.explanation: Gari and beans is a mixture of gari and beans.
questions.misconception: Gari and beans is a single substance.

questions.stem: What is salt solution used for?
hints: Salt solution is used in food.
It is used to add flavour.
questions.explanation: Salt solution is used for cooking and flavouring food.
questions.misconception: Salt solution is not used for anything.

questions.stem: What is concrete used for?
questions.explanation: Concrete is used for building houses, bridges, and other structures.
questions.misconception: Concrete is only used in labs.

questions.stem: State one use of a mixture in everyday life.
hints: Mixtures are used in food and construction.
questions.explanation: Mixtures are used for cooking (salt solution), building (concrete), and food (gari and beans).

questions.stem: Why is concrete useful in building?
options: It is strong and hard when it dries
questions.explanation: Concrete is useful in building because it is strong and hard when it dries.

questions.stem: Why are mixtures useful in everyday life?
options: They combine useful properties of different substances
They are only used in labs
questions.explanation: Mixtures are useful because they combine the properties of different substances to serve a purpose.

questions.stem: Explain why mixtures are useful in everyday life.
answer: they combine different substances to make something useful, like concrete for building
mixtures combine useful properties of substances
they are used in cooking, building and food
hints: Think about salt solution for cooking.
questions.explanation: Mixtures are useful because they combine different substances to make useful products like concrete for building and salt solution for cooking.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Mixtures are only made in science laboratories.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, mixtures are only made in labs
No, mixtures are common in everyday life, such as salt solution and concrete
No, mixtures are only made in factories
hints: Think about salt solution at home.
questions.explanation: Mixtures are common in everyday life, such as salt solution in cooking and concrete in building.

questions.stem: How do you prepare a salt solution?
options: Add salt to water and stir
Add sand to water and stir
Add salt to oil and stir
Add salt to cement and stir
hints: Salt solution is salt and water.
questions.explanation: To prepare a salt solution, add salt to water and stir until it dissolves.
questions.misconception: Salt solution is made with sand.

questions.stem: Describe how to prepare a sugar solution.
answer: add sugar to water and stir until it dissolves
mix sugar with water and stir
put sugar in water and stir
hints: Sugar is a solid, water is a liquid.
questions.explanation: To prepare a sugar solution, add sugar to water and stir until it dissolves.
questions.misconception: Sugar solution is made without water.

questions.stem: In groups, prepare a simple mixture (salt solution or sand and water). Describe the steps you took and state what type of mixture you made.

criteria.description: Stated the type of mixture (solid-liquid or solid-solid)
Named the components of the mixture

hints: Add a solid to a liquid.
questions.explanation: This is a practical task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.

questions.stem: Which mixture is used for food?
hints: Which mixture is used in cooking?
questions.explanation: Salt solution is used in food for cooking and flavouring.
questions.misconception: Salt solution is not for food.

questions.stem: Classify concrete according to its use.
hints: Concrete is used to build houses.
questions.explanation: Concrete is a building material used for construction.

questions.stem: Classify salt solution, concrete, and gari and beans according to their uses.
answer: salt solution - food; concrete - building; gari and beans - food
salt solution for food, concrete for building, gari and beans for food
salt solution: food; concrete: building; gari and beans: food
questions.explanation: Salt solution and gari and beans are used for food, while concrete is used for building.
questions.misconception: All mixtures have the same use.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.1.1 Recognise the relationship between the earth and the sun
indicator.objective: Describe the relative sizes of the earth and sun and their importance

questions.stem: Which is bigger: the sun or the earth?
questions.explanation: The sun is much larger than the earth.
questions.misconception: The earth is bigger than the sun.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the sizes of the earth and the sun?
options: The sun is much larger than the earth
The earth is much larger than the sun
They are about the same size
The earth is larger than the moon but smaller than the sun
hints: Stars are usually larger than planets.
questions.explanation: The sun is much larger than the earth.
questions.misconception: The sun and earth are the same size.

questions.stem: Which is larger, the earth or the sun?
hints: It is at the centre of the solar system.
questions.explanation: The sun is larger than the earth.

questions.stem: A learner says, 'The earth and the sun are the same size because they both look round.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, they are the same size
No, the sun is much larger than the earth
No, the earth is much larger than the sun
No, the moon is the largest
hints: Looking round does not mean same size.
The sun is a star, much bigger than a planet.
questions.explanation: The sun is much larger than the earth, even though both look round.
questions.misconception: The sun and earth are the same size.

questions.stem: Which body is the larger one in the earth-sun pair?
questions.explanation: The sun is the larger body; the earth is smaller.
questions.misconception: The earth is the larger body.

questions.stem: Describe the relative sizes of the earth and the sun.
answer: the sun is much larger than the earth
the sun is larger and the earth is smaller
the earth is smaller than the sun
hints: The sun is the larger body.
questions.explanation: The sun is much larger than the earth.
questions.misconception: The earth is larger than the sun.

questions.stem: If you were to compare the earth to the sun, which statement is correct?
options: The earth is much smaller than the sun
The earth is much larger than the sun
The earth is the largest body in the solar system
hints: The sun is the largest body in the solar system.
questions.explanation: The earth is much smaller than the sun.
questions.misconception: The earth is the largest body.

questions.stem: What does the sun give to the earth?
hints: The sun makes you feel warm.
questions.explanation: The sun gives light and heat to the earth.

questions.stem: Why is the sun important to life on earth?
options: It provides light and heat energy
questions.explanation: The sun is important because it provides light and heat energy needed for life on earth.
questions.misconception: The sun is not important because it is far away.

questions.stem: Give one reason why the sun is important to the earth.
questions.explanation: The sun is important because it provides light, heat and energy for life on earth.

questions.stem: How does the sun help plants?
options: It provides light for plants to make food
questions.explanation: The sun provides light, which plants use to make food.
questions.misconception: The sun is not important for plants.

questions.stem: Why is the earth important?
options: It is our home and supports life
questions.explanation: The earth is important because it is our home and supports life.

questions.stem: Why is the earth important to us?
answer: it is our home and supports life
it has water and air for life
hints: What does the earth have that supports life?
questions.explanation: The earth is important because it is our home and has water and air that support life.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the earth is important in the earth-sun relationship?
options: The earth is the planet where life exists
The earth is the largest body
The earth produces its own light
The earth is the centre of the solar system
questions.explanation: The earth is important because it is the planet where life exists.
questions.misconception: The earth is the centre of the solar system.

questions.stem: What does the earth do around the sun?
hints: The sun is at the centre.
questions.explanation: The earth moves around the sun.
questions.misconception: The sun moves around the earth.

questions.stem: Which body moves around the other: the earth or the sun?
answer: the earth moves around the sun
hints: The sun is at the centre.
questions.explanation: The earth moves around the sun.
questions.misconception: The sun moves around the earth.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'The sun moves around the earth.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, the sun moves around the earth
No, the earth moves around the sun
No, the moon moves around the sun
hints: The sun is at the centre.
questions.explanation: The earth moves around the sun, not the other way round.
questions.misconception: The sun moves around the earth.

questions.stem: What would happen if the earth were bigger than the sun?
options: The earth would not be able to move around the sun in the same way
The moon would become a planet
hints: The sun is at the centre because it is larger.
questions.explanation: If the earth were bigger than the sun, the relationship between them would be different, and the earth would not move around the sun in the same way.

questions.stem: Predict what would happen if the sun were much smaller than it is now.
answer: it would not be able to provide enough light and heat to the earth
the earth would receive less light and heat
it would not support life as it does now
hints: The sun provides light and heat.
A smaller sun would give less.
questions.explanation: If the sun were much smaller, it would not provide enough light and heat to support life on earth as it does now.
questions.misconception: Size does not matter for the sun's importance.

questions.stem: A learner says, 'The size of the sun does not matter because it is far away.' Is this correct?
options: No, the sun's large size is what allows it to provide enough light and heat to the earth
hints: The sun provides light and heat.
Its large size helps it produce and give out energy.
questions.explanation: The sun's large size is important because it allows it to provide enough light and heat to the earth.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.1.2 Show understanding of the roles of condensation, evaporation, transpiration and precipitation in the hydrological (water) cycle
indicator.objective: Explain how rain falls from clouds

questions.stem: What is evaporation?
options: Water changing from liquid to vapour
Water changing from vapour to liquid
questions.explanation: Evaporation is the change of water from liquid to vapour.
questions.misconception: Evaporation is the same as condensation.

questions.stem: What is condensation?
options: Water vapour changing into liquid droplets
hints: Think about droplets on a cold glass.
questions.explanation: Condensation is the change of water vapour into liquid droplets when it cools.
questions.misconception: Condensation is the same as evaporation.

questions.stem: What is precipitation?
answer: water falling from clouds as rain, snow, or hail
questions.explanation: Precipitation is water falling from clouds as rain, snow, or hail.

questions.stem: How are clouds formed?
options: Water vapour cools and condenses around dust particles
Rain falls upwards to form clouds
Wind blows clouds from the ground
questions.explanation: Clouds are formed when water vapour rises, cools and condenses around tiny dust particles in the air.
questions.misconception: Clouds are made by the sun directly.

questions.stem: What happens to water vapour when it rises and cools?
options: It condenses into tiny water droplets
questions.explanation: When water vapour rises and cools, it condenses into tiny water droplets that form clouds.
questions.misconception: Water vapour disappears in the sky.

questions.stem: Explain how clouds are formed.
answer: water vapour rises, cools and condenses around dust particles
water vapour cools and condenses into droplets
vapour rises and condenses to form clouds
questions.explanation: Clouds form when water vapour rises, cools and condenses around tiny dust particles in the air.
questions.misconception: Clouds are made by the sun.

questions.stem: Why do clouds form high in the sky?
options: Because water vapour rises and cools at higher altitudes
Because the sun pushes clouds up
Because clouds are lighter than air
hints: It cools as it goes higher.
questions.explanation: Clouds form high in the sky because water vapour rises with warm air and cools at higher altitudes, where it condenses into droplets.
questions.misconception: Clouds form because they are light.

questions.stem: How do raindrops form in clouds?
options: Tiny water droplets join together around dust particles and grow bigger
Wind blows raindrops from the ground
questions.explanation: Raindrops form when tiny water droplets in clouds join together around dust particles and grow bigger and heavier.

questions.stem: What happens to water droplets in a cloud when they become too heavy?
questions.explanation: When water droplets in a cloud become too heavy, they fall as rain.

questions.stem: Explain how raindrops form and grow in clouds.
answer: tiny water droplets join together around dust particles and grow bigger until they are heavy enough to fall
water droplets combine and grow around dust particles
droplets join and grow until they fall as rain
questions.explanation: Tiny water droplets in clouds join together around dust particles. As they combine, they grow bigger and heavier until they fall as rain.

questions.stem: Why do raindrops need tiny dust or smoke particles to form?
options: Water vapour condenses more easily around these particles
Dust particles are made of water
Dust particles push the rain down
hints: Vapour needs a surface to condense on.
questions.explanation: Water vapour condenses more easily around tiny dust or smoke particles, which act as surfaces for droplets to form on.
questions.misconception: Dust particles are made of water.

questions.stem: What causes raindrops to fall from clouds?
hints: Things fall down due to this force.
It pulls objects towards the earth.
questions.explanation: Gravity causes raindrops to fall from clouds to the ground.

questions.stem: What force causes rain to fall from clouds?
hints: It is the same force that makes objects fall.
questions.explanation: Gravity is the force that causes rain to fall from clouds.

questions.stem: A learner says, 'Rain falls because clouds push the water down.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, clouds push the water down
No, gravity pulls the raindrops down
No, the sun pushes the rain down
No, wind pushes the rain down
questions.explanation: Rain falls because gravity pulls the raindrops down, not because clouds push them.

questions.stem: Do all clouds produce rain?
options: No, not all clouds produce rain
hints: Some clouds are thin and wispy.
Not every cloud has enough water to rain.
questions.explanation: Not all clouds produce rain. Some clouds do not contain enough water droplets to fall as rain.

questions.stem: Why do some clouds not produce rain?
answer: they do not contain enough water droplets to fall as rain
the droplets are too small or light
they do not have enough water
hints: Clouds need enough water to rain.
questions.explanation: Some clouds do not produce rain because they do not contain enough water droplets to become heavy enough to fall.

questions.stem: Which of these best explains why some clouds do not produce rain?
options: They do not contain enough water droplets to fall
They are too high in the sky
hints: If droplets are few, no rain falls.
questions.explanation: Some clouds do not produce rain because they do not contain enough water droplets to fall as rain.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes part of the water cycle?
questions.explanation: The water cycle includes evaporation, then condensation, then precipitation (rain).
questions.misconception: The water cycle has a different order.

questions.stem: Explain how evaporation and condensation lead to rain in the water cycle.
answer: water evaporates, rises, cools and condenses into clouds, then falls as rain
evaporation puts vapour in the air, condensation forms clouds, and rain falls from clouds
water vapour rises, condenses into clouds, and then falls as rain
questions.explanation: Water evaporates into the air, rises, cools and condenses into clouds. The water droplets in clouds fall as rain.
questions.misconception: Rain falls directly from the sun.

questions.stem: Design a simple diagram showing how rain falls from clouds. Label the sun, evaporation, condensation (cloud formation), precipitation (rain), and gravity. Use arrows to show the direction of movement.

criteria.description: Showed the sun and evaporation from a water source
Showed water vapour rising and condensing into a cloud
Showed rain falling from the cloud
Labeled gravity as the force pulling the rain down
Used arrows to show direction of movement

hints: Start with the sun heating water.
Show vapour rising and forming a cloud.
questions.explanation: This is a drawing task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: Rain falls directly from the sun.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.1.3 Demonstrate understanding of how carbon and nitrogen are cycled in nature
indicator.objective: Know the functions of carbon within the environment

questions.stem: Which of these materials contains carbon?
hints: Pencils are made of graphite and clay.
Graphite is a form of carbon.
questions.explanation: A pencil contains carbon in the form of graphite. Graphite is a form of carbon used for writing.
questions.misconception: Carbon is only found in pencils.

questions.stem: Which of these is a source of carbon in the environment?
hints: Charcoal is made from burnt wood.
questions.explanation: Charcoal contains carbon. It is made from wood that has been burned without much air.

questions.stem: Name one material in the environment that contains carbon.
hints: Think about what you write with.
Think about what you burn for fuel.
questions.explanation: Materials that contain carbon include pencils (graphite), charcoal, wood, coal and food.
questions.misconception: Carbon is only found in pencils.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Carbon is only found in pencils.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, carbon is only in pencils
No, carbon is also found in charcoal, food and carbon dioxide
No, carbon is only found in water
No, carbon is only found in stones
questions.explanation: Carbon is found in pencils, but also in charcoal, food, carbon dioxide and many other materials.
questions.misconception: Carbon is only found in pencils.

questions.stem: What is the role of carbon in a pencil?
options: It makes the pencil smell good
hints: The dark part of the pencil is graphite.
questions.explanation: Carbon in the form of graphite helps the pencil write by leaving marks on paper.
questions.misconception: Carbon in pencils is for colour.

questions.stem: What is the role of carbon in charcoal?
options: It helps charcoal burn as fuel
questions.explanation: Carbon in charcoal helps it burn and produce heat for cooking and other uses.
questions.misconception: Charcoal does not use carbon for burning.

questions.stem: State one role of carbon in charcoal.
answer: it makes charcoal a good fuel
it provides heat when charcoal burns
questions.explanation: Carbon in charcoal helps it burn and produce heat.
questions.misconception: Carbon in charcoal is not useful.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Carbon in charcoal is only for colour.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, carbon is only for colour
No, carbon in charcoal is mainly for burning and producing heat
No, carbon in charcoal is for writing
No, carbon in charcoal is for drinking
questions.explanation: Carbon in charcoal is mainly for burning and producing heat, not just for colour.
questions.misconception: Carbon in charcoal is only for colour.

questions.stem: Which gas contains carbon and is used by plants to make food?
hints: Plants take in this gas from the air.
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is a gas that contains carbon. Plants use it to make food.
questions.misconception: Carbon dioxide is not related to carbon.

questions.stem: What do plants use carbon dioxide for?
hints: Plants need it to make food.
They take it from the air.
questions.explanation: Plants use carbon dioxide to make food.
questions.misconception: Plants do not use carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: How is carbon dioxide related to carbon?
options: Carbon dioxide does not contain carbon
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide contains carbon. It is a gas made of carbon and oxygen.
questions.misconception: Carbon dioxide is not related to carbon.

questions.stem: Why is carbon important in the environment?
options: It is part of all living things and helps plants make food
questions.explanation: Carbon is important because it is part of all living things and helps plants make food through carbon dioxide.
questions.misconception: Carbon has no function in the environment.

questions.stem: Give one reason why carbon is important in the environment.
answer: it is part of living things
plants use carbon dioxide to make food
questions.explanation: Carbon is important because it is part of all living things and helps plants make food through carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Carbon is only a pollutant.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, carbon is only a pollutant
No, carbon is also an essential part of living things and helps plants make food
No, carbon is only found in water
hints: Carbon is in all living things.
questions.explanation: Carbon is not only a pollutant; it is an essential part of living things and helps plants make food.

questions.stem: In a role-play about carbon, what would a learner acting as carbon in a pencil say?
questions.explanation: A learner acting as carbon in a pencil would say 'I help you write' because carbon in graphite helps pencils write.
questions.misconception: Carbon in pencils is for breathing.

questions.stem: In a role-play, how would you describe the function of carbon in charcoal?
answer: I help charcoal burn and give heat
I make charcoal a good fuel
I help produce heat when charcoal burns
questions.explanation: Carbon in charcoal helps it burn and produce heat, so a learner could say 'I help charcoal burn and give heat.'
questions.misconception: Carbon in charcoal is not useful.

questions.stem: In groups, role-play the functions of carbon in the environment. One learner acts as carbon in a pencil, another as carbon in charcoal, another as carbon dioxide used by plants. Each learner should say one sentence explaining their role. Present to the class.

criteria.description: Acted as carbon in a pencil and explained its role (writing)
Acted as carbon in charcoal and explained its role (burning/fuel)
Acted as carbon dioxide and explained its role (used by plants to make food)
Spoke clearly and participated in the role-play

hints: Think about the role of carbon in each material.
Say one sentence about what carbon does.
questions.explanation: This is a practical/role-play task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.

questions.stem: Is carbon part of the food we eat?
options: Yes, carbon is part of food
No, food does not contain carbon
questions.explanation: Yes, carbon is part of food because food comes from living things, and all living things contain carbon.

questions.stem: Why is carbon found in food?
answer: because food comes from living things and living things contain carbon
food is made from living things which contain carbon
all living things contain carbon, so food does too
hints: Food comes from plants and animals.
questions.explanation: Carbon is found in food because food comes from living things, and all living things contain carbon.

questions.stem: A learner says, 'Carbon is only found in non-living things like pencils and charcoal.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, carbon is only in non-living things
No, carbon is also found in living things and food
No, carbon is only found in water
No, carbon is only found in air
questions.explanation: Carbon is found in non-living things like pencils and charcoal, but it is also found in living things and food.
questions.misconception: Carbon is not part of living things.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.1.4 Recognise water and air as important natural resources
indicator.objective: Investigate ways of conserving water in the home, school and community

questions.stem: What does conserving water mean?
options: Using water wisely and avoiding waste
Using as much water as you want
hints: You still use water, but you do not waste it.
questions.explanation: Conserving water means using it wisely and avoiding waste.
questions.misconception: Conserving water means not using it at all.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes water conservation?
options: Using water carefully so it is not wasted
Using water only once a week
Using all the water in the house
questions.explanation: Water conservation means using water carefully and not wasting it.
questions.misconception: Water conservation means not using water.

questions.stem: What is water conservation?
answer: using water wisely and avoiding waste
using water carefully without wasting it
hints: It is about not wasting water.
questions.explanation: Water conservation is the wise use of water to avoid waste.
questions.misconception: Water conservation means not using water.

questions.stem: Which of these activities at home requires water?
hints: You need water to boil rice.
questions.explanation: Cooking requires water. Other activities like sleeping, reading and watching TV do not require water.
questions.misconception: Water is only used for drinking.

questions.stem: Which set lists activities at home that use water?
options: Watching TV, playing football, listening to radio
hints: Bathing and cooking both need water.
questions.explanation: Bathing, cooking and washing clothes are activities at home that require water.

questions.stem: Name two activities at home that require water.
hints: Think about what you do in the bathroom.
Think about what you do in the kitchen.
questions.explanation: Activities at home that require water include bathing, cooking, washing clothes and drinking.

questions.stem: Which of these actions wastes water?
options: Turning off the tap after use
hints: Which action lets water flow for no reason?
questions.explanation: Leaving a tap running wastes water. Turning off taps, using buckets and fixing leaks save water.
questions.misconception: Leaving a tap running does not waste water.

questions.stem: Which of these is a water-wasting action?
options: Turning off the tap while brushing
hints: A leak lets water drip away.
questions.explanation: Leaving a leaking pipe unfixed wastes water. The other actions help conserve water.
questions.misconception: Leaking pipes do not waste water.

questions.stem: Give one example of an action that wastes water.
answer: using a hose to wash a car
hints: Think about a tap left open.
questions.explanation: Actions that waste water include leaving taps running, ignoring leaks and using excessive water.

questions.stem: Ama leaves the tap running while she brushes her teeth. What is the best advice?
options: Turn off the tap while brushing
hints: Turning off the tap saves water.
You only need water to rinse.
questions.explanation: Ama should turn off the tap while brushing her teeth to conserve water.
questions.misconception: Leaving the tap running is fine.

questions.stem: Which of these is a way to conserve water at home?
options: Using a bucket instead of a hose to wash a car
hints: A bucket uses less water than a hose.
It is a way to save water.
questions.explanation: Using a bucket instead of a hose to wash a car conserves water.

questions.stem: Which method conserves water at school?
hints: Turn off taps when not in use.
questions.explanation: Turning off taps after use conserves water at school.

questions.stem: Give one way to conserve water at home.
answer: use a bucket instead of a hose
questions.explanation: Ways to conserve water at home include turning off taps, fixing leaks, using buckets and collecting rainwater.

questions.stem: A community wants to conserve water. Which plan is BEST?
options: Fix leaking pipes and educate people to turn off taps
questions.explanation: The best plan is to fix leaking pipes and educate people to turn off taps. This saves water in the community.

questions.stem: Why is conserving water important?
options: To ensure there is enough water for everyone
questions.explanation: Conserving water is important to ensure there is enough clean water for everyone now and in the future.

questions.stem: Why should we conserve water?
answer: to ensure there is enough water for everyone
water is limited and we need it for many things
questions.explanation: We should conserve water because it is limited and needed for drinking, cooking, washing and farming.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Water is everywhere, so we don't need to conserve it.' What is the best correction?
options: No, clean water is limited and we must use it wisely
No, water is only in rivers
hints: Clean water is not always available.
questions.explanation: Clean water is limited, so we must conserve it to ensure there is enough for everyone.

questions.stem: Design a simple flyer or poster encouraging people to conserve water. Include at least two water-saving actions and a short message.

criteria.description: Included at least two correct water-saving actions
Flyer is neat and easy to understand

hints: Think about turning off taps and fixing leaks.
questions.explanation: This is a drawing task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.

questions.stem: Write a short message for a poster encouraging water conservation.
answer: turn off the tap, save water
questions.explanation: A short message like 'Save water, save life' encourages people to conserve water.

questions.stem: List three rules you would put on a water-conservation poster for your school.

criteria.description: Listed three clear and correct rules for saving water

hints: Think about taps, leaks and using buckets.
questions.explanation: This is a written task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.1.4 Recognise water and air as important natural resources (indicator code printed as B6.2.1.5.2)
indicator.objective: Demonstrate that air supports burning

questions.stem: What is air made of?
options: A mixture of gases including oxygen
questions.explanation: Air is a mixture of gases, including oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Which gas in the air is needed for burning?
hints: It is the gas we breathe in to live.
questions.explanation: Oxygen is the gas in the air that is needed for burning.

questions.stem: Which gas in the air supports burning?
hints: It is also needed for breathing.
It makes up part of the air.
questions.explanation: Oxygen in the air supports burning.

questions.stem: Why does a fire need air?
options: Because air contains oxygen which supports burning
questions.explanation: A fire needs air because air contains oxygen, which supports burning.
questions.misconception: Air is not needed for burning.

questions.stem: What happens to a fire when it is deprived of air?
hints: Without air, the fire cannot continue.
questions.explanation: A fire goes out when deprived of air because it needs oxygen to keep burning.

questions.stem: Explain why air is necessary for burning.
answer: air contains oxygen which is needed for burning
oxygen in the air supports burning
fire needs oxygen from the air to burn
hints: What gas in air supports burning?
questions.explanation: Air is necessary for burning because it contains oxygen, which is needed for a fire to burn.
questions.misconception: Air is not needed for burning.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'A fire will burn forever if it has fuel.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, fuel is all a fire needs
No, a fire also needs oxygen from the air to keep burning
No, a fire needs water to keep burning
No, a fire needs sand to keep burning
hints: Without oxygen, the fire goes out.
questions.explanation: A fire needs both fuel and oxygen. Without oxygen from the air, the fire will go out.
questions.misconception: Fuel alone is enough for burning.

questions.stem: A burning candle is covered with a glass jar. What happens after a short time?
hints: The candle uses up the oxygen.
questions.explanation: When a burning candle is covered with a glass jar, the flame goes out because the candle uses up the oxygen inside the jar.
questions.misconception: The candle continues to burn in the jar.

questions.stem: Why does the candle flame go out when covered with a glass jar?
options: The oxygen inside the jar is used up
The candle runs out of wax
hints: The jar traps the air, and the oxygen is used up.
questions.explanation: The candle flame goes out because the burning candle uses up the oxygen inside the jar. Without oxygen, the flame cannot continue.
questions.misconception: The jar is cold, so the flame goes out.

questions.stem: In the candle-and-jar experiment, why does the flame go out?
answer: the candle uses up the oxygen in the jar
the oxygen inside the jar is used up
there is no more oxygen for burning
questions.explanation: The flame goes out because the candle uses up the oxygen trapped inside the jar, and fire cannot burn without oxygen.
questions.misconception: The jar blocks the flame physically.

questions.stem: In groups, carry out the candle-and-jar experiment. Light a candle, cover it with a glass jar, and observe what happens. Describe your observation and explain why it happens.

criteria.description: Observed that the candle flame goes out when covered
Explained that the candle uses up the oxygen in the jar

questions.explanation: This is a practical task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.

questions.stem: Why is air important for burning?
options: It contains oxygen which supports burning
questions.explanation: Air is important for burning because it contains oxygen, which supports burning.
questions.misconception: Air is not important for burning.

questions.stem: Why is air important for burning?
answer: it contains oxygen which supports burning
oxygen in air is needed for burning
questions.explanation: Air is important for burning because it contains oxygen, which is needed for fire to burn.
questions.misconception: Air has no effect on fire.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Air is only important for breathing.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, air is only for breathing
No, air is also important for burning because it contains oxygen
No, air is only important for plants
No, air is not important at all
questions.explanation: Air is important for breathing and also for burning because it contains oxygen.

questions.stem: If you cover a burning candle with a jar, what will happen?
options: The flame will move out of the jar
questions.explanation: The flame will go out because the candle uses up the oxygen inside the jar.

questions.stem: Predict what happens if you blow gently on a small flame.
answer: the flame may go out because the air blows it away
hints: Blowing removes the air around the flame.
What happens when you blow out a candle?
questions.explanation: Blowing gently on a small flame can put it out because it removes the air around the flame and the burning gases are blown away.
questions.misconception: Blowing always makes a fire bigger.

questions.stem: A learner fans a glowing charcoal fire with a piece of cardboard. What happens and why?
options: The fire glows brighter because more oxygen is supplied
The fire goes out because air is removed
questions.explanation: Fanning the fire supplies more oxygen from the air, which makes the fire glow brighter.
questions.misconception: Fanning always puts out a fire.

questions.stem: Which of these shows that air supports burning?
options: Blowing on a fire to make it burn brighter
hints: Blowing adds more air to the fire.
questions.explanation: Blowing on a fire to make it burn brighter shows that air (oxygen) supports burning.
questions.misconception: Blowing always puts out a fire.

questions.stem: Give one everyday example showing that air supports burning.
answer: blowing on a fire to make it burn brighter
using a fan to make a fire burn
opening a window to let air in for a fire
hints: Think about what makes a fire burn better.
questions.explanation: An everyday example is blowing on a fire or fanning it to make it burn brighter, because fresh air supplies more oxygen.

questions.stem: Why does covering a fire with a blanket put it out?
options: It cuts off the air and oxygen supply to the fire
It makes the fire too hot
It adds fuel to the fire
It blows air into the fire
questions.explanation: Covering a fire with a blanket puts it out because the blanket cuts off the air and oxygen supply needed for burning.
questions.misconception: Blankets add air to a fire.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.2.1 Demonstrate understanding of the life cycle of a plant
indicator.objective: Know the materials needed for the survival of plants in the environment (water, carbon dioxide, oxygen, sunlight)

questions.stem: Which of these is needed by plants for survival?
questions.explanation: Water is needed by plants for survival.

questions.stem: Which set lists materials needed for plant survival?
hints: Plants need gases from the air.
questions.explanation: Plants need water, carbon dioxide, oxygen and sunlight to survive.
questions.misconception: Plants only need water and sunlight.

questions.stem: Name two materials needed for plant survival.
questions.explanation: Plants need water, carbon dioxide, oxygen and sunlight.

questions.stem: Where do plants get carbon dioxide from?
hints: It is in the air around us.
questions.explanation: Plants get carbon dioxide from the air.
questions.misconception: Plants get carbon dioxide from the soil.

questions.stem: Where do plants get water from?
options: From the soil through their roots
questions.explanation: Plants get water from the soil through their roots.
questions.misconception: Plants get water from the air only.

questions.stem: Where does the sunlight that plants use come from?
hints: It is the brightest object in the sky.
questions.explanation: Plants get sunlight from the sun.
questions.misconception: Plants get sunlight from the moon.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Plants get all their food from the soil.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, plants get food from the soil
No, plants make their own food using sunlight, carbon dioxide and water
No, plants get food from the air only
No, plants get food from rocks
hints: Plants make food in their leaves.
They need sunlight, carbon dioxide and water.
questions.explanation: Plants do not get food directly from the soil. They make their own food using sunlight, carbon dioxide and water.
questions.misconception: Plants get food directly from the soil.

questions.stem: What is one role of water in plants?
options: It changes the colour of leaves
hints: Water is used in making food.
Plants need water to stay alive.
questions.explanation: Water helps plants make food and keeps them healthy.
questions.misconception: Water is not needed for plant survival.

questions.stem: Why do plants need water?
answer: to make food and stay healthy
to help make food and carry nutrients
questions.explanation: Plants need water to make food, carry nutrients and stay upright.

questions.stem: A plant is not watered for many days. What will happen?
options: The plant will wilt and may die
The plant will change colour to white
The plant will produce more flowers
hints: Plants need water to stay upright.
Without water, plants lose their firmness.
questions.explanation: Without water, the plant will wilt because water helps keep plant cells firm and supports the plant.

questions.stem: What do plants use carbon dioxide for?
hints: Plants make food in their leaves.
Carbon dioxide is one of the materials used.
questions.explanation: Plants use carbon dioxide to make food during photosynthesis.
questions.misconception: Plants do not need carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Why do plants need carbon dioxide?
answer: it is used to make food in the leaves
hints: Carbon dioxide is used in this process.
questions.explanation: Plants need carbon dioxide to make food through photosynthesis.
questions.misconception: Carbon dioxide is not needed by plants.

questions.stem: A plant is kept in a sealed clear box with no carbon dioxide. What will happen?
options: The plant will not be able to make food and will eventually die
The plant will produce more oxygen
hints: Carbon dioxide is needed for making food.
questions.explanation: Without carbon dioxide, the plant cannot make food and will eventually die.
questions.misconception: Plants do not need carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Why do plants need oxygen?
questions.explanation: Plants need oxygen for respiration, which releases energy for life processes.

questions.stem: Why is oxygen important for plants?
answer: it is used for respiration to get energy
questions.explanation: Oxygen is important for plants because they use it for respiration to release energy.
questions.misconception: Plants only produce oxygen; they do not need it.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Plants only give out oxygen; they do not need it.' What is the best correction?
options: Yes, plants only give out oxygen
No, plants need oxygen for respiration, just like animals
No, plants only need carbon dioxide
No, plants do not need any gases
questions.explanation: Plants need oxygen for respiration, even though they also produce oxygen during photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Why do plants need sunlight?
hints: Plants make food in their leaves.
questions.explanation: Plants need sunlight to make food through photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Explain why sunlight is important for plants.
answer: it provides energy for plants to make food
plants use sunlight to make their own food
hints: Plants make food using this energy.
questions.explanation: Sunlight is important because it provides the energy plants need to make food.

questions.stem: Draw a simple plant and label the materials it needs to survive. Show where each material comes from (e.g. water from soil, sunlight from sun, carbon dioxide from air).

criteria.description: Drew a plant with roots, stem and leaves
Labeled water and showed it coming from soil
Labeled sunlight and showed it coming from the sun
Labeled carbon dioxide and showed it coming from the air
Labeled oxygen as needed by the plant

hints: Think about what plants need to grow.
Show where each material comes from.
questions.explanation: This is a drawing task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: Plants only need water and sunlight.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.2.1 Demonstrate understanding of the life cycle of a plant
indicator.objective: Observe the life cycle of a plant (okra or maize plant)

questions.stem: What is the first stage of a plant's life cycle?
hints: It is small and can be planted.
It grows into a new plant.
questions.explanation: The seed is the first stage of the plant life cycle.
questions.misconception: A seed is not part of the life cycle.

questions.stem: Where does a new plant come from?
hints: It is planted in the soil.
questions.explanation: A new plant grows from a seed.

questions.stem: What is the first stage of a plant's life cycle?
hints: It is planted in the soil.
questions.explanation: The seed is the first stage of the plant life cycle.
questions.misconception: The life cycle starts with a flower.

questions.stem: What is germination?
options: The sprouting of a seed into a seedling
hints: It is when a seed starts to grow.
questions.explanation: Germination is the sprouting of a seed into a seedling.
questions.misconception: Germination is the same as growth.

questions.stem: What do we call the young plant that comes out of a germinating seed?
hints: It has just started to grow.
questions.explanation: The young plant that comes out of a germinating seed is called a seedling.
questions.misconception: A seedling is a mature plant.

questions.stem: Describe what happens during germination.
answer: a seed sprouts and a small seedling appears
the seed begins to grow into a seedling
a shoot comes out of the seed
hints: Think about a seed starting to grow.
questions.explanation: During germination, a seed sprouts and a small seedling appears.
questions.misconception: Germination is when the plant flowers.

questions.stem: What happens during the growth stage of a plant?
options: The seedling becomes a mature plant with more leaves
hints: It develops more leaves and a stronger stem.
questions.explanation: During the growth stage, the seedling grows into a mature plant with more leaves, a taller stem and deeper roots.

questions.stem: Which of these shows that a plant is in the growth stage?
options: It is getting taller and developing more leaves
questions.explanation: A plant in the growth stage gets taller and develops more leaves.
questions.misconception: Growth is the same as flowering.

questions.stem: What happens to a seedling during the growth stage?
answer: it grows into a mature plant with more leaves and a taller stem
it gets bigger and develops more leaves
hints: More leaves and a stronger stem.
questions.explanation: During the growth stage, the seedling grows into a mature plant with more leaves and a taller stem.
questions.misconception: The seedling stays the same size.

questions.stem: A pupil observes a maize plant that is taller than the seedling stage but has not yet produced flowers. What stage is the plant in?
hints: It has grown but not flowered yet.
questions.explanation: The plant is in the growth stage because it has grown taller but has not yet produced flowers.
questions.misconception: The plant is in the flowering stage.

questions.stem: What happens during the flowering stage of a maize plant?
hints: Maize plants produce tassels and silks.
questions.explanation: During the flowering stage, the maize plant produces flowers (tassels and silks).
questions.misconception: Maize plants do not produce flowers.

questions.stem: Why is the flowering stage important in the life cycle of a plant?
answer: flowers help the plant produce fruits and seeds
questions.explanation: The flowering stage is important because flowers help the plant produce fruits and seeds for the next generation.

questions.stem: A farmer notices that his okra plants have started producing yellow flowers. What stage of the life cycle are the plants in?
questions.explanation: The okra plants are in the flowering stage because they have started producing flowers.
questions.misconception: The plants are still in the growth stage only.

questions.stem: What happens after the flowering stage in the life cycle of a plant?
questions.explanation: After flowering, the plant produces fruits and seeds, completing the life cycle.
questions.misconception: The life cycle stops at flowering.

questions.stem: What is the final stage of the life cycle of a maize plant?
questions.explanation: The final stage is the production of fruits (cobs) and seeds, which can grow into new plants.
questions.misconception: The life cycle ends at flowering.

questions.stem: What does a plant produce at the end of its life cycle?
hints: These can grow into new plants.
questions.explanation: At the end of its life cycle, a plant produces fruits and seeds.

questions.stem: A maize cob is full of maize seeds. What does this show about the plant's life cycle?
options: The plant has completed its life cycle by producing seeds
The plant is still in the germination stage
The plant has not yet flowered
hints: The cycle is complete when seeds are formed.
questions.explanation: The cob full of seeds shows that the plant has completed its life cycle by producing seeds for the next generation.
questions.misconception: Seeds are not part of the life cycle.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly shows the life cycle of a maize plant?
questions.explanation: The correct sequence is: seed → germination → growth → flowering → fruiting/seeds.

questions.stem: Arrange these stages in the correct order: flowering, seed, growth, germination, fruiting.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: seed, germination, growth, flowering, fruiting.

questions.stem: In groups, plant a maize or okra seed and observe it over several weeks. Record the stages you observe (germination, growth, flowering, fruiting). Present your findings to the class.

criteria.description: Planted a seed and cared for it
Observed and recorded at least three stages of the life cycle
Arranged the stages in the correct order
Presented findings clearly to the class

hints: Plant the seed and water it.
Watch for germination, growth, flowers, and fruits.
questions.explanation: This is a practical task. Your teacher will mark it using the rubric.
questions.misconception: The life cycle stops at the mature plant.

indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B6.3.1.1 Recognise that different parts of the human body work interdependently to perform a specific function
indicator.objective: Explain the functions of organs in the excretory system of humans

questions.stem: Which organ is part of the excretory system?
hints: They filter blood to make urine.
questions.explanation: The kidneys are part of the excretory system.
questions.misconception: The kidneys are part of the digestive system.

questions.stem: Which set lists organs of the excretory system?
hints: Think about organs that remove waste products.
questions.explanation: The main organs of the excretory system are the kidneys, lungs, skin and liver.
questions.misconception: The stomach is part of the excretory system.

questions.stem: Name two organs of the excretory system.
questions.explanation: The excretory system includes the kidneys, lungs, skin and liver.

questions.stem: Which organ is NOT part of the excretory system?
hints: The stomach is part of digestion.
It does not remove waste from the body.
questions.explanation: The stomach is part of the digestive system, not the excretory system.
questions.misconception: The stomach is part of the excretory system.

questions.stem: What is the main function of the kidneys?
options: To remove urea and excess water as urine
questions.explanation: The kidneys remove urea and excess water from the blood and form urine.

questions.stem: The kidneys produce which excretory product?
hints: It is passed out of the body.
questions.explanation: The kidneys produce urine, which contains urea and excess water.

questions.stem: What do the kidneys remove from the blood?
questions.explanation: The kidneys remove urea and excess water from the blood, forming urine.

questions.stem: A person's kidneys are not working well. What is likely to happen?
options: Waste products build up in the blood
The person will digest food faster
hints: If they fail, waste stays in the blood.
questions.explanation: If the kidneys are not working well, waste products like urea build up in the blood, which is dangerous.
questions.misconception: Kidney failure has no effect on the body.
